summary.authors: Paul M. Harvey and Andrew Oldag

Observations were conducted over a continuous wavelength range of 1 to 4 µm using the pMIRAS high-speed spectrophotometer mounted on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-meter telescope during an immersion occultation event on August 28, 2001. (2006). The dust density gradient around AFGL 5440 follows a power law of ρ ∝ r⁻², consistent with a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow.
AFGL 5440 has a non-constant mass-loss history, with a significantly higher mass-loss rate in the past that produced the far-infrared emitting dust.
A substantial graphite component is required in the best-fit dust composition to match the IRAS 60 µm flux, despite general evidence against graphite in AGB stars.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents multi-spectral lunar occultation observations and radiative transfer modeling of the dust-enshrouded carbon-rich AGB star AFGL 5440 (OH 06.86-1.5), at a distance of approximately 2.25 kpc with a luminosity of 1.4 × 10⁴ L⊙. Observations were conducted over a continuous wavelength range of 1 to 4 µm using the pMIRAS high-speed spectrophotometer mounted on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-meter telescope during an immersion occultation event on August 28, 2001. The data reduction yielded approximately 100 light curves, each extracted from a buffer of 5000 frames centered on the occultation event, with a time resolution of 8 milliseconds per frame. Modeling with the DUSTY radiative transfer code—originally developed for AGB star shells—explored over 200 configurations varying dust optical depth, composition, grain size distribution, and density gradient, simultaneously fitting the occultation light curves and the spectral energy distribution described by Guandalini et al. (2006). Two comparison stars, IRC+00233 and HD 155292, were observed with the same instrument to calibrate the model and demonstrate that the AFGL 5440 data cannot be fit by a single-size uniform disk. The DUSTY modeling yielded a maximum dust temperature at the inner shell radius of Tmax = 950 K ± 50K, with an optical depth at 5 µm of 0.5 ± 0.1. The radial density gradient ρ ∝ r⁻² or the radiatively-driven hydrodynamic gradient produced the best fits. The inner dust shell was constrained to an angular radius of 11 mas (3.7 × 10¹⁴ cm), with the central stellar photosphere resolved at approximately 3 mas. The dust mass-loss rate was derived at 6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr, consistent with independent measurements by Groenewegen et al. (2002). A persistent unresolved issue is that no model with a reasonable density structure can fit the IRAS 60 µm flux without assuming a substantial graphite abundance or a significantly higher past mass-loss rate, implying a non-constant outflow history. The work demonstrates that high-spectral-resolution lunar occultations can separately resolve the stellar photosphere from the inner dust shell, providing strong constraints on AGB mass loss geometry.

Research Context
Mass loss from post-main-sequence stars contributes a large fraction of the heavy element abundance and solid particle content of the interstellar medium. The mechanisms of mass loss during the AGB phase are thought to involve both radiation pressure and stellar pulsation, but details are not well understood. Molecular line studies of extended envelopes around AGB stars have found periodic variations in mass-loss rates leading to "rings" in the radial distribution of molecular emission. Very deep imaging of IRC+10216 found similar phenomena in dust, but studying the inner regions requires angular resolutions well under 1 arcsec. At a distance of 1 kpc, the dust evaporation radius of a 10⁴ L⊙ star corresponds to 20 mas. Speckle interferometry and adaptive optics have enabled 0.1 arcsec resolution, while lunar occultation and multi-aperture interferometry have pushed to milli-arcsecond levels. Until recently, most interferometric observations were made in one or two relatively broad bands, lacking the spectral coverage needed to constrain circumstellar shell structure. AFGL 5440 was classified as a carbon-rich AGB star on the basis of its IRAS LRS spectrum.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can lunar occultation combined with multi-spectral coverage resolve the spatial structure of the innermost circumstellar dust shell in a carbon-rich AGB star? Can we independently constrain the inner radius of the dust shell, the optical depth, and the radial density gradient using DUSTY radiative transfer modeling? Does a single-size uniform disk model adequately fit the occultation data across the entire 1–4 µm bandwidth? The authors hypothesized that the combined emission from the central star and a circumstellar shell would require a more complex model than a uniform disk. The modeling was expected to constrain the dust density gradient in the innermost part of the shell to within a narrow range of optical depth and near-infrared to mid-infrared emission ratio. A central prediction was that the innermost dust emission (3–4 µm) would be best reproduced by models with a maximum temperature around 900–950 K and a density gradient near r⁻². The spectral energy distribution from Guandalini et al. was expected to provide independent but complementary constraints on the dust properties at different temperatures.

Methodological Details
The observations were made over a continuous range of wavelengths from 1 to 4 µm. A high-speed spectrophotometer pMIRAS was used, developed as a prototype for a more ambitious instrument. The instrument used a NaCl prism to disperse light imaged onto a 32×100 pixel portion of a 256×256 InSb array detector. The slit width was set at about 5 arcsec for typical seeing of 1.5 arcsec. The detector was read out every 8 milliseconds, with photon integration occurring over essentially the full 8 ms time. The instrument is read-noise limited shortward of 2.5 µm and background-limited longward of 3 µm. A typical observation consisted of taking 5000 frames centered on the occultation event. The data reduction used a cross-correlation algorithm to shift images and minimize spectral blurring. Wavelength calibration was performed by fitting the NaCl dispersion function to the observed positions of the J, H, K, and L atmospheric transmission maxima. The accuracy of wavelength calibration was good to ±0.01 λ throughout the 1–4 µm region. No flux calibration was attempted due to variable instrumental efficiency and non-photometric sky conditions during occultation. Stellar magnitudes were compared to published literature and found consistent within ±30%. Three stars were observed: AFGL 5440, IRC+00233, and HD 155292, with the latter two serving as calibration stars. IRC+00233 (M7) and HD 155292 (K2) are cool stars with no detectable circumstellar dust shell based on near-infrared and IRAS colors. Groenewegen et al. (2002) estimated the distance to AFGL 5440 to be 2.25 kpc. The reported distance and photometry imply a luminosity of 1.4 × 10⁴ L⊙.

Procedures And Architectures
The observations of AFGL 5440 were made during an immersion occultation event on 28 Aug 2001 at approximately 02:44:00 UT. The elevation of the Moon was 36°, the Sun was 17° below the horizon, and the lunar phase was 0.72. The position angle of the occultation event on the lunar limb was 54°. The pMIRAS instrument was mounted on the McDonald Observatory 2.7-m telescope. The data reduction produced approximately 100 light curves for which a few hundred frames centered on the occultation event were extracted. For wavelength calibration, the NaCl dispersion function was fitted to the telluric transmission maxima in the actual data for each occultation event. The fringe pattern of a lunar occultation is a convolution of the point source pattern over the telescope aperture, integration time, wavelength bandwidth, and source size/structure. The lunar shadow velocity, calculated by occultation prediction software, had to be fitted as an additional parameter due to uncertainties in lunar limb shape. The modeling procedure began with a uniform disk model, and a simple χ² test was used for the best model, allowing one or more parameters to vary. For comparison stars, both the angular size and lunar velocity were allowed to vary and fitted globally over the entire wavelength range. For AFGL 5440, more than 200 models were explored by varying input parameters and then varying the dust optical depth to find the best fit to the spectral energy distribution. The DUSTY code output included both model source images and the total energy distribution, making it ideal for simultaneous fitting of fringes and SED. The dust composition assumed for AFGL 5440 was a carbon-rich mix: amorphous carbon, silicon carbide, and graphite as major constituents. Two grain size distributions were compared: the MRN slope (Mathis et al. 1977) and the KMH shape (Kim et al. 1994) used by Ivezić & Elitzur for IRC+10216. The optical depth at 5 µm was varied between 0.3 and 0.6 to find the best fit. The radial density gradient was explored with values near r⁻², and also DUSTY's radiatively-driven wind gradient.

Key Results
The occultation fringes of AFGL 5440 cannot be fit by any single-size model over the entire 1–4 µm bandwidth. A single 11 mas uniform disk provides a passable fit in the mid-range (2.5–3.2 µm) but fringes are too sharp at long wavelengths and too broadened at short wavelengths. For IRC+00233, the best fit uniform disk size is between 4.5 and 5.0 mas, exceeding the 3.5 mas expected from blackbody calculations. For HD 155292, all uniform-disk models with a size less than about 3 mas fit the data reasonably well, consistent with the blackbody size of less than 1 mas. The maximum dust temperature at the inner radius of the shell is constrained to Tmax = 950 K ± 50K. Models with Tmax below 900 K do not have enough hot dust to fit occultation fringes at long wavelengths, while hotter models fail to fit the SED longward of 10 µm. The best-fit radial density gradient is close to ρ ∝ r⁻², or the DUSTY-calculated gradient for a radiatively driven wind. Models with a gradient of r⁻¹⁸ produce IRAS 60 µm flux better but do not fit the 5–20 µm energy distribution. Models with a gradient of r⁻².2 fit the energy distribution out to 20 µm and the occultation but have substantially worse fits to the IRAS 60 µm flux. The optical depth at the fiducial wavelength of 5 µm for the best-fit model is 0.5 ± 0.1, within the range of 0.3–0.6. The dust composition with the best fit includes a small amount of SiC together with comparable amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite. The dust mass-loss rate derived from the best-fit model is 6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr for the optical constants of amorphous carbon used by DUSTY. Groenewegen et al. (2002) computed a dust mass-loss rate of 5.1 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr from the IRAS 60 µm flux, slightly lower than the authors' derivation. A gas mass-loss rate of 3.1 × 10⁻⁵ M⊙/yr from millimeter CO observations implies a gas-to-dust mass ratio of 600. The inner dust shell radius is constrained to 11 mas (3.7 × 10¹⁴ cm), with the central stellar photosphere of 2500K ± 300K resolved at approximately 3 mas. The MRN slope and KMH shape grain size distributions both produce reasonably good fits, with no strong preference between them.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The constraint on Tmax = 950 K ± 50K means the inner radius is nearly a factor of two below the expected condensation temperatures of approximately 1900 K (Egan & Leung 1995). The 11 mas inner shell radius corresponds to an angular radius of 11 mas at the assumed distance of 2.25 kpc, while the central star diameter is 3 mas. The density constraint at 3–4 µm implies that the optical depth and the ratio of near-infrared to mid-infrared dust emission are constrained to a fairly narrow range for any given assumed dust emissivity. The fact that the best-fit dust density gradient matches the radiatively driven hydrodynamic gradient suggests that the circumstellar envelope is shaped by radiation pressure on dust grains. The requirement for graphite in the best-fit model to match the IRAS 60 µm flux contradicts the large amount of evidence against substantial graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. The inability to fit the 60 µm flux without graphite or a higher past mass-loss rate suggests a non-constant outflow where the mass-loss rate was greater in the past. The dust mass-loss rate of order 5–10 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr and gas mass-loss rate a few hundred times larger are consistent with the data. The time scale for the higher past mass-loss rate would be 500 years to a couple thousand years, comparable to the period of fluctuation seen by Mauron & Huggins (2000) for IRC+10216. The observation separates the stellar photosphere from the inner dust shell, providing the first multi-spectral resolution of these components for this star over the entire infrared wavelength region.

Contradictions And Limitations
The uniform-disk models for IRC+00233 and HD 155292 are limited by data of ±2 mas accuracy, beyond the required <1 mas resolution to reliably detect departures from a uniform disk. At ∼1.7 µm for IRC+00233, a substantially larger uniform-disk size provides a better ﬁt, but no good explanation is offered, possibly systematic noise or a real photosphere difference. For HD 155292, periodic electronic pickup had a non-negligible effect on the fringe patterns at shorter wavelengths, and the S/N was low enough that no effective narrow-band information exists beyond 2.5 µm. The models cannot fit the IRAS 60 µm flux without assuming a substantially higher mass-loss rate in the past, which would require modifications to the density law in the outer regions. The use of graphite in the best-fit model contradicts the substantial evidence against graphite in AGB stars, and the authors admit this is a problem that  The authors state they did not try to extract details of the stellar photosphere or examine all possible dust size/composition models due to wavelength coverage and spectral resolution limitations. The optical properties of different forms of amorphous carbon were not explored, which may affect the dust emissivity assumptions. The wavelength calibration has a probable accuracy of ±0.01 λ, but the exact uncertainty is not quantified. The exact time resolution is a strong function of the signal-to-noise ratio, but the functional dependence is not explicitly characterized. The spectral resolution R varies from ∼20 at the shortest wavelengths to ∼100 at the long end, and is uncompensated by seeing effects at short wavelengths.

Claims
Lunar occultation with multi-spectral coverage can resolve both the stellar photosphere and the inner dust shell of a carbon-rich AGB star. The single 11 mas uniform disk model produces fringes too sharp at long wavelengths and too broadened at short wavelengths, demonstrating the need for a composite structure. The best-fit model separately resolves the stellar photosphere at ∼3 mas from the dust shell at 11 mas. The DUSTY modeling, combining occultation fringes with the spectral energy distribution, yields a consistent maximum temperature of 950 K ± 50K. The single-source-size uniform disk of 11 mas provides a passable fit in the mid-wavelength range (2.5–3.2 µm), suggesting the shell is not spatially resolved over that band. The data is limited to ±2 mas accuracy, preventing detection of minor (10–30%) departures from a uniform disk in the comparison stars. This confirms that lunar occultation is a viable method for constraining the innermost circumstellar structure in AGB stars. The 11 mas inner radius constraint directly informs models of AGB mass loss geometry and the dust condensation location.
The dust density gradient around AFGL 5440 follows a power law of ρ ∝ r⁻², consistent with a radiatively driven hydrodynamic outflow. Models with a density gradient close to r⁻² or the DUSTY-calculated radiatively-driven wind gradient produced the best fits to both fringes and SED. Models with r⁻¹·⁸ produce the IRAS 60 µm flux better but do not fit the 5–20 µm SED shape. Models with r⁻²·² fit the 5–20 µm SED and occultation well but have substantially worse fits to the IRAS 60 µm flux. The best-fit dust mass-loss rate (6.5 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr) derived from the model is slightly higher than the Groenewegen et al. value (5.1 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr) from 60 µm, suggesting tension. The 60 µm flux requires a different density structure than the 5–20 µm emission, implying the power-law does not hold out to several arcseconds. The consistency with radiatively driven hydrodynamic models supports radiation pressure as a dominant mass-loss mechanism in AGB stars. The radial dependence of the dust density is constrained in the innermost part of the shell, where the occultation data has maximum sensitivity.
AFGL 5440 has a non-constant mass-loss history, with a significantly higher mass-loss rate in the past that produced the far-infrared emitting dust. No model with a reasonable density structure can fit the IRAS 60 µm flux without assuming a substantially higher mass-loss rate in the past. Models with only amorphous carbon and SiC (no graphite) fail to fit the 60 µm flux by factors of 3 or more. The 60 µm emitting dust is located at order 1 to a few arcseconds from the star, corresponding to a time 500–2000 years in the past. The authors acknowledge that explaining the 60 µm problem is beyond the scope of the study and the non-constant outflow explanation is  The dust mass-loss rate of order 5–10 × 10⁻⁸ M⊙/yr is consistent with the data, but the model cannot simultaneously reconcile inner and outer regions. The non-constant mass-loss rate contradicts the assumption of a steady-state outflow and implies temporal variation in AGB winds. The observation of the 60 µm problem by this work, in contrast to the superwind proposal by Suh (1997), points to a past-mass-loss increase rather than a recent one.
A substantial graphite component is required in the best-fit dust composition to match the IRAS 60 µm flux, despite general evidence against graphite in AGB stars. The best-fit composition included a small amount of SiC together with comparable amounts of amorphous carbon and graphite. The factor that drove inclusion of graphite was its relatively flat emissivity between 10 and 50 µm, enabling the IRAS 60 µm flux to be fit. Models with only amorphous carbon and SiC failed to fit the 60 µm flux by factors of 3 or more. The authors state this result is contrary to the large amount of evidence against substantial amounts of graphite in stars like AFGL 5440. Virtually all prior modeling efforts used dust emissivities appropriate for amorphous carbon and SiC, but with no graphite, contrary to this best-fit model. The inclusion of graphite in the best-fit model remains a controversial finding and may be an artifact of the emissivity assumptions at longer wavelengths. The dust emissivity ϵ ∝ λ⁻¹·³ of the best-fit model is consistent with Jura (2004) amorphous carbon, but the graphite addition remains a point of tension.

Data And Code Availability
The authors state that no data calibration for flux was performed, and no mention is made of data publication. The DUSTY code (Ivezić, Nenkova & Elitzur 1999) was used for modeling, which is a standard radiative transfer code for AGB shells. No mention is made of data or code availability; the publication is from 2007 and preprint archives may hold the data.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
More than 200 models were explored to understand the effect of varying input parameters on the quality of the fit. Models with Tmax below 900 K did not have enough hot dust to fit long-wavelength fringes. Models with hotter inner edges had even more difficulty reproducing the energy distribution longward of 10 µm. Models with density gradient r⁻¹·⁸ produced the IRAS 60 µm flux better but did not fit the 5–20 µm SED shape. Models with r⁻²·² fit the energy distribution out to 20 µm and the occultation, but had substantially worse fits to the IRAS 60 µm flux. The optical depth at 5 µm was varied between 0.3 and 0.6 to test sensitivity. The MRN slope (Mathis et al. 1977) and KMH shape (Kim et al. 1994) grain size distributions were compared; both produced reasonably good fits. Models that use only amorphous carbon and SiC (no graphite) fit the occultation data nearly as well as the best-fit model, but fail the 60 µm flux. A third model that fits the energy distribution but gives a poor fit to the occultation results (lack of enough warm dust close to the star) was discussed. The DUSTY radiatively driven density gradient was compared against the power-law gradient; both yielded comparable results for the inner shell.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows observed and model light curves for the 4.5 mas uniform disk model for a subset of wavelengths for IRC+00233. Figure 2 shows the χ² and S/N ratio as a function of wavelength over the entire observed band for the IRC+00233 model. Figures 3 and 4 show all uniform-disk models with size <3 mas fitting the data reasonably well for HD 155292. Figure 5 shows the observed light curves for AFGL 5440 indicating a single source size is insufficient to fit the 1–4 µm bandwidth. Figure 6 shows the results of trying to fit the data with an 11 mas uniform disk, exhibiting sharp long-wavelength fringes and broadened short-wavelength fringes. Figure 7 shows the fit to the spectral energy distribution for the best-fit DUSTY model. Figure 8 shows the fit to the occultation light curves for the best-fit DUSTY model. Figure 9 shows the quality of the fit versus wavelength for the best-fit model. Figure 10 illustrates the spatial profiles of the best-fit DUSTY model, showing the emission as a function of radius. Figures 11 and 12 show the energy distribution and model light curves for the best-fitting model using only amorphous carbon and SiC. Figures 13 and 14 show results for a third model that fits the energy distribution but gives a poor fit to the occultation results.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first multi-spectral resolution of the stellar photosphere (~3 mas) from the inner dust shell (11 mas) in a carbon-rich AGB star, constraining the dust temperature to 950 K ± 50K and the density gradient to ρ ∝ r⁻². 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative showing that the 11 mas uniform disk (the simplest source model) produces fringes that are too sharp at long wavelengths and too broadened at short wavelengths, combined with over 200 DUSTY models converging on Tmax = 950 K and ρ ∝ r⁻². 3. The future path requires resolving the 60 µm flux problem—which the current models cannot explain without assuming a non-constant mass-loss history or unphysical dust compositions—and developing higher-resolution multi-spectral occultation techniques to probe the shell structure beyond 500–2000 years into the past.

summary.title: Gluon Radiation of an Expanding Color Skyrmion in the Quark-Gluon Plasma
summary.authors: Jian Dai
summary.field_subfield: High Energy Physics - Phenomenology / Nuclear Theory
summary.executive_summary:
This paper calculates the density of states and energy spectrum of gluon radiation originating from the color current of an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion within a quark-gluon plasma (QGP). The QGP is modeled as an ideal relativistic fluid described by a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism, with an SU(2) group structure for the velocity field. The equation of state approximates radiation ($\epsilon = 3p$), yielding a free energy density $F = \beta \frac{4}{3} n^{4/3}$. A class of expanding soliton solutions is identified where the spatial scale $R(t)$ evolves as $R(t) \approx R_0(t/\tau + 1)^{4/3} \theta(t)$, characterized by a small parameter $\lambda = \tau/R_0 \ll 1$. Using the hedgehog ansatz for the skyrmion solution, the nonabelian current is derived as a multipole expansion, with the spherically symmetric lowest mode contributing to the radiation spectrum. Semiclassical calculations using a free parton picture (neglecting gluon self-interaction due to coupling hierarchy) yield the radiation amplitude. The density of states $n$ and energy spectrum $dE/dk$ are computed as functions of dimensionless momentum $\kappa = R_0 k$. The IR behavior is found to be $\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$ for small $k$, distinct from the $1/k$ form reported in prior literature for infinite medium sizes. The UV side shows a fast fall-off, while the intermediate energy is dominated by a smooth peak. The radiation is characterized by the coupling strength $\alpha = (2\pi^5/225)(g_{\text{eff}}^2/\beta^6)$. Three values of $\lambda$ (1/15, 2/15, 1/5) are numerically presented. The work situates itself between jet-quenching models (scattering-based) and gluon density saturation studies (initial state), proposing a hydrodynamic-color-current approach to gluon radiation by the expanding medium itself.

Key results include the functional forms $n = \alpha R_0 \lambda^2 \kappa^{-1/2} |\tilde{f}_{M\lambda}(\kappa)|^2$ and $dE/dk = \alpha \lambda^2 \kappa^{1/2} |\tilde{f}_{M\lambda}(\kappa)|^2$, with the characteristic IR behavior $\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$ for small $k$ when normalized by $1/\sqrt{\kappa}$. The paper concludes that this hydrodynamic approach offers a new mechanism to address elliptic flow eccentricity, both intrinsically via the nonabelian color current and exogenously via gluon radiation patterns, which the author identifies as a topic for follow-up work.

The IR behavior of the radiation spectrum is softened from $1/k$ to $1/\sqrt{k}$ due to the finite medium size $R_0$.
The hydrodynamic approach can address elliptic flow eccentricity both intrinsically via nonabelian color currents and exogenously via radiation patterns.

Semiclassical calculations using a free parton picture (neglecting gluon self-interaction due to coupling hierarchy) yield the radiation amplitude. The density of states $n$ and energy spectrum $dE/dk$ are computed as functions of dimensionless momentum $\kappa = R_0 k$. The IR behavior is found to be $\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$ for small $k$, distinct from the $1/k$ form reported in prior literature for infinite medium sizes. The UV side shows a fast fall-off, while the intermediate energy is dominated by a smooth peak. The radiation is characterized by the coupling strength $\alpha = (2\pi^5/225)(g_{\text{eff}}^2/\beta^6)$. Three values of $\lambda$ (1/15, 2/15, 1/5) are numerically presented. The work situates itself between jet-quenching models (scattering-based) and gluon density saturation studies (initial state), proposing a hydrodynamic-color-current approach to gluon radiation by the expanding medium itself.

Key results include the functional forms $n = \alpha R_0 \lambda^2 \kappa^{-1/2} |\tilde{f}_{M\lambda}(\kappa)|^2$ and $dE/dk = \alpha \lambda^2 \kappa^{1/2} |\tilde{f}_{M\lambda}(\kappa)|^2$, with the characteristic IR behavior $\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$ for small $k$ when normalized by $1/\sqrt{\kappa}$. The paper concludes that this hydrodynamic approach offers a new mechanism to address elliptic flow eccentricity, both intrinsically via the nonabelian color current and exogenously via gluon radiation patterns, which the author identifies as a topic for follow-up work.

Research Context
The study addresses gluon radiation during the hydrodynamic stage of the hot QCD matter or quark-gluon plasma (QGP) evolution. Medium-induced gluon radiation has been explored in the context of final-state partonic energy loss, known as "jet quenching." In jet quenching models, the spatially extended nuclear matter affects fragmentation and hadronization of hard partons produced in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. High $p_T$ hadronic observables are affected at collider energies, and the degree of medium modification characterizes hot QCD matter in the deconfined phase. The medium-induced radiation effect emerges from thermal QCD per se, with different approximation schemes giving consistent results. Gluon radiation has also been considered in the context of gluon density saturation in the initial stage, where a strongly interacting gluonic atmosphere is crucial for rapid local thermalization. The time evolution of the RHIC "fireball" influences observable particle production spectra, and the resulting state is modeled as a relativistic fluid undergoing hydrodynamic flow. Generalized fluid mechanics characterizing the long-distance transport of color charges has been developed for this purpose. A type of single skyrmion solution in color fluid was recently discovered as a non-static configuration. The time-dependent skyrmion expands in time, consistent with the expanding nature of the fireball generated in RHIC experiments. The pattern of gluon radiation pertaining to the color current of these non-static configurations is an important character of the color skyrmion. Prior work in the context of gluon density saturation extracted an asymptotic number density of $1/k$ at small $k$ for a medium taken to be infinitely large.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is to calculate the density of states and energy spectrum of gluon radiation for the color current of an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion in the QGP. The study uses a semiclassical approach to compute these radiation characteristics from the first principles of the nonabelian fluid mechanics. The hypothesis is that the expanding geometry of the skyrmion will lead to a distinct radiation spectrum compared to static or infinite-medium cases. The prediction is that there is a fast fall-off in the UV side of the spectrum, but a smooth peak dominates the intermediate energy. In the IR limit, the characteristic feature is predicted to be a long tail. The study hypothesizes a hierarchy between the partonic coupling $g_{YM}$ and the effective coupling $g_{\text{eff}}$, allowing the omission of gluon self-interactions. A second hypothesis is that the medium size, characterized by the soliton size $R_0$, will soften the IR behavior compared to infinite-medium treatments. The work also suggests that this hydrodynamical approach can address the eccentricity of elliptic flow both intrinsically via the nonabelian color current and exogenously via radiation patterns.

Methodological Details
The model is framed in the context of thermalization of hot QCD matter above the deconfinement transition temperature. Color charge transport is modeled by a nonlinear sigma model in a first-order formalism with a Lagrangian containing three terms. The velocity field is defined via a group element $U$ in an SU(2) group, with $\omega_\mu = -i/2 Tr(\sigma_3 U^\dagger \partial_\mu U)$. The equation of state approximates radiation with $\epsilon = 3p$, implying $F = \beta (4/3) n^{4/3}$ where $n = \sqrt{j_\mu j^\mu}$ is the invariant length. A class of expanding soliton solutions is identified where $U(x, t) = U(x/R(t))$ with $R(t) \approx R_0(t/\tau + 1)^{4/3} \theta(t)$. The condition $\tau \ll R_0$ enables the definition of a small parameter $\lambda = \tau/R_0$. The hedgehog ansatz is used to specify the solution: $U = \cos \phi + i \sigma \cdot \hat{x} \sin \phi$ with stereographic coordinates. The spatial coordinate $s$ is defined as the dimensionless $x/R(t)$. The sign of $\cos \phi$ signifies a topological charge, where the negative sign gives skyrmion number +1. The nonabelian current $J_a^\mu$ is related to the abelian current $j^\mu$ by the Eckart factorization $J_a^\mu = Q_a j^\mu$. The spherically symmetric part of the current is contained only in the third component and is expressed via a polynomial $P_6(s) = 1 - 7s^2 + 7s^4 - s^6$. The lowest multipole mode is considered alone, with higher polarization effects reserved for elsewhere.

Procedures And Architectures
Since transfer momentum between hard partons is much greater than between a hard parton and the soliton, the free parton picture is used. The gauge coupling in the Lagrangian becomes the coupling between a classical current and a free quantum field for gluon, neglecting gluon self-interaction. The semiclassical amplitude is given by the integral of the current dotted with the gluon wave function: $iM = g_{\text{eff}} \langle 1 | \int d^4x J_\mu \hat{A}_\mu^a | 0 \rangle$. The gluon wave function is $\langle 1 | \hat{A}_\mu^a(x) | 0 \rangle = \phi_a \epsilon_\mu e^{ik \cdot x} / \sqrt{2\omega}$. The spatial Fourier transformation of the current is performed analytically, yielding the polynomial $Q_4(x) = 5x^2 - 5x^3 + x^4$. The amplitude becomes $iM = B(k) \int d\omega t e^{-i\omega t} e^{-R(t) k Q_4(R(t) k)}$ with $B(k) = \pi^2 A(k)/120$. Substituting $R(t)$ leads to the integral over $t$ with variable $\eta = \omega\tau/(k R_0)^{3/4}$ and $\kappa = R_0 k$. The on-shell condition $\omega = k$ simplifies the expression, and with $\eta = \lambda \kappa^{1/4}$, the amplitude is factorized into a kinematic prefactor and a dimensionless integral $f_{M\lambda}(\kappa)$. The density of states is $n = 4\pi k^2 \sum_{c,h} |M|^2$ and the energy spectrum is $dE/dk = k dN/dk$. The dimensionless coupling constant is $\alpha = (2\pi^5/225)(g_{\text{eff}}^2 / \beta^6)$. The final expressions are $n = \alpha R_0 \lambda^2 \kappa^{-1/2} |\tilde{f}_{M\lambda}(\kappa)|^2$ and $dE/dk = \alpha \lambda^2 \kappa^{1/2} |\tilde{f}_{M\lambda}(\kappa)|^2$. The integral is defined as $f_{M\lambda}(\kappa) = \int_0^{\kappa^{3/4}} d\tau e^{i\lambda \kappa^{1/4} \tau - \tau^{4/3} Q_4(\tau^{4/3})}$.

Key Results
The density of states $n$ and energy spectrum $dE/dk$ are computed for three values of $\lambda$: 1/5, 2/15, and 1/15, shown in Figure 1. In the IR limit (small $\kappa$), the number density $n$ scales as $\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$ when normalized by $1/\sqrt{\kappa}$, as shown in Figure 2. This IR behavior ($\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$) is softer than the $1/k$ form found in prior work for infinitely large medium sizes. The spectrum shows a fast fall-off on the UV side and a smooth peak dominating the intermediate energy. In the UV (large $\kappa$), the spectrum decays rapidly, as expected for radiation from a finite source. The peak position and height depend on $\lambda$, with the 1/15 curve showing a lower and more shifted peak compared to 1/5. The coefficient $\alpha$ scales as $g_{\text{eff}}^2 / \beta^6$, relating the radiation strength to the coupling and the equation of state parameter. The hierarchy between medium-induced jet quenching ($\omega_C = 1/2 \hat{q} L^2$ with $\hat{q} \sim 0.04-0.16 \text{ GeV}^2/	ext{fm}$) and the characteristic medium radiation momentum $1/R_0$ is maintained. The radiation is a character of the color skyrmion, distinct from scattering-based radiation by the expanding medium. The result is presented as a semiclassical calculation validated by comparison with literature values.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The IR behavior $\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$ versus $1/k$ is attributed to the finite soliton size $R_0$ versus the infinite medium in prior work. The free parton picture is justified by the hierarchy between the partonic coupling $g_{YM}$ and the effective coupling $g_{\text{eff}}$, allowing the neglect of gluon self-interaction. The expansion of the skyrmion ($R(t)$) provides the dynamical mechanism for the radiation spectrum, distinct from static color-current models. The hydrodynamical approach opens the possibility of addressing elliptic flow eccentricity both intrinsically through the nonabelian color current and exogenously through radiation patterns. The work establishes a bridge between nonlinear sigma model descriptions of color fluid and semiclassical gluon radiation observables. The radiation pattern is identified as a defining character of the color skyrmion in the QGP.

Contradictions And Limitations
The approximation in equation (7) is valid only provided $\tau \ll R_0$. Only the lowest multipole mode of the nonabelian current is considered; effects of higher polarization are explicitly reserved for elsewhere. The free parton picture neglects gluon self-interaction ($F_{\mu\nu} F^{\mu\nu}$), which may fail if the coupling hierarchy is not strictly obeyed. The radiation is calculated in a semiclassical approach, so higher-order quantum corrections to the amplitude are not included. No quantitative comparison is given for the absolute magnitude of radiation, only qualitative features (fall-off, peak, tail) and scaling. The specific value of the coupling constant $g_{\text{eff}}$ is not fixed, so the absolute magnitude of $dE/dk$ cannot be determined without a numerical choice. The paper does not include a detailed error analysis or systematic uncertainty on the numerical integration of $f_{M\lambda}$.

Claims
The radiation spectrum of an expanding hydrodynamic skyrmion in the QGP exhibits a fast UV fall-off, a smooth intermediate peak, and a $\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$ IR tail. The UV side of the spectrum shows a fast fall-off as expected for finite-source radiation. A smooth peak dominates the intermediate energy region of the spectrum. In the IR, the number density scales as $1/\sqrt{k}$, verified by Figure 2. Numerical results for $\lambda = 1/15, 2/15, 1/5$ consistently show these features in Figure 1. Prior work by [6] extracted an asymptotic behavior of $1/k$ for small $k$, but that was for an infinitely large medium. The difference in IR power-law is attributed to medium size differences, not a fundamental contradiction. The radiation is a distinct channel for energy loss in the QGP, separable from jet-quenching scattering. The radiation pattern can serve as an observable to characterize the color skyrmion in the QGP.
The IR behavior of the radiation spectrum is softened from $1/k$ to $1/\sqrt{k}$ due to the finite medium size $R_0$. In [6], the asymptotic behavior of the number density at small $k$ is of the $1/k$ form. In our case, the asymptotic of the number density at small $k$ is $\sim 1/\sqrt{k}$. The difference comes from the fact that the medium size is taken to be infinitely large in [6] while in our case it is $R_0$. The scaling argument relies on the finite-source assumption which may be idealized. This distinction allows for a quantitative test of medium-size effects in QGP radiation models.
The hydrodynamic approach can address elliptic flow eccentricity both intrinsically via nonabelian color currents and exogenously via radiation patterns. This will be the topic of the follow-up to this work. The nonabelian color current carries the color information of the skyrmion. The author admits this is a proposed avenue for follow-up, not a result demonstrated in the current paper. The work extends the utility of the nonlinear sigma model from pure hydrodynamics to radiation observables.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The dependence on the expansion parameter $\lambda$ is explored with three values (1/15, 2/15, 1/5), showing how the peak height and position vary. The free parton approximation is justified by the coupling hierarchy $g_{YM} 
eq g_{\text{eff}}$, omitting gluon self-interaction. Only the lowest multipole mode is retained; higher modes are reserved for elsewhere, serving as an implicit ablation of higher-order current contributions.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents the density of states $n$ and energy spectrum $dE/dk$ for three expansion parameters $\lambda = 1/5, 2/15, 1/15$, plotted against dimensionless momentum $\kappa = R_0 k$. Figure 2 shows the IR scaling $n/(\kappa^{1/2})$ for $\lambda = 0.2$ in the small $\kappa$ limit, verifying the $1/\sqrt{k}$ asymptotic behavior. No tables of numerical data are provided beyond the visual information in Figures 1 and 2.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first semiclassical calculation of gluon radiation from an expanding color skyrmion in the QGP, yielding a distinct $1/\sqrt{k}$ IR tail and a smooth intermediate peak. 2. The strongest evidence is the analytical derivation of the $1/\sqrt{k}$ IR scaling from the finite soliton size $R_0$, contrast with the $1/k$ result for infinite media in prior literature. 3. The future path identified is addressing elliptic flow eccentricity both intrinsically through the nonabelian color current and exogenously via radiation patterns in follow-up work.

summary.title: ARE THERE MACH CONES IN HEAVY ION COLLISIONS? THREE-PARTICLE CORRELATIONS FROM STAR
summary.authors: JASON GLYNDWR ULERY FOR THE STAR COLLABORATION
summary.field_subfield: Nuclear Physics - Heavy Ion Collisions, Quark Gluon Plasma, Jet Correlations
summary.executive_summary:
This paper presents 3-particle azimuthal correlation results from the STAR experiment at RHIC (√sNN = 200 GeV) for pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions, focusing on a 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c trigger particle with two 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c associated particles. The primary objective was to investigate the away-side azimuthal structure of jet correlations, which in central Au+Au collisions shows a broadened, double-humped structure consistent with conical emission. The authors employ a 3-particle correlation analysis method where events are decomposed into a jet-like correlated component and a combinatorial background. The background consists of three terms: a hard-soft background (one jet-like associated particle, one flow-correlated), a soft-soft background (two associated particles independent of the trigger), and a trigger-flow term. The background is constructed from mixed-event techniques with v2 and v4 flow modulations added in pairwise or triplet-wise. 

Key findings include: (1) pp and d+Au results are similar with clear near-side (0,0) and away-side (π,π) peaks; (2) Au+Au collisions show additional on-diagonal broadening, interpreted as deflected jets; and (3) central Au+Au collisions exhibit off-diagonal peaks at approximately π ± 1.45 radians, consistent with Mach-cone conical emission. The Mach cone emission angle was tested as a function of associated particle pT (1 < pT < 2 GeV/c) and centrality, finding it remains constant (approximately 1.41–1.46 radians), which favors a hydrodynamic Mach cone over a pT-dependent ˇCerenkov radiation mechanism. Systematic uncertainties from v2 measurement variations, normalization window size, v4 parameterization, and multiplicity bias were quantified and shown to be robust. The results indicate that the conical emission structure is prominent in the 0–12% central Au+Au collisions triggered by the ZDC.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents 3-particle azimuthal correlation results from the STAR experiment at RHIC (√sNN = 200 GeV) for pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions, focusing on a 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c trigger particle with two 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c associated particles. The primary objective was to investigate the away-side azimuthal structure of jet correlations, which in central Au+Au collisions shows a broadened, double-humped structure consistent with conical emission. The authors employ a 3-particle correlation analysis method where events are decomposed into a jet-like correlated component and a combinatorial background. The background consists of three terms: a hard-soft background (one jet-like associated particle, one flow-correlated), a soft-soft background (two associated particles independent of the trigger), and a trigger-flow term. The background is constructed from mixed-event techniques with v2 and v4 flow modulations added in pairwise or triplet-wise. 

Key findings include: (1) pp and d+Au results are similar with clear near-side (0,0) and away-side (π,π) peaks; (2) Au+Au collisions show additional on-diagonal broadening, interpreted as deflected jets; and (3) central Au+Au collisions exhibit off-diagonal peaks at approximately π ± 1.45 radians, consistent with Mach-cone conical emission. The Mach cone emission angle was tested as a function of associated particle pT (1 < pT < 2 GeV/c) and centrality, finding it remains constant (approximately 1.41–1.46 radians), which favors a hydrodynamic Mach cone over a pT-dependent ˇCerenkov radiation mechanism. Systematic uncertainties from v2 measurement variations, normalization window size, v4 parameterization, and multiplicity bias were quantified and shown to be robust. The results indicate that the conical emission structure is prominent in the 0–12% central Au+Au collisions triggered by the ZDC.

Research Context
Heavy ion collisions create a medium that may be the quark gluon plasma (QGP). Two-particle jet-like azimuthal correlations show the away-side shape in central Au+Au collisions broadened with respect to pp. The away-side structure is consistent with several mechanisms: large angle gluon radiation, deflected jets, hydrodynamic conical flow, and ˇCerenkov radiation. Three-particle correlations can differentiate conical flow from ˇCerenkov radiation, which both have conical emission characteristics. The associated particle pT dependence of the emission angle can differentiate between hydrodynamic conical flow and ˇCerenkov radiation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the away-side broadening in Au+Au jet correlations arises from Mach-cone conical emission. The hypothesis is that 3-particle correlations will reveal off-diagonal peaks if conical emission is present. A predicted outcome is that Mach cone emission angle remains independent of associated particle momentum. The ˇCerenkov radiation model predicts an emission angle that decreases sharply with increasing associated particle momentum. The study hypothesizes that the off-diagonal signal magnitude should equal the on-diagonal signal if only conical emission contributes.

Methodological Details
The analysis uses charged trigger particles with 3 < pT < 4 GeV/c. Two charged associated particles have 1 < pT < 2 GeV/c. Data were taken in the STAR time projection chamber for pp, d+Au, and Au+Au collisions at √sNN = 200 GeV/c. The background is constructed using mixing events with flow modulation added pairwise. v2 values are obtained from reaction plane and 4-particle cumulant methods. The v4 parameterization used is v4 = 1.15v2^2 from data. The background is normalized to the signal within 0.8 < |∆φ| < 1.2 (zero yield at 1 radian or ZYA1). The ZDC-triggered Au+Au collisions cover centrality 0-12%. Centrality bins include 0-12%, 10-30%, 30-50%, and 50-80%. The 2-particle background B_inc is constructed by mixing events with flow added pairwise. The 3-particle soft-soft background B_inc^3 is obtained from mixing events where all three particles are from different events.

Procedures And Architectures
Events are treated as composed of two components: jet-like correlated particles and background. The hard-soft background is computed as the 2-particle jet-like correlation ˆJ2 folded with the normalized 2-particle background B_inc. The soft-soft background B_inc^3 accounts for correlations between the two associated particles independent of the trigger. The trigger-flow term B_inc,T^3 adds flow correlation between the trigger and associated particles. The total background is the sum of hard-soft, soft-soft, and trigger-flow terms. The α2 factor corrects for multiplicity bias from requiring a trigger particle. The β factor accounts for non-Poisson multiplicity distributions and ensures consistency between signal and background. Off-diagonal locations are determined from a double Gaussian fit to a strip projected to the off-diagonal. The signal is measured in 0.7 x 0.7 boxes in the ∆φ_a ∆φ_b plane.

Key Results
PP and d+Au results are similar with a near-side peak at (0,0) and an away-side peak at (π,π). The away-side peak displays diagonal elongation consistent with kT broadening. Peripheral Au+Au results show additional on-diagonal elongation of the away-side peak from deflected jets. Central Au+Au collisions display an off-diagonal structure at about π ± 1.45 radians. The off-diagonal signal increases with centrality and significantly deviates from zero in central Au+Au. The Mach cone emission angle is consistent with 1.45 ± 0.02 radians for the 0-12% ZDC-triggered data. The angle is consistent with constant as a function of associated particle pT between 1.41 and 1.5 radians. The angle remains constant at approximately 1.46 radians across centrality bins. The difference between on-diagonal and off-diagonal signals decreases with distance from (π,π). No strong pT dependence of the angles on associated particle pT is observed, favoring Mach cone emission. The off-diagonal peak angle for 0-12% Au+Au is 1.41 ± 0.02 radians, while 0-50% shows 1.45 radians.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The conical emission structure is attributed to Mach-cone shock waves generated by jets in the QGP. The constant emission angle with pT favors the hydrodynamic Mach cone interpretation over ˇCerenkov radiation. The difference between on-diagonal (cone + deflected jets) and off-diagonal (cone only) signals indicates deflected jet contributions. The observation of the structure in the 0-12% central data provided by the online ZDC trigger strengthens the evidence for conical flow. The results support the presence of a hydrodynamic medium where energy loss creates shock waves.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study acknowledges the away-side structure is consistent with many physics mechanisms beyond just conical emission. The hard-soft and trigger-flow backgrounds vary greatly with elliptic flow, though variations cancel to first order in sum. The analysis is restricted to a specific pT range (3-4 GeV/c trigger, 1-2 GeV/c associated) and cannot generalize to all regimes. The background estimation relies on the v4 = 1.15v2^2 parameterization, which may introduce model-dependent uncertainty. The study is a STAR preliminary result, not the final peer-reviewed paper. The v2 uncertainty (reaction plane vs 4-particle cumulant) is not precisely quantified as a single percentage but shown as robust.

Claims
Central Au+Au collisions exhibit an off-diagonal peak in 3-particle correlations consistent with Mach-cone conical emission. Off-diagonal peaks at π ± 1.45 radians are prominent in 0-12% central Au+Au. The angle is constant at 1.45 ± 0.02 radians, consistent with Mach cone expectation. The signal deviates significantly from zero in central collisions. The away-side structure is also consistent with deflected jets or large angle gluon radiation. The on-diagonal peak contains both deflected jet and conical emission contributions. The result favors hydrodynamic Mach cones over ˇCerenkov radiation. The constant angle confirms the Mach cone is not pT-dependent.
The conical emission angle is independent of associated particle pT and centrality. Angle at 1.41 ± 0.02 for ZDC 0-12% and 1.45 for 0-50% is nearly constant. A constant fit gives 1.46 radians across centrality. The angle remains constant for both mid-central and central Au+Au. The 0-12% point has been shifted for clarity, affecting direct visual comparison. The range of associated particle pT is limited to 1-2 GeV/c. This result discriminates against the ˇCerenkov radiation model which predicts decreasing angle with pT. The Mach cone interpretation is strengthened by this constant-angle result.

Data And Code Availability
The analysis method is rigorously described in reference 9, but no specific code or dataset repository is mentioned in this paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The signal is robust with respect to changing the v2 source from reaction plane to 4-particle cumulant. The hard-soft and trigger-flow backgrounds cancel their v2 variations to first order in the sum. The normalization window was doubled from 0.8-1.2 to 0.6-1.4, and the signal remained robust. Trigger particle v2 is affected by 20% from requiring a correlated particle. Systematic errors include v4 parameterization uncertainty and multiplicity bias effects on soft-soft background.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows raw 2-particle (a), 3-particle (b), soft-soft background (c), and hard-soft + trigger flow background (d) for 0-12% Au+Au. Figure 2 displays background-subtracted 3-particle correlations for pp, d+Au, and multiple Au+Au centrality bins. Figure 3 shows centrality dependence of average signal strengths in four regions with statistical and systematic error bars. Figure 4 shows away-side projections of a 0.7 radian strip for d+Au (left) and 0-12% Au+Au (right). Figure 5 shows emission angles vs associated pT (left) and centrality (right), with a constant fit of 1.46 radians. Figure 6 shows systematic checks: reaction plane v2 (a), 4-particle cumulant v2 (b), and doubled normalization window (c).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the observation of off-diagonal peaks in 3-particle correlations, interpreted as Mach-cone conical emission from jets in QGP. 2. The strongest evidence is the measured emission angle of ~1.45 radians which remains constant as a function of associated particle pT, favoring Mach cones over ˇCerenkov radiation. 3. The future path includes more comprehensive pT coverage, higher-statistics ZDC-triggered data, and more precise quantification of flow uncertainties to confirm the conical flow mechanism.

summary.title: A schematic model of scattering in PT −symmetric Quantum Mechanics
summary.authors: Miloslav Znojil
summary.field_subfield: Quantum Physics, PT-Symmetric Quantum Mechanics, Scattering Theory
summary.executive_summary: This theoretical paper derives analytical formulae for the reflection and transmission coefficients in one-dimensional quantum scattering with a PT-symmetric potential using a Runge-Kutta-discretized Schrödinger equation. The potential is of the form V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x), where Z(x) is real and even, and Y(x) is real and odd, satisfying the PT-symmetry condition. The author transforms the continuous Schrödinger equation into a discrete difference equation via Runge-Kutta discretization, replacing the continuous boundary conditions with discrete scattering versions defined on a lattice. The central methodological innovation is partitioning the doubly infinite system of linear algebraic equations into a finite-dimensional (2M-1)-dimensional tridiagonal non-square matrix problem, which is further reduced to a two-dimensional matrix inversion. The resulting scattering formulae (equations 20 and 21) express the reflection coefficient B and transmission coefficient C in terms of the input energy parameter φ and two key functions α and β, which carry all the dynamical information and are rational functions of the coupling constants. Example formulae are derived for M=2, M=3, and M=4, illustrating increasing algebraic complexity; for M=4, the determinant of the system matrix contains sums of 15 and 14 products of couplings, while the numerator of α involves 32 products. The author also notes an energy constraint E ∈ (0, 4/h^2) imposed by the requirement of a real energy variable φ. The paper demonstrates that the PT-symmetric scattering problem can be solved using standard non-matching and non-recurrent linear algebra techniques, revealing that the manifest asymmetry between "in" and "out" states is merely formal. The author also notes a close formal parallelism between scattering by Hermitian and non-Hermitian potentials, as both share the same form for transmission and reflection coefficients, with all differences encoded in the α and β functions. The paper frames this as a contribution to filling the relatively small gap in scattering studies for PT-symmetric potentials compared to bound-state studies.

The formalism for Hermitian and non-Hermitian scattering is identical, with all differences encoded in two functions α and β.
The manifest asymmetry between in and out states in PT-symmetric scattering is merely formal and does not impede tractability.

The paper frames this as a contribution to filling the relatively small gap in scattering studies for PT-symmetric potentials compared to bound-state studies.

Research Context
The PT-symmetric quantum mechanics program was initiated by the 1998 letter of Bender and Boettcher identifying real bound-state spectra in complex potentials. Subsequent developments clarified the existence of a non-trivial physical Hilbert space and identified PT-symmetry as P-pseudo-Hermiticity. The current literature abounds in studies of analytically continued, singular, and multidimensional PT-symmetric potentials. Despite these advancements, a comparatively small number of papers have been devoted specifically to the scattering problem. The present difference-equation-based study aims to fill this methodological gap in PT-symmetric scattering.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to derive explicit reflection and transmission coefficients for a one-dimensional PT-symmetric scattering problem using a Runge-Kutta-discretized approach. The one-dimensional scattering problem involves a PT-symmetric short-range potential V(x) = Z(x) + iY(x). The potential satisfies PT-symmetry conditions Z(−x) = Z(x) and Y(−x) = −Y(x) where both are real. The Runge-Kutta method is identified as a purely numerical recipe to address O(h^4) discretization errors. The two small parameters h and 1/M should be chosen and varied independently for quickest convergence.

The difference Schrödinger equation is rewritten as a doubly infinite system of linear algebraic equations. The system is partitioned into a finite-dimensional (2M−1)-dimensional tridiagonal non-square matrix problem. The definition of transmission and reflection coefficients has the same form in Hermitian and non-Hermitian contexts. All differences between Hermitian and non-Hermitian scattering are encoded in the two functions α and β. The manifest asymmetry between "in" and "out" states in PT-symmetric scattering is shown to be merely formal. The problem remains tractable by standard non-matching and non-recurrent techniques of linear algebra. The partitioning of the Schrödinger equation separates essential from inessential components, reducing the problem to 2D matrix inversion. The dynamical input is represented entirely by the four corners of the inverse matrix R. The formalism demonstrates a close formal parallelism between real and complex potential scattering. The author suggests the model may illuminate the non-Hermitian versions of the inverse scattering problem.

The model is a schematic, toy problem and the analysis is admitted to be short. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a theoretical framework for QED⊗QCD resummation, extending the Yennie-Frautschi-Suura (YFS) exponentiation theory to non-Abelian gauge theories. The central motivation is the requirement for a theoretical precision tag at the 0.67% level for LHC luminosity processes to match the 2% experimental precision tag, necessitating simultaneous control over multiple gluon and photon radiative effects. The new theory provides an exact rearrangement of the QCD perturbative series, combined with QED resummation, valid over the entire phase space without double-counting of effects to all orders in αs and α. The framework is applied to single heavy gauge boson production (W, Z) at hadron colliders, where the cross section is expressed as an exponentiated sum over hard gluon and photon emissions with residual matrix elements free of infrared singularities. Key semi-analytical results show that QED threshold corrections contribute at the .3% level at both LHC and Tevatron, stable under scale variations. The theory provides a firm basis for combining exact YFS-style resummation with HERWIG and PYTHIA parton showers through two shower-matching schemes: pT matching at the factorization scale and a more accurate shower-subtracted residual approach. The paper concludes that the complete O(α²s, ααs, α²) results needed for LHC physics are in progress, with the W production analysis ongoing. While the QCD resummation was established in Ref. [3] and Soft-Collinear Effective Theory (SCET) in Ref. [8] provides an alternative, this approach maintains exactness to all orders and is valid over the entire phase space. The theory forms a paradigm for precision electroweak measurements at LHC, FNAL, RHIC, and ILC.

Research Context
The LHC luminosity determination requires an experimental luminosity precision tag at the 2% level. To avoid compromising the over-all LHC luminosity determination, the theoretical precision tag on corresponding processes should be at the 0.67% level. This precision requirement dictates that multiple gluon and photon radiative effects must be controlled at the stated level. The existing QCD resummation theory, presented in Ref. [3], provides an exact rearrangement of the QCD perturbative series. This resummation is based on the N = 1 term in the exponent from the formal proof of exponentiation in non-Abelian gauge theories in the eikonal approximation. The resummation in Ref. [3] is augmented with residuals taking into account remaining contributions exactly to all orders in αs. Soft-collinear effective theory (SCET) in Ref. [8] provides an alternative approach for double resummation of soft and collinear effects. Results in Refs. [9–14] showed that QED contributions in structure function evolution lead to effects of ∼0.3%, almost half of the error budget. Similar size effects are expected from the threshold region of heavy gauge boson production. All these effects must be taken into account if one wants 1.0% for the theoretical precision tag.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to simultaneously exponentiate multiple gluon and multiple photon radiative effects in LHC physics processes without double-counting. The hypothesis is that a QED⊗QCD resummation theory, extending the YFS exponentiation to QCD, provides an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series valid over the entire phase space. The authors predict that the QED threshold corrections will be at the level of .3% at both LHC and Tevatron, sufficient for ≲1% precision. The theory is hypothesized to be valid over the entire phase space and applicable to an exact treatment via Monte Carlo methods. The framework should allow systematic improvement without double-counting of effects to all orders in both αs and α. The theory is expected to provide the needed theoretical precision tag for LHC luminosity processes.

Methodological Details
The primary process studied is parton-level single heavy boson production at hadron colliders, specifically q + ¯q′ → V + n(g) + X, where V = W ±, Z. The cross section is expressed as an exact exponentiated sum over n hard gluon and m hard photon emissions. Each emission produces a residual matrix element ˜¯βn,m free of all infrared singularities to all orders in αs(Q). The functions SUMIR(QCD) and DQCD, along with basic infrared functions, are specified in Ref. [3]. A compensation between non-Abelian IR virtual and real singularities isolates ˜¯βj and distinguishes QCD from QED. Exact O(α²s) and exact O(α) results for heavy gauge boson production are cited from Refs. [15–17] and [18–20] respectively. Semi-analytical methods are used with structure functions from Ref. [23] to examine QED⊗QCD threshold corrections. A Monte Carlo realization of the theory is noted to appear elsewhere in Ref. [24]. The approach is compared with standard QCD parton shower practices in HERWIG and PYTHIA. The current state of the art for shower/ME matching is Ref. [28], which combines an exact O(αs) correction with HERWIG.

Procedures And Architectures
The QED⊗QCD theory is obtained by simultaneously exponentiating the large IR terms in QCD and the exact IR divergent terms in QED. The new YFS residuals ˜¯βn,m represent the successive application of the YFS expansion first for QCD and subsequently for QED. The QCED functions are determined from their QCD analogs via substitutions: Bnls QCD → Bnls QCD + Bnls QED, ˜Bnls QCD → ˜Bnls QCD + ˜Bnls QED, and ˜Snls QCD → ˜Snls QCD + ˜Snls QED. The average Bjorken x values imply that QCD corrections occur an order of magnitude earlier than QED corrections. Two shower-matching approaches are proposed: pT matching of the shower from backward evolution with the matrix elements, and shower-subtracted residuals. In pT matching, gluon radiation at scales below the factorization scale µ is omitted in the residuals to avoid double-counting. The shower-subtracted residual approach expands the shower formula's perturbative expansion to match the exact calculated result at each order. The ratio rexp = σexp/σBorn is computed with and without QED, using the Born cross section formula from Eq. (4). The QED⊗QCD exponent γQCED = (2Q²f/απ + 2CF/αsπ)Lnls is used, with Lnls = ln x¹x²s/µ². The functions FYFS(γQCED) and δYFS(γQCED) are well-known from Ref. [22], involving Riemann’s zeta function of argument 2 and Euler’s constant. The Born cross section formula excludes the narrow resonance approximation to set a paradigm for precision studies. The full O(α²s, ααs, α²) results are in progress for all collider environments.

Key Results
The calculated rexp ratio at the LHC with QCED = QCD + QED is 1.1901. The calculated rexp ratio at the LHC with QCD alone is 1.1872. The calculated rexp ratio at the Tevatron with QCED = QCD + QED is 1.1911. The calculated rexp ratio at the Tevatron with QCD alone is 1.1879. QED effects are found to be at the .3% level at both LHC and FNAL. The results are stable under scale variations. The QED effect is similar in size to structure function results in Refs. [9–13]. Semi-analytical results for QED threshold effects agree with literature on Z production. As QED is at the .3% level, it is needed for LHC theory predictions at ≲1%.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The resummation is an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series, not a threshold approximation. Because it is valid over the entire phase space, it is readily applicable to an exact treatment via MC methods. The .3% QED effect is needed for LHC theory predictions at the 1% precision level. The theory provides a firm theoretical basis for the complete O(α²s, ααs, α²) results needed for LHC, FNAL, RHIC, and ILC physics. The QED⊗QCD resummation forms a paradigm for precision heavy vector boson studies.

Contradictions And Limitations
No Monte Carlo realization of the full theory is presented in this paper; it is noted to appear elsewhere. The analysis of W production is in progress and not completed. The N > 1 Gatherall exponent can be systematically included, but it is not done in the primary result. The paper applies the theory only to single heavy gauge boson production processes. The complete O(α²s, ααs, α²) results are stated to be in progress, not completed. The DGLAP evolution in the shower matching approach relies on a collinear limit regulator m_q, though independence of m_q should hold for m_q → 0.

Claims
YFS theory, when extended to non-Abelian gauge theory, allows simultaneous exponentiation of QED and QCD. The theory provides an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series valid over the entire phase space. The QCED functions are determined from QCD analogs via direct substitution of QED terms. The new YFS residuals represent successive application for QCD then QED. The paper notes that some confusion exists about the exactness since the result does not show an explicit ordered operator. The N > 1 Gatherall exponents are not systematically included in the primary result. The framework provides a firm basis for the complete O(α²s, ααs, α²) results needed for collider physics. It forms a paradigm for precision electroweak measurements at LHC and beyond.
The theory can be combined with HERWIG and PYTHIA parton showers to realize full MC event generators. Two shower-matching approaches (pT matching and shower-subtracted residuals) are proposed. The backward evolution of initial partons via the Les Houches procedure is compatible. The shower-subtracted approach achieves accuracy improved over the pT-matching scheme. A complete Monte Carlo realization is not presented in this paper. The full MC event generator realization is possible in principle but not demonstrated here. The framework allows systematic improvement with exact fully exclusive results order-by-order in αs.
QED threshold corrections at the .3% level are required for LHC theory predictions at the 1% precision level. Semi-analytical results show QED effects of .3% at both LHC and Tevatron. The experimental luminosity precision tag is 2%, requiring a 0.67% theoretical tag. The 1.0% precision tag requirement covers both QED and QCD effects. The W production analysis is still in progress. The paper only demonstrates threshold corrections, not the full emission spectrum. The .3% QED effect must be included to not compromise the over-all LHC luminosity determination.
The QED⊗QCD resummation provides an exact treatment valid over the entire phase space, unlike threshold resummation. Unlike threshold resummation, the resummation is valid over the entire phase space. It is readily applicable to an exact treatment in MC methods. The DGLAP evolution in the shower matching still uses a collinear limit regulator. The framework allows the inclusion of the shower formula's perturbative expansion to match the exact result.

Data And Code Availability
A Monte Carlo realization of the theory is noted to appear elsewhere in Ref. [24]. No code or data are provided in this paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The rexp results are stated to be stable under scale variations. Two shower-matching schemes are proposed and both are under investigation. The shower-subtracted residuals approach is noted to be more accurate in principle than the pT-matching scheme. The shower-subtracted residuals were verified for the exact O(α) luminosity Bhabha process.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the YFS exponentiation extended to non-Abelian gauge theories, providing a QED⊗QCD resummation theory that is exact to all orders in αs and α, valid over the entire phase space, and without double-counting of effects. 2. The strongest evidence is the semi-analytical rexp calculations showing that QED threshold corrections contribute at the .3% level at both LHC and Tevatron, consistent with structure function results and stable under scale variations, and the two proposed shower-matching schemes demonstrate a clear path to MC implementation. 3. The future path involves completing the O(α²s, ααs, α²) results, finishing the W production analysis, realizing the full Monte Carlo event generator, and applying the framework to other precision electroweak processes at the LHC, FNAL, RHIC, and ILC.

summary.title: ON GENERALIZED ENTROPY MEASURES AND PATHWAYS
summary.authors: A.M. MATHAI and H.J. HAUBOLD
summary.field_subfield: Mathematical Statistics, Information Theory, Statistical Mechanics
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical/mathematical developments paper presenting new entropy measures and pathway models
summary.executive_summary:
This paper presents a comprehensive examination of generalized entropy measures and pathway models, centered on the foundational role of the product probability property (PPP), also known as statistical independence, and the recursivity postulate. The authors argue that the term "independence" is a misnomer for events when interpreted via the product probability $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$, as this definition would make any event independent of the sure event, leading to inconsistencies with common sense. The paper demonstrates that the recursivity postulate, when combined with continuity, symmetry, zero-indifference, and normalization, uniquely characterizes Shannon entropy as a logarithmic functional. Consequently, additivity in Shannon entropy emerges not from independence itself but from the logarithmic form mandated by the recursivity postulate.

The paper introduces five generalized entropies of order $\alpha$: Rényi, Havrda-Charvát, Tsallis, Mathai, and Mathai's additive entropy, all of which converge to Shannon entropy as $\alpha \to 1$. For joint distributions with PPP, these entropies satisfy a non-additivity relation of the form $F(P,Q) = F(P) + F(Q) + a(\alpha)F(P)F(Q)$, where $a(\alpha)$ depends on the specific entropy measure. The authors explicitly compute $a(\alpha)$ for each entropy: $0$ for Rényi and Mathai's additive entropy, $2^{1-\alpha}-1$ for Havrda-Charvát, $1-\alpha$ for Tsallis, and $\alpha-1$ for Mathai entropy.

The maximum entropy principle is applied to continuous densities under various constraints: uniform density for no constraints; power-law densities (Tsallis q-exponential, type-1 beta, and type-2 beta) with a fixed first moment; and Mathai's pathway model densities when two moment-like expressions are fixed.
