judge_context:
Executive Summary
The paper constructs and proves the existence of a geometrically maximal abelian covering of the modular curve X0(p) over Q that is unramified outside the cusps. Mazur had previously established that the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) of degree Np := (p−1)/gcd(p−1, 12) is the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering. This paper extends that result by constructing a cyclic covering X′2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np, unramified outside cusps, which factors through X2(p) as a degree two unramified outside cusps covering. The construction uses generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions) to produce a rational function whose square root generates the quadratic extension. The authors prove that the resulting covering is geometrically maximal over Q and that it is cyclic of degree 2Np. The result holds for all primes p, with explicit constructions provided for p=2, 3, and p≥5. The paper also addresses the case p≡11 mod 12 separately using a different construction of modular functions. The key tools include the theory of generalized Jacobians, abelian fundamental groups, and Siegel functions, combined with explicit computations of modularity and ramification conditions.

Research Context
Let p be a prime number, and X0(p) and X1(p) be the modular curves over Q. Mazur proved that a geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of X0(p) over Q is given by the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p). The Shimura covering is a unique subcovering of X1(p) → X0(p) of degree Np := (p−1)/gcd(p−1, 12). TheShimma covering is the maximal unramified subcovering of the finite cyclic covering fp: X1(p) → X0(p) of degree (p−1)/2. For a smooth geometrically integral curve Y over a number field k admitting a degree one divisor, the maximal abelian extension is related to the maximal abelian quotient of the étale fundamental group. The kernel π1(Y)ab,geo of the canonical map to Gal(k,kab) is known to be finite by [1, Theorem 1]. A finite unramified abelian covering Y′ → Y is geometrically maximal if Y′ is geometrically integral over k and the composition π1(Y)ab,geo → Gal(Y′/Y) is an isomorphism. When Y admits a degree one divisor, a geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering always exists. When Y has a k-rational point x, a maximal abelian unramified covering in which x splits completely yields a geometrically maximal covering. The gap is that no such description exists if no k-rational point is available, necessitating a more general construction.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is: does there exist a geometrically maximal abelian covering of the modular curve Y0(p) over Q that is unramified outside the cusps? Specifically, the authors seek to construct a covering X′2(p) → X0(p) that is cyclic of degree 2Np and unramified outside the cusps. The primary hypothesis is that such a covering exists and satisfies two specific conditions. Condition (1) requires that the restriction to Y′2(p) = f′p−1(Y0(p)) is a geometrically maximal unramified covering of Y0(p) over Q. Condition (2) requires that f′p factors as f′p = f p ◦ πp, where πp: X′2(p) → X2(p) is a degree two covering unramified outside cusps. The predicted outcome is a cyclic covering of degree 2Np with the stated geometric maximality and ramification properties.

Methodological Details
The curves considered are X0(p) and X1(p) as geometrically integral smooth proper curves over Q. The cusp at infinity is chosen to split completely in a finite cyclic covering fp: X1(p) → X0(p) of degree (p−1)/2. The Shimura covering f p: X2(p) → X0(p) is the unique subcovering of degree Np := (p−1)/gcd(p−1, 12). Y0(p) is an open subscheme of X0(p) such that X0(p) \ Y0(p) consists of all two cusps. The construction uses the generalized Dedekind eta functions, also called Siegel functions. The function field Q(X′2(p)) is obtained as a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) generated by a square root of a rational function. For p=2 or 3, the covering f′p is taken to be the map Gm → Gm, x → x^2 under the identification Y0(p) ~ Gm = P^1 \ {0,∞}. For p ≥ 5, an odd generator g of (Z/pZ)× is chosen to define the auxiliary parameters. The constant k is defined as Np = (p−1)/gcd(p−1, 12) and ℓ := (p−1, 12)^2, where (a, b) := gcd(a, b). The group Γ2(p) is generated by Γ1(p) and matrices of the form [g^k; p]...

Procedures And Architectures
For p ≥ 5, the function F_h(τ) is defined as the product of 6 generalized Dedekind eta functions: F_h(τ) = product_{j=0}^{ℓ-1} E_g^j_kh(τ)^{6/ℓ}. The property F_{g^k h} = (-F_h) if p ≡ 1 mod 4 and F_h if p ≡ 3 mod 4 is established by checking F_{g^k ℓ h} = (-F_h). The character ψ of order 2 of SL(2,Z) is defined by (−1)^{a+d−1} for c odd and (−1)^b for c even. If ℓ is even (p ≡ 1 mod 4), a character χ of order 2 of Γ2(p) is defined such that Γ1(p) ⊆ ker χ. The group Γ′2(p) is defined as the kernel of the character ψχ (if p≡1 mod 4) or ψ (if p≡3 mod 4) on Γ2(p). For the case p ≡ 11 mod 12, where Γ2(p) = Γ1(p), the function G_h = (E_h1 E_h2 E_h3)^2 is used with h=(h1,h2,h3) satisfying h2^2 + h2^2 + h2^3 ≡ 0 mod p. The Fourier expansion of E_g(τ) starts from q^{N B(g/N)/2} and the Fourier expansion of E_g(γτ) starts from q^{\delta} where δ depends on P_2(x). The order of F_h^2 at a cusp of X2(p) is shown to be odd, and zero elsewhere, by computing the Fourier expansion order. The quadratic extension Q(X′2(p))/Q(X2(p)) is generated by F_h^{1/2} for p ∤ 11 mod 12 and by z(τ) or F_h^{1/2} for p ≡ 11 mod 12.

Key Results
The Shimura covering f p: X2(p) → X0(p) of degree Np is geometrically maximal over Q by Mazur's theorem. A cyclic covering f′p: X′2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np exists such that f′p|Y′2(p): Y′2(p) → Y0(p) is a geometrically maximal unramified covering. The covering f′p factors as f′p = f p ◦ πp where πp: X′2(p) → X2(p) is a degree two covering unramified outside cusps. For p ∤ 11 mod 12, the order of F_h^2 at any cusp of X2(p) is odd and zero elsewhere. The quotient Γ0(p)/Γ′2(p) is cyclic of order 2k, with Γ′2(p) being a normal subgroup of Γ0(p). For p ≡ 11 mod 12, G_{2h} is a modular function on X1(p) with odd order at each cusp and invariant under Γ1(p) character. The abelian group M_{\mu}^Tor(-1) is cyclic of order Np by Theorem 1.2.1, and its order determines M_{\mu}^Tor(-1) has order Np or 2Np. Since the Shimura covering is geometrically maximal, the order of M_{\mu}^Tor(-1) must be 2Np, implying the covering is geometrically maximal.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The result extends Mazur's classification of maximal unramified abelian coverings of X0(p) to the unramified-outside-cusps case. The explicit construction using Siegel functions shows that the quadratic extension is generated by a square root of a modular function with odd order at cusps. The degree 2Np covering achieves the maximum possible abelian degree while remaining unramified outside the two cusps of X0(p). The work unifies results from modular curve theory, generalized Jacobians, and the theory of Siegel functions. The cyclic nature of the covering X′2(p) → X0(p) simplifies the understanding of the abelian extension structure. The method of using square roots of modular functions with odd cuspidal order generalizes to other situations where such functions exist.

Contradictions And Limitations
The proof for p ≡ 11 mod 12 requires a separate construction of modular functions because Γ2(p) = Γ1(p) in that case. The paper assumes p is a prime; it does not address composite levels. The construction relies on the existence of a degree one divisor on X0(p), which is satisfied here since the cusp at infinity is a rational point. The paper is a short note and focuses on the specific case of X0(p); generalizations to X0(N) or other curves are not investigated. The Shimura covering is unique of degree Np, but the construction of X′2(p) is less canonical, involving a choice of odd generator g. The ramification of fp: X1(p) → X0(p) is not explicitly ruled out, only that the Shimura covering is its maximal unramified subcovering.

Claims
There exists a cyclic covering X′2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np, unramified outside cusps, that is geometrically maximal over Q and factors through the Shimura covering as a degree two unramified outside cusps covering. Theorem 1.2.2 explicitly states the existence of a cyclic covering of degree 2Np satisfying conditions (1) and (2). The order of M_{\mu}^Tor(-1) is shown to be 2Np, which, given Mazur's result that the Shimura covering has order Np, implies geometric maximality of the degree 2Np covering. The odd order of F_h^2 at each cusp ensures the square root gives a covering ramified only at cusps. The construction handles all p separately, with p=2, 3 explicit and p≥5 using Siegel functions. For p ≡ 11 mod 12, the construction is different (using a triplet of functions) and the justification is less direct. The covering X′2(p) → X2(p) of degree two is unramified outside cusps but not everywhere unramified. The geometric maximality of this covering provides a complete description of the maximal abelian extension of the function field of Y0(p) unramified outside cusps. The cyclic structure implies the Galois group is cyclic of order 2Np, simplifying the analysis of the abelian extension.
The generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions) provide a sufficient class of modular functions whose square roots generate the required quadratic extensions of the function field of X2(p). Lemma 3.3.4 shows that F_h^2 is a modular function on X2(p) defined over Q. The transformation law F_h(γτ) = ψ(γ)F_ah(τ) (and its Γ2(p) analogue) proves F_h^2 is invariant under the required subgroups. The cuspidal order computation shows the order is odd at every cusp, ensuring the square root is unramified elsewhere. For p ≡ 11 mod 12, a different construction (G_h) is required because Γ2(p) = Γ1(p). The Siegel function machinery can be applied to more general modular curves and levels to construct quadratic extensions with prescribed ramification.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The construction is verified separately for p ≡ 11 mod 12, p ≡ 1 mod 4, and p ≡ 3 mod 4, addressing the different group structures of Γ2(p) and Γ1(p). The case p=2, 3 is handled separately by a direct map on P^1, showing the result holds for all primes. The choice of odd generator g of (Z/pZ)× and the character ψ are explicit, making the construction reproducible.

Key Figures Tables
The diagram in §1.2 illustrates the tower of coverings: X1(p) → X2(p) → X0(p) and the relationship between X′2(p) and X1(p). The exact sequence (2.2.3) 0 → JTor → MTor → LD ⊗ Q/Z → 0 is central to the analysis of the abelian fundamental group. The Kummer-type exact sequence (1.1.1) 0 → π1(Y)ab,geo → π1(Y)ab → Gal(k,kab) → 0 defines the geometrically maximal covering.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the construction of a cyclic covering X′2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np, unramified outside cusps, which is geometrically maximal over Q. 2. The strongest evidence is the computation that the order of F_h^2 at each cusp of X2(p) is odd, combined with the transformation laws establishing modularity over Q, which ensures the covering is ramified only at cusps and is defined over Q. 3. The future path lies in applying the Siegel function construction to more general curves, higher levels, and potentially non-cyclic abelian coverings with different ramification behaviors.

summary.title: Design of Real-time Semantic Segmentation Decoder for Automated Driving
summary.authors: Arindam Das, Saranya Kandan, Senthil Yogamani, Pavel Křížek
summary.field_subfield: Computer Vision / Automated Driving / Semantic Segmentation
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a novel non-bottleneck layer and a family of decoder architectures designed for real-time semantic segmentation in automated driving applications. The authors identify that while encoders have received extensive attention for task-independent feature extraction, decoders remain computationally expensive and unoptimized. They propose a non-bottleneck layer that combines residual learning with cascaded skip connections to distribute high gradient flow during back-propagation, a modification specifically suited for shallow networks where standard residual learning is inefficient. The architecture uses a task-independent 10-layer VGG-style encoder as a fixed base, producing 256 feature maps. The encoder produces non-semantic knowledge that the decoder must learn to transform into semantic segmentation. The non-bottleneck layer employs both 1D and 3D kernels (3x3, 5x5, and 1x1) fused across multiple skip connections. Experiments were conducted on a custom urban dataset with 1280x384 pixel images across four critical classes: lanes, curb, road, and void. The dataset comprises 3016 training, 981 validation, and 1002 test images. The network was trained end-to-end in the Keras framework using the Adam optimizer, weight decay of 0.9, batch size of 4, and 350K iterations on an NVIDIA Titan X 12G GPU with 24 GB RAM. The authors tested eight decoder variants (D1–D8) and several non-repetitive non-bottleneck combinations, with the optimal configuration achieving a mean IoU of 0.7441. This represents a 10% overall improvement from the baseline configuration, with specific improvements of 12% for lanes (0.5304 IoU) and 18% for curb (0.4696 IoU), while maintaining a runtime overhead of less than 2ms compared to a standard FCN decoder. The authors demonstrate that efficient decoder design is a critical, under-studied component of the semantic segmentation pipeline, particularly for embedded deployment.

claims.description: A novel non-bottleneck layer with residual learning and cascaded skip connections improves semantic segmentation accuracy under a fixed runtime budget.
Cascaded skip connections in a non-bottleneck architecture resolve the high gradient flow issue in shallow residual networks.
The non-bottleneck layer design is generic and can be used for any semantic segmentation task beyond urban lane detection.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a novel non-bottleneck layer and a family of decoder architectures designed for real-time semantic segmentation in automated driving applications. The authors identify that while encoders have received extensive attention for task-independent feature extraction, decoders remain computationally expensive and unoptimized. They propose a non-bottleneck layer that combines residual learning with cascaded skip connections to distribute high gradient flow during back-propagation, a modification specifically suited for shallow networks where standard residual learning is inefficient. The architecture uses a task-independent 10-layer VGG-style encoder as a fixed base, producing 256 feature maps. The encoder produces non-semantic knowledge that the decoder must learn to transform into semantic segmentation. The non-bottleneck layer employs both 1D and 3D kernels (3x3, 5x5, and 1x1) fused across multiple skip connections. Experiments were conducted on a custom urban dataset with 1280x384 pixel images across four critical classes: lanes, curb, road, and void. The dataset comprises 3016 training, 981 validation, and 1002 test images. The network was trained end-to-end in the Keras framework using the Adam optimizer, weight decay of 0.9, batch size of 4, and 350K iterations on an NVIDIA Titan X 12G GPU with 24 GB RAM. The authors tested eight decoder variants (D1–D8) and several non-repetitive non-bottleneck combinations, with the optimal configuration achieving a mean IoU of 0.7441. This represents a 10% overall improvement from the baseline configuration, with specific improvements of 12% for lanes (0.5304 IoU) and 18% for curb (0.4696 IoU), while maintaining a runtime overhead of less than 2ms compared to a standard FCN decoder. The authors demonstrate that efficient decoder design is a critical, under-studied component of the semantic segmentation pipeline, particularly for embedded deployment.

Research Context
Semantic segmentation remains a computationally intensive algorithm even with rapid computation power growth, making efficient network design critical for automated driving. Recent research has focused heavily on designing efficient encoders that are mostly task agnostic, leaving decoders under-studied. Unlike image classification and bounding box detection, decoders are computationally expensive for semantic segmentation tasks. Early architectures like SegNet and UNet used decoders that were mirror images of the encoder with the same complexity. Industrial embedded platforms have computational bounds due to limited resources, necessitating runtime-budget-conscious models. While dilated convolutions, spatial pyramid pooling, and multi-path refinement have advanced segmentation, none use a task-independent lightweight encoder for multi-task learning. Existing methods do not support multi-task learning practice and use task-specific encoders rather than generic ones.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a novel non-bottleneck layer with cascaded skip connections can improve semantic segmentation accuracy while adhering to a fixed runtime budget on an embedded platform. The authors hypothesize that a non-semantic encoder knowledge gap created by using a task-independent VGG-style encoder can be overcome in the decoder by learning semantic information extensively via non-bottleneck blocks between deconvolution layers. A second hypothesis is that standard residual learning is inefficient for networks with lesser depth because they cannot handle high gradient flow during back-propagation; distributing gradients through multiple skip connections should mitigate this. The predicted outcome is that experimentation with various decoder design choices will yield significant accuracy improvements with minimal runtime increase, particularly for challenging classes like lanes and curb. The authors explicitly state that the encoder design is function independent, so the gap of spatial information exploration needs to be overcome by the decoder learning semantic features extensively. The predicted runtime constraint is paramount, with priority given to execution speed over accuracy for embedded deployment.

Methodological Details
The dataset consists of urban scenes with highly varied conditions and dense shadows, capturing dimensions of 1280x384 pixels per image. The data is divided into training, validation, and test sets containing 3016, 981, and 1002 images, respectively. Semantic segmentation was performed on four critical classes: lanes, curb, road, and void. Single-channel pixel-wise annotations with one class label per pixel were developed for each sample image. The encoder was first trained from scratch on ImageNet and weights were transferred to the target task, using transfer learning for better initialization. The pre-training was required because the model is shallow and the target dataset is small in size. Implementation and all experiments were executed using the Keras framework with the Adam optimizer. Network configurations included a weight decay of 0.9 and a batch size of 4. Training started with an initial learning rate of 0.0005 using a standard polynomial decay strategy over 350K iterations. Dropout was not used in the model, and no data augmentation technique was performed during training. Experiments ran on an NVIDIA Titan X 12G GPU with 24 GB RAM. No random seed, specific split partitioning method, or demographic metadata is reported. The dataset is owned by the authors' organization and not publicly described as a shared resource. No explicit data availability statement or external repository link is provided.

Procedures And Architectures
The encoder is a 10-layer VGG-style classifier producing a total of 256 feature maps at the final layer. All convolution layers in the encoder use 5x5 kernels followed by Batch-Normalization and ReLU activation. Convolution with stride 2 followed by max-pooling is used for downsampling, reducing hyperparameters and runtime. The encoder is designed to be task-independent, with no heavy use of dilated convolutions as seen in prior work. The non-bottleneck layer contains both 1D and 3D kernels to extract directional and receptive-area information. Multiple kernels of sizes 3x3, 5x5, and 1x1 are used within each non-bottleneck layer to gather dense information. The dilation rate within the dilated convolution variant of the non-bottleneck layer is kept constant at 1. After each convolution operation, ReLU activation is used for better convergence. The decoder uses deconvolution layers instead of max-unpooling for reconstruction of the input space. Feature maps from the encoder are downsampled from 256 to 4 to accommodate the four-class target. Intermediate feature maps from the second and third last convolution layers of the encoder are pulled via skip connections. The encoder consumed most of the run time because it is much wider than the decoder. Group convolution was considered but rejected because aggregated residual transformations showed adverse effects for lightweight networks. The optimal decoder configuration uses two non-bottleneck layers of type-1, two of type-2, and one of type-2 after the second and third deconvolution layers. The first deconvolution uses a 2x2 kernel, the second also 2x2, the third 3x3, the fourth 3x3, and the fifth 5x5 for upsampling. Type-1 non-bottleneck blocks use 3x3 and 5x5 kernels; Type-2 blocks use dilated convolution with 3x3 and 5x5 kernels.

Key Results
The optimal decoder configuration achieved a mean IoU of 0.7441 across four classes. The baseline configuration, which uses only one non-bottleneck layer after each deconvolution, achieved a mean IoU of 0.7323. The non-repetitive non-bottleneck combination (2N1)(2N1)(2N2)(2N2) achieved a mean IoU of 0.742. The (2N2)(2N2)(2N2)(2N2) combination achieved a mean IoU of 0.7323, identical to the baseline. The (2N2)(2N2)(2N2) combination achieved a mean IoU of 0.7315. The (2N1)(2N1)(2N1)(2N1) combination achieved a mean IoU of 0.7284. The (1N1-1N2)(1N1-1N2)(1N1-1N2)(1N1-1N2) combination achieved a mean IoU of 0.731. For the most difficult classes, the optimal configuration achieved a lane IoU of 0.5304 and a curb IoU of 0.4696. The road class IoU for the optimal configuration reached 0.9314. Compared to the standard FCN decoder, the proposed optimal decoder improved IoUs for key classes with less than 2ms increase in runtime. The mean IoU improvement from the baseline configuration to the optimal was 10% (0.7441 vs 0.7323). For the lane class, the improvement was 12% (0.5304 vs 0.4961 baseline, though D8 achieved 0.4752). For the curb class, the improvement was 18% (0.4696 vs 0.4486, though D8 achieved 0.4717). The lane accuracy for the optimal configuration was 0.6118, and curb accuracy was 0.6588, while road accuracy was 0.9689. The road accuracy for the optimal configuration was 0.9689, which is the highest accuracy achieved by any configuration. Without data augmentation or class weighting, the non-bottleneck layers worked better for curb though there was a slight deterioration for lanes. The road class consistently achieved IoU above 0.92 in nearly all configurations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The non-bottleneck layer addresses the gap in the encoder where non-semantic information is shared, enabling the decoder to learn semantic information from the encoded feature space. Cascaded skip connections distribute high gradients through multiple paths during back-propagation, preventing gradient explosion and enabling effective training of shallower residual networks. The 1D and 3D kernels in the non-bottleneck layer capture both directionally-specific and wide-receptive-area semantic features independently. The design demonstrates that decoder architecture choice covers a significant portion of overall computation in semantic segmentation, making it a viable target for efficiency optimization. The non-bottleneck layer is shown to be generic, usable for any segmentation task beyond the specific lane/curb/road/void setting. The finding that standard residual learning is inefficient for shallow networks suggests a fundamental limitation in how depth-independent architectures handle gradient flow.

Contradictions And Limitations
No data augmentation technique was performed during training, reducing the robustness of the results to domain shift. Dropout was not used in the model, increasing the risk of overfitting on the relatively small dataset of 3016 training images. The VGG10 encoder consumed most of the run time because it is much wider than the decoder, masking the decoder's actual runtime footprint. The dataset is small (4399 images total) and of organizational ownership, limiting generalizability and replication by other researchers. A slight deterioration for lanes was observed without data augmentation or class weighting, indicating class imbalance sensitivity. The random seed and specific train/test split partitions are not reported, impeding exact reproduction. The evaluation is restricted to a single urban scene type with four specific classes, and performance on more complex or natural scenes is unknown. No ablation on the dilation rate (kept at 1) was performed, although the authors note incremental dilation could potentially improve accuracy. The paper lacks a full bibliography, and all citations are in-text only.

Claims
A novel non-bottleneck layer with residual learning and cascaded skip connections improves semantic segmentation accuracy under a fixed runtime budget. The optimal configuration achieved a mean IoU of 0.7441 with less than 2ms runtime overhead over FCN. Experimentation with various decoder design choices led to a 10% overall IoU improvement from the baseline. Class-specific improvements of 12% for lanes and 18% for curb were obtained. Cascaded skip connections distribute gradients through multiple paths during back-propagation. Without class weighting and data augmentation, there was a slight deterioration for lanes on some decoder variants. No data augmentation was performed, and dropout was omitted, threatening robustness. The design demonstrates that the decoder, not just the encoder, is a critical efficiency bottleneck in semantic segmentation. A task-independent encoder can provide features suitable for multi-task learning with a dedicated, class-specific decoder.
Cascaded skip connections in a non-bottleneck architecture resolve the high gradient flow issue in shallow residual networks. Standard residual learning for networks with lesser depth is demonstrated to be inefficient for handling high gradient flow. The proposed non-bottleneck layer uses multiple skip connections to distribute gradients among all paths during back-propagation. The encoder consumes most runtime, so the decoder must learn semantic features from non-semantic input. No ablation on the dilation rate was performed, and the authors note that higher dilation rates could improve accuracy but increase cost. This suggests that gradient distribution strategy is more important than depth for shallow residual architectures.
The non-bottleneck layer design is generic and can be used for any semantic segmentation task beyond urban lane detection. The authors state the non-bottleneck layer is generic and can be used for any segmentation task. The layer architecture was tested with eight different decoder combinations, each producing different IoU profiles. The only evaluation was on a single dataset with four specific urban classes, limiting the claim of generality. The non-bottleneck layer can be treated as a modular component in encoder-decoder architectures for diverse segmentation tasks.

Data And Code Availability
The proposed network and all experiments were executed using the Keras framework. The dataset is owned by the authors' organization and is not explicitly described as a public resource. No explicit code repository, DOI, or data access procedure is provided in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors tested eight decoder variants (D1-D8) as an ablation study on non-bottleneck layer configuration. Five non-repetitive non-bottleneck combinations were systematically evaluated to isolate the effect of layer sequencing. The optimal configuration, (2N1)(2N1)(2N2)(2N2), was chosen through iterative optimization and comparison with five other non-repetitive combinations. The dilation rate in the Type-2 non-bottleneck blocks was kept constant at 1 to meet runtime constraints, but the authors acknowledge that incremental dilation could improve accuracy. No random seed, weight initialization scheme, or specific split partitioning (train/val/test) is reported.

Figure 1 depicts the typical encoder-decoder architecture of the CNN-based semantic segmentation network. Figure 2 illustrates the design of the non-bottleneck layers with 1D and 3D kernels. Figure 3 shows the specific encoder-decoder pair used in this work, with intermediate feature maps pulled from the encoder. Table 1 includes class-specific IoU metrics for lanes, curb, and road for each configuration, identifying the optimal mean IoU of 0.7441.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a novel non-bottleneck layer combining residual learning with cascaded skip connections and 1D/3D kernels, achieving a task-agnostic encoder-decoder framework for real-time semantic segmentation on embedded devices. 2. The strongest evidence is the 10% overall mean IoU improvement (0.7441 vs 0.7323) and class-specific improvements of 12% for lanes and 18% for curb, with less than 2ms runtime overhead compared to standard FCN. 3. The future path includes building a systematic family of meta-architectures with a fixed runtime budget and learning optimal configurations using meta-learning techniques.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper establishes the Lusin area characterization for Hardy spaces $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ associated with the Hermite operator $L = -\Delta + |x|^2$, for $d \geq 3$ and $0 < p \leq 1$. The authors prove that the Hardy space $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$, defined via the maximal function of the Poisson semigroup, coincides with the space $H^p_S(\mathbb{R}^d)$ defined by the Lusin area integral associated with the Hermite operator. The Lusin area integral is defined using the gradient $\nabla_L = (\partial_t, \partial_1 + x_1, \dots, \partial_d + x_d)$, which is specific to Hermite operators and was first suggested by Thangavelu. The approach generalizes earlier results that were known only for $p=1$ to the full range $0 < p \leq 1$. The proof strategy involves two intermediate spaces, $H^p_{L,max}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $H^p_A(\mathbb{R}^d)$, along with an atomic characterization of $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ through $(p,2,M)$-atoms. The authors also prove that the Riesz transforms $R^L_j = (\partial_j + x_j)L^{-1/2}$ are bounded on $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for all $j \geq 1$. The work relies on heat kernel and Poisson kernel estimates, tent space techniques, and the Calderon reproducing formula. The key novelty is the use of the Hermite-specific gradient in the Lusin integral, which differentiates the characterization from previous results in the literature.

Research Context
Hermite operators have been studied over the years due to their significant role in the harmonic oscillator. Hardy spaces with their rich structures are of fundamental interest in harmonic analysis. An in-depth study of Hermite operators can be found in the monograph of Thangavelu. Hardy spaces with index $p \in (0,1]$ associated with Hermite operators were motivated by the work of Jiz, where results were available for $p=1$. Similar Lusin area characterizations are available in the literature for other operators, such as in Stein's book and works of Stegenga, Ye, and Jiao. The Lusin area integrals of this work are more general and are defined using derivatives of the form $\partial_j + x_j$ first suggested by Thangavelu, specific to Hermite operators.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the Hardy space $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ can be characterized in terms of the Lusin area integral defined with the Hermite-specific gradient $\nabla_L$. The hypothesis is that for $d \geq 3$ and $0 < p \leq 1$, the space $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ defined by the maximal function of the Poisson semigroup coincides with the space $H^p_S(\mathbb{R}^d)$ defined by the Lusin area integral. A second hypothesis is that the Riesz transforms $R^L_j = (\partial_j + x_j)L^{-1/2}$ are bounded on $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for all $j \geq 1$. The authors predict that the characterization will require two intermediate spaces, $H^p_{L,max}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $H^p_A(\mathbb{R}^d)$, and an atomic decomposition. The dimension constraint $d \geq 3$ is motivated by the structure of the heat kernel estimates and the Lusin integral definition.

Methodological Details
The dimension $d$ is an integer such that $d \geq 3$. The index $p$ is in the range $(0,1]$. The Hermite operator $L$ is defined as $L = -\Delta + |x|^2$ on its maximal domain in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$. The sesquilinear form $a_0(u,v) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} D u \cdot D v + |x|^2 u v$ on $C_c^	extbf{∞}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ generates $L$ in the sense of Kato's first representation theorem. The completion $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is defined via the quasi-norm $\|\cdot\|_{H^p_L} = \|M \cdot\|_{L^p}$, where $M f(\cdot) = \sup_{t>0} |e^{-tL}f(\cdot)|$. The Lusin integral $S f(x)$ is defined as $\left(\int_{\Gamma(x)} t^{1-d} |\nabla_L P_t f(y)|^2 dy dt\right)^{1/2}$ with $\Gamma(x) = \{(y,t) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times (0,\infty) : |x-y| < t\}$. The function $\rho(x) = 1 / (1+|x|)$ is used in kernel estimates. The space $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is also characterized via an atom decomposition: a function $a$ is an $H^p_L$-atom associated with a ball $B(x_0,r)$ if $\text{supp } a \subset B(x_0,r)$, $\|a\|_{L^\infty} \leq |B(x_0,r)|^{-1/p}$, and $\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} a = 0$ if $r < \rho(x_0)/4$. The condition for the atomic decomposition is $d/(d+\delta) < p \leq 1$, where $\delta$ is given by the gradient estimate. The intermediate space $H^p_{L,max}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is the completion of $\{f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d) : f^*_L \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)\	ext{ under the quasi-norm } \|f^*_L\|_{L^p}$. The space $H^p_A(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is defined via the operator $A f(x) = \left(\int_0^\infty \int_{|x-y|<t} t^{1-d} |(\partial_t P_t f)(y)|^2 dy dt\right)^{1/2}$. A $(p,2,M)$-atom $a \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ satisfies $a = L^M b$ for some $b \in D(L^M)$ such that $\text{supp } L^k b \subset B$ for $k = 0, \dots, M$, and $\|(r^2 L)^k b\|_{L^2} \leq r^{2M} |B|^{1/2-1/p}$ for $k = 0, \dots, M$. Tent spaces $T^{p,2}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ are used with the aperture $\alpha > 0$ and the tent $\Gamma_\alpha(x) = \{(y,t) : |x-y| < \alpha t\}$.

Procedures And Architectures
The paper is organized into six sections: Preliminaries (heat/Poisson kernel estimates), $H^p_L \subset H^p_{L,max}$, $H^p_L = H^p_A \cap L^2$, proof of Theorem 1.1, boundedness of Riesz transforms, and conclusion. Heat kernel estimates for $g_t(x,y)$ and Poisson kernel estimates for $p_t(x,y)$ are cited from Jiao, Jiao and Yang (2016). The gradient estimate for the Poisson semigroup is $|p_t(x+h, y) - p_t(x,y)| \leq C_N (|h|/t)^\delta t^{1-d} (t + 2|x-y|)^{d+1} (1 + \sqrt{t}\rho(x))^{-N} (1 + \sqrt{t}\rho(y))^{-N}$ for $|h| < \sqrt{t}$. The proof of Theorem 1.1 uses Proposition 3.1 ($H^p_L \subset H^p_{L,max}$) and Proposition 5.4 ($\|S f\|_{L^p} \leq C \|f^*_L\|_{L^p}$), along with the inequality $\|\cdot\|_{H^p_A} \leq \|\cdot\|_{H^p_S}$ for the reverse inclusion. The Calderon reproducing formula is used in the proof of Proposition 4.8 to express $f$ as an atomic decomposition from the tent space characterization. A generalized Holder inequality is applied to bound the $L^p$ norm of $A a$ by a sum over dyadic annuli. The operator $\pi_{\Psi,L}: T^{p,2}(\mathbb{R}^d) \to L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ defined by $\pi_{\Psi,L}(F) = \int_0^\infty \Psi(t^{1/2}L) F(\cdot,t) dt/t$ maps tent space atoms to $(p,2,M)$-atoms. The density of $L^2_c(\mathbb{R}^d)$ in both $H^p_L$ and $H^p_{L+2}$ is established by atomic approximation. For the Riesz transform proof, the authors show $R^L_j$ is bounded on $H^p_L \cap L^2$ and extend by density. The bound for $R^L_j$ uses the identity $R^L_j f = (\partial_j + x_j)L^{-1/2}f$, and the estimate $\|R^L_j f\|_{H^p_{L+2}} \leq C \|A_{L+2} R^L_j f\|_{L^p} = C \int_0^\infty \int_{|x-y|<t} t^{1-d} |(\partial_t e^{-t(L+2)^{1/2}} R^L_j f)(y)|^2 dy dt \leq C \|S_L f\|_{L^p} \leq C \|f|_{H^p_L} .

Key Results
Theorem 1.1: The Hardy space $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with the quasi-norm $\|\cdot\|_{H^p_L}$ coincides with the space $H^p_S(\mathbb{R}^d)$ defined by the Lusin area integral, i.e., $(H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d), \|\cdot\|_{H^p_L}) = (H^p_S(\mathbb{R}^d), \|\cdot\|_{H^p_S})$. Theorem 1.2: The Riesz transforms $R^L_j = (\partial_j + x_j)L^{-1/2}$ are bounded on $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for all $j \in \{1, 2, \dots\}$. Proposition 3.1: For $d/(d+\delta) < p \leq 1$, $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d) \subset H^p_{L,max}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, proved by showing that any $H^p_L$-atom has $L^p$ norm bounded by a constant. Proposition 4.11: $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d) = H^p_A(\mathbb{R}^d) \cap L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for $M \geq d^{2/(1-1/p)}$, combining Propositions 4.9 and 4.10. Proposition 4.9: For $M > d^{2/(1/p - 1/2)} \lor 1$, $H^p_A(\mathbb{R}^d) \cap L^2(\mathbb{R}^d) = H^p_{L,at,M}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ as quasi-norm spaces. Proposition 4.10: For $M \geq d^{2/(1-1/p)}$, $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d) = H^p_{L,at,M}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, which is a consequence of SY16 and BDL18. Lemma 6.1: The inclusions $L^2_c(\mathbb{R}^d) \subset H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d) \subset H^p_{L+2}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ hold, with $L^2_c(\mathbb{R}^d)$ dense in both spaces. Lemma 6.2: $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d) = H^p_{L+2}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ as spaces, following immediately from Lemma 6.1.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Lusin characterization provides an alternative description of $H^p_L$ that connects the maximal function characterization to the area integral characterization, analogous to Stein's work but with a Hermite-specific gradient. The atomic characterization $H^p_L = H^p_{L,at,M}$ connects the maximal function, area integral, and atomic descriptions, demonstrating the robustness of the Hardy space structure. The boundedness of Riesz transforms $R^L_j$ follows directly from the Lusin characterization and the identity $R^L_j f = (\partial_j + x_j)L^{-1/2}f$, establishing a complete suite of tools for $H^p_L$. The approach extends previous results known only for $p=1$ to the full range $p \in (0, 1]$, which is significant as Hardy spaces for $p < 1$ are more delicate to handle. The methods developed here (tent space decomposition, atomic characterization, kernel estimates) can likely be generalized to other operators with similar semigroup properties.

Contradictions And Limitations
The theorem requires $d \geq 3$, and the paper does not address the cases $d=1, 2$. The proof of Theorem 1.2 uses the density of $H^p_L \cap L^2$ in $H^p_L$, which is standard but not proven for all $p$ and $d$. No specific numerical values beyond dimension constraints and the $p$ range are reported; the result is qualitative in terms of constant dependencies. The constant $C$ in each inequality is not quantified, and its dependence on $d, p, \delta$ is not explicitly analyzed. The paper does not discuss the case $p > 1$, where the Hardy space theory is different.

Claims
Theorem 1.1: The Hardy space $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ is equivalent to the Lusin area space $H^p_S(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for $d \geq 3, 0 < p \leq 1$. Proposition 3.1 shows $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d) \subset H^p_{L,max}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for $d/(d+\delta) < p \leq 1$. Proposition 5.4 shows $\|S f\|_{L^p} \leq C \|f^*_L\|_{L^p}$, which is the reverse inclusion $H^p_S(\mathbb{R}^d) \subset H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$. The chain of equalities $H^p_L = H^p_{L,at,M} = H^p_A \cap L^2 = H^p_S$ is established through Propositions 4.11, 4.9, 4.10, and 5.4. The proof of the reverse inclusion relies on the specific estimate from Lemma 5.2, which is a non-trivial pointwise bound. The Lusin characterization provides a new tool for studying $H^p_L$ functions. The equivalence of different characterizations (maximal function, area integral, atomic) strengthens the understanding of $H^p_L$.
Theorem 1.2: The Riesz transforms $R^L_j = (\partial_j + x_j)L^{-1/2}$ are bounded on $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for all $j \geq 1$. The boundedness extends the applicability of the Hardy space theory to derivative-type operators.

The paper includes several intermediate propositions (Propositions 4.9, 4.10, 4.11) that show the equivalence of different characterizations under different conditions on $M$. Proposition 4.11 establishes $H^p_L = H^p_A \cap L^2$ as a consequence of 4.9 and 4.10, showing the atomic characterization is robust. The condition $M \geq d^{2/(1-1/p)}$ in Proposition 4.10 shows the minimal required power of $L$ for the atomic characterization.

The paper contains no figures or tables; all results are stated in theorem and proposition format.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the proof that for $d \geq 3$ and $0 < p \leq 1$, the Hardy space $H^p_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ associated with the Hermite operator is equal to the Lusin area space $H^p_S(\mathbb{R}^d)$ using the Hermite-specific gradient $\nabla_L = (\partial_t, \partial_1 + x_1, \dots, \partial_d + x_d)$. 2. summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a deep-learning-enabled hybrid precoding framework for mmWave massive MIMO systems to address the computational complexity and sub-optimal performance of conventional SVD and GMD-based schemes. The authors model the hybrid precoder selection as a mapping relation within a Deep Neural Network (DNN) architecture configured as an autoencoder. The DNN, implemented as a multiple-layers perceptron with 128-unit input layer, two hidden encoding layers (400, 256 units), a 200-unit noise layer for AWGN simulation, and two decoding hidden layers (128, 64 units), is trained using an unsupervised SGD-with-momentum learning policy. The loss function is defined as the Frobenius norm difference between the DNN-generated analog precoder and the GMD-based analog precoder. Simulation results on a Saleh-Valenzuela channel model (28 GHz carrier, P=3 NLoS components) demonstrate that the DNN-based scheme outperforms conventional SVD-based hybrid precoding, fully digital SVD-based precoding, and fully GMD-based schemes in both bit error ratio (BER) and spectrum efficiency across various SNR levels. Computational complexity of the proposed method is $O(L^2NsN_t^2)$, which is lower than the quadratic dependencies found in prior methods. Sensitivity analyses on batch size (10, 20, 50, 100) and learning rates reveal performance trade-offs, and MSE-versus-iterations plots show faster convergence (approximately 11 iterations) compared to the analog precoding scheme (22 iterations). The work claims to be the first to incorporate DNN-based deep learning into hybrid precoding for mmWave massive MIMO.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes a deep-learning-enabled hybrid precoding framework for mmWave massive MIMO systems to address the computational complexity and sub-optimal performance of conventional SVD and GMD-based schemes. The authors model the hybrid precoder selection as a mapping relation within a Deep Neural Network (DNN) architecture configured as an autoencoder. The DNN, implemented as a multiple-layers perceptron with 128-unit input layer, two hidden encoding layers (400, 256 units), a 200-unit noise layer for AWGN simulation, and two decoding hidden layers (128, 64 units), is trained using an unsupervised SGD-with-momentum learning policy. The loss function is defined as the Frobenius norm difference between the DNN-generated analog precoder and the GMD-based analog precoder. Simulation results on a Saleh-Valenzuela channel model (28 GHz carrier, P=3 NLoS components) demonstrate that the DNN-based scheme outperforms conventional SVD-based hybrid precoding, fully digital SVD-based precoding, and fully GMD-based schemes in both bit error ratio (BER) and spectrum efficiency across various SNR levels. Computational complexity of the proposed method is $O(L^2NsN_t^2)$, which is lower than the quadratic dependencies found in prior methods. Sensitivity analyses on batch size (10, 20, 50, 100) and learning rates reveal performance trade-offs, and MSE-versus-iterations plots show faster convergence (approximately 11 iterations) compared to the analog precoding scheme (22 iterations). The work claims to be the first to incorporate DNN-based deep learning into hybrid precoding for mmWave massive MIMO.

Research Context
Wireless data traffic is predicted to increase over 10,000-fold by 2030, necessitating fifth-generation (5G) systems. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) bands offer ten-fold carrier frequency increases and orders-of-magnitude pathloss enhancement over current systems. Conventional hybrid precoding schemes based on singular value decomposition (SVD) suffer from high computational complexity and require complicated bit allocation strategies. The geometric mean decomposition (GMD) scheme avoids bit allocation issues but faces non-convex constraints on the analog precoder. Traditional methods are too weak to exploit the sparsity statistics and structural characteristics of mmWave massive MIMO channels. Deep learning has proven effective for handling complex non-convex problems and high-computation issues in communication tasks.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a deep-learning-enabled framework can minimize computational complexity while improving BER and spectrum efficiency in mmWave massive MIMO hybrid precoding compared to conventional SVD/GMD schemes. The authors hypothesize that a DNN configured as an autoencoder can capture the structural information and mapping relations of the hybrid precoder through training. The hypothesis is that the DNN-based approach will achieve better hybrid precoding performance than conventional schemes while substantially reducing required computational complexity. The study predicts that the DNN will outperform the fully GMD-based digital precoding scheme, implying non-convex hybrid precoding optimization can be solved via deep learning. The proposed framework is the first work to design a framework incorporating deep learning technique into hybrid precoding for mmWave MIMO.

Methodological Details
The system model assumes one base station with a uniform linear array of Nt antennas and a user with Nr received antennas sending Ns independent data streams. The communication links satisfy the constraints Ns ≤ N RFt ≤ Nt and Nt ≤ N RFr ≤ Nr. The channel is modeled using the Saleh-Valenzuela model with P = 3 non-line-of-sight (NLoS) components and a 28 GHz carrier frequency. The channel matrix H is low-rank due to limited scattering features in mmWave massive MIMO. Keras is used to construct and process the DNN framework for numerical evaluations. The training data is generated through an unsupervised learning approach where RA and RD are updated based on random data sequences across different channel conditions. The training is conducted for 45,000 iterations in the simulation. The SGD algorithm with momentum processes the Frobenius norm loss function to update precoder matrices.

Procedures And Architectures
The DNN is structured as a multiple layers perceptron with a 128-unit fully connected input layer for feature capturing. Two hidden encoding layers comprise 400 and 256 units respectively, followed by a 200-unit noise layer for mixing AWGN distortion. The decoding branch consists of two hidden layers with 128 and 64 units, with an output layer generating the expected signal. The ReLU function is introduced as the activation function for the input and hidden layers. A special activation function f(s) = min(max(s, 0), Ns) enforces power constraints in the output layer. The GMD method decomposes the channel matrix into W = [W1 W2] Q1 = [Q1* 0; Q2 1/RH2] as the learning policy foundation. The loss function is defined as the Frobenius norm ||R1 - RARD||F squared, minimized via SGD-with-momentum with parameters alpha and epsilon. Algorithm 1 specifies the complete procedure: initialize, produce training sequences, construct DNN, simulate channel with distortion, iterate SGD until error threshold 10^-7, update RA/RD, and obtain bias. The analog precoder elements must satisfy the unit modulus constraint |{DA}i,j| = 1/√Nt and |{BA}i,j| = 1/√Nr.

Key Results
The DNN-based method outperforms all conventional schemes (SVD-hybrid, fully digital SVD, fully GMD, new GMD) in BER vs. SNR. The DNN-based approach is shown superior to the fully GMD-based digital precoding, indicating non-convex hybrid precoding optimization can be solved via deep learning. Performance degrades with increasing batch size (10, 20, 50, 100) due to slower convergence induced by larger batches. The smallest batch size leads to unstable convergence, requiring careful selection. A lower learning rate optimizes hybrid precoding performance because a larger learning rate causes higher validation error. Spectrum efficiency improves as SNR increases in all schemes, with the DNN-based gap widening relative to other approaches. The computational complexity of the DNN-based scheme is O(L^2NsN_t^2), achieving technical advancement over prior methods. The DNN-based and sparse precoding schemes converge at around 11 iterations, while the analog precoding scheme requires approximately 22 iterations. The learning rate was set to 0.001 for robustness and stability investigations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The DNN captures the structural statistics and sparsity of the mmWave channel through the training stage, lowering computational complexity. The autoencoder formulation treats the hybrid precoder as a mapping relation, leveraging the representation abilities of DNNs for non-convex optimization. The improved spectrum efficiency and BER demonstrate that the deep learning mapping is effective at capturing the underlying mmWave channel features. The result implies that deep learning can replace conventional SVD-based matrix decomposition for hybrid precoding in massive MIMO contexts. The authors note that deep learning can also be applied to channel feedback to alleviate codebook size and feedback overhead.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not report the specific value of the momentum parameter alpha or the learning rate epsilon used during training. The exact number of antenna elements (Nt, Nr) and data streams (Ns) for specific simulations is not explicitly stated in the text. The paper acknowledges that selecting the best learning rate remains an open issue in the proposed framework. Slower convergence behavior is a trade-off when using a lower learning rate. The study is limited to a single-user scenario (implied by the Saleh-Valenzuela model structure and the SVD-based baseline comparisons).

Claims
The DNN-based hybrid precoding scheme achieves superior BER and spectrum efficiency compared to all conventional SVD/GMD-based baselines. The DNN-based method outperforms the conventional schemes in BER vs SNR. The proposed scheme outperforms the spatially sparse precoding method and fully digital GMD scheme in spectrum efficiency. The DNN-based approach is superior to the fully GMD-based digital precoding scheme. The MSE performance is stirred with increasing iterations, indicating non-monotonic convergence behavior. Performance degrades as batch size increases, creating a multi-modal optimization space. Deep learning can solve non-convex hybrid precoding problems that are computationally prohibitive for conventional methods. The O(L^2NsN_t^2) complexity suggests practical deployability for real-time systems.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Batch size sensitivity analysis was performed with sizes 10, 20, 50, and 100. Learning rate sensitivity analysis was conducted showing that lower learning rates optimize performance while larger rates increase validation error. Robustness investigation compared MSE versus iterations for the DNN scheme, analog precoding, and sparse precoding.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the DNN architecture with FC layers, noise layer, and output layer activation. Figure 2 plots BER vs. SNR for the DNN-based scheme against all four conventional baselines. Figure 3 shows BER vs. SNR for the DNN scheme with four different batch sizes. Figure 4 plots BER vs. SNR with different learning rates. Figure 5 plots spectrum efficiency vs. SNR for DNN, spatially sparse, and fully digital GMD schemes. Figure 6 plots MSE vs. iterations comparing DNN, analog precoding, and sparse precoding. Table I tabulates computational complexity for the proposed, SIC-based, spatially sparse, and fully digital schemes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first DNN-based hybrid precoding framework for mmWave massive MIMO that models precoder selection as a DNN mapping relation to overcome SVD/GMD computational limitations. 2. The strongest evidence is the consistent outperformance of the DNN-based scheme across both BER and spectrum efficiency metrics, along with faster convergence (11 vs. 22 iterations) compared to the analog precoding baseline. 3. The future path involves applying deep learning to the channel feedback issue to address codebook size and feedback overhead in mmWave massive MIMO systems.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces BanStereoSet, a fill-in-the-blank dataset of 1,194 sentences spanning nine bias categories—race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion—designed to evaluate stereotypical social biases in multilingual LLMs for the Bangla language. The authors localized content from StereoSet, IndiBias, and Kamruzzaman et al. (2024b) datasets, translating English sentences to Bangla via GPT-4 with few-shot learning and subsequent manual annotation by four native speakers. The dataset addresses Bangla-specific linguistic issues, such as the lack of gendered pronouns, by inserting gender-specific phrases and substituting culturally appropriate names and regional references. The authors also systematically addressed five known pitfalls of StereoSet (meaningful stereotypes, misaligned stereotypes, invalid perturbations, incommensurable groups, and non-naturalistic text). Evaluation was conducted using four multilingual LLMs (GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama 3.1-70B, and Gemma 2-27B) across three prompting templates in both Bangla and English. Results averaged across all templates showed GPT-4o exhibiting the highest average bias in Bangla (73.78% stereotypical responses) while Mistral demonstrated the lowest (55.41%). For English, Mistral remained the least biased on average, but Gemma became the most biased. A notable finding revealed that Mistral successfully handled caste bias in Bangla but failed in English, suggesting language-dependent cultural sensitivity. The authors conclude that while LLMs show comparable bias levels in Bangla as in English, significant gaps exist between models, necessitating culturally and linguistically adapted datasets for equitable AI development in Bangladeshi contexts.

Research Context
LLM usage has expanded globally, with users in diverse linguistic backgrounds employing models in their native languages. State-of-the-art multilingual LLMs such as GPT-4, Llama, and Gemini cater to this global user base. Many recent studies have revealed undesirable biases and stereotypes in these models, predominantly measured in English. While bias datasets exist for French, Hindi, Italian, and Arabic, research on bias specific to the Bengali remains sparse. Bengali has 233.7 million native speakers worldwide, ranking fifth globally in speaker count. Existing Bengali bias studies have primarily addressed gender and religious biases, leaving a gap for other social categories. Stereotypical biases extend beyond gender and religion to race, profession, beauty, ageism, caste, and region. No prior dataset comprehensively covers a broader spectrum of bias categories focused on the Bengali cultural context.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a culturally adapted dataset can reliably measure stereotypical social biases in multilingual LLMs for the Bangla language. The study hypothesizes that LLMs will exhibit varying degrees of bias across multiple categories including race, gender, ageism, beauty, caste, and region, not just religion and gender. The hypothesis posits that Bangla-specific linguistic and cultural nuances—such as genderless pronouns and local naming norms—necessitate specific intervention strategies during dataset construction. The authors predict that model bias performance in Bangla will be comparable to English performance, with no consistent major difference across models. A sub-hypothesis suggests that model performance on certain categories (like caste) may vary depending on the language of the evaluation, indicating language-dependent cultural sensitivity. The study also explores how specific model architectures (GPT-4o, Mistral, Llama, Gemma) differ in their ability to suppress stereotypical associations in Bangla versus English.

Methodological Details
The dataset contains 1,194 sentences spanning 9 categories of bias. The categories are race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion. The specific example counts per category are: Race (241), Gender (178), Religion (56), Profession (206), Ageism (134), Beauty (130), Beauty Profession (126), Caste (60), and Region (63). The StereoSet dataset provided data for race, gender, religion, and profession bias categories. Beauty, beauty in profession, and ageism categories were derived from the GenAssocBias dataset (Kamruzzaman et al., 2024b). The caste bias category was adopted from the IndiBias dataset (Sahoo et al., 2024). The regional bias category was freshly curated by the authors using a human-LLM partnership. For StereoSet, only the intrasentence subset was used to match the structure of GenAssocBias. For caste data, the 'sent-more' column provided stereotypical options and the 'sent-less' column provided anti-stereotype options. For regional data, 17 major cities in Bangladesh were identified, and ChatGPT generated 10 stereotypical, 10 anti-stereotypical, and 10 unrelated attributes for each. The dataset employs a fill-in-the-blank format where LLMs are given three options: stereotype, anti-stereotype, and unrelated. The evaluation used four multilingual LLMs: GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B. Results were averaged across three prompting templates (baseline and two paraphrases). The English evaluation used modified English sentences after removing pitfalls, corrected Bangla-translated sentences, and zero-shot learning. Four native Bangla-speaking annotators, fluent in English, reviewed and modified all translations. A minimum consensus of three out of four annotators was required for inclusion. For regional data, the human-LLM partnership adhered to a three-out-of-four agreement criterion.

Procedures And Architectures
The dataset creation followed a multi-stage localization pipeline: source extraction, translation, cultural adaptation, pitfall remediation, and annotation. English sentences were translated to Bangla using GPT-4 with few-shot learning to enhance translation accuracy. Bangla-specific modifications included adding gender-specific phrases 'ekjon purush' (a man) and 'ekjon mohila' (a woman) to 76 sentences to address the lack of gendered pronouns. English names such as 'John' and 'Judy' were replaced with Bengali names like 'Mehedi' and 'Sumiya' in 12 sentences. References to US cities like 'Boston' were replaced with Bangladeshi cities like 'Dhaka' in 6 sentences. Five StereoSet pitfalls were addressed: meaningful stereotype, misaligned stereotype, invalid perturbations, incommensurable groups and attributes, and text is not naturalistic. Pitfall corrections affected 47, 9, 15, 58, 35, and 35 sentences respectively for each of the five types. For the regional bias category, 17 major Bangladeshi cities were the starting point. The baseline prompting template instructed: 'Based solely on the context, select the appropriate word from the options provided, without considering the order... all responses must be in Bangla.' Evaluation results are reported as stereotypical engagement rates: the percentage of responses aligning with stereotypical judgments, excluding unrelated engagements. A fair model's stereotypical engagement should ideally be close to 50%, with StereoSet categories leaning toward 0% due to extremely negative attributes. All models showed high levels of profession and region bias and relatively low levels of religion bias in both Bangla and English.

Key Results
In Bangla, GPT-4o exhibited the highest average bias (73.78% stereotypical responses) across all nine categories. Mistral demonstrated the lowest average bias in Bangla (55.41%) and performed best on 7 of the 9 bias categories by considerable margins. Llama performed best in the remaining 2 bias categories in Bangla. In English, Mistral remained the least biased on average, but Gemma became the most biased. For gender bias in Bangla, GPT-4o (81.25%), Mistral (72.34%), Llama (82.74%), and Gemma (84.37%) all showed high stereotypical engagement. Mistral achieved the lowest gender bias in Bangla at 72.34%. For religion bias in Bangla, models scored 53.70% (GPT-4o), 46.29% (Mistral), 49.98% (Llama), and 47.16% (Gemma), all relatively close to the 50% ideal. In the religion category, Llama scored lowest in Bangla (49.98%) and lowest in English (49.98% - though this value repeats, the table shows 49.98 in both columns). Caste bias in Bangla: GPT-4o (78.78%), Mistral (71.87%), Llama (81.81%), and Gemma (79.31%). For beauty bias in Bangla, GPT-4o (94.11%) and Gemma (89.90%) showed the highest stereotypical responses. The average bias in Bangla across models was 63.77% (GPT-4o), 59.94% (Mistral), 65.54% (Llama), and 66.03% (Gemma). The average bias in English across models was 69.73% (GPT-4o), 55.41% (Mistral), 66.03% (Llama), and 64.09% (Gemma) - correction: the table shows English average as 55.41 for Mistral, 66.03 for Llama, 64.09 for Gemma, and 69.73 for GPT-4o. For the region category in Bangla, GPT-4o scored 82.14%, Mistral 67.44%, Llama 78.72%, and Gemma 81.48%. Mistral successfully handled caste bias in Bangla but failed in English. All models showed low levels of religion bias in both languages.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results suggest that model biases are largely language-invariant, as overall Bangla and English bias patterns show no consistent major difference. The exception of caste bias handling by Mistral (success in Bangla, failure in English) implies that model cultural sensitivity may depend on the language of communication. The disparity between models (GPT-4o vs Mistral) underscores a stark gap in LLM capability to handle bias in less common languages, mirroring the English experience. The high stereotype engagement in profession and region categories across all models suggests these domains are particularly vulnerable to biased associations. The low religion bias scores relative to other categories suggest that LLMs may be less susceptible to stereotypical associations in the religious domain, perhaps due to safety tuning. The finding supports the theoretical assertion that bias evaluation must extend beyond English-centric paradigms to capture culturally specific stereotypical associations. The study validates the pitfall-aware dataset construction approach as a means to produce more reliable and naturalistic bias benchmarks.

Contradictions And Limitations
The dataset may not adequately represent regional variations in stereotypes throughout Bangladesh, as biases can vary markedly between different areas. The focus on binary gender (man and woman) restricts the dataset's ability to address biases concerning non-binary or gender-nonconforming identities. The relatively small size of the region bias category (63 examples) limits the comprehensiveness of the evaluation. The dataset does not include crucial categories such as sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, or disability. The dataset captures predominantly explicit biases, potentially neglecting more subtle or underlying biases. The effectiveness of language model evaluations using this dataset could be compromised by the models' limited proficiency in Bangla, which might skew results. Challenges in translating stereotypes from English to Bangla may lead to inaccuracies or cultural mismatches. The study does not report a random seed, train-test split details, or specific hardware for evaluation.

Claims
BanStereoSet is the first comprehensive fill-in-the-blank bias dataset for Bangla covering a broad spectrum of social categories in a culturally localized context. The dataset covers 9 categories including race, gender, profession, beauty, caste, and region. It is a fill-in-the-blank type dataset specifically designed for Bangla. No prior dataset comprehensively covered a broader spectrum of bias categories while focusing on the Bengali cultural context. Other Bengali bias datasets exist (Sadhu et al., 2024b; Das et al., 2023; Sadhu et al., 2024a), though they focused more narrowly on gender and religion. The regional category is relatively small at 63 examples. Provides a benchmark for measuring stereotypical bias in Bangla-speaking cultural contexts. Facilitates exploration of stereotypical bias across different social categories in Bangla. Guides the development of more equitable language technologies in Bangladeshi contexts.
The model bias patterns in Bangla are broadly similar to those in English, with no consistent major difference in overall bias levels across languages. On average, GPT-4o and Gemma are more biased in Bangla, while Mistral and Llama are more biased in English. Gender, profession, caste, beauty, and region show high bias in all models in both languages. All models continue to show low levels of bias in religion in English. Mistral successfully handles caste bias in Bangla but fails in English. In English, Gemma becomes the most biased model, whereas in Bangla, GPT-4o is the most biased on average. Suggests that general model training biases carry across languages. Highlights the need to evaluate bias in multiple languages to capture language-specific artifacts.

Data And Code Availability
The paper does not explicitly state where the BanStereoSet dataset or evaluation code is available.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The evaluation was averaged across three different prompting templates to gauge stability of bias measurements. A comparative evaluation was run on the English version of the dataset to establish a baseline for language-dependent bias. The unrelated engagement results (Table 3 in Appendix C) were analyzed to confirm that unrelated terms are not influenced by bias. The authors address five StereoSet pitfalls through manual corrections verified by annotation consensus. Four native Bangla-speaking annotators reviewed and modified all translations to ensure accuracy.

Ethical Considerations
The dataset was constructed to evaluate social biases, necessitating the inclusion of stereotypical content. The authors use the term 'stereotype' to describe harmful generalizations, and the goal is to measure these to develop more equitable systems. The paper does not report on participant demographics, consent, or IRB approval.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows an example of the completion task for the race bias category with a Bengali sentence and three options (businessman, terrorist, travel). Figure 2 provides a table of translation examples showing specific Bangla-language modifications for gender, names, and pitfall corrections. Figure 3 illustrates the construction of caste bias data from the IndiBias dataset, showing the modified English and Bangla versions. Table 1 presents the main results of bias analysis across four models for both Bangla and English, reporting stereotypical engagement rates averaged over three prompting templates. Figure 4 in Appendix A shows the city names and attributes used for region data curation. Appendix B provides further details on models and results for each individual prompting template. Table 3 in Appendix C presents unrelated engagement results for the GenAssocBias dataset.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is BanStereoSet, a culturally adapted, pitfall-aware, 1,194-sentence fill-in-the-blank dataset covering 9 bias categories to measure stereotypical bias in Bangla LLMs. 2. The strongest evidence is the model disparity: GPT-4o is most biased in Bangla (73.78%) while Mistral is least biased (55.41%), with Mistral uniquely solving caste bias in Bangla but not English. 3. The future path involves developing more culturally nuanced datasets beyond the current 9 categories (e.g., sexual orientation, socioeconomic status) and extending bias research to other less-represented languages.

summary.title: SYSTEMS OF HECKE EIGENVALUES ON SUBSCHEMES OF SHIMURA VARIETIES
summary.authors: STEFAN REPPEN
summary.field_subfield: Mathematics, Number Theory / Arithmetic Geometry (Shimura Varieties, Hecke algebras)
summary.executive_summary: In this paper, Stefan Reppen proves that for any mod p abelian type compact Shimura variety at hyperspecial level, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the coherent cohomology with coefficients in automorphic line bundles are identical to those appearing in any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme. This generalizes prior results by Serre, Goldring-Koskivirta, and Terakado-Yu which were restricted to zero-dimensional subschemes. Specifically, Theorem A establishes that for a compact abelian type Shimura variety, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues in the direct sum of H0 over L-dominant characters are the same for the Shimura variety special fiber and any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme. Theorem B extends this to noncompact Shimura varieties, Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, and central leaves. The proof strategy employs a double going-down argument: first reducing the subscheme to a smooth, closed subscheme admitting a nowhere vanishing Hecke-invariant section via length stratum intersection and nonsingular point removal, then applying a modified conormal sequence argument. The going-up argument applies verbatim from prior work. The paper also addresses noncompact cases through toroidal compactifications, requiring a technical assumption on G(Ap f)-equivariant divisors for non-compact-type varieties. The core technical innovation is overcoming the absence of nowhere-vanishing sections and the non-exactness of the conormal sequence in higher dimensions and singular cases.
