Executive Summary
In this paper, Stefan Reppen proves that for any mod p abelian type compact Shimura variety at hyperspecial level, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the coherent cohomology with coefficients in automorphic line bundles are identical to those appearing in any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme. This generalizes prior results by Serre, Goldring-Koskivirta, and Terakado-Yu which were restricted to zero-dimensional subschemes. Specifically, Theorem A establishes that for a compact abelian type Shimura variety, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues in the direct sum of H0 over L-dominant characters are the same for the Shimura variety special fiber and any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme. Theorem B extends this to noncompact Shimura varieties, Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, and central leaves. The proof strategy employs a double going-down argument: first reducing the subscheme to a smooth, closed subscheme admitting a nowhere vanishing Hecke-invariant section via length stratum intersection and nonsingular point removal, then applying a modified conormal sequence argument. The going-up argument applies verbatim from prior work. The paper also addresses noncompact cases through toroidal compactifications, requiring a technical assumption on G(Ap f)-equivariant divisors for non-compact-type varieties. The core technical innovation is overcoming the absence of nowhere-vanishing sections and the non-exactness of the conormal sequence in higher dimensions and singular cases.

Research Context
The mod p fiber of an abelian type Shimura variety at good reduction carries an action of the prime-to-p Hecke algebra. Several well-studied subschemes, including Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, Newton strata, and central leaves, are invariant under this action. Serre showed that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the cohomology of a mod p modular curve are the same as those appearing in the cohomology of the supersingular locus. Goldring-Koskivirta generalized this to Hodge-type Shimura varieties at good reduction, showing the eigenvalues coincide with the unique zero-dimensional Ekedahl-Oort stratum. Terakado-Yu extended this to any central leaf contained in the basic Newton stratum, using the existence of a nowhere vanishing Hecke-invariant section on zero-dimensional subschemes. The prior works were restricted to smooth subschemes of dimension 0. Higher dimensional and possibly singular subschemes remain unaddressed in the previous literature.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can the systems of Hecke eigenvalues in coherent cohomology of automorphic bundles on a compact abelian type Shimura variety be related to those on arbitrary Hecke-equivariant closed subschemes? The hypothesis is that for any (prime-to-p) Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme, the sets of Hecke eigenvalues are identical. The paper further hypothesizes that analogous results hold for noncompact Shimura varieties and nonclosed subschemes like Ekedahl-Oort and length strata. The predicted outcome is that a generalized going-down argument, constructing a smooth closed subscheme with a nowhere-vanishing section, will resolve the obstacles posed by higher dimensions and singularities. The expected method is to intersect the subscheme with the smallest length stratum it meets and successively remove nonsingular points to isolate a suitable subscheme.

Methodological Details
The paper assumes (G, X) is a Shimura datum of abelian type, with G = Gc (the cuspidal quotient). A prime p not equal to 2 is fixed over which G is unramified. K is a sufficiently small open compact subgroup of G(Ap f) of the form KpKp, where Kp is a hyperspecial subgroup. SK denotes the special fiber of the Kisin-Vasiu integral canonical model of the Shimura variety. The transition maps between special fibers for different hyperspecial subgroups are finite étale. The stack of G-zips G-Zipµ is a smooth algebraic κ-stack of dimension 0 isomorphic to a quotient stack [E\G]. For Hodge-type, there exists a smooth surjective morphism ζK from SK to G-Zipµ. An automorphic vector bundle is defined as isomorphic to ζ∗KV(r) for some representation r: P → GL(V). The Hodge line bundle ω is defined as det ΩSK and is associated with the L-representation (Lie(G)/Lie(P))∨. The Ekedahl-Oort stratification is indexed by the Weyl group subset IW and the closure relation is given by partial ordering. Length strata are defined by the length function l: W → N on IW. Hasse invariants Haw of H0([E\Gw], ωr) whose nonvanishing locus is exactly [E\Gw] are used for the going-up argument. Central leaves C(x) are defined via Dieudonné module isomorphisms and are locally closed in SK(κ). The Hecke action is defined via the restricted tensor product of unramified Hecke algebras at places of ramification and p. A system of Hecke eigenvalues appears in a module if there is an eigenvector for the action of H.

Procedures And Architectures
The proof of Theorem A proceeds by decomposing SK into length strata and inductively defining a sequence of closed subschemes. Let i0 be the minimum index such that YK intersects SK,i0. Z(0)K is defined as (YK ∩SK,i0)red and Z(i)K is defined as (Z(i-1)K \ Z(i-1),sm)red for i ≥ 1. Because YK is Noetherian, the sequence Z(i)K terminates at a minimal index m such that Z(m)K is smooth. Lemma 2.4.5 ensures that Z(i)K form a G(Ap f)-equivariant system of closed subschemes. The going-down argument relates eigenvalues on SK to ZK using a conormal-like argument with the Hasse invariant. The going-up argument applies the arguments of Goldring-Koskivirta verbatim. For the nonclosed case, the argument uses the closure of YK in SΣK and relates the nonvanishing locus of a Hecke-equivariant section. In the noncompact case, the toroidal compactification SΣK and the boundary divisor D are used. For non-compact-type varieties, an extra assumption is made that there exists a G(Ap f)-equivariant divisor D′ such that ωk(−D′) is ample for large k.

Key Results
Theorem A: For a compact abelian type Shimura variety, M(YK) ↭H M(SK) for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme YK. The systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in H0(SK, V(η)) and H0(YK, V(η)) are identical. Theorem B: For nonclosed subschemes YK, M(SK) ⇝H M(YK) always holds. If YK is an Ekedahl-Oort stratum or a length stratum, M(YK) ↭H M(SK) holds. If SK is proper and CK is a central leaf closed in the Ekedahl-Oort stratum containing it, M(SK) ↭H M(CK). If YK meets the basic locus, then M(SK) ↭H M(YK) for locally closed YK. If YK = ζ∗KY for a closed substack Y of G-Zipµ, then M(YK) ↭H M(SK). If M(YK) ↭H M(SK) and there is a Hecke-equivariant section, then M(YK) ↭H M(YK,h). Corollary 3.2.7: For any two G(Ap f)-equivariant systems of closed subschemes, the Hecke eigenvalues appear in both. The conormal sequence IK/I2 → ΩSK|ZK → ΩZK → 0 is G(Ap f)-equivariant and its associated map is injective on Symn.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The result demonstrates that the Hecke eigenvalues of automorphic line bundles are determined by the geometric structure of the Shimura variety's special fiber, regardless of the subscheme. The method generalizes Serre's and Goldring-Koskivirta's results from zero-dimensional strata to arbitrary dimensions and singular schemes. The key mechanism is the construction of a smooth closed subscheme ZK with a nowhere-vanishing Hasse invariant from any Hecke-equivariant subscheme. The Hasse invariant provides the substitute for the nowhere-vanishing section that was available only in the zero-dimensional case. The use of the conormal exact sequence with the Hasse invariant extends the 'going-down' argument beyond the smooth dimension 0 restriction. The result implies that Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, and central leaves capture the full range of Hecke eigenvalues for any abelian type Shimura variety.

Contradictions And Limitations
The theory of toroidal compactifications for abelian type Shimura varieties has not yet been fully developed, limiting the noncompact treatment. The noncompact results require an additional assumption on the existence of a G(Ap f)-equivariant divisor D′ making ωk(−D′) ample. The assumption G = Gc is a technical requirement to obtain a smooth surjective morphism to G-Zipµ, though it might be removable. The going-down argument does not require Hasse invariants, but the going-up argument does, creating a technical asymmetry in the proof. The conormal sequence is neither exact nor consists of locally free sheaves in the singular case, necessitating the extra going-down step. The proof for noncompact varieties relies on the assumption that if (G, X) is not compact-type, it is of Hodge type.

Claims
The systems of Hecke eigenvalues in coherent cohomology with automorphic line bundle coefficients of a compact abelian type Shimura variety are the same as those in any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme. The proof constructs a smooth closed subscheme ZK of YK with a nowhere-vanishing Hasse-invariant section. Lemma 3.2.1 shows that eigenvalues in Symn(ΩSK|YK)⊗V(η) appear in some V(ηi). Lemma 3.2.2 establishes M(YK) ⇝H M(ZK) given an injective Hasse-invariant section. Lemma 3.2.4 establishes M(ZK) ⇝H M(YK) by Serre vanishing and Hasse invariant multiplication. The inductive construction ensures ZK is smooth, closed, and equivariant. The nonclosed case only yields M(SK) ⇝H M(YK), not equality, unless YK is also closed. The noncompact case requires the G(Ap f)-equivariant ample divisor assumption for non-compact-type varieties. This unifies the spectral data of all major subschemes (Ekedahl-Oort, length, Newton, central leaves) with the full Shimura variety. The result holds for arbitrary dimensions, overcoming the zero-dimensional restriction of prior work.
Ekedahl-Oort strata and length strata capture all Hecke eigenvalues of the Shimura variety special fiber. Theorem B applies directly to Ekedahl-Oort and length strata because they are closed and Hecke-equivariant. Hasse invariants exist for both EO and length strata, providing the necessary sections. Corollary 3.3.3 explicitly states the equality of eigenvalue systems for these strata. Central leaves are only guaranteed to satisfy the equality if they are closed in the Ekedahl-Oort stratum containing them. This provides a practical way to study all Hecke eigenvalues via computable finite-dimensional strata.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The assumption G = Gc is noted as technical; the author mentions that for Hodge type, G = Gc always holds. The going-up argument is applied verbatim from prior work, meaning its validity is inherited rather than re-verified in this paper. Lemma 2.4.6 handles the conormal sequence equivariance, which is the core algebraic infrastructure for the proof.

Key Figures Tables

Gj] =  igcup_{i≤j} [E
Gi]. Equation (3.2.3) is the central surjection H0(ZK, Symn(I/I2)⊗V(η)⊗ωar) → H0(ZK, J n/J n+1 ⊗V(η)⊗ωar).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the proof that systems of Hecke eigenvalues in automorphic line bundle cohomology of a compact abelian type Shimura variety are identical to those in any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme, extending prior zero-dimensional results to arbitrary dimensions. 2. The strongest evidence is the double going-down/going-up argument: reducing to a smooth closed subscheme with a nowhere-vanishing Hasse invariant, then applying a modified conormal sequence argument for the going-down step and the original Goldring-Koskivirta argument verbatim for going-up. 3. The future path involves addressing noncompact varieties (requiring additional technical assumptions), nonclosed subschemes, and generalizing the method to other types of Shimura varieties beyond abelian type.

summary.title: Anomalous Hall effect from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling
summary.authors: Longju Yu, Hong Jian Zhao, Yurong Yang, Laurent Bellaiche, and Yanming Ma
summary.field_subfield: Condensed Matter Physics / Spintronics / Magnetoelectrics
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical study combining symmetry analysis and first-principles calculations
summary.executive_summary: The paper establishes a phenomenological theory for spontaneous and electric-field driven anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in crystalline magnets using group-theoretical symmetry analysis. The authors demonstrate that both type-I and type-III magnetic point groups (90 in total) host AHE components driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields via linear or nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. A key finding is that such electric-field driven Hall conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter (+L to -L), providing a direct probe of magnetic state. The theory predicts that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling—previously largely unexplored for AHE—can generate significant Hall conductivities. The authors identify Cr2O3 and CoF2 as representative candidate materials, with Cr2O3 exhibiting conductivities > 100 S/cm under 4 MV/cm electric fields via first-order response, and CoF2 yielding conductivities > 200 S/cm via second-order response. The work highlights nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling as a novel avenue for probing magnetic orders in spintronics, offering complementary means to the conventional detection of magnetization through linear AHE or other methods.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The paper establishes a phenomenological theory for spontaneous and electric-field driven anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in crystalline magnets using group-theoretical symmetry analysis. The authors demonstrate that both type-I and type-III magnetic point groups (90 in total) host AHE components driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields via linear or nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. A key finding is that such electric-field driven Hall conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic order parameter (+L to -L), providing a direct probe of magnetic state. The theory predicts that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling—previously largely unexplored for AHE—can generate significant Hall conductivities. The authors identify Cr2O3 and CoF2 as representative candidate materials, with Cr2O3 exhibiting conductivities > 100 S/cm under 4 MV/cm electric fields via first-order response, and CoF2 yielding conductivities > 200 S/cm via second-order response. The work highlights nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling as a novel avenue for probing magnetic orders in spintronics, offering complementary means to the conventional detection of magnetization through linear AHE or other methods.

Research Context
While AHE spontaneously occurs in ferromagnets or antiferromagnets with magnetization, electric-field induced AHE via linear magnetoelectric coupling has been recently reported, but nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling remains largely unexplored. The AHE is a topology-related transport phenomenon of interest in spintronics for efficient probing of magnetic orders, such as data readout in memory devices. The prior literature (Refs. 1-21) establishes AHE in ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic materials with specific magnetic configurations or tiny magnetization. Recent studies demonstrate gate voltage inducing AHE via linear magnetoelectric coupling, including layer and electric Hall effects. The group-theoretical approach for determining magnetization existence in crystalline materials is established by prior work on magnetic point groups.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether AHE can be induced by electric fields via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling and which magnetic point groups support such effects. The hypothesis is that symmetry analysis can establish the phenomenological theory for both spontaneous and electric-field driven AHE in crystalline materials. The authors predict that both type-I and type-III magnetic point groups exhibit spontaneous AHE or electric-field induced AHE from linear or nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. The prediction is that nonlinear magnetoelectric AHE is accommodated by a wide spectrum of MPGs, where Hall conductivity is achieved by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields. The hypothesis includes that electric-field driven anomalous Hall conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic orders. The authors further hypothesize that specific magnetic materials, namely Cr2O3 and CoF2, are representative candidates hosting the predicted effect.

Methodological Details
The study uses a group-theoretical symmetry analysis to establish the phenomenological theory for AHE in crystalline materials. The symmetry analysis covers the entire 122 magnetic point groups, excluding the 32 type-II MPGs that exhibit time-reversal symmetry forbidding magnetization. The authors identify 90 type-I and type-III magnetic point groups that support spontaneous or electric-field driven AHE. Candidate materials are selected from the MAGNDATA database, which categorizes materials by magnetic point group. Cr2O3 and CoF2 are chosen because they have no more than 10 ions per primitive cell, making computational costs affordable. Cr2O3 has a Néel temperature of 307 K and belongs to the ¯3′m′ magnetic point group. CoF2 has a Néel temperature of 39 K and belongs to the 4′/mm′m MPG of the P4′/mmm′ magnetic space group. First-principles calculations are performed to verify the phenomenological theory in the two candidate materials.

Procedures And Architectures
The anomalous Hall conductivity is expressed via the Berry curvature integral in the intrinsic mechanism, where σαβ = ∫ (2π)⁻³ f(εnk)Ωγ dk. The Hall vector M ≡ (σzy, σxz, σyx) is defined such that AHE is described by J = M × E, analogous to magnetization behavior. Time-reversal symmetry and Onsager reciprocity require σαβ(+L) = −σαβ(−L), indicating reversal of AHE with magnetic order. The effective magnetic field Bαeff is expanded in powers of electric field: Bαeff = λα + Σ λαβEβ + Σ λαβγEβEγ + Σ λαβγδEβEγEδ. The coefficients λα, λαβ, λαβγ, and λαβγδ characterize spontaneous, first-order, second-order, and third-order magnetoelectric couplings. For Cr2O3, the effective fields are Bxeff = λxxEx and Byeff = λxxEy, where the shared λxx implies σzy and σxz are symmetrically related. For CoF2, the effective fields are Bxeff = λxxzExEz, Byeff = −λxxzEyEz, and Bzeff = λzxx(E²x − E²y). First-principles calculations use a chemical potential defined relative to the Fermi level to explore conductivity as a function of doping.

Key Results
The symmetry analysis identifies 90 type-I and type-III magnetic point groups that support spontaneous or electric-field driven AHE components. In Cr2O3 (+L order), σzy is driven by Ex, σxz by Ey, and σyx by Ez or E²y, with conductivities exceeding 100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm. The maximum value of σyx in Cr2O3 driven by Ey = 4 MV/cm via third-order response is less than 20 S/cm. Switching Cr2O3 from +L to −L reverses the sign of the electric-field induced Hall conductivities, verified by first-principles. In CoF2, the Hall conductivities respond via second-order magnetoelectric coupling: σyx by E²x or E²y, σzy by ExEz, and σxz by EyEz. At Ex = Ez = 2√2 MV/cm and Ey = Ez = 2√2 MV/cm (total 4 MV/cm), CoF2 exhibits σzy and σxz reaching 10 S/cm. An electric field of Ex = 4 MV/cm or Ey = 4 MV/cm in CoF2 can yield σyx larger than 200 S/cm. Reversing the magnetic order parameter in CoF2 reverses the anomalous Hall conductivities, confirming the prediction. Ten magnetic point groups exhibit quenching of bi-axial or tri-axial Hall conductivities under specific field directions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reversible nature of electric-field driven AHE by magnetic order reversal provides a direct method to probe magnetic state in magnets. Nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling, previously unexplored for AHE, is established as a key mechanism for creating exotic transport phenomena. The correspondence between (σzy, σxz, σyx) and (Mx, My, Mz) establishes the Hall vector M as a magnetization-like vector under symmetry. The similarity between Cr2O3 σzy and σxz components stems from the shared λxx coefficient, reflecting underlying symmetry constraints. The work offers alternative avenues for the probe of magnetic orders, complementing conventional linear magnetoelectric coupling methods.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper omits type-II MPGs from the discussion because they possess time-reversal symmetry that forbids electric-field induced magnetization, potentially limiting generality. The quenching behavior in 10 MPGs is noted as a limitation where Hall conductivity vanishes for specific field directions, which could impede device realization. First-principles results for CoF2 show lower conductivities (10 S/cm) compared to Cr2O3 (>100 S/cm) for bi-axial responses, suggesting material-specific variation in coupling strengths. The quenching occurs in the regime of fourth-order magnetoelectric coupling, which may be practically difficult to access or engineer. The paper is a theoretical work combined with first-principles validation; no experimental verification of the predicted Hall conductivities is reported.

Claims
Type-I and type-III magnetic point groups host AHE driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. Symmetry analysis identified 90 type-I and type-III MPGs supporting AHE. The effective magnetic field expansion explicitly shows terms up to third order (and fourth order in special cases). Table I codifies the Hall conductivity components for all 90 MPGs by field type. Type-II MPGs do not support this effect, limiting applicability to specific magnetic structures. Quenching occurs in 10 MPGs for specific field directions, meaning the effect is not universal across all field orientations. This prediction opens new search avenues for magnetoelectric materials. Device designs could utilize bi-axial or tri-axial fields to access multiple Hall components.
Cr2O3 and CoF2 are representative materials exhibiting electric-field induced AHE via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. Cr2O3 yields σzy, σxz > 100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm. CoF2 yields σyx > 200 S/cm at 4 MV/cm. Both materials show Hall conductivity reversal upon magnetic order parameter switching. Effective fields Bxeff and Byeff for both materials match symmetry predictions. CoF2's bi-axial responses (10 S/cm) are an order of magnitude lower than Cr2O3's first-order responses (>100 S/cm). The first-principles results are for a single configuration (+L), not exploring full temperature/field ranges. Experimental realization of the AHE in these materials would confirm the theory and enable spintronic applications. The material-specific coupling strengths suggest that further screening of MPGs is necessary for device identification.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The quenching behavior analysis identifies 10 MPGs where Hall conductivity vanishes for specific field directions. The 4mm.1 MPG case demonstrates that when |Ex| = |Ey|, the fourth-order σyx component is quenched. The similarity between Cr2O3 Figs. 2(a) and (b) is attributed to the shared λxx coefficient, serving as a self-consistency check. The resemblance between CoF2 Figs. 2(e) and (f) is similarly attributed to the effective field structure.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the crystal and magnetic structures for Cr2O3 and CoF2 with magnetic moments as red arrows. Figure 2 panels (a)-(d) depict Cr2O3 anomalous Hall conductivities as a function of chemical potential for Ex, Ey, Ey, and Ez. Figure 2 panels (e)-(h) show CoF2 Hall conductivities driven by [Ex, Ez], [Ey, Ez], Ex, and Ey. Table I lists all 90 type-I and type-III MPGs with color-coded spontaneous, uni-axial, bi-axial, and tri-axial driven AHE components. Supplementary Table 9 provides the effective magnetic field expressions for the 90 MPGs. Supplementary Table 10 gives the specific effective magnetic fields for the ¯6m2.1 MPG. Supplementary Table 12 summarizes the quenching of bi-axial and tri-axial Hall conductivities in 10 MPGs.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is a symmetry-based phenomenological theory establishing that AHE in crystalline magnets can be induced by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields via linear or nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling across 90 magnetic point groups. The strongest evidence is the first-principles verification in Cr2O3 (>100 S/cm at 4 MV/cm via first-order) and CoF2 (>200 S/cm via second-order), with both exhibiting predicted Hall conductivity reversal upon magnetic order parameter switching. The future path lies in experimental demonstration of these electric-field driven Hall conductivities and the identification of additional candidate materials from the MAGNDATA database, enabling a new diagnostic tool for magnetic state readout in spintronic devices.

summary.title: Enabling Real-Time Conversations with Minimal Training Costs
summary.authors: Wang Xu, Shuo Wang, Weilin Zhao, Xu Han, Yukun Yan, Yudi Zhang, Zhe Tao, Zhiyuan Liu, Wanxiang Che
summary.field_subfield: Computer Science - Conversational AI / Large Language Model Duplex Systems
summary.type_of_paper: Research paper presenting a novel decoding strategy for real-time duplex interactions
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces DUplex decOding (DUO), a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy that enables large language models (LLMs) to support real-time duplex conversational interactions with minimal additional training. Conventional LLM-powered dialogue systems operate on a turn-based paradigm, precluding real-time interaction during response generation. Prior work has proposed duplex models (e.g., MiniCPM-Duplex, LSLM) that use time-division-multiplexing strategies, but these require substantial computational resources for model retraining because the decoding procedure diverges significantly from the backbone model's original training format. DUO addresses this by processing input and output channels simultaneously in each decoding cycle: the output channel generates tokens autoregressively while the input channel prefills the key-value cache and predicts the next tokens. Two state tokens (<1> for user query, <2> for non-query text) signal whether a query should be addressed or ignored, allowing the model to suspend the original output channel and transition to the new query when interrupted. The method requires only 10K training samples (versus 5,000K for MiniCPM-Duplex) and was trained for only 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs over approximately 25 minutes, compared to 10,000 steps on 40 A100 GPUs over 36 hours for the baseline. Human evaluation across 40 multi-turn voice-based dialogue sessions by three participants shows that MiniCPM-Duo achieves superior responsiveness and human-likeness compared to MiniCPM-Duplex, with comparable factuality and faithfulness. Standard benchmark results (CMMLU, MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K, etc.) confirm that MiniCPM-Duo preserves the model's original capabilities while adding duplex functionality. The paper concludes that channel-division-multiplexing preserves the training data format, minimizing retraining costs and enabling real-time interactive feedback including non-awakening and interrupt interactions.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces DUplex decOding (DUO), a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy that enables large language models (LLMs) to support real-time duplex conversational interactions with minimal additional training. Conventional LLM-powered dialogue systems operate on a turn-based paradigm, precluding real-time interaction during response generation. Prior work has proposed duplex models (e.g., MiniCPM-Duplex, LSLM) that use time-division-multiplexing strategies, but these require substantial computational resources for model retraining because the decoding procedure diverges significantly from the backbone model's original training format. DUO addresses this by processing input and output channels simultaneously in each decoding cycle: the output channel generates tokens autoregressively while the input channel prefills the key-value cache and predicts the next tokens. Two state tokens (<1> for user query, <2> for non-query text) signal whether a query should be addressed or ignored, allowing the model to suspend the original output channel and transition to the new query when interrupted. The method requires only 10K training samples (versus 5,000K for MiniCPM-Duplex) and was trained for only 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs over approximately 25 minutes, compared to 10,000 steps on 40 A100 GPUs over 36 hours for the baseline. Human evaluation across 40 multi-turn voice-based dialogue sessions by three participants shows that MiniCPM-Duo achieves superior responsiveness and human-likeness compared to MiniCPM-Duplex, with comparable factuality and faithfulness. Standard benchmark results (CMMLU, MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K, etc.) confirm that MiniCPM-Duo preserves the model's original capabilities while adding duplex functionality. The paper concludes that channel-division-multiplexing preserves the training data format, minimizing retraining costs and enabling real-time interactive feedback including non-awakening and interrupt interactions.

Research Context
LLMs have enabled applications such as question answering and coding assistance that augment human capabilities through conversation. The quality of the interaction experience is important for practical human-computer interaction. Traditional turn-based chat systems inherently limit the interactive experience by requiring one party to passively wait while the other responds. Human conversations involve simultaneous listening and thinking, which turn-based patterns fail to capture. Recent studies have proposed duplex models to address the challenge of concurrent input and output processing. Zhang et al. (2024) introduced MiniCPM-Duplex, which employs a time-division-multiplexing strategy where input and output are split and mixed in a time slice format. Ma et al. (2024) introduced LSLM, which combines channels for autoregressive generation and real-time turn-taking detection with three fusion strategies. However, these existing duplex approaches often demand significant computational resources for model retraining because the designed procedure diverges substantially from the backbone model. The gap is the need for a duplex mechanism that preserves the original training format to minimize retraining overhead.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a channel-division-multiplexing decoding strategy can equip LLMs with duplex capabilities while minimizing training costs. The hypothesis is that by optimizing the decoding strategy rather than retraining the model on a mixed time-slice format, duplex abilities can be added with minimal additional training. The proposed method employs parallel decoding of queries and responses, implementing a channel-division-multiplexing strategy rather than time-division-multiplexing. The model is predicted to support both non-awakening interaction (filtering out background dialogues) and interruption interaction (pausing generation to address the latest query). Two state tokens are hypothesized to effectively signal whether a query should be addressed or ignored during the channel transition. The prediction is that DUO will enhance the naturalness and human-likeness of user-AI interactions with minimal training costs compared to time-division-multiplexing approaches. The paper explicitly states that the proposed method requires only minimal additional training to learn the state of the query, contrasting with the heavy retraining needed by MiniCPM-Duplex.

Methodological Details
The foundation model used is MiniCPM-2.4B (Hu et al., 2024), with MiniCPM-Duplex serving as the baseline since both are derived from the same checkpoints. A total of 10K samples were constructed from Duplex-UltraChat (Zhang et al., 2024) to train the model, a significantly smaller dataset than the 5,000K samples used for MiniCPM-Duplex. The dataset was constructed by adapting Duplex-UltraChat into a standard turn-based format with appended state tokens. To simulate non-awakening interaction scenes, ChatGPT was used to generate non-query text, with the prompt optimized to make the text relevant to the context. Each user's content in the dataset was appended with the <1> state token since all queries required a response. Training hyperparameters for MiniCPM-Duo include a learning rate of 1e-5, a constant learning rate scheduler, a batch size of 112, and a maximum sequence length of 4,096. The loss is calculated on both the state tokens and the output text. MiniCPM-Duo was trained for 400 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for approximately 25 minutes. In contrast, MiniCPM-Duplex was trained for 10,000 steps on 40 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for 36 hours. The input channel predicted tokens α is set to 4. The decoding strategy was implemented based on the Ouroboros repository. The human evaluation involved 40 multi-turn dialogue sessions recorded with three participants, each holding a Bachelor's degree. The human evaluators ranked dialogues on five criteria: responsiveness, human-likeness, faithfulness, factuality, and overall experience. The standard benchmarks included CMMLU, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, ARC-e, ARC-c, and HellaSwag, all evaluated via the UltraEval platform.

Procedures And Architectures
DUO processes inputs and outputs cyclically, where in each cycle the output channel generates new tokens autoregressively while the input channel prefills the key-value cache and predicts the next tokens. As illustrated in Figure 1, a new input channel is established when a user interprets the model's generation at time step t1 while the model generates output autoregressively. Tokens generated by the input and output channels after t1 do not attend to each other despite sharing the same prefix tokens, preserving language modeling in each channel. The attention mask is modified to accommodate the token dependency while ensuring channels remain independent during parallel generation. Upon processing the input tokens, the output channel persists in generating tokens rather than terminating immediately, maintained until either the model responds to the new query or the output sequence is completed. Two state tokens are used to signal the status of the user's query: <1> denotes that the input is a user query, and <2> denotes that the new input is non-query text. When the model predicts state token <1>, the original output channel is suspended and the input channel seamlessly transitions to become the new output channel. When state token <2> is predicted, the model continues to respond to the original query and the input channel is disregarded. Otherwise, the key-value cache of the predicted input would be disregarded and the next processing cycle continues. DUO processes the input and output simultaneously by optimizing the decoding strategy, functioning as a channel-division-multiplexing system where the data format remains largely unchanged. In contrast to MiniCPM-Duplex's time-division-multiplexing which splits and mixes input and output in a time-slice format, DUO's data format remains consistent with the original training data. DUO can be efficiently implemented using Flex-Attention which facilitates non-standard attention mechanisms. All operations are accomplished through the management of the key-value cache, and DUO does not increase the number of forward passes compared to standard decoding. The model generates output concurrently while the key-value cache of the input is prefilled and the next tokens of input are predicted in each time slice.

Key Results
In human evaluation across 40 multi-turn sessions, MiniCPM-Duo demonstrated superior responsiveness and human-likeness compared to MiniCPM-Duplex. MiniCPM-Duo maintains comparable levels of factuality and faithfulness with MiniCPM-Duplex, and exhibits a substantial advantage in overall performance. For the overall satisfaction criterion, MiniCPM-Duo wins more frequently than MiniCPM-Duplex, as shown in Figure 2. On standard benchmarks, MiniCPM-Duo achieves comparable results with MiniCPM-Duplex and the base MiniCPM model, preserving original capabilities. CMMLU: MiniCPM-Duo (50.66) slightly exceeds MiniCPM-Duplex (50.56) and the base model (51.30). MMLU: MiniCPM-Duo (53.13) is comparable to MiniCPM-Duplex (53.76) and the base model (53.45). BBH: MiniCPM-Duo (36.51) performs similarly to MiniCPM-Duplex (35.81) and the base model (37.25). HumanEval: MiniCPM-Duo (51.83) slightly exceeds MiniCPM-Duplex (51.81) and the base model (50.00). MBPP: MiniCPM-Duo (38.19) is comparable to MiniCPM-Duplex (38.30) and the base model (38.09). GSM8K: MiniCPM-Duo (42.15) is comparable to the base model (42.30) and lower than MiniCPM-Duplex (46.10). ARC-e: MiniCPM-Duo (84.93) is comparable to MiniCPM-Duplex (85.19) and the base model (84.60). ARC-c: MiniCPM-Duo (70.48) slightly exceeds MiniCPM-Duplex (69.43) and the base model (69.80). HellaSwag: MiniCPM-Duo (59.78) significantly underperforms compared to the base model (61.40) and MiniCPM-Duplex (60.79). When MiniCPM-Duplex is trained on the same 10K dataset scale as MiniCPM-Duo, its performances drop, and the duplex capability of inadequately trained MiniCPM-Duplex is relatively poor. MiniCPM-Duplex requires substantial computational resources to learn the time-slice format, whereas DUO solely trains the model to recognize the state of the user's query.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The theoretical core of DUO is channel-division-multiplexing, which preserves the original training data format by processing input and output streams independently in each decoding cycle. This contrasts with time-division-multiplexing (used by MiniCPM-Duplex), which splits and mixes input and output in a time-slice format, requiring extensive retraining because the decoded sequence differs from the original training distribution. By maintaining the original data format, DUO preserves the model's inherent language modeling capabilities while adding duplex functionality via a decoding-level modification. The mechanism enables real-time interactive feedback including non-awakening interaction and interrupt interaction, which are not addressed by MiniCPM-Duplex. The case study in Figure 3 demonstrates adaptive behavior: when a user interrupts, state token <2> results in deletion of the new input, while state token <1> triggers a seamless transition to a new output channel. The findings imply that duplex capability can be added to LLMs as a decoding-level augmentation rather than requiring full fine-tuning on mixed-data formats. The substantial computational savings (25 minutes vs 36 hours) suggest that such decoding-level interventions can dramatically reduce the overhead of deploying interactive LLM systems.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study acknowledges that experiments primarily focused on language models, potentially limiting the generalizability of findings to other domains. The authors state they aim to extend DUO to multimodal settings in future research. The human evaluation was conducted with only three participants, which may limit the statistical robustness of the preference rankings. The comparison on HellaSwag shows a significant performance drop for MiniCPM-Duo (59.78) compared to the base model (61.40) and MiniCPM-Duplex (60.79), suggesting some capability erosion on certain reasoning tasks. The GSM8K result (42.15) is lower than both MiniCPM-Duplex (46.10) and the base model (42.30), indicating mixed effects on math reasoning. The baseline comparison assumes both models are derived from the same checkpoints, but differences in training scale (5,000K vs 10K samples) may confound direct comparisons. The paper does not report a full ablation study on the state token prediction length (α set to 4) or its effect on performance. There is no explicit report on whether the duplex decoding increases latency beyond standard decoding, though the paper claims it doesn't increase forward passes.

Claims
DUO achieves real-time duplex capabilities with minimal training costs compared to time-division-multiplexing approaches. MiniCPM-Duo required only 10K samples, while MiniCPM-Duplex required approximately 5,000K samples. Training took 400 steps on 8 A100 GPUs over 25 minutes, versus 10,000 steps on 40 A100 GPUs over 36 hours for the baseline. DUO does not increase the number of forward passes compared to standard decoding. The data format remains largely unchanged, with only the addition of some state tokens. The method can be efficiently implemented using Flex-Attention for non-standard attention mechanisms. On HellaSwag, MiniCPM-Duo scored 59.78, a significant drop from the base model's 61.40. On GSM8K, MiniCPM-Duo scored 42.15, lower than the base model's 42.30. The human evaluation was conducted with only three participants, potentially limiting the generality of the preference rankings. The channel-division-multiplexing approach suggests that duplex capabilities can be added as a decoding-level augmentation rather than full fine-tuning. The substantial training cost reduction makes duplex LLMs more accessible for deployment in production conversational systems.
DUO enables both non-awakening interaction and interrupt interaction, while MiniCPM-Duplex does not address non-awakening interactions. The case study in Figure 3 demonstrates the model handling both user silence during generation and user interruption with state tokens. The authors state DUO is capable of handling non-awakening interactions, an aspect that MiniCPM-Duplex does not address. Two state tokens are used: <1> to signal user query and <2> to signal non-query text, enabling the model to decide whether to respond. There is no quantitative measurement provided specifically for non-awakening interaction performance, only the qualitative case study. This broader capability makes DUO more suitable for real-world voice assistants that face background speech and frequent interruptions.

Data And Code Availability
The decoding strategy was implemented based on the Ouroboros repository: https://github.com/thunlp/Ouroboros. The interactive demo for evaluation was hosted at https://github.com/thunlp/duplex-model. The paper does not explicitly state whether the trained DUO weights or the full dataset are publicly available.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The paper reports that when MiniCPM-Duplex is trained on the same 10K dataset scale as MiniCPM-Duo, its performances drop and duplex capability is relatively poor. The input channel predicted tokens α is set to 4, but no ablation on this value is reported. The state tokens are trained end-to-end with the output, and the paper does not report ablation of individual state token behaviors. Standard benchmarks (CMMLU, MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, ARC-e, ARC-c, HellaSwag) serve as the robustness check for preserving model capabilities. The human evaluation was conducted across 40 multi-turn sessions with three participants to assess human-likeness, responsiveness, and factuality.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the channel-based parallel decoding architecture: Top Left shows the new decoding branch when a user interrupts; Right shows non-attending output/input channels; Left Bottom shows channel transition via state tokens. Figure 2 presents the human evaluation comparison between MiniCPM-Duo and MiniCPM-Duplex on responsiveness, human-likeness, factuality, faithfulness, and overall satisfaction. Figure 3 is a case study showing a conversation about Southgate College where the model handles user silence (generating answer) and an interrupt (predicting <2> and discarding new input). Figure 5 shows the training example for MiniCPM-Duplex (time-division-multiplexing), and Figure 6 shows the training example for DUO (channel-division-multiplexing). Table 1 reports performance on standard benchmarks: CMMLU (51.30, 48.53, 50.56, 50.66), MMLU (53.45, 53.76, 52.89, 53.13), BBH (37.25, 36.35, 35.81, 36.51), HumanEval (50.00, 49.39, 51.81, 51.83), MBPP (38.09, 38.30, 34.70, 38.19), GSM8K (42.30, 46.10, 40.26, 42.15), ARC-e (84.60, 85.19, 83.12, 84.93), ARC-c (69.80, 70.05, 69.43, 70.48), HellaSwag (61.40, 60.79, 50.85, 59.78).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is DUplex decOding (DUO), a channel-division-multiplexing strategy that adds duplex capability to LLMs via a decoding-level modification that preserves the original training data format, requiring only 10K samples and 400 training steps on 8 A100 GPUs (25 minutes) versus 5,000K samples and 10,000 steps over 36 hours for time-division-multiplexing. 2. The strongest evidence is the human evaluation of 40 multi-turn voice-based dialogue sessions where MiniCPM-Duo achieved superior responsiveness and human-likeness over MiniCPM-Duplex while maintaining comparable factuality and faithfulness, with standard benchmarks confirming that DUO preserves most of the base model's capabilities with only minor regressions on HellaSwag and GSM8K. 3. The future path lies in extending DUO to multimodal settings, as noted by the authors who state the approach is inherently designed for versatility and can be adapted by treating input tokens as features extracted from encoders for various modalities, broadening potential applications beyond text-only conversations.

summary.authors: Lina Zhang, Qiyuan Pan, Yun Soo Myung, De-Cheng Zou

summary.executive_summary: This paper investigates the spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes, which are spherically symmetric, regular (singularity-free) black hole solutions within Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics theory. The authors demonstrate that a tachyonic instability, triggered by the nonminimal coupling between a scalar field and the electromagnetic field, leads to the formation of scalarized charged black holes (SCBHs). Two coupling forms are analyzed: quadratic, \tilde{f}(\phi) = 1 - \alpha\phi^2, and exponential, \tilde{f}(\phi) = e^{-\alpha\phi^2}, where \alpha\geq \alpha_{n=0}(g) is the instability threshold. The study finds that infinite (n = 0, 1, 2, \cdot \cdot \cdot) branches of SCBHs with magnetic charge g emerge from the Bardeen background at various bifurcation points. For a representative nonextremal Bardeen black hole with mass M = 0.5 and magnetic charge g = 0.2, the outer horizon radius is found to be r⁺ = 0.935. The instability thresholds for three magnetic charges are numerically determined: \alpha_{th}(0.175) = 17.338, \alpha_{th}(0.200) = 12.712, and \alpha_{th}(0.250) = 7.251. These thresholds coincide with the n = 0 bifurcation points, indicating that the instability threshold for Bardeen black holes marks the formation of the largest n = 0 branch of SCBHs. The n = 0 branch, representing the fundamental scalarized solution, is found to be stable against radial perturbations for both quadratic and exponential couplings, while other branches (n \neq 0) are expected to be unstable. For g = 0.2 and quadratic coupling, the n = 0 branch is obtained at \alpha = 13.048; for exponential coupling, it is obtained at \alpha = 13.667. The metric function N(r) of the SCBH solution has a horizon at ln r = −0.0683, slightly shifted from the Bardeen horizon at ln r = −0.0671. The stability analysis, performed by solving the Schrödinger-type equation for l = 0 scalar perturbations, confirms that the n = 0 branch is stable with \Omega < 0 for all investigated magnetic charges. The authors conclude that since the n = 0 branch is stable, it can serve as an end point of the Bardeen black hole solution and has potential observational implications.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes, which are spherically symmetric, regular (singularity-free) black hole solutions within Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics theory. The authors demonstrate that a tachyonic instability, triggered by the nonminimal coupling between a scalar field and the electromagnetic field, leads to the formation of scalarized charged black holes (SCBHs). Two coupling forms are analyzed: quadratic, \tilde{f}(\phi) = 1 - \alpha\phi^2, and exponential, \tilde{f}(\phi) = e^{-\alpha\phi^2}, where \alpha\geq \alpha_{n=0}(g) is the instability threshold. The study finds that infinite (n = 0, 1, 2, \cdot \cdot \cdot) branches of SCBHs with magnetic charge g emerge from the Bardeen background at various bifurcation points. For a representative nonextremal Bardeen black hole with mass M = 0.5 and magnetic charge g = 0.2, the outer horizon radius is found to be r⁺ = 0.935. The instability thresholds for three magnetic charges are numerically determined: \alpha_{th}(0.175) = 17.338, \alpha_{th}(0.200) = 12.712, and \alpha_{th}(0.250) = 7.251. These thresholds coincide with the n = 0 bifurcation points, indicating that the instability threshold for Bardeen black holes marks the formation of the largest n = 0 branch of SCBHs. The n = 0 branch, representing the fundamental scalarized solution, is found to be stable against radial perturbations for both quadratic and exponential couplings, while other branches (n \neq 0) are expected to be unstable. For g = 0.2 and quadratic coupling, the n = 0 branch is obtained at \alpha = 13.048; for exponential coupling, it is obtained at \alpha = 13.667. The metric function N(r) of the SCBH solution has a horizon at ln r = −0.0683, slightly shifted from the Bardeen horizon at ln r = −0.0671. The stability analysis, performed by solving the Schrödinger-type equation for l = 0 scalar perturbations, confirms that the n = 0 branch is stable with \Omega < 0 for all investigated magnetic charges. The authors conclude that since the n = 0 branch is stable, it can serve as an end point of the Bardeen black hole solution and has potential observational implications.

Research Context
Spontaneous scalarization is a dynamic process that imparts scalar hair to black holes without changing weak-field predictions. The phenomenon is a strong gravity phase transition caused by tachyonic instability from nonminimal coupling. Black hole spontaneous scalarization has been extensively studied, including rotation, spin-induced, and scalar-Gauss-Bonnet cases. Scalarized black holes are entropically favorable compared to bald solutions, and their n = 0 branches are stable. Bardeen proposed the first regular black hole solution, spherically symmetric and free of singularities. The physical source of Bardeen black holes was initially unclear, with nonlinear electromagnetic sources proposed to explain the matter content. Regular black holes are of great interest for understanding fundamental issues including singularities and nonlinear electrodynamics. In this context, the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theory with exponential and quadratic scalar couplings has been previously explored. The work aims to study the spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes by introducing two scalar field couplings.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether Bardeen black holes undergo spontaneous scalarization under quadratic and exponential scalar couplings. A key hypothesis is that a tachyonic instability will exist above a threshold value of the coupling parameter α. The study predicts that infinite branches of scalarized charged black holes will emerge from the Bardeen background. The n = 0 branch is expected to be the largest and potentially the most physically relevant branch. The authors predict that both quadratic and exponential couplings will lead to scalarization and that the stability of the n = 0 branch can be established. A subsidiary hypothesis is that the instability threshold α_{th}(g) will correspond to the n = 0 bifurcation point. The paper also aims to verify whether the instability threshold depends on the magnetic charge g. The ultimate goal is to demonstrate that the n = 0 branch is stable against radial perturbations, making it an end point of the Bardeen solution. Observational implications are sought for the stable n = 0 branch of SCBHs.

Methodological Details
The theoretical framework is Einstein-nonlinear electrodynamics theory coupled with a scalar field. The action contains the scalar curvature, a scalar field term, and a coupling function ˜f(ϕ) times the nonlinear electromagnetic Lagrangian L(F). L(F) is a nonlinear function of F = F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}, with a specific form parameterized by s = |g|/(2M). Two coupling forms are considered: ˜f(ϕ) = 1 −αϕ^2 (quadratic) and ˜f(ϕ) = e^{−αϕ^2} (exponential), with parameter α. The Bardeen solution is obtained by setting ϕ = 0 and solving the field equations for M and g. A representative nonextremal Bardeen black hole is chosen with M = 0.5 and g = 0.2. From f(r) = 0, the outer horizon radius for g = 0.2 and M = 0.5 is r⁺ = 0.935. The scalar perturbation equation is analyzed using the separation of variables, ϕ(t, r, θ, φ) = u(r)/r e^{−iωt} Y_{lm}. The l = 0 mode is selected for assessing the instability, as it is permissible for scalar perturbations. The radial scalar equation is transformed into a Schrödinger-type equation in tortoise coordinates r^∗. The scalar potential V(r) is explicitly derived from the metric and coupling. The threshold of instability α_{th}(g) is determined numerically by solving the linearized scalar equation with purely ingoing/outgoing wave boundary conditions. To verify the instability bound, static scalar solutions are found by solving the linearized equation with ω = 0. For g = 0.2, the first three bifurcation points are found at α ≈ 12.712, 75.114, and 190.590. Three magnetic charges g = 0.175, 0.200, and 0.250 are analyzed to check g-dependence of the threshold. The n = 0 branch is constructed numerically using a metric ansatz and shooting from near-horizon to asymptotic regions. The near-horizon expansion provides coefficients m1, δ1, and ϕ1 determined by the coupling and horizon radius. The asymptotic solution incorporates the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner mass M and the scalar charge Qs. Stability of the SCBH solution is tested by solving the perturbed Schrödinger equation with vanishing boundary conditions. For exponential coupling, the equation is solved in exponential form by imposing outgoing/ingoing wave boundary conditions.

Procedures And Architectures
The computational process proceeds in four steps: detecting tachyonic instability, predicting SCBH bifurcation points, obtaining the n = 0 branch, and performing stability analysis. The scalar potential V(r) for the Bardeen background is derived analytically: V(r) = f(r) [l(l + 1)/r^2 + 2M(r^2 − g^2(2 + 3α))/(g^2 + r^2)^{5/2}]. For the SCBH construction, a metric ansatz ds^2 = −N(r)e^{−2δ(r)}dt^2 + dr^2/N(r) + r^2(dθ^2 + sin^2θdφ^2) and scalar ϕ(r) are used. Three coupled ODEs for {δ(r), m(r), ϕ(r)} are derived from the field equations: δ'(r) + rϕ'^2(r) = 0; a mass-equation; and the scalar equation. Near-horizon coefficients m1, δ1, ϕ1 are calculated: m1 = 3g^2Mr^2_+ / (g^2 + r^2_+)^{5/2} + ˜f(ϕ₀); δ1 = −r_+ϕ₁^2; ϕ1 = 3g^2Mr_+ / (g^2 + r^2_+)^{5/2} + 6g^2Mr₂ / ˜f'(ϕ₀) − 36g⁴M²r₄ / ˜f(ϕ₀)^2. The shooting method is employed to match the near-horizon and asymptotic solutions, with ϕ₀ and δ₀ as shooting parameters. For the quadratic case, the n = 0 branch is obtained at α = 13.048 for g = 0.2. For the exponential case, the n = 0 branch is obtained at α = 13.667 for g = 0.2. The SCBH metric function N(r) has a horizon at ln r = −0.0683, while the Bardeen horizon is at ln r = −0.0671. For stability analysis, radial perturbations are introduced: ds^2_RP = −N(r)e^{−2δ(r)}[1 + ϵH₀(t, r)]dt^2 + dr^2/N(r)[1 + ϵH₁(t, r)] + r^2(dθ^2 + sin^2θdφ^2); ϕ = ϕ(r) + ϵδϕ(t, r)/r. ϵ ≪ 1 is the control parameter for perturbations. All perturbed fields except the scalar field δϕ are considered redundant for l = 0. The Schrödinger-type equation for scalar perturbations is d²ϕ₁(r)/dr*² − [Ω^2 + V_{SCBH}(r)]ϕ₁(r) = 0. The potential V_{SCBH}(r) is explicitly given and involves N(r), δ(r), ˜f(ϕ), and their derivatives. For the quadratic case, the numerical solver confirms stability against the l = 0 mode. For the exponential case, the re-defined scalar field ˜ϕ₁(r) is solved with outgoing wave at infinity and ingoing wave at the horizon. The stability results for three values of g (0.175, 0.200, 0.250) are presented in Fig. 6.

Key Results
The n = 0 branch of SCBHs exists for coupling parameters α ≥ α_{n=0}(g) with both quadratic and exponential couplings. The Bardeen black hole is stable for α < α_{th}(g) and unstable for α ≥ α_{th}(g), with the instability marking the formation of the n = 0 SCBH branch. For M = 0.5 and g = 0.2, the outer horizon radius of the Bardeen black hole is r⁺ = 0.935. The instability thresholds are α_{th}(0.175) = 17.338, α_{th}(0.200) = 12.712, and α_{th}(0.250) = 7.251. The bifurcation points for g = 0.2 are α_{n=0} ≈ 12.712, α_{n=1} ≈ 75.114, and α_{n=2} ≈ 190.590, with α_{th}(0.200) = α_{n=0}(0.200) = 12.712. The quadratic coupling n = 0 SCBH solution is obtained at α = 13.048 with a horizon at ln r = −0.0683, slightly shifted from the Bardeen horizon at ln r = −0.0671. The exponential coupling n = 0 SCBH solution is obtained at α = 13.667 for the same parameters. The n = 0 SCBH branch is stable against the l = 0 scalar mode, with the perturbation mode Ω being negative in Fig. 6. The stability of the n = 0 branch is independent of the magnetic charge g, holding true for g = 0.175, 0.200, and 0.250. The exponential coupling does not affect the stability of the scalarized Bardeen black holes. The bifurcation point α_{n=0}(g) increases as g decreases, meaning tachyonic instability is harder to realize for smaller magnetic charges. Infinite branches of SCBHs are expected, with n ≠ 0 branches expected to be unstable against radial perturbations. The n = 0 branch is stable against radial perturbations, making it an end point of the Bardeen black hole solution. Figure 1 shows the α-dependent potential V(r, α) for g = 0.2, with negative regions indicating instability; the negative region's width and depth increase with α. Figure 3 shows the first three static scalar solutions ϕ(z) for M = 0.5, g = 0.2, with nodes indicating the branch number n = 0, 1, 2. Figure 4 shows the metric functions N(r), δ(r), ϕ(r) and the Bardeen f(r) for the n = 0 branch at α = 13.048 (quadratic) and α = 13.667 (exponential). Figure 5 shows the scalar potentials V_{SCBH}(r) around the n = 0 branch for quadratic coupling at α = 12.713, 13.048, 14.110, revealing small negative near-horizon regions that turn out to be stable. Figure 6 shows the growth rate Ω as a function of α, with negative Ω values indicating stability.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Spontaneous scalarization is interpreted as a strong gravity phase transition induced by the nonminimal coupling between scalar fields and spacetime curvature or matter. The n = 0 branch represents the fundamental scalarized solution and, due to its stability, can be interpreted as a physical end point of the Bardeen black hole solution. The stability of the n = 0 branch against radial perturbations allows for potential observational implications, as the solution is a legitimate equilibrium configuration. The instability threshold α_{th}(g) marks the boundary between the bald Bardeen solution and the n = 0 scalarized branch, confirming the bifurcation structure predicted by scalarization theory. The exponential coupling does not qualitatively change the stability or structure of the scalarized solution compared to the quadratic coupling. The violation of the strong energy condition at the center of the Bardeen black hole supports its identification as a regular black hole. The fact that α_{th}(g) increases as g decreases suggests that magnetic charge plays a role in regulating the threshold for spontaneous scalarization. The existence of infinite branches (n = 0, 1, 2, ...) suggests a rich structure of scalarized solutions, of which the n = 0 branch is the most stable and physically accessible. The stability of the n = 0 branch, combined with its near-equality to the Bardeen metric at large r, suggests that scalarization introduces small but measurable deviations from general relativity predictions.

Contradictions And Limitations
A small negative region in the near-horizon of V_{SCBH} with α = 12.713 does not necessarily imply instability, as the full numerical solution is required to confirm decay. The potential V_{SCBH} only exhibits small negative regions in the near-horizon, and the stability is confirmed through the full eigenvalue problem rather than just potential positivity. The stability of higher branches (n ≠ 0) is assumed to be unstable based on prior references rather than demonstrated explicitly in this work. The radial perturbation analysis only considers the l = 0 mode; higher angular momentum modes are not addressed and their stability is not established. The shooting method for SCBH construction requires an approximate near-horizon expansion, which may limit the accuracy near the horizon. The analysis is limited to stationary, spherically symmetric cases and does not include dynamical evolution or time-dependent perturbations beyond the linear mode analysis. The coupling forms are restricted to quadratic and exponential; other coupling functional forms are not explored. No explicit parameter range is given for the coupling strength α beyond the instability threshold; arbitrary values above α_{th} are used. The matching procedure between near-horizon and asymptotic regions involves an approximation that may introduce errors near the horizon. The shooting method requires choosing two shooting parameters (ϕ₀, δ₀), and the convergence and uniqueness of the matching solution are not explicitly discussed. The paper does not explicitly report the numerical methods, tolerance values, or software used for the ODE shooting and eigenvalue problems. There is no mention of random seeds, grid spacing, or convergence checks for the numerical solutions. The shooting method for matching near-horizon and asymptotic regions is a well-established procedure but its accuracy near the horizon depends on the order of the expansion used. The paper does not report the full parameter space explored for g beyond the three values g = 0.175, 0.200, 0.250.

Claims
Bardeen black holes undergo spontaneous scalarization at a threshold of the coupling parameter α, forming infinite branches of scalarized charged black holes. The tachyonic instability of the Bardeen background is demonstrated by the Schrödinger potential V(r) developing a negative region near the horizon for α ≥ α_{th}(g). Numerical solution of the linearized scalar equation yields the n = 0 branch at α = 13.048 (quadratic) and α = 13.667 (exponential) for g = 0.2, M = 0.5. The n = 0 branch is found to be stable against radial perturbations (Ω < 0) for both quadratic and exponential couplings. The instability threshold α_{th}(g) exactly coincides with the n = 0 bifurcation point α_{n=0}(g). Static scalar solutions are obtained for three distinct bifurcation points α_{n=0}, α_{n=1}, α_{n=2} corresponding to branches with zero, one, and two nodes respectively. A negative potential region in V_{SCBH} near the horizon does not always imply instability, as shown by the stable n = 0 branch solutions. The n = 0 branch is obtained for α ≥ α_{n=0}(g), but only the first three branches are explicitly computed and analyzed. The stability is only confirmed for the l = 0 mode; higher angular momentum modes are not analyzed. The n = 0 branch is a stable equilibrium solution that could serve as an end point of the Bardeen solution with potential observational signatures. The instability threshold α_{th}(g) marks the critical coupling where scalarization occurs, with the threshold depending on the magnetic charge g. The exponential coupling does not qualitatively alter the scalarization physics compared to the quadratic coupling.
The n = 0 branch of SCBHs is stable against radial (spherically symmetric) perturbations for both quadratic and exponential couplings, across all investigated magnetic charges. The Schrödinger-type equation for l = 0 perturbations yields a fully negative Ω for the n = 0 branch at all three g values (0.175, 0.200, 0.250). The instability thresholds and bifurcation points are consistent with the stability boundary. The SCBH potentials V_{SCBH} for n = 0 exhibit a large positive region outside the horizon, consistent with stability. The instability of the Bardeen background (α ≥ α_{th}) corresponds to the region where SCBH solutions emerge, while the stable Bardeen solution (α < α_{th}) has no corresponding scalarized branch. For exponential coupling, the stability is confirmed using the exponential version of the perturbation equation with the appropriate boundary conditions. The potentials V_{SCBH} contain small negative regions near the horizon, which might traditionally be associated with instability. The stability is only established for the spherically symmetric l = 0 mode; general stability (all l) is not proven. The stability analysis uses a linear perturbation approach; nonlinear stability is not addressed. The stable n = 0 branch is a viable physical solution and could potentially be observed in gravitational-wave or other astrophysical contexts. The stability of the n = 0 branch for both coupling forms shows the robustness of the scalarization phenomenon to the specific form of the nonminimal coupling.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Three magnetic charges g = 0.175, 0.200, and 0.250 are examined to test g-dependence of the instability threshold. Two coupling forms—quadratic and exponential—are analyzed to compare the effects of the nonminimal coupling functional form. Three branch numbers n = 0, 1, 2 are computed for the static scalar solutions, showing bifurcation points at different α values. The radial perturbation analysis is limited to the l = 0 mode, and higher l modes are not included as ablations. For exponential coupling, the stability equation is solved in exponential form, providing a cross-check of the quadratic coupling results. The near-horizon expansion coefficients are checked against the shooting method matching, with no explicit error analysis reported.

Figure 5(b) shows the same for exponential coupling, with a large positive region outside the horizon confirming stability. Figure 6(a) shows the growth rate Ω as a function of α for the quadratic coupling with three g values, with negative Ω indicating stability. Figure 6(b) shows the same for exponential coupling, confirming stability with negative Ω across all three g values.

1. The core contribution is the first demonstration of spontaneous scalarization of Bardeen black holes under both quadratic and exponential scalar couplings, establishing infinite branches of SCBHs with a stable n = 0 fundamental branch. 2. summary.title: Three-dimensional topological valley photonics
summary.authors: Wenhao Li, Qiaolu Chen, Ning Han, Xinrui Li, Fujia Chen, Junyao Wu, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Haoran Xue, Yihao Yang

summary.executive_summary: This work presents a theoretical and experimental framework for three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics, moving beyond the two-dimensional (2D) valley photonics that has dominated the field to date. The 3D framework is characterized by a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley contrasting physics, enabling the manipulation of light in three dimensions. Unlike 2D valley photonics, which typically suffer from out-of-plane losses and are limited to planar geometries, the 3D system supports triple pairs of valleys at the corners of the 3D Brillouin zone, characterized by valley Chern vectors rather than scalar valley Chern numbers. This vectorial nature enables the creation of vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states, whose propagation directions are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The 3D photonic crystal architecture employs a diamond-like lattice with nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor couplings, fabricated with perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres and rods. The inversion symmetry is broken by differentiating the sphere diameters (D1 = 6.4 mm, D2 = 3.6 mm), which gaps out nodal line degeneracies to form a complete photonic bandgap. Experimental verification employs a vectorial chiral source array with four sources at relative positions, exciting and outcoupling Bloch modes with specific phase windings. At 13.8 GHz, outcoupling fields exhibit directions of -32.9° and +32.9° for Vy- and Vy+, respectively, confirming the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature through the pump-probe measurement. Furthermore, the work demonstrates robust canalized valley surface states on all faces of the sample, with nearly-linear dispersion at 14.6 GHz and flat isofrequency contours, confirmed both experimentally and numerically. The right-hand-thumb rule is explicitly verified through boundary-crossing measurements, showing that the valley Chern vector direction and the circulating surface state propagation direction are intrinsically linked. The authors conclude that the orbital moments of 3D valley states offer a means to control the angular momentum of light, while the highly directional outcoupling can serve as narrow-beam antennae, and the robust canalized surface states inspire novel 3D topological photonic devices. The concept can be extended to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals.
