judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work presents a theoretical and experimental framework for three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics, moving beyond the two-dimensional (2D) valley photonics that has dominated the field to date. The 3D framework is characterized by a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley contrasting physics, enabling the manipulation of light in three dimensions. Unlike 2D valley photonics, which typically suffer from out-of-plane losses and are limited to planar geometries, the 3D system supports triple pairs of valleys at the corners of the 3D Brillouin zone, characterized by valley Chern vectors rather than scalar valley Chern numbers. This vectorial nature enables the creation of vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states, whose propagation directions are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The 3D photonic crystal architecture employs a diamond-like lattice with nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor couplings, fabricated with perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres and rods. The inversion symmetry is broken by differentiating the sphere diameters (D1 = 6.4 mm, D2 = 3.6 mm), which gaps out nodal line degeneracies to form a complete photonic bandgap. Experimental verification employs a vectorial chiral source array with four sources at relative positions, exciting and outcoupling Bloch modes with specific phase windings. At 13.8 GHz, outcoupling fields exhibit directions of -32.9° and +32.9° for Vy- and Vy+, respectively, confirming the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature through the pump-probe measurement. Furthermore, the work demonstrates robust canalized valley surface states on all faces of the sample, with nearly-linear dispersion at 14.6 GHz and flat isofrequency contours, confirmed both experimentally and numerically. The right-hand-thumb rule is explicitly verified through boundary-crossing measurements, showing that the valley Chern vector direction and the circulating surface state propagation direction are intrinsically linked. The authors conclude that the orbital moments of 3D valley states offer a means to control the angular momentum of light, while the highly directional outcoupling can serve as narrow-beam antennae, and the robust canalized surface states inspire novel 3D topological photonic devices. The concept can be extended to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals.

Research Context
Prior work in valley photonics has been limited to two-dimensional (2D) systems where the photonic confinement along the third dimension is obtained in a nontopological way such as total internal reflection. These 2D valley systems support valley states with a single polarization and suffer from out-of-plane losses that constrain light manipulation to planar geometries. The complete photonic bandgap, in which light with any polarization is forbidden to propagate in any direction in three dimensions, has remained a significant challenge. Valley photonics offers a readily accessible method for achieving topologically robust photonic devices suitable for real-world applications including lasers, on-chip communication, and quantum optics. Valley photonics does not necessitate breaking time-reversal symmetry or incorporating synthetic spin-orbital coupling but simply requires a reduction of inversion symmetry to guarantee local nonzero Berry curvature.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics framework with a complete photonic bandgap can be developed and experimentally verified. The 3D framework hypothesizes that triple pairs of valleys at the corners of the 3D BZ, characterized by valley Chern vectors rather than scalar valley Chern numbers, enable vectorial valley-contrasting physics. The authors predict that this vectorial nature will enable the creation of vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. A key hypothesis is that the valley Chern vectors and the circulating propagation direction of the valley surface states are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The framework aims to demonstrate robust canalized valley surface states on all surfaces of a specifically shaped sample, a capability not previously achieved by any 3D photonic topological insulators.

Methodological Details
The 3D photonic crystal is a diamond-like lattice with lattice constant a = 20 mm, where lattice vectors are a1 = (a/2, a/2, 0), a2 = (0, a/2, a/2), and a3 = (a/2, 0, a/2). Carbon atoms are replaced by perfect electric conductor (PEC) spheres, and bonds are replaced by PEC rods. Each face-centered-cubic (fcc) unit cell contains two spheres with diameters D1 and D2. Each nearest sphere is connected by PEC rods with diameter B1 = 2.4 mm. Next-nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B2 = 1.2 mm to suppress high-order modes and obtain a clean bandstructure. For the symmetric case where ∆D = 0, the inversion symmetry is preserved and D1 = D2 = 5 mm, producing nodal lines along Wα±-X. When ∆D ≠ 0, the inversion symmetry is broken and the nodal line degeneracies are gapped out to form a complete photonic bandgap. The broken symmetry configuration uses D1 = 6.4 mm and D2 = 3.6 mm, which defines the ∆D value and breaks inversion. The six valleys are located at (±π/a, 2π/a, 0), (0, ±π/a, 2π/a), and (2π/a, 0, ±π/a) for Wx±, Wy±, and Wz±. The topological boundary states are achieved by modifying on-site boundary potentials: the (001) surface is covered with a metallic plate. To satisfy the boundary condition, the diameter of the outmost metallic sphere D3 is set to 4 mm, and the distance h between the plate and the sphere is set to 6.25 mm. The metallic plate features perforations for inserting the source and probe with a hole interval of a/2.

Procedures And Architectures
The k · p method is applied to obtain the effective Hamiltonian near each valley, with mass term m = (ω1 - ω2)/2 induced by breaking inversion symmetry. The vectorial chiral source array is configured with four sources at relative positions (0, 0, 0), (−a/2, −a/2, 0), (−a/2, 0, −a/2), and (0, −a/2, −a/2). To implement phase winding on x-y, y-z, and x-z planes, the relative phase delay of each source is set to (0, π/2, π, 3π/2) for Wy− and (0, −π/2, −π, −3π/2) for Wy+. The chirality-matched source array selectively excites and outcouples Bloch modes through the vectorial chiral source array. The pump-probe measurement verifies the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature by selectively exciting and observing chiral Bloch modes. Far-field radiation patterns are measured to verify that outcoupling directions agree well with calculated results. Surface field distributions are mapped and Fourier-transformed along the L4-Wx−-L1 direction to obtain the surface dispersion spectrum. The right-hand-thumb rule is tested by positioning the source at the center of the (001) surface and measuring field distributions on the (001) and (010) surfaces.

Key Results
The outcoupling fields at 13.8 GHz exhibit different directions: −32.9° for clockwise phase winding (Wy−) and +32.9° for counterclockwise winding (Wy+), relative to the 0° direction for X. The directional outcoupling beams in the far-field are single-directional in 3D space, unlike the 2D case where radiation is restrained in the plane and diverges vertically. The valley Chern vector is calculated as (±1/2, 0, 0) for Wx±, (0, ±1/2, 0) for Wy±, and (0, 0, ±1/2) for Wz±, verifying the vectorial topological nature. The measured surface transmission maintains high values within the complete photonic bandgap while the bulk transmission is substantially lower, verifying the existence of surface states. The surface field distribution at 14.6 GHz reveals a nearly-linear surface dispersion in the bandgap around the Wx− valley. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction, corresponding to the Wx− valley, confirming the canalization behaviour. The flat isofrequency contours of the surface states have been confirmed both experimentally and numerically, indicating the group velocity preserves for different transverse wavevectors. The chiral valley surface states can be supported on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces, with the propagation direction locked to each valley. The Wx− surface states propagate along +y on the (001) surface, along −z on the (010) surface, along −y on the (001) surface, and along +z on the (010) surface, forming a closed loop. The surface states smoothly pass through the sharp corner with high transmission, verifying the valley-locking property without intervalley scattering. Fourier-transformed field distributions on both the (001) and (010) surfaces reveal that only surface states around the Wx− valley are excited, experimentally confirming the valley-locking property. The measured isofrequency contours before and after the bend at 14.6 GHz match simulated contours, with carnation arrows indicating the group velocity direction normal to the contours.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The vectorial nature of the 3D valley states means the orbital moments provide a means to control the angular momentum of light, with highly directional outcoupling serving as a mechanism for creating narrow-beam antennae. The robust canalized valley chiral surface states may inspire innovative 3D topological photonic devices for guiding and trapping light in an unprecedented way. The canalization is an intrinsic property of the surface states because the group velocity preserves for different transverse wavevectors, leading to flat isofrequency contours. The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic relation between the VCVs and the valley surface states, which are both determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. Unlike the 2D case, the radiated beams in 3D are single-directional, providing the opportunity for directional antenna design.

Contradictions And Limitations
The experimental demonstration is performed at lower frequencies (around 13.8-14.6 GHz), and the authors note that the concept can be extended to higher frequencies including terahertz and optical ranges. The paper does not report the specific random seed, exact sample fabrication details beyond sphere/rod dimensions, or the exact fabrication process for the PEC materials. The outcoupling at 13.8 GHz shows a contribution from states at X that coexist with valley states at the same frequency, which may complicate selective excitation. The boundary condition is satisfied when h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm, but the paper does not explore sensitivity to variations in these parameters.

Claims
The 3D topological valley photonics framework with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley contrasting physics enables directional control and robust surface propagation in three dimensions. The outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz are -32.9° and +32.9°, confirming the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature. The surface transmission is high within the bandgap while bulk transmission is substantially lower, verifying surface states. The right-hand-thumb rule relates the VCV direction to the circulating propagation loops on all surfaces. At 13.8 GHz, states at X coexist with valley states at the same frequency, potentially complicating state selection. The boundary condition is satisfied only at specific parameters h = 6.25 mm and D3 = 4 mm, and robustness to parameter variations is not tested. The highly directional outcoupling can serve as narrow-beam antennae for 3D waveguiding and directional radiation. The concept can be extended to higher frequencies including terahertz and optical ranges using all-dielectric diamond-like crystals.
The canalized surface states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction, confirmed both experimentally and numerically by flat isofrequency contours. Measured surface transmission shows high transmission within the bandgap while bulk is lower. The nearly-linear surface dispersion at 14.6 GHz is confirmed by Fourier-transformed measurements and simulations. Measured isofrequency contours at 14.6 GHz match simulated contours with group velocity arrows normal to the contours. The canalization was previously explored at the topological transition point in twisted van der Waals bilayers, suggesting it may not be a unique feature of valley photonics. The canalization presents promising opportunities for imaging and lensing applications.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The ∆D = 0 case with inversion symmetry is compared to the ∆D ≠ 0 case with broken inversion symmetry to demonstrate the bandgap opening. The next-nearest-neighbor coupling rods with diameter B2 = 1.2 mm are explicitly included to suppress high-order modes and ensure topological band separation. The surface field distributions are Fourier-transformed to obtain the dispersion, and are compared against simulated contours to verify the nearly-linear dispersion. The outcoupling direction of the valley states is compared with the free-space light dispersion at 13.8 GHz to verify the momentum-space analysis.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) shows the cubic cell with two sublattices and the diamond-like lattice with PEC spheres and rods, and the fcc unit cell. Figure 1(b) presents the band structure of the 3D VPC with ∆D = 0 and ∆D ≠ 0 cases, showing nodal lines and the gapped phase. Figure 1(c) shows the 3D Brillouin zone of the fcc unit cell with the six valleys marked by red and blue dots and nodal lines by dashed lines. Figure 1(d) shows simulated eigenstates on the (001) surface for the first band at Wz± valleys with Poynting vectors and phase information. Figure 1(e) shows simulated Berry curvature components of the first band at Wz±, verifying the vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Figure 2(a) illustrates the vectorial chiral source array with four sources and relative phase delays for Wy-. Figure 2(b) shows the momentum-space analysis of Wy-, X, and Wy+ with outcoupling directions and the free-space light dispersion at 13.8 GHz. Figure 2(c) shows the experimental setup with four scanned planes at φ = 90°, θ = −32.9°, θ = 0°, and θ = +32.9°. Figure 2(d) shows measured electric field distributions of outcoupling waves in the y-z plane at 13.8 GHz with theoretical refraction direction arrows. Figure 2(e) shows measured outcoupling far-field radiation patterns at Wy-, X, and Wy+ in planes from (c). Figure 3(a) shows the 3D VPC with the modified (001) surface covered by a metallic plate with h and D3 parameters. Figure 3(b) shows the experimental setup for surface state demonstration. Figure 3(c) shows the projected surface BZ onto the (001) surface with the simulated isofrequency contour at 14.6 GHz. Figure 3(d) shows simulated surface dispersion with bulk and surface states distinguished. Figure 3(e) shows normalized measured transmission with the bulk bandgap shadowed. Figure 3(f) shows the measured field distribution at 14.6 GHz with the propagation direction indicated. Figure 3(g) shows the measured and simulated surface dispersion around the Wx- valley. Figure 3(h) shows the measured and simulated isofrequency contour of surface dispersion at 14.6 GHz with the first BZ indicated. Figure 4(a) illustrates the direction of VCVs and the propagation loops of valley surface states at three pairs of valleys showing the right-hand-thumb rule. Figure 4(b) shows the measured field distributions before (#1) and after (#2) the bend on the (001) and (010) surfaces. Figure 4(c) shows the measured transmission of bulk and surface states before and after the bend in the bandgap. Figure 4(d) shows the measured isofrequency contours of the field distribution before and after the bend at 14.6 GHz with carnation arrows indicating group velocity.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first theoretical and experimental development of three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap, characterized by triple pairs of valleys with valley Chern vectors and vectorial valley-contrasting physics, enabling 3D control of light. 2. The strongest evidence is the direct verification of the vectorial valley-contrasting Berry curvature through the -32.9° and +32.9° outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz, combined with the experimental observation of nearly-linear, canalized surface states on all faces of the sample at 14.6 GHz with confirmed flat isofrequency contours. 3. The future path is the extension of the 3D valley photonics concept to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals, with applications in 3D waveguiding, directional antenna design, and orbital angular momentum control of light.

summary.authors: Xu Han, Xianda Chen, Zhenghan Cai, Pinlong Cai, Meixin Zhu, Xiaowen Chu

summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces Words2Wheels, a framework that automatically generates customized driving policies from natural language user commands without prior driving data. Traditional methods for driving style customization rely on either predefined styles requiring expert input or data-driven techniques like Inverse Reinforcement Learning, both of which struggle with limited style data in Robotaxi scenarios and the inability to prioritize style metrics according to user preferences. Words2Wheels bridges user input to policy via a Style-Customized Reward Function, stored in a Driving Style Database containing reward codes, pre-trained Style Policies, and statistical features. The framework leverages GPT-4o-2024-08-06 with Retrieval-Augmented Generation to select relevant reward functions, generates new ones when no match exists, and trains policies using Proximal Policy Optimization. A Statistical Evaluation module, employing Chain-of-Thought reasoning over reserved test data, validates alignment with user commands by comparing metrics such as speed, jerk, and time headway against natural driving statistics. Experiments on the HighD car-following dataset with 10 human volunteers (1,000 events) show that 72% of participants preferred Words2Wheels-generated styles over IDM, while 9.2% preferred IDM and 18.8% judged them equal. Case studies across 40 commands at three levels of directness (Level I direct, Level II indirect strong hints, Level III indirect mild hints) show 85-97.5% success rates. The framework also features a fuzzy memory that recalled all associated styles except for one snowing case. Code and demo are available at yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces Words2Wheels, a framework that automatically generates customized driving policies from natural language user commands without prior driving data. Traditional methods for driving style customization rely on either predefined styles requiring expert input or data-driven techniques like Inverse Reinforcement Learning, both of which struggle with limited style data in Robotaxi scenarios and the inability to prioritize style metrics according to user preferences. Words2Wheels bridges user input to policy via a Style-Customized Reward Function, stored in a Driving Style Database containing reward codes, pre-trained Style Policies, and statistical features. The framework leverages GPT-4o-2024-08-06 with Retrieval-Augmented Generation to select relevant reward functions, generates new ones when no match exists, and trains policies using Proximal Policy Optimization. A Statistical Evaluation module, employing Chain-of-Thought reasoning over reserved test data, validates alignment with user commands by comparing metrics such as speed, jerk, and time headway against natural driving statistics. Experiments on the HighD car-following dataset with 10 human volunteers (1,000 events) show that 72% of participants preferred Words2Wheels-generated styles over IDM, while 9.2% preferred IDM and 18.8% judged them equal. Case studies across 40 commands at three levels of directness (Level I direct, Level II indirect strong hints, Level III indirect mild hints) show 85-97.5% success rates. The framework also features a fuzzy memory that recalled all associated styles except for one snowing case. Code and demo are available at yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/.

Research Context
Autonomous driving technology faces limitations in delivering command-based driving styles, with existing methods either relying on predefined styles requiring expert input or data-driven techniques like Inverse Reinforcement Learning. Prior work relied heavily on expert input, making the style design process cumbersome and subjective, requiring frequent adjustments. Data-driven approaches use methods such as clustering and Inverse Reinforcement Learning to derive driving policies but require small amounts of driving data to match specific styles. Obtaining such data is particularly difficult in Robotaxi scenarios, leading to issues with style matching. The metrics used to quantify driving styles are diverse, and the inability to prioritize these metrics according to user preferences restricts the effectiveness of style matching. These methods are limited to selecting from existing styles and cannot customize a style based on user needs, known as the generalization problem. Foundation model approaches can adjust specific behaviors like speed and lane changes but fall short in adjusting the overall driving policy at the style level.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether Words2Wheels can automatically generate customized driving policies from natural language user commands without prior driving data. The framework proposes a Style-Customized Reward Function to bridge user input and a Style-Customized Driving Policy, with reward functions guiding the RL policy to optimize long-term rewards. The hypothesis is that by leveraging LLMs and RAG, Words2Wheels can generalize to new commands and styles without user behavior data due to zero-shot generation capabilities. The framework is predicted to outperform existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability, offering a novel solution for customized AV driving behavior.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on the car-following scenario using the HighD dataset collected by a 4K resolution camera mounted on a drone flying over a roadway. The data extraction and kinematic model for car-following behavior were based on FollowNet. To ensure objectivity of the Statistical Evaluation module, 15% of the data was reserved as a test set. User commands were categorized into three levels based on directness: Level I direct, Level II indirect with strong hints, and Level III indirect with mild hints. The Driving Style Database was populated with 8 initial styles, including data-driven reward functions derived using clustering plus IRL from [26] and human-designed rewards from [42], [47], [48]. Ten volunteers with valid driving license were recruited, each presented with 5 user commands and testing 20 events per command, totaling 1,000 tested events. The experiments followed the approach outlined in [54] for categorizing user commands across three levels of directness. The Statistical Evaluation module uses a reserved test dataset to collect relevant data and calculate metrics such as speed, acceleration, jerk, spacing, and time headway.

Procedures And Architectures
GPT-4o-2024-08-06 was used as the base LLM with the temperature set to 0.3 for deterministic text generation. In style selection, k = 3 relevant style rewards are selected from the database, and n = 2 statistical metrics are chosen in Statistical Evaluation. The process applies RAG principles where the LLM selects the top k relevant style rewards, which can be parallelized for efficiency. If no match is found, the LLM generates m new reward functions based on the most relevant Style Reward, producing new Style Policies via RL in parallel. For Style Policy generation from Style Reward, Proximal Policy Optimization was employed for training. Each RL training was run 5 times using different seeds, and the Style Policy with the highest reward was selected. The Statistical Evaluation module employs a Chain-of-Thought approach to select n relevant metrics and compare against natural data statistics provided in JSON format. The prompt includes a brief introduction to metrics and natural driving behavior statistics from the test set to provide a baseline. The LLM's generation goes beyond simple parameter adjustments and may involve logic modifications or restructuring to handle generalization challenges effectively.

Key Results
In human preference testing, Words2Wheels was judged as a better match to the user command than IDM in 72% of events, while IDM was preferred in only 9.2%. In 18.8% of events, both models were judged as equally effective by participants. For 'I’m going to be late for the date', 72% preferred Words2Wheels, 12.5% preferred IDM, and 15.5% were even. For 'I am getting car sick and prefer a smooth ride', 64% preferred Words2Wheels, 10.5% preferred IDM, and 25.5% were even. For 'Drive as fast as you can', 72.5% preferred Words2Wheels, 8.5% preferred IDM, and 19% were even. For 'Safety first. I have plenty of time', 79.5% preferred Words2Wheels, 3.5% preferred IDM, and 17% were even. For 'The cars behind us are honking, might be urging us,' 72% preferred Words2Wheels, 11% preferred IDM, and 17% were even. For 'I’m going to be late for the train,' the generated style exhibited higher speed, acceleration, and jerk, while for 'Safety first,' it showed greater spacing, time headway, and relative speed. The fuzzy memory function successfully recalled all associated driving styles except for the case involving 'It’s snowing and visibility has decreased.' Case studies across 40 commands showed 97.5% accuracy for Level I, 95% for Level II, and 92.5% for Level III, totaling 85% recall across all categories. In Case 26, the LLM intentionally selected the Style Reward with the highest jerk value as a counterexample. When acceleration and jerk values were negative, the LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition, indicating a gap in physics reasoning.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Words2Wheels is the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies to align with natural language user commands. The Driving Style Database acts as a repository that manages the increasing variety of driving styles and supports the automated policy customization, continuously expanding the style range. The framework reduces reliance on RL by using the Driving Style Database as a fuzzy memory, enhancing efficiency through recall of similar previous commands. The Statistical Evaluation module provides objective style evaluation, reducing biases from subjective judgments during policy assessment. The framework demonstrates that Style Rewards are less complex than user commands or traffic scenarios, enabling efficient retrieval of Style Policies.

Contradictions And Limitations
The aggressive style showed higher speeds and greater acceleration, but also a larger time headway, which aligned less well with expectations. The normal style showed higher jerk, possibly because the LLM did not prioritize these metrics correctly during generation. The LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition when acceleration and jerk values were negative, indicating a potential gap in physics-aware reasoning. The framework was tested only on the car-following scenario, limiting generalization to more complex driving tasks such as intersection navigation or lane changes. The number of commands in the generation test was limited to 4 styles for demonstration, and the full range of possible user commands was not explored. The randomization seed for the 5 RL training runs is not explicitly reported, making exact policy reproduction challenging. The training was run 5 times per command, but the specific convergence criteria and final policy hyperparameters are not fully detailed.

Claims
Words2Wheels automatically generates customized driving policies from natural language user commands without prior driving data, generalizing to new commands through zero-shot reward generation. The 40-command case study achieved 85-97.5% success across three levels of directness. Generation capability experiments demonstrated aligned styles (higher speed for 'late,' greater spacing for 'safety') when no matched style existed in the database. The fuzzy memory successfully recalled all associated styles except one snowing case, showing strong cross-command generalization. In Case 26, the LLM intentionally selected the Style Reward with the highest jerk value as a counterexample. Negative acceleration and jerk values led to interpretations conflicting with human intuition. Success rates dropped from 97.5% for Level I to 92.5% for Level III commands. The framework provides a scalable, data-efficient way to personalize AV driving behavior without large-scale style data collection. The approach could be extended to other robotic control tasks requiring style-aware policy generation from natural language.
Human users prefer Words2Wheels-generated driving styles over the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) for style-aware car-following. In 1,000 tested events with 10 volunteers, participants judged Words2Wheels as a better match in 72% of cases, while IDM was preferred in only 9.2%. For 'Safety first,' 79.5% preferred Words2Wheels versus 3.5% for IDM. For 'Drive as fast as you can,' 72.5% preferred Words2Wheels versus 8.5% for IDM. IDM was preferred in 9.2% of events, showing it still holds some preference among users. In 18.8% of events, the two models were considered equally effective by participants. The human preference was limited to 10 volunteers and 5 user commands, which may not generalize to all users and scenarios. The results validate the practical utility of style-customized policies in real-world user scenarios. The gap between Words2Wheels and IDM performance suggests room for further refining the policy generation and statistical evaluation.

Data And Code Availability
Code and demo are available at yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/, including implementation details and visual demonstrations.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
To ensure robustness, each command was run 5 times and averaged, with 5 RL training runs per command using different seeds. The PPO training was unstable at times, necessitating multiple runs to select the best policy with the highest reward. A reserved 15% test set was used to prevent overfitting and provided benchmarks for evaluation. The generation experiment limited the initial styles to 4 to better demonstrate the generation capability. For the fuzzy memory, 3 experimental sets with predefined memories were tested with 5 similar inputs each. In repeated experiments, sometimes the newly generated style was selected as the best suited, and sometimes the existing style was.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the workflow: Words2Wheels automatically generates customized driving policies in alignment with user commands. Figure 2 shows the Driving Style Database architecture, storing Style Rewards, Style Policies, and statistical features in JSON format. Figure 3 details the RAG-based command cognition, style matching, and style reward generation process. Figure 4 illustrates the Statistical Evaluation module comparing policy statistics to natural data from the test set. Figure 5 compares customized policies over style-aware metrics for three user commands (aggressive, normal, conservative). Figure 6 evaluates generated policies when no aligned styles were provided in the database. Figure 7 shows the User Interface of the visualization tool for comparing driving style alignment between two models. Table I defines three levels of user commands: Level I direct, Level II indirect with strong hints, and Level III indirect with mild hints. Table II summarizes human preference results across 5 commands and 10 volunteers, totaling 1,000 tested events. Table III presents case studies across 40 commands, showing performance metrics for Rational Priorities, Rational Metrics, Rational Retrieval, and Rational Generation. Table IV tests the fuzzy memory function with three experimental sets of similar commands.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is Words2Wheels, the first framework to automatically generate style-customized driving policies from natural language commands without prior driving data. 2. The strongest evidence is that in 1,000 human preference events, 72% of participants preferred Words2Wheels over IDM, and case studies achieved 85-97.5% success across three command levels. 3. The future path includes expanding to more complex driving scenarios beyond car-following, refining the Statistical Evaluation module, and incorporating a Feedback and Reflection module to improve reward functions.

It is predicted that Words2Wheels will outperform existing methods in accuracy, generalization, and adaptability."

methodological_details:
"The study focuses on the car-following scenario using the HighD dataset collected by a 4K resolution camera mounted on a drone. For the Statistical Evaluation module, 15% of the data was reserved as a test set. User commands were categorized into three levels based on directness: Level I direct, Level II indirect with strong hints, and Level III indirect with mild hints. The Driving Style Database was populated with 8 initial styles: some were data-driven reward functions derived using clustering plus IRL from [26], others were human-designed reward functions based on [42], [47], [48]. For the experiments, 10 volunteers with valid driving license were recruited, each presented with 5 user commands and testing 20 events per command, totaling 1,000 tested events."

procedures_and_architectures:
"The framework uses GPT-4o-2024-08-06 as the base LLM with temperature set to 0.3. In style selection, k=3 relevant styles are selected, and in Statistical Evaluation, n=2 metrics are chosen. The process follows RAG principles where the LLM selects top k style rewards from the database. If no match is found, the LLM generates m new reward functions based on the most relevant style. For Style Policy generation from Style Reward, Proximal Policy Optimization is employed, with training run 5 times using different seeds. The Statistical Evaluation module uses Chain-of-Thought reasoning to select n relevant metrics and compare with natural data statistics provided in JSON format."

summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary GX 9+9, an established atoll source, using the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) instruments aboard AstroSat. The source was observed on July 25, 2020 (Obs. ID: A09_018T01_9000003774), and was detected in the soft/banana state, characterized by a disk-dominated energy spectrum within the 0.7–25.0 keV range. The authors performed flux-resolved spectral analysis across three distinct flux levels (FL1: 450–570 counts/s; FL2: 570–650 counts/s; FL3: 650–770 counts/s), utilizing the simultaneous SXT and LAXPC data. The best-fit spectral model was identified as const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), with the thermal Comptonization model (ThComp) employed rather than the standard nThComp. Key spectral parameters including electron temperature (kTe), fractional scattering (fs), disk temperature (Tin), disk normalization (Ndbb), and inner-disk radius (Rin) were extracted for each flux level, along with total unabsorbed flux. The estimated average inner-disk radius during the observation was 16.57±1.29 km (referenced as 16.54±1.78 km in the conclusion), consistent with previous estimates of 27±4 km at a different distance and inclination. The timing analysis, performed solely on LAXPC data due to its high time resolution, utilized a multi-Lorentzian approach to the power density spectrum in the 0.003 Hz to 1 Hz frequency range. No quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) were detected; instead, a broad-band noise (BBN)-like feature was identified centered at ~0.1 Hz (with a characteristic frequency derived from a centroid frequency of ~0.04 Hz and half-width of ~0.09 Hz). The energy-dependent temporal modeling, based on the Garg et al. [29] propagative formalism, revealed that the fractional scattering and inner-disk temperature variations drive the observed BBN variability, with a positive phase lag (0.11±0.08) indicating perturbation moving towards the coronal region. The paper concludes that GX 9+9 is transitioning towards a softer state and emphasizes the need for further multi-mission observations due to the source's relatively under-studied status and the poor data quality of the individual observation.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a spectro-temporal investigation of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary GX 9+9, an established atoll source, using the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) instruments aboard AstroSat. The source was observed on July 25, 2020 (Obs. ID: A09_018T01_9000003774), and was detected in the soft/banana state, characterized by a disk-dominated energy spectrum within the 0.7–25.0 keV range. The authors performed flux-resolved spectral analysis across three distinct flux levels (FL1: 450–570 counts/s; FL2: 570–650 counts/s; FL3: 650–770 counts/s), utilizing the simultaneous SXT and LAXPC data. The best-fit spectral model was identified as const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), with the thermal Comptonization model (ThComp) employed rather than the standard nThComp. Key spectral parameters including electron temperature (kTe), fractional scattering (fs), disk temperature (Tin), disk normalization (Ndbb), and inner-disk radius (Rin) were extracted for each flux level, along with total unabsorbed flux. The estimated average inner-disk radius during the observation was 16.57±1.29 km (referenced as 16.54±1.78 km in the conclusion), consistent with previous estimates of 27±4 km at a different distance and inclination. The timing analysis, performed solely on LAXPC data due to its high time resolution, utilized a multi-Lorentzian approach to the power density spectrum in the 0.003 Hz to 1 Hz frequency range. No quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) were detected; instead, a broad-band noise (BBN)-like feature was identified centered at ~0.1 Hz (with a characteristic frequency derived from a centroid frequency of ~0.04 Hz and half-width of ~0.09 Hz). The energy-dependent temporal modeling, based on the Garg et al. [29] propagative formalism, revealed that the fractional scattering and inner-disk temperature variations drive the observed BBN variability, with a positive phase lag (0.11±0.08) indicating perturbation moving towards the coronal region. The paper concludes that GX 9+9 is transitioning towards a softer state and emphasizes the need for further multi-mission observations due to the source's relatively under-studied status and the poor data quality of the individual observation.

Research Context
GX 9+9 is a neutron star low-mass X-ray binary (NS-LMXB) identified during a sounding rocket mission. The source is an established atoll source tracing a ‘C’-pattern in the hardness-intensity diagram. Atoll sources exhibit two primary states: the hard island state at lower luminosities and the soft banana state at higher luminosities. The soft banana state is further classified into upper and lower states, with Comptonization dominating in the hard state and thermal disk emission in the soft. The source has a 4.2-hour X-ray and optical waveband modulation period. Distance is assumed to be between 5 kpc and 10 kpc, with compact NS mass of 0.2–0.45 M☉ and radius of 0.3–0.6 R☉. It is often detected in a luminous soft state with ~220 mCrab of X-ray flux in the 2–20 keV band. Previous spectral modeling included power law, blackbody plus Comptonization, disk plus Comptonized blackbody, and double blackbody with broad iron line. A simultaneous X-ray and optical timing investigation was previously conducted using SAAO and RXTE. The authors note that AstroSat’s LAXPC offers larger effective area and wider energy coverage compared to RXTE. GX 9+9 is not a well-studied source, necessitating more detailed investigation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is to study the spectro-temporal properties of GX 9+9 using AstroSat data and compare the constancy between spectral and temporal analyses. The authors attempt to estimate various source characteristics including inner-disk radius, flux, and inner-disk temperature. Based on the HID, the source was hypothesized to be in the soft banana state during the observation. The study hypothesizes that spectral parameter variations with increasing X-ray flux reflect a transition towards a softer state. The timing hypothesis is that BBN features, rather than QPOs, dominate the variability, and their radiative origin can be identified. The authors aim to identify the radiative origin of observed variability by modeling energy-dependent temporal properties. The study tests the consistency of spectral and temporal findings and compares estimated source characteristics with previously reported results.

Methodological Details
The study used the AstroSat Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) instruments. The single archival observation has Obs. ID: A09_018T01_9000003774 and was taken on July 25, 2020. LAXPC has three identical counters; however, counters 10 and 30 suffered abnormal gains since 2018, so only LAXPC 20 data was used. LAXPC operates over a wide energy band from 3-80 keV. SXT is an imaging instrument working in the low energy range of 0.3-8.0 keV. Good time interval data were extracted excluding South Atlantic Anomaly and Earth occultation-free regions. Scientific level-2 data were produced using the standard pipeline of LAXPC software version Oct. 13, 2022. SXT level-1 data were processed through AS1SXTLevel2-1.4b SXT pipeline to generate cleaned level-2 event files. The standard background file was SkyBkg_comb_EL3p5_Cl_Rd16p0_v01.pha and the response file was sxt_pc_mat_g0to12.rmf. SXT count rate exceeded the pileup threshold of 40 counts/sec during the observation. To mitigate pileup, an annular zone with outer radius 13 arcmin and inner radius 2 arcmin was used for SXT extraction. 2% model systematic error was incorporated for background uncertainty estimation. A gain fit was applied to SXT data with a slope of 1 and free offset parameter typically between 0.02-0.09. Both LAXPC and SXT spectrums were optimally grouped using ftool ftgrouppha. For timing analysis, only LAXPC data were considered due to high timing resolution of order of microseconds. The SXT and LAXPC data were used simultaneously for spectral analysis, with the combined energy range being 0.7–25.0 keV. The source flux was segregated into three distinct levels: FL1 (450–570 counts/s), FL2 (570–650 counts/s), and FL3 (650–770 counts/s). Spectral fitting used XSPEC (version 12.13.0c) with HEASOFT (6.31.1). The level of confidence for parametric errors was set at 90%. The source optical depth was frozen at 9 to constrain parameter estimation. Edge models for instrumental features at 2.4 keV were included for better fit. The source distance was taken as 10 kpc (D10 = 1), and inclination was fixed at 60 degrees for Rin calculation. The color-correction factor k was set to 1.7 in the Rin calculation.

Procedures And Architectures
The HID was constructed by plotting overall count rate in the 3–20 keV band against X-ray photon count ratio in 6–20 keV and 3–6 keV ranges. The best-fit spectral model was determined to be const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb) after the blackbody-only model gave reducedχ2 > 2. ThComp (thermal Comptonization) was used instead of nThComp as an improved version. 1000 log bins were used for the convolution model with  The 'const' parameter was used for cross-calibration, with LAXPC 20 spectrum as base (constant fixed at 1) and SXT constant free. The 'cflux' XSPEC model was used to estimate total unabsorbed flux in the extended 0.01–100 keV range. Inner-disk radius Rin was calculated using the formula Rin = k²(Ndbb/cosθ)^(1/2) * D10. The PDS was generated for the full flux in the 3–20 keV energy range over a frequency range of 0.003 Hz to 1 Hz. A multi-Lorentzian approach was used to fit the PDS at different flux levels. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected in individual FLs, so PDS of full flux was analyzed. The characteristic frequency νc was obtained from νc = √ (νo² + HWHM) with νo ≈ 0.04 Hz and HWHM ≈ 0.09 Hz. The RMS and phase lag spectra were obtained using the LAXPC subroutine laxpc_find_freqlag at the centroid frequency. The energy-dependent temporal modeling adopted the propagating model by Garg et al. [29] assuming truncated disk and hot electron corona. Soft seed photons originate from the truncated disk and are Comptonized in the coronal region. The temporal model fit was performed in rms and phase lag spectra, varying δkTin and δfs with time delay w.r.t. fs. The time lag was related to phase lag by time lag = phase lag / 2πf where f is the peak/central frequency.

Key Results
Based on the HID form, the source was confirmed to be in the soft banana state at the time of observation. For FL1, the spectral parameters were: NH = 0.16±0.01, kTe = 4.14±0.20 keV, fs = 0.14±0.02, Tin = 1.87±0.03 keV, Ndbb = 19.67±1.35, Rin = 18.18±0.62 km, with χ²/dof = 152.95/118. For FL2, the spectral parameters were: NH = 0.16±0.02, kTe = 4.12±0.26 keV, fs = 0.17±0.04, Tin = 2.02±0.06 keV, Ndbb = 16.07±1.68, Rin = 15.96±1.02 km, with χ²/dof = 103.86/111. For FL3, the spectral parameters were: NH = 0.16±0.02, kTe = 3.69±0.22 keV, fs = 0.34±0.10, Tin = 2.04±0.12 keV, Ndbb = 15.57±2.03, Rin = 15.50±1.92 km, with χ²/dof = 120.96/109. The full flux spectral parameters were: NH = 0.15±0.01, kTe = 4.17±0.20 keV, fs = 0.15±0.03, Tin = 1.95±0.04 keV, Ndbb = 16.96±1.15, Rin = 16.83±0.54 km, with χ²/dof = 130.33/117. The total unabsorbed flux in the 0.01–100 keV band was 5.94×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² for FL1, 6.51×10⁻⁹ for FL2, and 7.30×10⁻⁹ for FL3. The maximum unabsorbed flux of 7.30×10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² is comparable to 7.8×10⁻⁹ reported by Iaria et al. [12] in the 0.1–100 keV range. The average estimated inner-disk radius was calculated as 16.57±1.29 km from the formula (referenced as 16.54±1.78 km in the conclusion). This Rin is relatively consistent with the previously reported 27±4 km by Iaria et al. [12] (who used θ~43° and 5 kpc). A BBN-like feature was detected in the PDS centering at ~0.1 Hz, with a characteristic frequency νc ≈ 0.1 Hz derived from νo ≈ 0.04 Hz and HWHM ≈ 0.09 Hz. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected in the discrete FLs analyses. The energy-dependent temporal model yielded a reduced χ² of ~0.80 (6.39/8). The best-fit parameters for the temporal model were: δkTin = 0.56±0.10%, δfs = 81±32%, and phase lag = 0.11±0.08. The RMS at ~0.1 Hz increases with energy, while the phase lag shows a decreasing trend with energy. The positive phase lag value indicates that the variation in inner-disk temperature initially introduced the perturbation, which moved towards the coronal region as variation in the fraction of seed photons Comptonized. Further additional variations of parameters were not considered because of bad χ² values (>2).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The variation in spectral parameters with increasing X-ray flux (decreasing kTe, increasing Tin) suggests the source is transitioning towards a softer state. The fractional scattering and inner-disk temperature variations are identified as the causes of the broad-band noise variability, based on the Garg et al. [29] formalism. The positive phase lag confirms the propagation of perturbation from the inner disk to the coronal region, consistent with a truncated-disk/corona radiative model. The estimated Rin of ~16.54–16.57 km, though lower than the previously reported 27±4 km, is attributed to different assumed distance (10 kpc vs 5 kpc) and inclination (60° vs 43°). The propagating model has been successfully applied to GRS 1915+105, MAXI 1535-571, H 1743-322, and 4U 1608-52 to explain energy variability, reinforcing its applicability to GX 9+9. The constancy (or lack thereof) between spectral and temporal parameters helps constrain the radiative mechanism producing stochastic variability in atoll sources.

Contradictions And Limitations
The data quality was noted as poor, constraining the results. GX 9+9 is not a well-studied source, limiting the contextual comparisons available. The Rin value quoted in the text (~16.57±1.29 km) differs from the Rin value quoted in the conclusion (16.54±1.78 km). No QPOs were detected, which restricts the applicability of propagation models designed for QPOs. The phase lag error bars were consistent within data points, making reliance on the phase lag uncertain. The reduced χ² values in the spectral fitting (152.95/118 for FL1) are very high, indicating the model may not fully capture the spectral complexity. Additional variations of parameters were rejected due to bad χ² values (>2), limiting the model completeness. The study is constrained by a single archival observation, preventing time-resolved state transition analysis.

Claims
GX 9+9 is in the soft banana state and transitioning towards a softer state during the observation, evidenced by decreasing kTe and increasing Tin across flux levels. The HID form confirms the source was in the soft banana state at the time of observation. kTe decreases from 4.14 to 3.69 keV (FL1 to FL3) while Tin increases from 1.87 to 2.04 keV. The total unabsorbed flux increases from 5.94 to 7.30 × 10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² across the three flux levels. The high spectral reduced χ² values suggest the model may not fully describe the data. The source was not monitored over a long enough duration to confirm a state transition. The source's spectral evolution constrains the physics of accretion disk-corona coupling in atoll sources. Future multi-mission observations will be necessary to track state transitions more robustly.
The observed broad-band noise (BBN) at ~0.1 Hz is driven by variations in inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering, with perturbation propagating from the disk to the corona. A BBN-like feature was detected centering at ~0.1 Hz with νc ≈ 0.1 Hz. The temporal model yielded a positive phase lag of 0.11±0.08, indicating outward perturbation propagation. The reduced χ² for the temporal model was good at ~0.80 (6.39/8). The RMS at ~0.1 Hz increases with energy, consistent with propagating-perturbation expectations. The phase lag error bars are consistent within data points, making the trend less certain. The model was restricted to kTin and fs variations; additional parameter variations gave bad χ² (>2). The Garg et al. propagating model is validated as a physical description of BBN in atoll sources. The positive phase lag constrains the geometrical arrangement of the truncated disk and corona.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The blackbody-only spectral model (bbodyrad) was rejected as it gave reducedχ2 > 2 and was unable to explain observational data. The nThComp model was replaced by the improved ThComp thermal Comptonization model. The multi-Lorentzian approach was applied to different flux levels, but no QPOs or BBN were detected in individual FLs, necessitating analysis of full-flux PDS. Adding heating rate and optical depth variations to the temporal model resulted in insignificant χ² values (>2), justifying the selection of kTin and fs variations. The edge model at 2.4 keV was added to improve the fit.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the HID of the source with a binning time of 32s, plotting 3–20 keV count rate against X-ray photon count ratio in 6–20 keV and 3–6 keV, with each color representing different flux levels. Figure 2 displays the best-fit spectrum of FL1, FL2, and FL3 from top to bottom in the 0.7–25 keV energy range, with red and black points representing SXT and LAXPC 20 data, respectively. Figure 3 (left) shows the PDS fit with two Lorentzians, and Figure 3 (right) shows the energy-dependent temporal modeling of fractional RMS and phase lag for the representative FL1 segment. Table 1 presents the best-fit spectral parameters (NH, kTe, fs, Tin, Ndbb, Rin, χ²/dof) for each flux level and the full flux, as well as energy-dependent temporal modeling parameters (δkTin, δfs, phase lag, χ²/dof).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a spectro-temporal analysis of the atoll source GX 9+9 using simultaneous AstroSat SXT and LAXPC data, confirming the source is in the soft banana state and that its BBN variability is driven by propagating perturbations from the inner disk to the corona. 2. The strongest evidence is the energy-dependent temporal model achieving a reduced χ² of ~0.80, with a positive phase lag (0.11±0.08) and RMS energy-dependent trend consistent with propagation, and spectral parameters showing flux-dependent evolution consistent with a softer state transition. 3. The future path involves further multi-mission observations of the under-studied source GX 9+9 to confirm state transition dynamics, improve spectral parameter constraints, and explore the full range of variability characteristics beyond a single archival observation.

summary.title: Dense-TSNet: Dense Connected Two-Stage Structure for Ultra-Lightweight Speech Enhancement
summary.authors: Zizhen Lin, Yuanle Li, Junyu Wang, Ruili Li
summary.field_subfield: Speech Enhancement / Signal Processing (Ultra-lightweight)
summary.executive_summary: Dense-TSNet is an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement network designed to address the complexity and size bottlenecks of deep neural network-based models in resource-constrained environments such as edge devices. The core contribution is a novel Dense Two-Stage (Dense-TS) architecture that replaces dilated convolutions in the classic Two-Stage structure with a network composed entirely of densely connected Two-Stage modules. This dense connectivity is hypothesized to smooth the loss landscape in narrow lightweight models with fewer channels, preventing premature convergence and enabling better late-stage training. The architecture further incorporates the Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB), which captures global, channel, and local perspectives through three CNN-based sub-modules: a Large Kernel Extractor (LKE) for long-range low-frequency features, a Channel Attention (CA) module for channel reweighting, and a Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG) for local spatial modeling. The model is trained on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset with an FFT size of 400, window length of 400, and hop length of 100, using the AdamW optimizer for up to 1,000,000 steps with a batch size of 2. Evaluation metrics include PESQ (-0.5 to 4.5), CSIG, CBAK, and COVL (1 to 5). The proposed Dense-TSNet achieves a compact model size of approximately 14K parameters, making it the first speech enhancement model with approximately 10K parameters to the authors' knowledge. In comparative experiments against the classic Two-Stage baseline (6-channel, 14K parameters) and other lightweight models, Dense-TSNet achieves a PESQ of 3.05, CSIG of 4.51, CBAK of 3.58, and COVL of 3.86, outperforming the classic baseline and several existing lightweight approaches. An ablation study confirms that all three MVGB sub-modules and the Consistency Magnitude Loss improve performance over their respective ablations. A sensitivity analysis of the Metric Loss weight (λ2/λ1) reveals that while PESQ improves with larger weights, it introduces pseudohallucination distortion at higher values, leading the authors to default to the Consistency Magnitude Loss alone. Source codes will be released upon paper acceptance, and audio samples are available at the author's GitHub repository.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Dense-TSNet is an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement network designed to address the complexity and size bottlenecks of deep neural network-based models in resource-constrained environments such as edge devices. The core contribution is a novel Dense Two-Stage (Dense-TS) architecture that replaces dilated convolutions in the classic Two-Stage structure with a network composed entirely of densely connected Two-Stage modules. This dense connectivity is hypothesized to smooth the loss landscape in narrow lightweight models with fewer channels, preventing premature convergence and enabling better late-stage training. The architecture further incorporates the Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB), which captures global, channel, and local perspectives through three CNN-based sub-modules: a Large Kernel Extractor (LKE) for long-range low-frequency features, a Channel Attention (CA) module for channel reweighting, and a Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG) for local spatial modeling. The model is trained on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset with an FFT size of 400, window length of 400, and hop length of 100, using the AdamW optimizer for up to 1,000,000 steps with a batch size of 2. Evaluation metrics include PESQ (-0.5 to 4.5), CSIG, CBAK, and COVL (1 to 5). The proposed Dense-TSNet achieves a compact model size of approximately 14K parameters, making it the first speech enhancement model with approximately 10K parameters to the authors' knowledge. In comparative experiments against the classic Two-Stage baseline (6-channel, 14K parameters) and other lightweight models, Dense-TSNet achieves a PESQ of 3.05, CSIG of 4.51, CBAK of 3.58, and COVL of 3.86, outperforming the classic baseline and several existing lightweight approaches. An ablation study confirms that all three MVGB sub-modules and the Consistency Magnitude Loss improve performance over their respective ablations. A sensitivity analysis of the Metric Loss weight (λ2/λ1) reveals that while PESQ improves with larger weights, it introduces pseudohallucination distortion at higher values, leading the authors to default to the Consistency Magnitude Loss alone. Source codes will be released upon paper acceptance, and audio samples are available at the author's GitHub repository.

Research Context
Speech enhancement aims to improve speech quality and intelligibility in noisy environments for applications such as voice calls, video recording, and automatic speech recognition. Recent research inspired by TSTNN utilizes the Two-Stage (TS) architecture for deep feature extraction, reshaping and partitioning spectral data to address spectral distribution characteristics. TSNN also features an encoder-decoder with a dilated dense block that improves information flow stability and enhances local and large-scale feature dependency. In the time-frequency domain, some models focus solely on amplitude information while others enhance complex spectrograms to improve both amplitude and phase. CMGAN uses a dual-decoder structure for amplitude and complex spectrograms, and MP-SEnet directly estimates amplitude and phase spectrograms. Loss functions in speech enhancement typically compute the Lp-norm distance between estimated and target spectrograms, but MetricGAN addresses non-differentiable assessment metrics using learned evaluation metrics from a discriminator. Despite the strong performance of deep neural network-based methods, these come with increased model complexity, and new methods like Transformer or Mamba face challenges with optimized deployment operators. Research on single-channel speech enhancement models with around 10K parameters is still limited, underscoring the need for innovative approaches to develop effective models at this scale for practical applications in edge devices.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is: how can a speech enhancement model be designed with approximately 10K parameters that maintains competitive performance while overcoming the uneven loss landscape challenges inherent in narrow lightweight architectures? The authors hypothesize that replacing dilated convolutions in the classic Two-Stage structure with dense connections (the Dense-TS architecture) will smooth the loss landscape in narrower models, ensuring more robust refinement of the objective function in later training stages. A second hypothesis is that incorporating multi-view features—global, channel, and local—through a CNN-based Multi-View Gaze Block will enhance feature extraction capabilities without the deployment overhead associated with Transformers or Mamba. The authors predict that the proposed Dense-TSNet will achieve a compact model size of approximately 14K parameters while delivering performance competitive with or exceeding existing lightweight methods, making it suitable for resource-constrained environments. A third hypothesis concerns the loss function: while Metric Loss improves objective perceptual quality scores, its combination with consistency loss may introduce pseudohallucination distortion at high weights, suggesting that Consistency Magnitude Loss alone may be preferable for subjective perception.

Methodological Details
For experiments, the authors utilized the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset known for its high-fidelity utterances, segmented into two-second intervals for the short-time Fourier transform. The STFT employed an FFT size of 400, a window length of 400, and a hop length of 100 to convert the speech signal into the time-frequency domain. The training process was conducted with a batch size of 2, using the AdamW optimizer, and was carried out for up to 1,000,000 steps. Evaluation metrics include PESQ, which ranges from -0.5 to 4.5, and MOS-based metrics CSIG, CBAK, and COVL, each with a range of 1 to 5. The Dense-TSNet model has a size of only 14K parameters, making it the first speech enhancement model with approximately 10K parameters to the authors' knowledge. The classic Two-Stage architecture performs well with a channel count of 64 but faces limitations for ultra-lightweight networks with a narrow architecture that may cause uneven loss landscapes. The training curves compare the 6-channel version of the classic Two-Stage framework and the 4-channel version of the Dense-TS framework, both using the MVGB approach, to evaluate the hypothesis about the loss landscape. Source codes will be released after paper acceptance, and audio samples can be found at the author's GitHub repository.

Procedures And Architectures
The Dense-TSNet inputs only the magnitude spectrum and performs time-frequency feature extraction through the Dense-TS structure with the TS-MVGB. The Dense-TS structure replaces dilated convolutions in the Dilated Dense Block with Two-Stage modules, resulting in a network composed entirely of densely connected Two-Stage modules. Features are mapped to a high-dimensional space using 1×1 convolutions, and the dilated dense block is omitted in the encoder, proceeding directly to the Two-Stage feature extraction block. The TS-MVGB output is a serial connection of time-MVGB and freq-MVGB: TS-MVGBi(x) = freq-MVGB(time-MVGB(x)). Dense connections merge shallow and deep features, and a residual connection is added beyond the dense structure; the final output is 0.2 ∗skip_depth−1 + x. For each layer i in the Dense-TS: input channels Ci = dense channel × (i + 1) and output channels Cout = dense channel. The Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB) consists of three sub-modules: Large Kernel Extractor (LKE), Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG), and Channel Attention (CA). The LKE is composed of pointwise convolutions, Simple Gate, large kernel depthwise convolutions, Instance Norm, HardSwish, and pointwise convolutions. The LKE is divided into two branches: Channel Attention reallocates weights to each channel, while the LSG focuses on local information within the feature map. The LSG consists of depth-wise convolution, point-wise convolution, and Learnable-Sigmoid activation, inspired by the Learnable-Sigmoid activation function used in MP-SENet. Channel Attention reallocates weights to each channel, allowing the module to focus more on important channels while suppressing less significant ones. After each Two-Stage module, a convolutional layer as Adjust-Conv is used to adjust the channel count and further integrate time-frequency information. Features undergo L-Sigmoid activation and 1×1 convolution to decode the magnitude spectrum mask, which is then multiplied by the noisy magnitude spectrum to produce the network's output. The Consistency Magnitude Loss LMagConsis is defined as the expected squared minimum distance between the twice-STFTed speech magnitude spectrum and the clean speech magnitude spectrum. The Metric Loss uses the PESQ metric via a discriminator: LD = E∥D(Xm, Xm) - 1∥^2 + E∥D(Xm, Xconsis) - Q_PESQ∥^2, with LD = E∥D(Xm, Xconsis) - 1∥^2 as LMetric. The total generator loss is LG = λ1 LMagConsis + λ2 LMetric, with λ2 set to 0 by default.

Key Results
Dense-TSNet achieves a PESQ score of 3.05, CSIG of 4.51, CBAK of 3.58, and COVL of 3.86, outperforming the classic Two-Stage baseline (PESQ 2.96, CSIG 4.45, CBAK 3.58, COVL 3.78) with the same parameter count of 14K. Dense-TSNet achieves 356M MACs, which is slightly lower than the classic Two-Stage framework's 388M MACs, demonstrating improved efficiency with the same parameter count. Compared to TSTNN (0.92M parameters, PESQ 2.96), PHASEN (20.9M parameters, PESQ 2.99), MANNER-S-5.3GF (0.90M parameters, PESQ 3.06), CCFNet(Lite) (160K parameters, PESQ 2.87), and DeepFilterNet (1.78M parameters, PESQ 2.81), Dense-TSNet achieves superior PESQ with significantly fewer parameters. In the ablation study, removing the Large Kernel Extractor (w/o LKE) reduces PESQ from 3.05 to 2.79, CSIG from 4.51 to 4.31, CBAK from 3.58 to 3.47, and COVL from 3.86 to 3.61. Removing Channel Attention (w/o CA) reduces PESQ to 2.86, CSIG to 4.38, CBAK to 3.53, and COVL to 3.69. Removing the Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (w/o LSG) reduces PESQ to 2.97, CSIG to 4.46, CBAK to 3.57, and COVL to 3.79. Removing Consistency Loss reduces PESQ to 2.96, CSIG to 4.45, CBAK to 3.58, and COVL to 3.79, showing that the consistency loss provides a measurable improvement. The SSNR value for Dense-TSNet is 8.16, compared to 8.62 for w/o LKE, 8.91 for w/o CA, 8.69 for w/o LSG, and 8.79 for w/o Consistency Loss. In the loss function study, the only Consistency Magnitude Loss configuration (P=1) yields PESQ 3.05, magnitude error 0.022, phase error 2.56, and complex error 0.13. When P = 200 (λ2/λ1 = 200), PESQ increases to 3.28, but magnitude error rises to 0.057, phase error to 2.73, and complex error to 0.15. At P = 400 (λ2/λ1 = 400), PESQ drops to 3.04, magnitude error increases to 0.800, phase error to 3.95, and complex error to 0.41, with training reported to fail. The only complex loss configuration yields PESQ 2.60, magnitude error 0.075, phase error 2.73, and complex error 0.10. The training curves (Fig. 4) show that while the classic Two-Stage framework converges faster in the early stages, Dense-TSNet achieves better performance in the later stages, validating the smoother loss landscape hypothesis.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Dense-TS architecture is interpreted as providing a smoother loss landscape for narrow lightweight models, which prevents the early convergence to suboptimal solutions that plagues the classic Two-Stage structure when channel counts are reduced. The Multi-View Gaze Block's multi-perspective feature extraction is attributed to its ability to jointly capture long-range low-frequency features (LKE), channel-wise salient features (CA), and local spatial details (LSG) in a single pass. The choice of loss function underscores that while Metric Loss (PESQ-based) can improve objective scores, its unsupervised application in speech enhancement can introduce pseudohallucination artifacts, suggesting that direct consistency in the magnitude domain is sufficient for perceptual quality. The model demonstrates that an ultra-lightweight configuration (approximately 14K parameters) can achieve competitive speech enhancement performance, suggesting that architectural design (dense connections, multi-view attention) can compensate for reduced parameter capacity.

Contradictions And Limitations
The training curves show that the classic Two-Stage structure converges faster in the early stages than Dense-TSNet, though it ultimately reaches lower final performance. At P = 200, the PESQ score increases to 3.28 but a pseudohallucination distortion is introduced affecting perceptual quality, revealing a trade-off between objective metric improvement and subjective quality. At P = 400, training is reported to fail, indicating that the Metric Loss cannot be scaled indefinitely as a loss regularizer. The authors acknowledge that lightweight networks cannot fully fit complex multi-domain features due to having fewer parameters compared to state-of-the-art methods, a fundamental constraint they address through structural design rather than parameter scaling. The SSNR values in the ablation study show that removing LSG (SSNR 8.69) has a smaller impact than removing LKE (SSNR 8.62) or CA (SSNR 8.91), suggesting that local spatial modeling may be less critical than global or channel-wise features. The paper does not report on the specific random seeds, train-test split details beyond the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, or demographic information of any speakers, limiting reproducibility.

Claims
Dense-TSNet is the first speech enhancement model with approximately 10K parameters achieving competitive performance. The Dense-TSNet model has a size of only 14K parameters, which is the first to achieve a speech enhancement model with approximately 10k parameters to the authors' knowledge. In Table I, Dense-TSNet achieves PESQ 3.05, CSIG 4.51, CBAK 3.58, and COVL 3.86 with only 14K parameters and 356M MACs. The classic Two-Stage baseline requires 14K parameters and 388M MACs to achieve PESQ 2.96, CSIG 4.45, CBAK 3.58, and COVL 3.78. The MANNER-S-5.3GF model achieves a higher PESQ of 3.06 with only 0.90M parameters, although its CSIG (4.42), CBAK (3.58), and COVL (3.77) are lower than Dense-TSNet. The classic Two-Stage framework converges faster in the early stages than Dense-TSNet, although it ultimately reaches lower final performance. The result suggests that dense connectivity can mitigate the performance degradation typically seen in narrow lightweight architectures, enabling deployment on extremely resource-constrained edge devices.
The Dense-TS architecture smooths the loss landscape, enabling better late-stage training in narrow lightweight models. Fig. 4 shows that while the classic Two-Stage structure converges faster in early stages, Dense-TSNet achieves better performance in the later stages. The improvement is attributed to the smoother loss landscape provided by the dense connections in the narrower model. The 4-channel Dense-TSNet (14K parameters) achieves PESQ 3.05 compared to the 6-channel classic Two-Stage (14K parameters) achieving PESQ 2.96. The classic Two-Stage framework converges faster in the early training phases, which may delay convergence or require longer training for Dense-TSNet. Dense connectivity appears to be a viable alternative to increasing channel width for improving training dynamics in lightweight models.
The Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB) with its three CNN-based sub-modules captures complementary global, channel, and local perspectives for effective speech enhancement. Ablation results show w/o LKE (PESQ 2.79, SSNR 8.62), w/o CA (PESQ 2.86, SSNR 8.91), and w/o LSG (PESQ 2.97, SSNR 8.69), all significantly underperforming the full Dense-TSNet (PESQ 3.05, SSNR 8.16). The LKE establishes a global perspective, the CA reallocates weights to each channel, and the LSG focuses on modeling local information within the feature map. The LKE uses large kernel depthwise convolutions to provide a large receptive field to capture long-range low-frequency features. Removing CA (SSNR 8.91) has less of a negative impact than removing LSG (SSNR 8.69) or LKE (SSNR 8.62), suggesting the relative importance of these views may vary. CNN-based multi-view attention provides an efficient alternative to Transformer-based self-attention for both feature extraction and deployment convenience.
Consistency Magnitude Loss alone is sufficient and preferable to Metric Loss in this context. The only Consistency Magnitude Loss configuration yields PESQ 3.05, which is comparable to the full Dense-TSNet with Metric Loss included. At P = 200, the PESQ increases to 3.28 but a pseudohallucination distortion is introduced, affecting perceptual quality. At P = 400, training fails, and the PESQ drops to 3.04 with much higher magnitude error. The authors conclude: we do not employ LMetric in Dense-TS. The PESQ score increases with P (λ2/λ1), reaching 3.28 at P = 200, suggesting that Metric Loss does contribute to objective score improvement before artifacts appear. When objective metric improvement compromises subjective quality, the simplest sufficient consistency loss should be preferred in speech enhancement tasks.

Data And Code Availability
Source codes will be released after paper acceptance, and audio samples can be found at https://github.com/huaidanquede/Dense-TSNet. The experiments were conducted on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The ablation study on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset validates each component of the MVGB: removing LKE drops PESQ by 0.26, removing CA by 0.19, and removing LSG by 0.08. A sensitivity analysis of the loss function weight λ2/λ1 = P reveals that PESQ increases from 3.05 to 3.28 as P goes from 1 to 200, but magnitude error increases from 0.022 to 0.057. At P = 400, training fails and magnitude error reaches 0.800, with PESQ dropping to 3.04. The training curves in Fig. 4 show the 6-channel classic baseline vs. 4-channel Dense-TS, confirming the smoother loss landscape effect in later stages.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the overall architecture of Classic Two-Stage (a) and Dense-TS (b) frameworks, plus the serial Two-Stage modules (c) and Multi-View Gaze Block (d). Figure 2 details the internal components of the LKE, LSG, and CA within the Multi-View Gaze Block. Figure 3 illustrates the training criteria of Dense-TSNet with the Continuity Magnitude Loss and Metric Loss formulas. Figure 4 presents the training curves of Dense-TS and Classic-TS for PESQ and magnitude error, showing faster early convergence for Classic-TS and better late-stage performance for Dense-TSNet. Figure 5 shows the training curves of Dense-TS and Classic-TS at P = 200 (a) and LMagConsis only (b), with pseudohallucination distortion visible at P = 200. Table I compares Dense-TSNet (14K, 356M, PESQ 3.05) with the classic Two-Stage baseline (14K, 388M, PESQ 2.96) and five other lightweight methods. Table II reports ablation study results on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, showing the individual contributions of LKE, CA, LSG, and Consistency Loss. Table III compares loss function configurations, showing the PESQ, magnitude error, phase error, and complex error for Only Consistency Mag, P = 1, P = 200, P = 400, and Only complex.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a Dense Two-Stage architecture that uses dense connectivity instead of dilated convolutions in a Two-Stage framework to smooth the loss landscape in narrow lightweight models, achieving 3.05 PESQ with approximately 14K parameters, the first speech enhancement model at this scale. 2. The strongest evidence is the ablation study showing that all three MVGB sub-modules (LKE, CA, LSG) contribute significantly to performance, and the sensitivity analysis demonstrating that while Metric Loss can increase PESQ, it introduces pseudohallucination distortion at P = 200. 3. The future path is stated by the authors: we will continue to explore methods for further compressing model size.

summary.title: Recurrent Interpolants for Probabilistic Time Series Prediction
summary.authors: Yu Chen, Marin Biloš, Sarthak Mittal, Wei Deng, Kashif Rasul, Anderson Schneider
summary.field_subfield: Machine Learning / Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
summary.type_of_paper: Methodological paper with synthetic and real-world experiments
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes Recurrent Interpolants, a novel framework for probabilistic time series prediction that blends the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of diffusion-based stochastic interpolants. The authors extend the theory of stochastic interpolants to a general conditional generation framework with extra control features, enabling the model to condition on a large context window encoded by an RNN. The method addresses the scalability issues of standard generative models (whose model size depends on both feature dimension and window length) while capturing the sophisticated, high-dimensional distributions typical of time series. The framework is evaluated on synthetic two-dimensional datasets (8gaussians, Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll) using Wasserstein distance, and on four real-world multivariate forecasting datasets (Exchange rate, Solar, Traffic, Wiki) using Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS-sum). On real-world data, the SI-based model outperforms DDPM, SGM, and FM-based baselines on three out of four datasets, and outperforms the pure recurrent baseline (Vec-LSTM) on all four. A key theoretical contribution is Theorem 1, which extends stochastic interpolants to arbitrary joint distributions under a continuous-time interpretation, avoiding characteristic functions for a more user-friendly analysis. The method uses importance sampling with a Beta distribution to stabilize training over the diffusion time integral. Code will be made publicly available for the camera-ready version.

claims.description: The conditional stochastic interpolants method is a suitable generative module for probabilistic time series prediction, outperforming diffusion and flow-based baselines.
The RNN+SI framework achieves competitive performance by combining recurrent sequential modeling with generative diffusion.
Starting from an initial distribution proximate to the terminal data distribution improves generative model learning for time series.

top_influential_citations.Song et al., 2021: The score-based generative model (SGM) framework provides the score function formulation that is adapted into the SI architecture for time series prediction.

top_influential_citations.Lipman et al., 2022: The flow matching framework is used as a primary baseline, providing the vector field approach that contrasts with the SI velocity and score approach.

top_influential_citations.Ho et al., 2020: The DDPM framework (denoising diffusion probabilistic models) provides the standard diffusion baseline against which the SI method is compared.
