judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes Recurrent Interpolants, a novel framework for probabilistic time series prediction that blends the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of diffusion-based stochastic interpolants. The authors extend the theory of stochastic interpolants to a general conditional generation framework with extra control features, enabling the model to condition on a large context window encoded by an RNN. The method addresses the scalability issues of standard generative models (whose model size depends on both feature dimension and window length) while capturing the sophisticated, high-dimensional distributions typical of time series. The framework is evaluated on synthetic two-dimensional datasets (8gaussians, Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll) using Wasserstein distance, and on four real-world multivariate forecasting datasets (Exchange rate, Solar, Traffic, Wiki) using Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS-sum). On real-world data, the SI-based model outperforms DDPM, SGM, and FM-based baselines on three out of four datasets, and outperforms the pure recurrent baseline (Vec-LSTM) on all four. A key theoretical contribution is Theorem 1, which extends stochastic interpolants to arbitrary joint distributions under a continuous-time interpretation, avoiding characteristic functions for a more user-friendly analysis. The method uses importance sampling with a Beta distribution to stabilize training over the diffusion time integral. Code will be made publicly available for the camera-ready version.

Research Context
Sequential models like RNNs and Transformers are de facto tools for multivariate time series forecasting in a probabilistic fashion. Despite their ability to capture dependencies, challenges emerge in modeling high-dimensional complex distributions and cross-feature dependencies. Recent work addresses this by employing diffusion or flow-based generative models for probabilistic imputation and forecasting. However, scalability issues arise because generative model size depends on both feature dimension and window length, unlike recurrent models. Time series data points exhibit strong correlations, suggesting that future distributions are close to the current distribution. Previous studies support the idea that starting from an initial distribution proximate to the terminal data distribution alleviates learning challenges and reduces inference complexity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to combine the computational efficiency of RNNs with high-quality probabilistic modeling of the diffusion model for large-scale time series prediction. The hypothesis is that a generative model starting from an initial distribution proximate to the terminal data distribution will alleviate learning challenges and enhance sample quality. The authors propose that the longer temporal dependency can be encoded by an RNN while the generative model focuses on modeling the instantaneous distribution. The framework aims to offer a computationally friendly approach for generative model-based predictions where the model size is not proportional to the time window length.

Methodological Details
The study evaluates the method on several synthetic two-dimensional datasets including Circles, Moons, Rings, and Swissroll. These datasets are cited as coming from Chen et al., 2021 and Lipman et al., 2022. Real-world datasets include Exchange rate, Solar, Traffic, and Wiki, commonly used for probabilistic forecasting tasks. Preprocessing follows the steps in Salinas et al., 2019. Probabilistic forecasting is evaluated by Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS-sum), normalized RMSE, and point-metrics normalized deviance. Metrics calculation is provided by the gluonts package. For synthetic experiments, all models use the same neural networks and hyperparameters to ensure fair comparison. Training uses importance sampling with a Beta distribution to handle the integral over diffusion time. The context window length P is not explicitly specified, though it is referred to as the context window.

Procedures And Architectures
The architecture combines a recurrent neural network with a conditional stochastic interpolants module. The RNN encodes the context window xt−P:t−1 into a history prompt ht. The score and velocity functions depend on both the current state and the history prompt condition. The model learns a joint distribution p(xt+1, xt|xt−P:t−1) of the pair (xt+1, xt) given past observations. During inference, the RNN first encodes context into ht, then SI transports xt to the target distribution via the forward SDE. For multiple-step prediction, the step-by-step prediction is run recursively. The SI module is trained by minimizing velocity and score losses over diffusion time s ∈ [0, 1] sampled from a Beta distribution. The loss functions include velocity term Lb and score term Ls as defined in equations 15 and 16. The model uses the same neural networks for all generative baseline comparisons to ensure fairness.

Key Results
On synthetic datasets, SI achieves Wasserstein distances ranging from 0.12 to 0.75 across five datasets. Specifically, SI (sqrt, linear) achieves 0.59 on 8gaussians, 0.29 on Circles, 0.51 on Moons, 0.22 on Rings, and 0.37 on Swissroll. On the Exchange rate dataset, SI achieves 0.007±0.001 CRPS-sum, outperforming FM (0.009±0.001), DDPM (0.008±0.001), and SGM (0.008±0.002). On the Solar dataset, SI achieves 0.391±0.017 CRPS-sum, outperforming FM (0.419±0.027), SGM (0.364±0.029), and DDPM (0.359±0.061). On the Traffic dataset, SI achieves 0.133±0.002, while FM produces an extremely large value of 64.256±62.596. On the Wiki dataset, SI achieves 0.080±0.007, SGM 0.008±0.002, DDPM 0.084±0.023, and FM 0.108±0.026. Comparing to the pure recurrent model Vec-LSTM (0.133±0.002), SI and other generative models outperform it on all four datasets. Figure 4 demonstrates precise forecast paths on the Solar dataset with median prediction and 50th/90th confidence intervals.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The main theoretical contribution is Theorem 1, which extends stochastic interpolants to arbitrary joint distributions with a continuous-time interpretation. The framework benefits from the efficient training and computation inherited from RNNs while enjoying the high-quality probabilistic modeling of diffusion models. The approach is more natural for time series because it maps between dependent data points rather than from noise to data at each step. The model captures the uncertainty even when the scale of different dimensions varies significantly, as shown in the Solar forecast. The method guarantees that x1 follows the marginal distribution ρ1 and the sample pair (x0, x1) satisfies the joint density ρ(x0, x1).

Contradictions And Limitations
On the Traffic dataset, the FM model achieves 64.256±62.596, which appears as an outlier and may indicate training instability for flow matching on this dataset. The authors note that only on Traffic does FM achieve better performance, though this contradicts my reading of the table which shows SI is better. On Wiki data, FM cannot capture the data distribution, and the authors could not find satisfying flow matching hyperparameters. The SI (sqrt, trig) scheduler actually performs worse than SI (sqrt, linear) on all synthetic datasets, contrary to the statement that most combinations work well. The context window length P is not explicitly specified, and preprocessing details from Salinas et al., 2019 are not elaborated upon. The paper does not report specific training hyperparameters such as learning rate, batch size, or number of training epochs. The theorem proof in the appendix relies on continuous-time analysis that may differ from standard characteristic function-based SI proofs.

Claims
The conditional stochastic interpolants method is a suitable generative module for probabilistic time series prediction, outperforming diffusion and flow-based baselines. On three out of four real-world datasets, SI achieves better CRPS-sum than DDPM, SGM, and FM. SI outperforms FM on Exchange rate (0.007 vs 0.009), Solar (0.391 vs 0.419), and Traffic (0.133 vs 64.256). On the Traffic dataset, the FM score of 64.256±62.596 is extremely high, suggesting an issue with the FM baseline rather than a failure of SI. On the Wiki dataset, SGM achieves the best score (0.008±0.002), not SI (0.080±0.007). SI is a strong candidate for conditional generation in multivariate probabilistic forecasting tasks. The method can be extended to other conditional generation tasks beyond time series, such as image inpainting or imputation.
The RNN+SI framework achieves competitive performance by combining recurrent sequential modeling with generative diffusion. SI, SGM, and DDPM all outperform the pure recurrent model Vec-LSTM (0.133±0.002) on all four datasets. The framework captures the data distribution and provides meaningful confidence intervals, as shown in Figure 4. The performance gain over the pure recurrent baseline is small in some cases, e.g., on Exchange rate where SI (0.007) and Vec-LSTM (0.133) differ significantly in scale but both outperform FM. The authors do not report the exact magnitude of improvement over the recurrent baseline in a single consolidated metric. Generative models should be integrated with recurrent structures rather than used in-isolation for time series tasks. Carefully modeling the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction.
Starting from an initial distribution proximate to the terminal data distribution improves generative model learning for time series. The method maps between dependent data points rather than noise to data, which is more natural for continuous time series. The SI framework constructs a two-way generative SDE mapping from one distribution to another, maintaining dependency between x0 and x1. The paper does not provide an ablation study explicitly comparing starting from noise versus starting from the current time point to quantify the improvement. The FM baseline, which starts from noise, achieves 64.256 on Traffic, which may be due to dataset characteristics rather than the starting distribution. The approach can reduce inference complexity and improve sample quality by shortening the transport path. This principle can be generalized to any conditional generative task where the starting point can be anchored to prior data.

Data And Code Availability
The authors state that the code will be publicly available for the camera-ready version.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors test four gamma-interpolant function combinations: quad, sqrt, trig, and linear schedules for the SI model. They also explore both linear and cosine noise schedulers for diffusion-like models. The synthetic experiment is used to investigate properties with respect to varying data sizes, model sizes, and training lengths. The SI (sqrt, trig) configuration performs worse than SI (sqrt, linear) on all five synthetic datasets, contradicting the generalization claim.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the α(s), β(s), and γ(s) schedules of the stochastic interpolant, with examples of quad, sqrt, and trig gamma functions. Figure 2 presents the model diagram combining RNN context encoding with SI conditional generation, illustrating the flow from context to prediction. Figure 3 displays generated samples from DDPM, SGM, FM, and SI on Circles, Moons, Rings, and Swissroll datasets. Figure 4 shows forecast paths on the Solar dataset with median prediction and 50th/90th confidence intervals on 6 of 137 variate dimensions. Figure 5 illustrates the overall system architecture combining RNN, diffusion, and noise components for conditional time series prediction. Table 1 reports Wasserstein distance between generated samples and true data across 8gaussians, Circles, Moons, Rings, and Swissroll for eight model variants. Table 2 reports CRPS-sum scores for Exchange rate, Solar, Traffic, and Wiki datasets across four model families plus the Vec-LSTM baseline.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the combination of RNN efficiency for encoding temporal dependencies with stochastic interpolants for high-quality conditional generative modeling of the next time point distribution. 2. The strongest evidence is the CRPS-sum results on four real-world datasets, where SI outperforms FM on three out of four datasets and outperforms the pure recurrent baseline on all four. 3. The future path lies in extending the continuous-time SI framework to more complex conditional generation tasks beyond time series forecasting and generalising the conditional interpolation principle.

summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid (University of Milan-Bicocca); Nicolò Pianta (University of Milan-Bicocca); Simone Bonizzoni (University of Milan-Bicocca); Piercarlo Mustarelli (University of Milan-Bicocca); Riccardo Ruffo (University of Milan-Bicocca)
summary.field_subfield: Energy Storage / Electrochemistry (Aqueous Electrolytes)
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a comprehensive physicochemical and electrochemical characterization of highly concentrated aqueous binary acetate salt electrolytes (CH3COOK/CH3COONa) for use in sodium-ion battery applications. The authors systematically varied CH3COONa concentration (1–7 mol kg⁻¹) while keeping CH3COOK constant at 20 mol kg⁻¹, investigating thermal (DSC), rheological (viscosity), transport (conductivity), and electrochemical properties. The 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOK + 7 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COONa (7N20K) composition emerged as the optimal electrolyte, exhibiting a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C and a stability window up to 3 V under ideal conditions. Viscosity and conductivity measurements confirmed the 'water-in-salt' regime, with the 7N20K electrolyte maintaining a low liquidus temperature (implied by lack of crystallization at relevant cycle temperatures) and exhibiting a stability window on the cathodic side that suppresses hydrogen evolution. The electrolytes were classified as 'structure-making salts' with a glass transition temperature (Tg) that increases with salt concentration. For proof-of-concept battery application, carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) was used as an anode in the 7N20K electrolyte, delivering a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹ (vs. 96 mAh g⁻¹ cathodic), 96% average charge efficiency, 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles at 1C, and a charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV. In contrast, the same electrode in 1 M NaAc gave 96 mAh g⁻¹ cathodic / 36 mAh g⁻¹ anodic with 40% efficiency, highlighting the superiority of the WISE electrolyte. A diffusion coefficient of ~10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹ was calculated. The work establishes that highly concentrated acetate binary systems can achieve the conductivity, ESW, and kinetic performance required for practical alkaline-ion batteries, overcoming the limitations of less-soluble fluorinated salts and conventional dilute aqueous systems.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a comprehensive physicochemical and electrochemical characterization of highly concentrated aqueous binary acetate salt electrolytes (CH3COOK/CH3COONa) for use in sodium-ion battery applications. The authors systematically varied CH3COONa concentration (1–7 mol kg⁻¹) while keeping CH3COOK constant at 20 mol kg⁻¹, investigating thermal (DSC), rheological (viscosity), transport (conductivity), and electrochemical properties. The 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOK + 7 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COONa (7N20K) composition emerged as the optimal electrolyte, exhibiting a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C and a stability window up to 3 V under ideal conditions. Viscosity and conductivity measurements confirmed the 'water-in-salt' regime, with the 7N20K electrolyte maintaining a low liquidus temperature (implied by lack of crystallization at relevant cycle temperatures) and exhibiting a stability window on the cathodic side that suppresses hydrogen evolution. The electrolytes were classified as 'structure-making salts' with a glass transition temperature (Tg) that increases with salt concentration. For proof-of-concept battery application, carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) was used as an anode in the 7N20K electrolyte, delivering a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹ (vs. 96 mAh g⁻¹ cathodic), 96% average charge efficiency, 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles at 1C, and a charge transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV. In contrast, the same electrode in 1 M NaAc gave 96 mAh g⁻¹ cathodic / 36 mAh g⁻¹ anodic with 40% efficiency, highlighting the superiority of the WISE electrolyte. A diffusion coefficient of ~10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹ was calculated. The work establishes that highly concentrated acetate binary systems can achieve the conductivity, ESW, and kinetic performance required for practical alkaline-ion batteries, overcoming the limitations of less-soluble fluorinated salts and conventional dilute aqueous systems.

Research Context
Conventional non-aqueous organic carbonate electrolytes for Li-ion batteries suffer from low flashpoints, high melting points, high viscosities, and thermal instability of LiPF6 in the presence of moisture. The thermodynamic electrochemical stability window of pure water is limited to 1.23 V, and kinetic extension to 1.5 V using diluted salts remains insufficient to compete with organic counterparts. Early high-concentration strategies (e.g., McKinnon and Dahn, 1985) used LiAsF6 in PC, and the Water-in-Salt (WISE) concept was later established by Suo et al. at 21 mol kg⁻¹ LiTFSI, enabling a 3 V window. Fluorinated salts such as LiTFSI, NaFSI, and KOTF provide expanded stability windows but introduce environmental concerns due to severe oral/dermal toxicity and high costs. The lack of suitable, highly soluble, cost-effective salts at concentrations above 20 mol kg⁻¹ was identified as a major bottleneck for WISE implementation. Cost-effective and highly soluble salts include LiCl, CH3COONa (NaAc), and CH3COOK (KAc), with KAc recently investigated for potassium-ion batteries and supercapacitors. Previous reports by the group showed 32 mol kg⁻¹ KAc with 1 mol kg⁻¹ (CH3COO)2Zn enabling a 2.0 V Zn-MnO2 rechargeable cell, and 32 mol kg⁻¹ KAc with 7 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOLi with C-TiO2/LiMnO4. NASICON compounds offer stable structures with large ionic channels and low solubility, making them ideal for matching cell voltage to electrolyte ESW.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a binary aqueous acetate electrolyte with 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOK and variable CH3COONa (up to 7 mol kg⁻¹) can achieve the transport properties, thermal stability, and electrochemical window required for alkaline-ion batteries. The authors hypothesized that the water-in-salt regime would be achieved as salt concentration increases, characterized by a shifting glass transition temperature and reduced water activity. It was predicted that the most concentrated formulation (7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc) would provide the optimal balance between ionic conductivity and electrochemical stability. The hypothesis that sodium-ion intercalation into carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 could be demonstrated reversibly at about -0.7 V vs. SHE was tested as proof-of-concept. It was expected that the WISE electrolyte would improve anodic and cathodic capacity, charge efficiency, and capacity retention compared to the 1 M NaAc diluted electrolyte. The activation energy for charge transfer was expected to reflect good kinetic properties, with a low value supporting efficient ion transport.

Methodological Details
The electrolytes were prepared by dissolving 99% purity NaAc and KAc from Alfa Aesar in high-quality Milli-Q water (σ = 6.7 µS cm⁻¹) under sonication. Four binary electrolyte concentrations were tested: 1 N 20 K (1 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc), 2.5 N 20 K, 5 N 20 K, and 7 N 20 K, along with a 1 M NaAc control. The electrode material, carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 NASICON (CLTP), was synthesized via a one-pot route: 1.78 g NH4H2(PO4)3, 40 ml ethanol, 3.51 g Ti(OC4H9)4, 0.52 g CH3COOLi·2H2O, and 0.58 g C6H12O6. The mixture was stirred for 4 h at 55°C, heated to 80°C for gelation, dried under vacuum at 100°C, and calcined at 800°C for 6 h under argon flux. The ramp rate was 5°C min⁻¹ and gas flow 50 ml min⁻¹; pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 (LTP) was synthesized by omitting glucose. X-ray diffraction was performed using Rigaku Miniflex 600 (Cu Kα radiation) over 10° to 80° range with 0.02° step and 1 deg min⁻¹ scan speed. SEM analysis was conducted with Zeiss Gemini 450. Viscosity was measured with MCR Rheometer 102 (Anthon Paar) using a 50 mm parallel plate, shear rates 10–300 s⁻¹, at 10, 20, 30, and 40°C. DSC used DSC 1Star (Mettler Toledo) with STARe software over -120°C to 90°C: cooling 30 to -120 at 1°C min⁻¹, 5 min isotherm, then heating to 90 at 1°C min⁻¹. Conductivity was measured by EIS with a dip probe cell (two platinum foils, cell factor 1.04 cm⁻¹) under N2 flux, 1 Hz to 200 kHz, 25 mV amplitude, 5 to 70°C. For organic electrolyte benchmarking, PVDF:carbon black (8:1:1 wt%) slurries in NMP were cast on Al; active loads were ~2.4 mg cm⁻² (Li), ~2.7 mg cm⁻² (Na), ~1.7 mg cm⁻² (K). For aqueous measurements, carbon cloth current collectors were dip-coated; active material load was ~6 mg cm⁻². The NASICON electrodes were tested in 1.0 M LiPF6 in EC/DMC, 1 M NaClO4 in PC/FEC, and 0.8 M KPF6 in EC/DEC for organic benchmarks. ESW was estimated in flooded three-electrode cells: glassy carbon work, Pt mesh counter, double junction SCE reference. GCPL technique was used with 0.1 C, 0.5 C, 1 C, 5 C, 10 C cycling; 1C defined as 136 mA g⁻¹, corresponding to 2 alkaline ions. EIS for interface kinetics: 20°C to 70°C, 1 kHz to 100 kHz, 50 mV sinusoid, under N2 in Faraday cage.

Procedures And Architectures
The 7N20K electrolyte (20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc + 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc) was identified as the optimal water-in-salt formulation, balancing conductivity with a 3 V stability window. DSC analysis identified the glass transition (Tg) below -70°C, cold crystallization (Tc) below -20°C, and melting (Tm) around 0°C for the electrolyte solutions. Ionic conductivity vs. temperature followed VTF behavior: σ(T) = A T^(α-1) exp(Ea/kBT), where α is the fragility parameter. Molar conductivity (Λm) vs. fluidity (η⁻¹) plots confirmed all electrolytes as quasi-ideal, with the 7N20K solution following Kohlrausch's law at 25°C (Λo = 52.90 ohm⁻¹ cm² mol⁻¹). Viscosity measurements followed Arrhenius behavior: η = η_inf exp(Ea/RT), consistent with the VTF-described ionic transport. For the electrode/electrolyte interface, the EIS spectra exhibited a depressed semicircle followed by a straight Warburg line, with a charge-transfer activation energy and a diffusion coefficient calculated from the Warburg coefficient. The NASICON electrode (rhombohedral, R-3c space group, JCPDS 35-0754) was designed for Na⁺ intercalation at approximately -0.7 V vs. SHE.

Key Results
The 7N20K electrolyte exhibited an ionic conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C, preserving a level comparable to organic counterparts despite the 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc addition. DSC revealed Tg shifted to higher temperatures with increasing salt concentration, confirming the transition to the water-in-salt regime for the acetate binary. The 5N20K electrolyte showed a cold crystallization exotherm at -28.06°C and the 7N20K electrolyte at -33.70°C, while 1N20K and 2.5N20K remained in the glassy state throughout the DSC cooling protocol. In ideal conditions (small surface area, electrocatalytic electrode in flooded cell), the 7N20K electrolyte showed an electrochemical stability window up to 3 V. The electrochemical stability window expanded notably on the cathodic side with increasing salt concentration, confirming suppression of hydrogen evolution by reduced water activity. In a sodium-ion battery proof-of-concept using CLTP/7N20K, the first cycle showed anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, cathodic capacity of 104 mAh g⁻¹, and an average charge efficiency of 96%. At a cycling rate of 1C (136 mA g⁻¹), the CLTP/7N20K interface provided an average anodic specific capacity of 68 mAh g⁻¹ with 99.0% average charge efficiency. After 60 cycles at 1C, the CLTP/WISE interface maintained 90% capacity retention. In comparison, the CLTP in 1 M NaAc (diluted) gave cathodic capacity of 96 mAh g⁻¹ and anodic of 36 mAh g⁻¹ (40% efficiency), demonstrating that WISE electrolyte enhanced specific capacity by approximately 2.3 mAh g⁻¹ (anodic) and 68 mAh g⁻¹ (cathodic). The charge transfer activation energy for the NASICON/electrolyte interface was calculated as 0.12 eV, indicating very good kinetic properties. The calculated diffusion coefficient at room temperature was ~10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹, consistent with literature reports for similar systems. The Kohlrausch law of strong electrolytes at 25°C yielded a molar conductivity at infinite dilution of 52.90 ohm⁻¹ cm² mol⁻¹ for the acetate system.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The shift of Tg with increasing concentration is attributed to growing ion-ion and ion-solvent interactions, characterizing the transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt. The acetate electrolytes behaved as 'structure-making salts' because no sample exhibited a decrease in viscosity with increasing salt concentration, signifying reduced water activity. The formation of an internal liquid structure, where available water cannot effectively shell cations, promotes direct anion-cation interaction and modifies local hydrogen bonding. The VTF behavior and Arrhenius viscosity indicate that ionic transport and bulk rheology are governed by correlated molecular mechanisms, and the electrolyte remains quasi-ideal. The low liquidus temperature of the 7N20K electrolyte compared to fluorinated alternatives (35°C–50°C) provides a practical operational advantage for preventing cell failure due to salt crystallization. The NASICON structure (rhombohedral) with large channels accommodates alkaline ions efficiently, and the preferential introduction of Na⁺ over K⁺ in a mixed electrolyte is justified by the smaller ionic radius. The results demonstrate that a 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc base with up to 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc can deliver the performance required for alkaline-ion batteries without the toxicity/cost of fluorinated salts. The study establishes that aqueous acetate systems can reach the WISE regime with practical concentrations (27 mol kg⁻¹ total) that exceed the 21 mol kg⁻¹ LiTFSI benchmark while maintaining 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ conductivity.

Contradictions And Limitations
The ESW measurement uses a large amount of electrolyte and a quasi-ideal electrocatalytic electrode with a small surface area, which may lead to overestimated decomposition limits. The paper does not report the exact salt composition (KAc/NaAc molar ratio) at which the maximum achievable ESW is reached, only the 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc point. The 7N20K electrolyte showed a stability window of up to 3 V in 'ideal' conditions, but the practical operating window is not quantified in a full cell. No information on electrolyte decomposition product analysis or passivation layer formation on the NASICON surface is provided. The EIS measurements were performed on a partially sodiated electrode, and the number of mobile ions was estimated (n = 1.7), which adds uncertainty to the diffusion coefficient calculation. The study does not include a comprehensive aging study beyond 60 cycles, nor does it characterize electrolyte degradation products over time. The temperature range for EIS (20–70°C) and conductivity (5–70°C) is limited; extrapolation of VTF parameters beyond this range may be unreliable. The paper lacks a direct comparison of the 7N20K electrolyte with other WISE systems (e.g., LiTFSI-based) under identical cell conditions, other than the cited Reber et al. liquidus values.

Claims
The 7N20K (20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc + 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc) electrolyte is the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability for sodium-ion batteries. The electrolyte exhibits a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C, comparable to organic counterparts. The electrochemical stability window extends to 3 V under ideal conditions. DSC confirms the Tg shifts to higher temperatures, signifying the water-in-salt regime. Viscosity measurements confirm the electrolyte is a structure-making salt. The stability window of 3 V is only achievable under 'ideal' conditions with a small surface area and electrocatalytic electrode. The 7N20K electrolyte can serve as a drop-in replacement for organic electrolytes in sodium-ion batteries with comparable performance and enhanced safety. The 3 V window, combined with the low-potential NASICON anode, enables a viable cell voltage for energy storage applications.
The carbon-coated NASICON electrode demonstrates reversible alkaline-ion intercalation with excellent kinetics and capacity retention in the 7N20K electrolyte. First cycle anodic capacity is 85 mAh g⁻¹ with 90% retention after 60 cycles. Charge transfer activation energy is a very low 0.12 eV. Diffusion coefficient is ~10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹, consistent with literature. The aqueous electrolyte improves the diffusion of alkaline ions inside the electrode structure. The number of mobile ions (n = 1.7) is an estimate, introducing uncertainty in the diffusion coefficient calculation. The 7N20K concentration has 2.85 times lower sodium concentration than potassium concentration, yet sodium is preferentially inserted. NASICON-based electrodes are compatible with highly concentrated aqueous electrolytes for alkaline-ion batteries. The very good kinetic properties suggest efficient rate capability and fast charging potential.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information files are available free of charge, including shear stress vs. shear rate curves, XRPD patterns, SEM images, and thermal analysis data. Additional electrochemical characterization of NASICONs in organic electrolytes is included in the Supporting Information. There is no explicit mention of code availability (e.g., for EIS modeling, VTF fitting, or diffusion calculations).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A comparative control of 1 M NaAc was tested against the 7N20K electrolyte to isolate the effect of concentration on capacity and efficiency. Pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 (LTP) was synthesized without C6H12O6 to serve as a control for the carbon-coating effect. XRD of both LTP and CLTP confirmed phase purity with no crystalline secondary phases. EIS was measured in a Faraday cage to avoid interference from the surrounding environment. The VTF behavior was verified across the temperature range, and consistency between DSC-derived Tg and VTF-derived T₀ was checked. Walden plots at different temperatures (Figure 4a) confirmed quasi-ideal electrolyte behavior, with the ideal dissociation line as a reference.

Ethical Considerations
The paper does not discuss ethical considerations, animal studies, or human subject protections.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows DSC thermograms with ENDO direction bottom, showing Tg < -70°C, Tc < -20°C, and Tm ≈ 0°C for all electrolytes. Figure 2a displays ionic conductivity vs. temperature for all concentrations, following VTF behavior; Figure 2b shows conductivity decreasing with concentration. Figure 3a reports viscosity vs. temperature following Arrhenius behavior; Figure 3b shows viscosity evolution over temperature. Figure 4a shows molar conductivity vs. fluidity (η⁻¹) at different temperatures, with the ideal line as reference; Figure 4b shows Kohlrausch's law fit at 25°C. Figure 5 presents LSV profiles vs. SHE for all electrolyte samples, with a 0.1 mA cm⁻² threshold for water decomposition. Figure 7a shows preferential sodium insertion in CLTP in 7N20K; Figure 7b shows superior capacity and efficiency in 7N20K vs. 1 M NaAc. Figure 8 displays EIS spectra (depressed semicircle + Warburg line); Figure 9 shows the Arrhenius plot of charge transfer resistance. Table 1 lists all electrolytes with compositional parameters; Table 2 reports molar conductivities, activation energies, T₀, Tg, and DSC liquidus data. Table 3 summarizes anodic and cathodic decomposition potentials (in mV) for all samples under the ideal cell conditions.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of the 7N20K (20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc + 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc) binary electrolyte as a practical water-in-salt system that combines a 3 V stability window with 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ conductivity and no salt crystallization at cycling temperatures, making it viable for sodium-ion batteries without fluorinated salts. 2. The strongest evidence is the combined suite of DSC (Tg shift, low liquidus), Arrhenius viscosity (structure-making behavior), VTF conductivity (quasi-ideal behavior), and the 85 mAh g⁻¹ anodic capacity with 90% retention and 0.12 eV activation energy in a practical NASICON/electrolyte interface. 3. The future path lies in expanding the 7N20K electrolyte design to different cation/anion combinations (e.g., K+/Li+ or Zn2+/Na+), performing full cell cycling studies, and developing multi-electrode systems with NASICON-based cathode materials to achieve complete sodium-ion battery architectures.

summary.title: Freeze-Float System for High-throughput Measurement of Ice Nucleation
summary.authors: Yuki Kamijo (The University of Tokyo); Ratmir Derda (University of Alberta)
summary.field_subfield: Physics / Cryobiology - Ice Nucleation - Freeze-float Assay
summary.type_of_paper: Methodology and system development paper (extension of a proof-of-concept)
summary.executive_summary: This paper develops a high-throughput freeze-float selection platform for ice nucleation measurement, expanding on a previous proof-of-concept implementation that accommodated 50 1 µL droplets in a 1 cm² cuvette. The authors address the limitation of thermal lag in larger silicone oil containers by transitioning to 48 cryovials each capable of holding 40 droplets, increasing throughput by a factor of 38 to 1920 droplets per experiment. Key methodological innovations include automated droplet generation using the Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handler, achieving 30 1 µL droplets dispensed at 1 droplet per 2 seconds, and controlled-rate cooling using the Asymptote VIA freezer at -0.5 °C/min. Droplet monodispersity was confirmed at 9.2% (standard deviation of radii 2.86×10⁻⁵ m over mean 3.10×10⁻⁴ m), equating to ≤ ±0.09 °C expected dispersion in nucleation temperature via the Swanson approximation. In the 96-deep-well plate system, the cell-to-cell thermal gradient was reduced from a p-value of 4.4×10⁻⁷ under constant cooling to p = 0.31 under linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min). With the Asymptote freezer, the interwell freezing temperature dispersion was further reduced to p = 0.83 with a standard deviation of 0.73, representing 36% lower overall dispersion compared to the 96-well plate system (p = 0.31, σ = 1.6). Ice nucleation was detected at -7.1 ±0.59 °C in INA-containing droplets versus -12.3 °C in INA-free droplets, confirming consistent behavior with previous experiments while demonstrating improved detection accuracy. The paper notes that while throughput increased significantly, droplet stability during transport was insufficient due to static electricity caused by the Biomek 3000, preventing successful off-site system integration. The conclusion section is partially truncated in the text, but the work establishes a scalable, validated platform for high-throughput ice nucleation assays.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper develops a high-throughput freeze-float selection platform for ice nucleation measurement, expanding on a previous proof-of-concept implementation that accommodated 50 1 µL droplets in a 1 cm² cuvette. The authors address the limitation of thermal lag in larger silicone oil containers by transitioning to 48 cryovials each capable of holding 40 droplets, increasing throughput by a factor of 38 to 1920 droplets per experiment. Key methodological innovations include automated droplet generation using the Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handler, achieving 30 1 µL droplets dispensed at 1 droplet per 2 seconds, and controlled-rate cooling using the Asymptote VIA freezer at -0.5 °C/min. Droplet monodispersity was confirmed at 9.2% (standard deviation of radii 2.86×10⁻⁵ m over mean 3.10×10⁻⁴ m), equating to ≤ ±0.09 °C expected dispersion in nucleation temperature via the Swanson approximation. In the 96-deep-well plate system, the cell-to-cell thermal gradient was reduced from a p-value of 4.4×10⁻⁷ under constant cooling to p = 0.31 under linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min). With the Asymptote freezer, the interwell freezing temperature dispersion was further reduced to p = 0.83 with a standard deviation of 0.73, representing 36% lower overall dispersion compared to the 96-well plate system (p = 0.31, σ = 1.6). Ice nucleation was detected at -7.1 ±0.59 °C in INA-containing droplets versus -12.3 °C in INA-free droplets, confirming consistent behavior with previous experiments while demonstrating improved detection accuracy. The paper notes that while throughput increased significantly, droplet stability during transport was insufficient due to static electricity caused by the Biomek 3000, preventing successful off-site system integration. The conclusion section is partially truncated in the text, but the work establishes a scalable, validated platform for high-throughput ice nucleation assays.

Research Context
The previous publication reported a first proof-of-concept implementation of the freeze-float selection system. The system accommodated up to 50 1 µL droplets at once in a 1 cm² geometry cuvette. The cuvette separated samples having ice-nucleating activity from those without. Due to the low thermal conductivity of silicone oil, scaling the container footprint introduced significant thermal lag. Setting up more than 5-10 cuvettes in the same freezer resulted in non-uniform results with differences of a few degrees. High-throughput screening (HTS) in multi-well plates for biochemical assays is a well-established method. HTS was originally developed for drug discovery in the pharmaceutical industry. The transition to HTS results in shortened screening time, reduced sample volume, and lower overall costs. Miniaturization using 3456-well microtiter plates enabled over 100,000 assays per day with volumes under 5 µL. Automated liquid dispensing and plate handling robotics further increased throughput and reproducibility. Droplets-based assays offer chemical and physical compartmentalization to avoid cross-contamination of samples. Droplet microfluidic assays showed a million-fold reduction in reagent consumption and 300-fold throughput increase over HTS-multiwell assays. Droplet-based assays have measured tens of thousands of ice nucleation events at one experiment. Polydispersity is detrimental in ice-nucleation studies because the freezing temperature is directly proportional to the logarithm of droplet diameter. Swanson and co-worker showed droplet diameter and homogeneous freezing temperature can be expressed as y = ln(x) - 26.8. This approximation yields a 2.3 °C difference between 1 mm and 0.1 mm diameter droplets.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central goal was to expand the freeze-float selection system to higher throughput and accuracy. Increased efficiency of screening with fewer manipulation steps was a stated functional advantage. Increased accuracy of measurement via increased sample size was targeted. Increased uniformity of temperature distribution by incorporating the controlled-rate freezer was a stated advantage. It is hypothesized that droplet freezing is a random nucleation process accelerated by ice nucleators. Stochastic freezing behavior results in inherent distributions with spread freezing temperature even among identical droplets. Expanding the vessel from a 1 cm² footprint cuvette with 50 droplets to 48 cryovials with 40 droplets each increases throughput by a factor of 38. A controlled-rate freezer at -0.5 °C/min is hypothesized to improve cell-to-cell temperature uniformity. More than 30 droplets are concluded sufficient to observe a reliable freezing temperature. The confidence interval formula n ≈ (2k CI / σ)² with k = 1.96 for 95% confidence was used. Linear cooling at -0.25 °C/min is hypothesized to reduce cell-to-cell thermal gradients in the 96-deep-well plate system. The controlled-rate cooling system is expected to provide better INA detection compared to the commodity freezer freeze-float.

Methodological Details
30 1 µL droplets were dispensed into the silicone oil layer of a 96 deep well plate. The Biomek 3000 (Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, IN) robotic liquid transfer system enabled automated parallel droplet generation. Droplets were dispensed at a standard rate of 1 droplet per 2 seconds. Up to 40 uniform droplets were generated in each of 96 wells, reaching ~3800 droplets at once in ~15 minutes. For dispersion testing, 60 1 µL droplets were prepared with fluorescein dye in a 12 well plate filled with silicone oil. Fluorescent images were acquired by ChemiDoc MP (Bio-Rad, CA). Droplet diameters were measured using Matlab automated circle detection program Droplet_Dispersion.m. The polydispersity was defined as the standard deviation of the radii of the droplets divided by the mean radius. The measured standard deviation of the radii was 2.86×10⁻⁵ m and the mean radius was 3.10×10⁻⁴ m. The calculated polydispersity was 9.2%, indicating sufficiently uniform volume for the robotic system. Based on the Swanson relation, no more than ±0.09 °C dispersion in nucleation temperature was expected. HFE-7500 was always placed at the bottom of the system as a cushion layer to avoid droplet destabilization. The Biomek 3000 static electricity was removed using Auto-set Ion Pump #19500 (Charles Water, MA). Wet filter paper was placed below the plastic plate to minimize static accumulation during droplet system movement. 48 cryovials, each with 50 µL HFE-7500 cushion layer, 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant, and 20 aqueous droplets. Each cryovial contained 20 droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax marked with fluorescein dye and 20 droplets of INA-free milli Q water marked with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye. The Asymptote VIA freezer accommodated up to 48 cryovials in an instrument-specific metal holder. A custom-made glass lid enabled automated image recording by a generic digital camera.

Procedures And Architectures
Droplet generation was performed by Biomek 3000, replacing manual repeat pipetting from the previous report. Simple modification to the Biomek program allowed changing droplet number and size parameters. The 96 deep well plate was compatible with the robotic liquid handling machine. A 96-well validation experiment used 30 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax colored with yellow fluorescein dye in a 96 deep well system. The droplet freezing and floating behavior was recorded using a commodity freezer from the previous publication. Python script KStest.ipynb was used to compare freezing temperature distributions from two different samples. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was employed to show if freezing temperature profiles were drawn from the same distributions. For the 96-well plate, constant temperature was set to -28 °C in a generic freezer. Linear cooling was performed at -0.25 °C/min. The Asymptote VIA freezer (Asymptote, Cambridge, UK) provided high accuracy control and constant rate cooling down to -0.5 °C/min. Each cryovial contained 50 µL HFE-7500 cushion layer, 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant floating layer, and 20 droplets with INA (1 mg/mL Snomax) and 20 INA-free droplets. The controlled cooling rate was applied through the cryovials in the metal holder. The Asymptote freezer accommodated up to 48 cryovials. The custom-made glass lid enabled automated image recording by a generic digital camera. For the validation experiment, INA droplets were marked with yellow fluorescein dye and INA-free droplets with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye.

Key Results
The Biomek 3000 successfully prepared 30 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax in a 96 deep well system. The INA droplets showed droplet freezing behavior with good agreement with the previous report. In the 96 deep well plate at constant temperature -28 °C, the freezing temperature showed a p-value of 4.4×10⁻⁷, indicating significant well-to-well variation. With linear cooling at -0.25 °C/min, the cell-to-cell thermal gradient was decreased to p = 0.31. The mean freezing times between cells under linear cooling were 47.4 and 50.6 min, increasing the freezing time range. In the Asymptote freezer, INA droplets froze at -7.1 ±0.59 °C, while INA-free droplets did not freeze until -12.3 °C. The mean freezing temperature in the commodity freezer was -7.5 ±0.97 °C, suggesting the controlled cooling rate provided better INA detection. In the 96 deep well system, well-to-well variability and interwell dispersion in freezing time showed p = 0.31 with standard deviation 1.6. In the Asymptote freezer, the distribution of freezing showed less well-to-well freezing temperature difference with p = 0.83 and standard deviation 0.73. The Asymptote freezer showed 36% lower overall dispersion in freezing temperature compared to the 96-well plate system. The Asymptote freezer accommodated 48 cryovials, each containing 40 droplets, increasing throughput by a factor of 38.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The stochastic nature of ice nucleation, with inherent freezing temperature distributions among identical droplets, necessitates a large sample size for reliable temperature determination. The increased sample size of 1920 droplets per experiment (vs 50 in the previous publication) enhances the precision of freezing temperature measurement and INA detection. Controlled linear cooling reduces the cell-to-cell thermal gradient, mitigating the non-uniform temperature results caused by the low thermal conductivity of silicone oil. The controlled cooling rate at -0.5 °C/min in the Asymptote freezer provides better INA differentiation compared to commodity freezer freeze-float. The findings support the freeze-float selection paradigm as a scalable, high-throughput approach for ice nucleation measurement. The method establishes that uniform droplet generation via automated pipetting and controlled cooling are sufficient conditions for high-throughput ice nucleation assays.

Contradictions And Limitations
The low thermal conductivity of silicone oil limits the cuvette footprint and introduces non-uniform temperature distribution when multiple cuvettes are used. Static electricity from the Biomek 3000 caused droplet coalescence during system transport, preventing successful off-site use. In the 96 deep well plate system, linear cooling reduced the thermal gradient (p = 0.31) but increased the range of freezing times, with mean freezing times of 47.4 and 50.6 min. The droplets generated by the robotic system had a polydispersity of 9.2%, and while expected dispersion was ≤ ±0.09 °C, the actual measurements may be limited. The paper's conclusion section is truncated in the text, leaving the final quantification of INA detection accuracy incomplete. The authors note that when the system needs to be transferred a certain distance, droplet stability was not sufficient. The paper does not report the exact random seed or specific calibration details beyond model and hardware names.

Claims
The Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handling system enables automated, uniform, and high-throughput droplet generation for ice nucleation assays. Biomek 3000 dispensed 30 1 µL droplets into a 96 well plate at 1 droplet per 2 seconds. The system generated 40 uniform droplets per well, reaching ~3800 droplets in ~15 minutes. Droplet polydispersity was measured at 9.2% with standard deviation of radii 2.86×10⁻⁵ m. The expected freezing temperature dispersion was no more than ±0.09 °C. Droplet stability was not sufficient during transport, with static electricity causing coalescence. The paper notes it was not successful to combine the droplets generation system for off-site use. Automated droplet generation reduces manipulation steps and increases throughput. The Biomek 3000 is compatible with multiple multi-well plate geometries.
The Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer provides uniform cell-to-cell cooling and improved ice-nucleation detection accuracy. The Asymptote freezer reduced cell-to-cell thermal gradient from p = 4.4×10⁻⁷ to p = 0.31. The Asymptote freezer showed 36% lower overall freezing temperature dispersion than the 96-well plate system. The interwell freezing temperature difference in the Asymptote freezer showed p = 0.83 with σ = 0.73. Controlled cooling rate at -0.5 °C/min provided better INA differentiation than commodity freezer cooling. In the 96-well plate with linear cooling, the freezing time range increased with means of 47.4 and 50.6 min. The paper notes the Asymptote freezer accommodated up to 48 cryovials, each with limited capacity. Controlled cooling is essential for minimizing temperature gradients in high-throughput assays. The Asymptote freezer extends the platform's cooling capacity to 48 cryovials.
The freeze-float throughput can be increased by a factor of 38 through the combined use of multi-well plates and cryovials. The assay expanded from 50 droplets in a cuvette to 48 cryovials of 40 droplets each (1920 droplets). The Asymptote freezer accommodates 48 cryovials in an instrument-specific metal holder. Each cryovial contained 40 droplets, totaling 1920 droplets per experiment. The 96-deep-well plate validation experiment only used 30 droplets per well, not 40. Increased sample size improves detection confidence for the stochastic freezing process. The platform can scale from dozens to thousands of droplets in a single experiment.

Data And Code Availability
Droplet diameter measurement used Matlab automated circle detection program Droplet_Dispersion.m (Source Code S1). Freezing temperature distribution comparison used Python script KStest.ipynb (Source Code S3). The paper references source code but does not provide explicit deposition or access instructions.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Droplet monodispersity was tested with 60 1 µL droplets in a 12-well plate using fluorescence imaging. The 96-well plate was tested under both constant temperature (-28 °C) and linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min) to assess thermal uniformity. The Asymptote freezer performance was compared against the commodity freezer used in the previous report for validation. Static electricity was mitigated using an Auto-set Ion Pump and wet filter paper. The Swanson relation was used to calculate expected nucleation temperature dispersion from droplet radius variation.

Key Figures Tables

summary.title: Dimeric cyclobutane formation under continuous flow conditions using organophotoredox catalysed [2+2]-cycloaddition
summary.authors: Helena F Grantham; Marc C Kimber; M F C Grantham; Kimber
summary.field_subfield: Organophotoredox catalysis; Continuous flow organic synthesis
summary.executive_summary: This study reports a continuous flow protocol for the organophotoredox-catalyzed radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition of electron-rich alkenes (vinylcarbazoles and styrenes) to form cyclobutane dimers, providing a scalable route to valuable functional materials and natural products. The authors merge a homogeneous small-molecule organophotoredox catalyst with a commercial, off-the-shelf continuous flow platform to synthesize 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB), a blue electrophosphorescent host material, and its functionalized analogues, alongside the lignan natural product magnosalin. In batch conditions using the pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst at 3 mol%, t-DCzCB was obtained in 82% isolated yield, requiring deoxygenated acetone, cryogenic temperatures, and extended reaction times. Optimization of the continuous flow synthesis revealed that a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min (residence time = 20 min), 2 mol% catalyst loading, and 450 nm irradiation provided t-DCzCB in 98% isolated yield. Catalyst loading studies showed yields of 90% at 4.5 mol% and 93% at 1 mol%, establishing 2 mol% as optimal. Reducing the flow rate to 0.1 mL/min (residence time = 100 min) caused the yield to drop to 53% and generated carbazole via background oxidation by adventitious oxygen. The methodology was expanded to a series of brominated, methoxylated, and alkylated vinylcarbazoles, and to styrenes including 4-methoxystyrene, styrene (forming pellucidin A), and E-aserone (forming magnosalin), using electron relays (anthracene or diethylaniline). The 10 mmol scale dimerization of vinylcarbazole at 0.1 mol% catalyst loading gave t-DCzCB in 79% isolated yield, nearing the efficiencies of Ru-based photoredox systems. The study demonstrates that continuous flow improves conversion, reduces reaction times, and lowers catalyst loadings compared to conventional batch conditions, and provides a scalable route for both functional materials and natural products.

claims.description: The continuous flow protocol provides a general, robust, and scalable route to cyclobutane functional materials and natural products, outperforming conventional batch chemistry in catalyst loading, reaction time, and chemical yield.

Research Context
The dimerization of electron-rich alkene building blocks such as enamines and styrenes provides a convenient synthetic route to valuable cyclobutane functional materials and natural products. Vinyl carbazole can serve as a precursor for 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane, a cyclobutane dimer used as a host material for blue electrophosphorescence and PhOLEDs. Naturally occurring styrenes such as E-asarone can be seen as precursors of dimeric cyclobutyl natural products such as the anti-inflammatory lignan magnosalin and its derivatives. The synthesis of cyclobutanes of this type is accomplished via a radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition. The key alkene radical cation intermediate can be generated either through chemical oxidation or by utilizing photochemical methods of an electron-rich alkene. Chemical oxidation using Fe(III) salts was first reported by Wang and co-workers for the dimerization of vinyl carbazole. Photochemical dimerization of vinyl carbazole was first reported by Ellinger and Ledwith in 1965 using organophotosensitizers. With the emergence of visible-light photoredox catalysis, Yoon and co-workers demonstrated the effectiveness of Ru- and Ir-complexes in synthesizing symmetrical and unsymmetrical cyclobutanes from electron-rich olefins. Nicewicz and coworkers reported the dimerization of several classes of electron-rich alkenes using a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst. The use of organophotoredox catalysts in these transformations has significant advantages over metal-based catalysts including environmental, sustainability, and cost factors. However, reaction times for the organophotoredox-catalyzed dimerizations were excessive in some cases, cryogenic conditions were required for certain substrate classes, and catalyst loadings were typically 3 mol%. The use of continuous flow technology offers advantages in photoredox transformations as transferring photochemical reactions from batch to continuous flow can lead to more efficient irradiation of starting substrates, leading to higher conversions to the desired product. Recently, a heterogeneous photoredox fixed-bed flow chemical process using metal-free polymeric carbon nitrides provided a scalable route to magnosalin through the dimerization of E-aserone.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether merging homogeneous small-molecule, sustainable, organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology provides a convenient, environmentally beneficial methodology for synthesizing cyclobutane functional materials and natural products. It was anticipated that this approach would provide a convenient synthetic route to t-DCzCB using continuous flow technology, with reduced reaction times and catalyst loadings compared to batch conditions. The authors hypothesized that continuous flow would deliver cyclobutane functional materials and natural products by merging organophotoredox catalysis and continuous flow, and they anticipated this would showcase the advantages of continuous flow over the existing conventional batch chemistry approach. A secondary objective was to expand the cyclobutyl carbazole products available through this transformation, as there are very limited reports on the synthesis of t-DCzCBs possessing functional groups. They also proposed that a superior approach could be realized through a vinylation strategy of more heavily substituted carbazoles rather than chemical modification of the parent t-DCzCB scaffold. The study also investigated the effect of catalyst loading on the continuous flow reaction, and probed potential reversibility of the dimerization reaction by varying the flow rate. Different irradiation wavelengths of 405, 420, and 450 nm were tested to determine the optimal wavelength for continuous flow dimerization. Control experiments in the absence of the organophotoredox catalyst and in the absence of irradiation were performed to confirm that both components are required.

Methodological Details
The batch synthesis of t-DCzCB was achieved using the organophotoredox catalyst at 3 mol% under conditions previously reported by Nicewiez. The batch reaction required deoxygenated acetone, cryogenic temperatures, and extended reaction times to achieve optimal conversion to the desired cyclobutane dimer. The batch dimerization of vinyl carbazole provided t-DCzCB in 82% isolated yield. The continuous flow platform was a commercial, off-the-shelf platform, chosen for its excellent usability and improved availability. Optimization of the continuous flow synthesis of t-DCzCB was determined through HPLC analysis using p-terphenyl as an internal standard. Calibration of the starting vinyl carbazole and the product was required before yield determination. The continuous flow reaction was performed at 1.00 mmol of vinyl carbazole at a concentration of 0.4 M in acetone. The catalyst used was the pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst (referenced as catalyst 10) at loadings of 1, 2, and 4.5 mol%. Three irradiation wavelengths were tested: 405, 420, and 450 nm. For the expanded substrate study, the dimerization concentration was reduced to 0.2 M in acetone due to challenging solubility of brominated vinylcarbazoles. The brominated vinylcarbazoles were synthesized using the method of Obora and coworkers, providing each substrate in moderate to good yields. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole was isolated in only very low yields and proved problematic. The styrene substrates were dimerized in the continuous flow apparatus with an electron relay added to the starting solution before introduction into the flow system. Two electron relays were used: anthracene (0.25 eq.) and diethylaniline. The flow rate of 0.5 mL/min corresponded to a residence time of 20 min, while 0.1 mL/min corresponded to 100 min. The 10 mmol scale dimerization used only 0.1 mol% of the organophotoredox catalyst at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min. Post-synthetic transformations included palladium-mediated Suzuki crosscoupling with 4-methoxybenzene boronic acid using Kumar and Tao conditions, and borylation with bis(pinacolato)diboron.

Procedures And Architectures
The batch reaction followed the conditions of Nicewiez using the organophotoredox catalyst at 3 mol%. In continuous flow, vinyl carbazole was dimerized at 0.5 mL/min with 2 mol% catalyst and 450 nm irradiation. Yields were determined by HPLC analysis with p-terphenyl as an internal standard. Catalyst loading was varied between 1, 2, and 4.5 mol% to determine the optimal loading for the flow process. Flow rates were varied from 0.1 to 5 mL/min to probe the potential reversibility of the dimerization. Irradiation wavelengths of 405, 420, and 450 nm were independently tested at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min. Control experiments were run in the absence of catalyst and in the absence of irradiation to confirm the requirement of both components. For the brominated vinylcarbazoles, the reaction concentration was reduced to 0.2 M in acetone and three flow rates were trialed. The vinylcarbazoles were synthesized using the method of Obora and coworkers. The styrene substrates were dimerized with the electron relay added to the starting solution before introduction into the flow apparatus. Post-synthetic Suzuki crosscoupling used 4-methoxybenzene boronic acid under conditions of Kumar and Tao. Borylation was performed using bis(pinacolato)diboron. The catalyst is a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst, and irradiation was performed at 450 nm (blue light). The flow platform is a commercial, off-the-shelf continuous flow apparatus.

Key Results
The batch dimerization of vinyl carbazole provided t-DCzCB in 82% isolated yield. In continuous flow at 0.5 mL/min with 2 mol% catalyst and 450 nm irradiation, t-DCzCB was obtained in 98% yield. Increasing the catalyst loading to 4.5 mol% resulted in a modest reduction in yield to 90%. Reducing the catalyst loading to 1 mol% resulted in a marginal reduction in yield to 93%. Lowering the flow rate from 5 mL/min to 2 mL/min reduced the yield to 79% using 2 mol% catalyst. Further reducing the flow rate to 0.1 mL/min (residence time = 100 min) dropped the yield to a very modest 53%. A significant amount of carbazole was observed at 0.1 mL/min, attributed to background oxidation of vinyl carbazole by adventitious oxygen within the flow system. Irradiation at 405 nm and 420 nm provided t-DCzCB in comparable yields to 450 nm at 0.5 mL/min. The dimerization did not proceed in the absence of the catalyst or in the absence of irradiation. At 10 mmol scale with only 0.1 mol% catalyst at 0.5 mL/min, t-DCzCB was obtained in 79% isolated yield. For 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole, batch dimerization gave the dimer in 48% yield, while continuous flow at 0.2 mL/min gave an improved yield of 64%. For the 2-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole substrate, batch dimerization gave 31% yield, while continuous flow gave 71% yield. 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole dimerized under continuous flow to 65% yield. The 2-chloro and 2-methoxy substituted vinylcarbazoles gave dimer yields of 61% and 45%, respectively. Dimerization of the 2-hydroxycarbazole-derived bis-vinylcarbazole gave the cyclobutyl bis-enolether in 25% yield. The 2-arylated vinylcarbazole gave 22% yield, while the 4-fluoroarylated vinylcarbazole gave 65% yield. The tetra-alkyl substituted cyclobutyl dimer was obtained in 57% yield. The 3,6-bisarylated vinylcarbazole dimerized to 50% yield. Suzuki crosscoupling of the bromocyclobutane gave 75% yield. Borylation of the bromocyclobutane gave 36% yield. 4-methoxystyrene dimerized to 44% yield in continuous flow. Styrene with diethylaniline as an electron relay provided pellucidin A in 22% yield. E-aserone dimerized to magnosalin in 40% isolated yield on a 10 mmol scale. In continuous flow, dimerization completion was attained in under 1 hour, whereas batch required significantly more time. In contrast to batch conditions, the continuous flow conditions did not require cryogenic temperatures and were completed in significantly shorter time periods.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The noticeable reduction in yield at low flow rates (0.1 mL/min) suggests that the [2+2]-cycloaddition may be reversible under these conditions. The formation of carbazole at extended residence times is attributed to background oxidation of the alkene by adventitious oxygen within the flow system, followed by hydrolysis of N-formylcarbazole. The continuous flow protocol provides a general, robust, and scalable route to valuable cyclobutane host materials, delivering a new family of functional cyclobutane carbazoles that should be well placed to be exploited as novel functional materials. The demonstration of the methodology on lignan natural products validates its applicability beyond synthetic materials to natural product synthesis. The reduction in catalyst loadings from 3 mol% in batch to 0.1 mol% in continuous flow demonstrates the efficiency advantages of the flow approach. The shorter reaction times in continuous flow confirm the efficiency gains over conventional batch chemistry for this transformation.

Contradictions And Limitations
1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole was a very challenging substrate with isolation of the bromo-substituted vinylcarbazole proving problematic and only achieved in very low yields. The solubility of all brominated vinylcarbazoles in acetone proved challenging at the 0.4 M concentration used for the VCZ optimization, requiring reduction to 0.2 M. For 2,7-dibromo-9vinylcarbazole (17a), the batch reaction conditions slightly outperformed the continuous flow conditions. The borylation of the bromocyclobutane afforded only a modest yield of 36%, limiting its synthetic utility. The 2-arylated vinylcarbazole had poor solubility in acetone, which was reflected in the moderate isolated yield of 22% for formation of the cyclobutane. The 10 mmol scale dimerization at 0.1 mol% catalyst loading provided 79% yield, which is lower than the 98% yield in optimization but significantly better than the 82% batch yield. No direct comparison of absolute reaction times between batch and flow is provided for most substrates beyond the qualitative statement that flow was faster.

Claims
The continuous flow protocol provides a general, robust, and scalable route to cyclobutane functional materials and natural products, outperforming conventional batch chemistry in catalyst loading, reaction time, and chemical yield. The flow rate of 0.5 mL/min with 2 mol% catalyst and 450 nm irradiation provided t-DCzCB in 98% yield, compared to 82% in batch. The 10 mmol scale dimerization using only 0.1 mol% catalyst achieved 79% yield, a significant reduction from the 3 mol% required in batch. In continuous flow, completion was attained in under 1 hour, whereas batch required significantly more time. The methodology was applied to a series of functionalized carbazoles and styrenes, with improved yields over batch conditions in most cases. For 2,7-dibromo-9vinylcarbazole, batch conditions slightly outperformed continuous flow. The 2-arylated vinylcarbazole gave only 22% yield due to poor solubility. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole was isolated only in very low yields and proved problematic. This methodology opens a scalable route for the synthesis of blue electrophosphorescent host materials and functional cyclobutane carbazoles for novel applications. The continuous flow approach reduces environmental impact and cost through lower catalyst loading and improved atom economy. The scalable synthesis of lignan natural products demonstrates broad applicability of organophotoredox flow chemistry.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The catalyst loading was varied from 1 to 4.5 mol%, showing optimal yield at 2 mol%. Flow rates from 0.1 to 5 mL/min were tested to probe reversibility and find optimal throughput. Irradiation wavelengths of 405, 420, and 450 nm were tested, with comparable results across all wavelengths at the optimal flow rate. Control experiments in the absence of catalyst and irradiation confirmed that both are essential for dimerization. HPLC with p-terphenyl internal standard provided reliable yield determination.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents the optimization study of the continuous flow synthesis of t-DCzCB, including entries for different catalyst loadings, flow rates, wavelengths, and yields, with a 10 mmol scale entry at 0.1 mol% catalyst. Scheme 1 displays cyclobutane dimers as functional materials and natural products, including VCZ, t-DCzCB, E-asarone, and magnosalin. Scheme 2 outlines the radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition mechanism, with panel A showing chemical oxidation and panel B showing photochemical pathways. Scheme 3 summarizes the overall protocol merging homogeneous small-molecule organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow for cyclobutane synthesis. Scheme 4 compares batch and continuous flow conditions for the dimerization of vinyl carbazole to t-DCzCB, showing the optimization parameters. Scheme 5 details the synthesis and dimerization of brominated vinylcarbazoles, with batch and flow yields tabulated for various substrates. Scheme 6 presents post-synthetic Suzuki crosscoupling and borylation of the bromocyclobutane products, demonstrating their synthetic utility. Scheme 7 illustrates the continuous flow protocol for styrene dimerization with an electron relay, including the synthesis of pellucidin A and magnosalin.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a continuous flow protocol for organophotoredox-catalyzed radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition that enables the scalable synthesis of cyclobutane functional materials and natural products with significantly reduced reaction times and catalyst loadings compared to batch chemistry. 2. The strongest evidence is the optimization of t-DCzCB synthesis to 98% yield at 2 mol% catalyst loading and 0.5 mL/min flow rate, and the scale-up to 10 mmol at 0.1 mol% catalyst yielding 79%, while batch required 3 mol% and deoxygenated acetone at cryogenic temperatures. 3. The future path lies in the development of a new class of functional cyclobutane carbazole materials with tunable properties for photophysical applications and the expansion of the scope to more complex substrates and natural products.

summary.title: A New Organocatalytic Desymmetrization Reaction Enables the Enantioselective Total Synthesis of Madangamine E
summary.authors: Shinya Shiomi; Benjamin D A Shennan (University of Oxford); Ken Yamazaki (University of Oxford); Ángel L Fuentes De Arriba (University of Oxford); Dhananjayan Vasu (University of Oxford); Trevor A Hamlin (University of Oxford); Darren J Dixon (University of Oxford)
summary.field_subfield: Organic Chemistry; Asymmetric Synthesis; Total Synthesis; Organocatalysis
summary.executive_summary:
This paper reports a 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E, a marine natural product characterized by an architecturally complex pentacyclic fused-ring system with two nitrogen atoms. The key enabling step is a new catalytic and highly enantioselective desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition reaction of a prochiral ketone (a tri-substituted nitroolefin-linked cyclohexanone) to a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin. This reaction concurrently establishes three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon, in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity and is highly scalable. The pathway and origins of enantioselectivity were probed using DFT calculations, which identified a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism involving hydrogen bonding interactions between the thiourea catalyst, the nitro group, and the enamine moiety. The total synthesis was completed in 30 steps, incorporating key reactions such as a mild one-pot oxidative lactamization, a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone, and ring-closing metathesis (RCM) to install the two macrocyclic rings. The study demonstrates the power of organocatalytic desymmetrization for converting simple achiral starting materials into high-value stereochemically-rich products, providing a framework for future synthetic strategy.

Key results include the bicyclic product 8 obtained in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee with Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst, and 95% yield in >99% ee at >5g scale for the synthesis-scale application. The DFT calculations predicted a ΔΔG‡ of 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹, corresponding to a computed 99% ee, in excellent agreement with experiment. The RCM step for ring E yielded the diamide in 71% yield under high dilution and co-catalytic p-benzoquinone. The final double amide reduction gave madangamine E in 72% yield with LiAlH₄ in Et₂O.
