The 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E is achieved, with the AC bicyclic core installed early via the key desymmetrization reaction.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper reports a 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E, a marine natural product characterized by an architecturally complex pentacyclic fused-ring system with two nitrogen atoms. The key enabling step is a new catalytic and highly enantioselective desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition reaction of a prochiral ketone (a tri-substituted nitroolefin-linked cyclohexanone) to a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin. This reaction concurrently establishes three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon, in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity and is highly scalable. The pathway and origins of enantioselectivity were probed using DFT calculations, which identified a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism involving hydrogen bonding interactions between the thiourea catalyst, the nitro group, and the enamine moiety. The total synthesis was completed in 30 steps, incorporating key reactions such as a mild one-pot oxidative lactamization, a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone, and ring-closing metathesis (RCM) to install the two macrocyclic rings. The study demonstrates the power of organocatalytic desymmetrization for converting simple achiral starting materials into high-value stereochemically-rich products, providing a framework for future synthetic strategy.

Key results include the bicyclic product 8 obtained in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee with Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst, and 95% yield in >99% ee at >5g scale for the synthesis-scale application. The DFT calculations predicted a ΔΔG‡ of 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹, corresponding to a computed 99% ee, in excellent agreement with experiment. The RCM step for ring E yielded the diamide in 71% yield under high dilution and co-catalytic p-benzoquinone. The final double amide reduction gave madangamine E in 72% yield with LiAlH₄ in Et₂O.

Research Context
The madangamine family, isolated from marine sea sponges of the Xestospongia genus, is characterized by an architecturally complex pentacyclic fused-ring system with two nitrogen atoms. Three of the rings constitute a diazatricyclic core common to all family members, while the D ring differs in each and every madangamine. Since their isolation, madangamines have attracted significant attention with numerous reported strategies to polycyclic core fragments, yet only two total syntheses and one formal synthesis have been reported. Amat reported the first asymmetric total synthesis of madangamine D in 2014, while Chida and Sato demonstrated a unified total synthesis of madangamine's A, C, and E in 2017. There existed a need for a synthetic strategy that enables the conversion of relatively simple achiral starting materials to high-value stereochemically-rich products within a broader framework. Efficient routes that enable rapid generation of structural and stereochemical complexity are of particularly high importance given the role of natural products in medicinal chemistry. The authors envisioned that the development of highly enantio- and diastereoselective organocatalytic desymmetrization reactions would demonstrate the enabling power of such a synthetic strategy.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question was whether a catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization of tri-substituted nitroolefin-linked cyclohexanones could be developed to establish the AC bicyclic motif of the madangamine family. The authors hypothesized that the AC bicyclic motif would be well-suited for construction from a catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reaction, providing a rigid scaffold for further elaboration. It was predicted that a single chirality inducing step could install all the ensuing stereochemical information from the desymmetrization reaction. The authors aimed to establish a new, highly efficient organocatalytic desymmetrization of tri-substituted nitroolefin-linked cyclohexanones and apply it to the total synthesis of madangamine E. The key intermediate, ketone 5, was to be accessed from prochiral cyclohexanone 6 in isomerically pure form using the developed desymmetrization reaction. The DFT calculations were hypothesized to reveal the crucial substrate/catalyst interactions in the enantio-determining step of the catalytic cyclization.

Methodological Details
Methyl-substituted nitroolefin 7 was selected as the ideal model substrate for developing the enantioselective intramolecular Michael addition reaction. An oxidative radical nitration was employed to construct 7 in 3 steps from commercially available 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal. A range of chiral single enantiomer primary and secondary amine organocatalysts was investigated, including trans-cyclohexanediamine and proline-derived scaffolds. The reactions were performed in dichloromethane at 20 mol% catalyst loading in the presence of benzoic acid as a co-catalyst. Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f provided the desired bicyclic Michael adduct 8 in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee. A simplified bifunctional primary amine catalyst 9e also yielded 8 in 51% yield as a single diastereoisomer in 96% ee. For the synthesis-scale application, nitroolefin 17E treated with 20 mol% catalyst 9f and 20 mol% benzoic acid provided bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield and near-perfect enantio-and diastereoselectivity at >5g scale. The β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin 17 was accessed through a multistep route starting from 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal with reductive amination, tosylation, oxidative cleavage, Henry reaction, dehydration, and Michael addition. The Michael addition of the organo-zinc-copper complex to the branched nitroalkane 14 gave 90% yield and was proven highly scalable. Selenoxide elimination proceeded in 52% yield over 3 steps with E:Z = 3.8:1. The RCM step employed Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst in PhMe at 110 °C with co-catalytic p-benzoquinone at very high dilution. The final double amide reduction used excess LiAlH₄ in Et₂O at 72% yield. The total synthesis was completed in 30 steps.

Procedures And Architectures
The key step is a desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition of a 4-aminocyclohexanone derivative possessing a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin. The catalyst is a Jacobsen's thiourea-based bifunctional primary amine organocatalyst. The DFT calculations employed 16 possible transition structures for the stereoselectivity-determining C-C bond forming step. TS1 emerged as the most energetically favorable transition structure by ΔΔG‡ = 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ compared to the second-lowest-energy transition structure. The Michael addition is highly exergonic with ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹. The catalytic cycle is summarized in Figure 2B and proceeds through hemiaminal Int1, imine Int2, enamine Int3, and iminium-nitronate Int4. The reaction was performed at 20 mol% catalyst loading with benzoic acid as co-catalyst in dichloromethane. For the RCM step, Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst was used in PhMe at 110 °C with p-benzoquinone as a co-catalyst. The final step used excess LiAlH₄ in Et₂O to reduce the diamide to the tertiary alcohol, which was then further reduced to the amine. The intermediate methyl enol ether 19 was formed upon treatment of ketone 20 with catalytic p-toluenesulfonic acid in methanol. Reduction of the nitro group with LiAlH₄ provided a primary amine, which was protected as a Boc-PMB-amine and then converted to ketone 20 in 70% yield over 4 steps. The oxidative lactamization employed Iwabuchi's conditions with catalytic quantities of AZADO, copper chloride, 2,2'-bipyridine, and DMAP open to air.

Key Results
Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f provided the desired bicyclic Michael adduct 8 in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee from the model substrate. A simplified bifunctional primary amine catalyst 9e also yielded 8 in 51% yield as a single diastereoisomer in 96% ee. Treatment of 17E with 20 mol% catalyst 9f and 20 mol% benzoic acid provided bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield with near-perfect enantio- and diastereoselectivity at >5g scale. The DFT-computed ΔΔG‡ of 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ corresponds to a computed 99% ee, in excellent agreement with the experimental 99% ee. The Michael addition is highly exergonic with ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹, confirming it as an irreversible and stereoselectivity-determining step. RCM of 29 with Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst gave diamide 30 in 71% yield. The final double amide reduction gave synthetic madangamine E in 72% yield using excess LiAlH₄ in Et₂O. The total synthesis was completed in 30 steps. The selenoxide elimination yielded 52% over 3 steps with E:Z = 3.8:1. The Wittig homologation with a rigorous reaction mixture quench improved the yield of aldehyde 23 to 86% from a low 26%.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The near-perfect selectivity profile is rationalized by a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism where TS1 is stabilized by several hydrogen bonding interactions with the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. The cooperative mechanism is consistent with the thiourea activating the ketone, the nitro group coordinating with the thiourea, and the enamine participating in hydrogen bonding. The DFT calculations show that when the nitro group is replaced by an α,β-unsaturated ester, the intramolecular protonation reaction is preferred over the intermolecular protonation. This mechanistic difference is attributed to the pKa difference between nitronate (pKa = 17), thiourea (pKa = 20), and enolate (pKa = 30). The deprotonation of the thiourea by the enolate is favorable, whereas the deprotonation by the nitronate is unfavorable, explaining the mechanistic divergence. The irreversible nature of the C-C bond formation through TS1 ensures that the kinetically preferred transition state determines the stereochemistry of the product. The study demonstrates the utility of catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization for constructing high-value saturated molecular scaffolds and the rapid, atomeconomical generation of stereochemical complexity.

Contradictions And Limitations
Most tested catalysts (9a-9d, 9g-9k) failed to provide the cyclised product 8 and instead gave complex product mixtures. Amat's Wittig reaction of an octenoate phosphonium salt was largely unsuccessful despite extensive experimentation, attributed to competing deleterious deprotonation due to subtle bond geometry and flexibility of ketone 3. All attempts to form the macrocyclic E ring via RCM resulted in no desired cyclisation because of the distant spatial arrangement of the terminal alkenes. The selenoxide elimination demonstrated strong dependence on the solvent mixture, with Et₂O:CH₂Cl₂ (2:1) proving optimal. The Wittig homologation under standard reaction conditions gave only 26% yield of aldehyde 23, requiring a rigorous quench to achieve 86%. The O-protonation of the nitronate VI is facile, but the formed aci-nitro species VII is less electronegative at the α-position, preventing further protonation. The cyclobutane intermediate V can form but is energetically unstable and easily reopens with a low energy barrier.

Claims
A new catalytic and highly enantioselective desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition reaction of a prochiral ketone to a tethered β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin concurrently establishes three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon, in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity. Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f provided bicyclic adduct 8 in 70% yield in 99% ee. The DFT-computed ΔΔG‡ of 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ predicted 99% ee in excellent agreement with experiment. The synthesis-scale application yielded 95% in near-perfect enantio- and diastereoselectivity at >5g scale. The reaction is highly exergonic with ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹, confirming its irreversible nature. Most tested catalysts (9a-9d, 9g-9k) failed to provide the cyclised product 8, giving only complex mixtures. A simplified bifunctional amine catalyst 9e only yielded 51% in 96% ee, inferior to 9f. This provides a new method for constructing stereogenic quaternary carbon centres from β,β'-dialkylsubstituted nitroolefins. The reaction enables conversion of simple achiral starting materials to high-value stereochemically-rich products.
The 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E is achieved, with the AC bicyclic core installed early via the key desymmetrization reaction. The total synthesis was completed in 30 steps. The final double amide reduction yielded madangamine E in 72% using excess LiAlH₄. RCM of 29 gave diamide 30 in 71% yield using Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst. All analytical data were highly consistent with that reported by Chida and Sato and by the isolation team of Andersen. Amat's Wittig reaction of an octenoate phosphonium salt was largely unsuccessful despite advice from the original authors. All attempts to form the macrocyclic E ring via RCM resulted in no desired cyclisation initially. The early introduction of stereochemical information enabled the completion of the total synthesis. This demonstrates the utility of catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization in the synthesis of high-value saturated molecular scaffolds.

Data And Code Availability
The supporting information contains detailed synthetic procedures and computational methods.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The performance of a range of chiral single enantiomer primary and secondary amine organocatalysts was investigated to probe the narrow catalyst structure allowance. The DFT calculations included a conformational search identifying 16 possible transition structures, with TS1 emerging as the most energetically favorable. The selenoxide elimination efficiency demonstrated strong dependence on the solvent mixture, with Et₂O:CH₂Cl₂ (2:1) proving optimal. The Wittig homologation was optimized by incorporating a rigorous reaction mixture quench at 60 °C for 3 hours, improving yield from 26% to 86%.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the architecturally complex pentacyclic fused-ring system of the madangamine family with two nitrogen atoms. Figure 1B shows a formal synthesis of madangamine A. Figure 1C illustrates the pentacyclic skeleton retrosynthetically, with the end-game relying on tetracyclic ketone 3. Figure 2A shows the enantioselective desymmetrising intramolecular Michael addition to α,β-unsaturated esters previously reported by the group. Figure 2B presents the catalytic cycle including hemiaminal Int1, imine Int2, enamine Int3, and iminium-nitronate Int4. Figure 2C and Figure 3 show the DFT calculations for the intramolecular Michael addition of nitroolefin 7 as a model substrate. Figure 4A shows the restructured route to access nitroolefin 17, starting from 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal. Figure 4B shows the application of the organocatalytic enantioselective desymmetrization to the synthesis-scale substrate 17E.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a new organocatalytic desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition that concurrently establishes three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon, in near-perfect enantioselectivity (99% ee) from tri-substituted nitroolefin-linked cyclohexanones. 2. The strongest evidence is the 30-step total synthesis of madangamine E, achieved with the bicyclic core installed in 95% yield (>99% ee) at >5g scale, with DFT calculations (ΔΔG‡ = 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ predicting 99% ee) in excellent agreement with experiment. 3. The future path involves the application of catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization as a general strategy for the rapid, atomeconomical generation of stereochemical complexity in high-value saturated molecular scaffolds.

summary.title: Tuning the Dielectric Response in a NC Material through Nanoparticle Morphology
summary.authors: Archita Adluri; Brett Henderson; Irina Paci
summary.field_subfield: Materials Science, Computational Dielectrics, Condensed Matter Physics
summary.executive_summary: This computational study investigates how the morphology—size, shape, and orientation—of molecular-scale silver (Ag) nanoparticle inclusions affects the dielectric response of a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix. Utilizing Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) and the Modern Theory of Polarization implemented in the Quantum Espresso code, the authors model the low-frequency electronic and ionic polarization of nanocrystalline (NC) composites. The study considers rod-like and disk-like Ag inclusions with sizes ranging from 8 to 32 atoms, embedded in an MgO host with bulk permittivity 8-9.8 and bandgap 7.8 eV. Key findings demonstrate dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30–100% relative to the bare matrix, with asymmetric inclusions (rods and disks) yielding significantly greater enhancements than spherical inclusions at comparable volume loadings. Specific results include over 70% enhancement for multi-layer disks (332, 432, 442) at similar volume loading to the bare matrix, and a ~30% increase for a spherical Ag8 inclusion at ~4% volume ratio. Born effective charge (BEC) tensor maps reveal that local field enhancements and depolarization regions are concentrated at the Ag-MgO interface, extending up to ~3 Å from the inclusion edge. The work establishes that at the molecular nanoparticle scale (<30 atoms), discrete quantum effects dominate, making morphology a primary design lever for tuning dielectric properties in high-k applications. Limitations include the LDA functional's underestimation of bandgaps, periodic boundary conditions imposing volume-averaged values, and computational constraints preventing study of inclusions larger than ~40 atoms. The authors propose future extensions to other matrices (SiO2, HfO2) and transition metal dopants (Cu, Co, Fe).

Executive Summary
This computational study investigates how the morphology—size, shape, and orientation—of molecular-scale silver (Ag) nanoparticle inclusions affects the dielectric response of a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix. Utilizing Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) and the Modern Theory of Polarization implemented in the Quantum Espresso code, the authors model the low-frequency electronic and ionic polarization of nanocrystalline (NC) composites. The study considers rod-like and disk-like Ag inclusions with sizes ranging from 8 to 32 atoms, embedded in an MgO host with bulk permittivity 8-9.8 and bandgap 7.8 eV. Key findings demonstrate dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30–100% relative to the bare matrix, with asymmetric inclusions (rods and disks) yielding significantly greater enhancements than spherical inclusions at comparable volume loadings. Specific results include over 70% enhancement for multi-layer disks (332, 432, 442) at similar volume loading to the bare matrix, and a ~30% increase for a spherical Ag8 inclusion at ~4% volume ratio. Born effective charge (BEC) tensor maps reveal that local field enhancements and depolarization regions are concentrated at the Ag-MgO interface, extending up to ~3 Å from the inclusion edge. The work establishes that at the molecular nanoparticle scale (<30 atoms), discrete quantum effects dominate, making morphology a primary design lever for tuning dielectric properties in high-k applications. Limitations include the LDA functional's underestimation of bandgaps, periodic boundary conditions imposing volume-averaged values, and computational constraints preventing study of inclusions larger than ~40 atoms. The authors propose future extensions to other matrices (SiO2, HfO2) and transition metal dopants (Cu, Co, Fe).

Research Context
The demand for new high-κ dielectric materials is driven by energy storage and processing power limits of traditional single-phase materials. Nanocomposite materials combining a standard dielectric matrix with high- and mid-κ inclusions have been advanced as tunable avenues for device engineering. A specific need exists for materials with tunable dielectric constants for transistors, high-density charge storage, and quantum computing applications. Traditional Si/SiO₂ gate materials have been replaced by silicon-germanium, hafnium oxides, and nitrogen-doped structures to address leakage at shrinking scales. Molecular nanoparticles (mNPs) with up to ~100 atoms bridge the gap between single-atom dopants and traditional metallic nanoparticles. Unlike traditional nanoparticles, mNPs are insulating, lack a band structure, and provide highly polarizable electron density requiring quantum mechanical treatment. Effective medium approximations are suitable for macroscale mixtures but do not capture the quantum response and local field effects dominating complex-structured dielectrics. A previous study from the authors used the modern theory of polarization to model Ag⁸/MgO NCs and found significant interfacial effects exceeding expected polarization.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how the distribution and shape of mNP inclusions affect the dielectric capacity of a metal-oxide material. The authors hypothesize that at mNP scales of <30 atoms, size, shape, and orientation greatly alter electron behavior and consequently the atomic-scale polarization. The study specifically compares three rod-like and five disk-like inclusions relative to the bare matrix. It is predicted that asymmetric inclusions will provide orientation-dependent dielectric enhancements that differ from simple volume-loading scaling. The Born effective charge tensor is employed to isolate the local electronic polarization contribution from the matrix response. The authors expect that larger, more asymmetric inclusions will generate stronger local fields due to increased available polarizable electrons. The study also examines whether the 'quantum of polarization' effects arising from periodic boundary conditions introduce systematic artifacts in the calculated permittivity.

Methodological Details
The matrix material is magnesium oxide (MgO), selected for its cubic crystal structure, isotropic polarization, and low number of polarizable d-electrons. MgO has a bulk dielectric constant of 8–9.8 and a bandgap of 7.8 eV. Inclusions are molecular-scale silver (Ag) nanoparticles, built on an ideal Ag fcc lattice. Three rod-like and five disk-like inclusions were modeled with sizes ranging from 8 to 32 atoms. The matrix extended 2 MgO layers beyond the inclusion edge in each direction to prevent periodic image interaction while maintaining cell size control. The loading ratio was maintained between 3–5% in terms of atom counts, equating to volume loading since inclusion and matrix atoms occupy approximately the same volume. The CPMD method was implemented in Quantum Espresso versions 6.0 and 6.6. The plane-wave-basis set was constructed using the LDA functional. Mg atoms used Bachelet-Hamann-Schluter norm-conserving pseudopotentials; O and Ag used Rappe-Rabe-Kaxiras-Joannopoulos ultra-soft pseudopotentials from MaterialsCloud. Wavefunction cutoff (wfcut) was set at 50–60 Ry; charge density (rhocut) cutoff at 560 Ry. Total energy convergence was set to 10⁻⁸ (increased from standard 10⁻⁴) and force threshold at 10⁻⁴. Electron masses were initialized at 300 a.u. and increased to 450 a.u. after damped minimization. All calculations employed periodic boundary conditions with Brillouin zone sampling at the Γ point. Stress relaxation was performed by continuously updating cell size and volume during the damped dynamics and structure minimization steps. Thermostats were not applied, and temperatures were not controlled; test runs between 200 and 600 K showed negligible geometric temperature effects. The Born effective charge tensor was calculated by differencing forces under zero-field and static polarization conditions, normalized to the bulk matrix.

Procedures And Architectures
Model construction utilized Avogadro software to build Ag fcc lattice inclusions embedded in MgO. The electronic structure calculation proceeded in six steps: initial electron minimization with Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization, followed by damped dynamics to minimize ions/electrons, and a lattice vector relaxation step. Polarization calculation used a static field of 0.001 a.u. applied along the z-axis. The low-frequency dielectric constant (εr) is calculated as εr = 1 + 4π(P_damped - P_relax)/ε_field. The damped dynamics step (P_damped) accounts primarily for ionic polarization. The relaxed electronic structure step (P_relax) allows electrons to fully polarize and Ag electron density to migrate into the Ag-MgO interface. A clamped-ion step computed electronic polarization and Born effective charges, coupling electronic response to fixed ionic positions. The fully-relaxed static polarization was computed by releasing ionic clamps while the static field remained applied. Post-processing included mathematical corrections for the 'quantum of polarization' effect—box edge jumps due to matrix distortion during simulations. The Brillouin zone was sampled at the Γ point for all calculations.

Key Results
Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30–100% were observed across inclusion sizes from 8 to 32 atoms. A spherical Ag8 inclusion at ≈4% volume loading yielded an ≈30% increase in εr relative to the bare matrix. Asymmetric rod-like and disk-like inclusions further enhanced the dielectric response beyond the spherical case at comparable volume ratios. Multi-layer disk inclusions (332, 432, 442) exhibited more than 70% enhancement in εr over the matrix permittivity at similar volume loading. The inclusion of silver atoms distorted the local MgO structure up to ~3 Å from the mNP edge. Rod-like inclusions oriented parallel to the field showed higher ε∥ (9.23 vs bulk) compared to perpendicular ε⊥. Disk442, with twice the x,y dimensions of Rod223, produced more than twice the polarization increase of Rod223 at similar loading. 2D disk nanoparticles (421, 441) showed a decrease in polarization relative to the bulk in both directions because electrons could not move in the z-direction. The BEC maps for the 224 rodlike inclusion revealed enhancement of the polarization field in matrix regions adjacent to NP poles, with depolarization (red/yellow) in the equatorial region. The BEC plots showed forces contributed mainly by atoms at the matrix-nanoparticle interface, with perpendicular depolarization affecting only interfacial atoms. The perpendicular depolarization field never decayed to normal bulk values, extending over large regions of the cell.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The discrete quantum behavior of mNPs (<30 atoms) enables the manipulation of local field enhancements at the Ag-MgO interface as a design parameter for dielectric materials. Asymmetric inclusions (rods/disks) break spatial symmetry, enabling orientation-dependent polarization effects that go beyond simple volume-ratio scaling. Disk-shaped mNPs exhibit stronger polarization than rods of similar size, attributed to more available moving electrons with greater spatial freedom in the nanoparticle. The Born effective charge tensor maps confirm that the increased permittivity is driven by local charge redistribution at the interface, not by a uniform shift in matrix ionic charges. The 'reach' of the induced field is physically longer and stronger when the NP is oriented parallel to the field, creating larger areas of increased effective polarizability. Interfacial effects are identified as the dominant mechanism, which can be exploited since the mNPs are encapsulated by the matrix, isolating the interfacial response from bulk effects. The quantum of polarization effect, coupled with cell distortion from asymmetric inclusions, introduces multiply-defined polarization values requiring post-processing corrections.

Contradictions And Limitations
The LDA functional inherently underestimates bandgaps, although the authors argue that the DFT performance should mirror the nanoparticle bandgap rather than the bulk MgO bandgap. The calculated εr values are volume-averaged and do not account for surface charge or edge effects, rendering them not 'true' dielectric constants for real materials. The periodic boundary conditions introduce artifacts where electrons can polarize into neighboring image cells, shifting polarization values by multiples of n × box-length. Computational constraints limited the study to inclusions with <40 atoms; larger inclusions may exhibit metallic behavior that the current models cannot fully capture. The BEC plots for perpendicular polarization converged to nominal (+2, -2) values within a very short distance, indicating a smaller field and weaker effect. The paper acknowledges that the perpendicular response in the matrix can sometimes dominate, resulting in a dielectric constant lower than for the pure matrix.

Claims
Nanoparticle morphology—specifically shape and orientation—is a first-order control variable for tuning the dielectric response of metal-oxide NC composites. Asymmetric disk inclusions (332, 432, 442) provided >70% enhancement at similar volume loading to spherical inclusions. Rod-shaped inclusions with parallel orientation showed ε∥ of 9.23, while perpendicular orientation produced weaker depolarization. Disk442 produced more than twice the polarization increase of Rod223 at similar loading, demonstrating shape-dependent scaling. 2D disk nanoparticles (421, 441) showed a decrease in polarization relative to bulk, indicating that some geometries inhibit rather than promote enhancement. The perpendicular depolarization field never decays to bulk values, suggesting the effect can persist over large regions and interfere with dielectric response. Dielectric constant tuning can be achieved by selecting inclusion shape and orientation, offering a design lever independent of doping concentration. Close control on NP orientation is required, particularly in crystal systems with directional polarization where perpendicular response can dominate.
Born effective charge tensor maps reveal that the local field enhancement and depolarization are interfacial phenomena localized within ~3 Å of the inclusion surface. The local structure distortion only extended to the nearest neighbors of the inclusions (up to around 3 Å from the edge). BEC plots showed that forces contributing to increased ε∥ or decreased ε⊥ were mainly due to atoms at the matrix-nanoparticle interface. The enhancement is strongly localized to two layers of matrix ions at the interface, while the weaker depolarization field extends over larger regions. The perpendicular depolarization field, though weaker, is extended over large regions of the cell, contradicting the idea of strictly localized interfacial effects. Interfacial engineering through encapsulation can isolate and exploit the local field enhancement, making NCs attractive for selective dielectric tuning. The localized nature of the effect means that aggregation of inclusions could lead to destructive interference or excessive screening.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Temperature-controlled test runs between 200 and 600 K confirmed that geometric temperature effects were negligible due to MgO's high melting temperature and ionic rigidity. The %loading was kept between 3–5% atom counts to ensure sufficient matrix separation between periodic images. The BEC calculations confirmed that oscillating forces persist even after ions are clamped, supporting the electron-dynamics interpretation. Maximum Wannier function calculations were attempted but failed to converge for nanoparticles larger than 8 atoms due to delocalization.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows an example NC with a Ag8 inclusion, illustrating the local MgO lattice distortion. Table 1 presents εr values for all rod-like and disk-like inclusions across different sizes. Figure 4 displays the six-step CPMD procedure from electronic structure calculation to lattice vector relaxation. Figure 5 outlines the polarization calculation procedure, from clamped-ion to fully-relaxed static polarization. Figure 6 presents the mathematical corrections for polarization jumps during post-processing. Figure 9 shows a smeared BEC plot of normalized Born charges, revealing local field enhancements and depolarization regions.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that molecular-scale (8–32 atom) Ag inclusions in MgO yield 30–100% dielectric enhancement through orientation- and shape-dependent interfacial field modifications. 2. The strongest evidence is the >70% enhancement in disk inclusions (332, 432, 442) at similar volume loading to the bare matrix, corroborated by BEC maps showing localized interfacial charge redistribution within ~3 Å. 3. The future path involves extending the framework to other matrices (SiO2, HfO2), transition metal dopants (Cu, Co, Fe), and studying the quantum-mechanical transition to metallic behavior at larger inclusion sizes.

summary.title: Low density interior in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expels ions to the subsurface
summary.authors: Shahrazad M A Malek, Ivan Saika-Voivod, Styliani Consta
summary.field_subfield: Computational physical chemistry; supercooled aqueous nanodroplets
summary.executive_summary:
This study uses molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the spatial distribution of Na+ ions within supercooled aqueous nanodroplets containing 100 to 1100 water molecules at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. The authors report direct computational evidence that supercooled nanodroplets develop a heterogeneous solvent structure: a low-density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water molecules surrounded by a higher-density, more disordered subsurface. At supercooling, a single Na+ ion is expelled from the low-density core and peaks within approximately 0.1 nm of the subsurface density maximum, whereas at room temperature, the ion distribution is nearly uniform across the droplet interior. 

To analyze the single-ion distribution, the authors introduce a reference analytical model of "electrostatic confinement" (EC), which expresses the droplet energy as the sum of electrostatic and surface energies of a deformable dielectric droplet. The model predicts that an ion is subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, with a spring constant K(ε) that peaks at a relative dielectric constant of ε ≈ 2.73. The model predictions agree with the simulation findings at room temperature but not at supercooling, where the heterogeneous water structure dominates. For multiple ions, the subsurface localization persists at 200 K, and the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann (NPB) equation—which predicts exponential decay toward the center at 300 K—cannot describe the distribution at supercooling. 

The authors note that for the smallest system (N = 100 H2O), the low-density core is absent due to large relative shape fluctuations and immediate ion solvation of the Na+ ion. The study anticipates serving as a starting point for investigating supercooled electrosprayed droplets used to preserve macromolecule conformations in native mass spectrometry. Key results include: the EC model predicts r^2 < 12 Å excursions for a single charge at N = 1000; NPB fits at 300 K yield λPB ≈ 1.2 nm for 776 H2O and 1.3 nm for 1100 H2O, compared to a theoretical λPB ≈ 0.8; and for 8 Na+ ions in 1100 H2O at 200 K, two peaks appear at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm, indicating subsurface localization.

claims.description: A low-density, tetrahedrally ordered core forms in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets and expels single and multiple Na+ ions to a more disordered, higher-density subsurface.
The electrostatic confinement model, predicting a harmonic potential for a single ion in a flexible droplet, explains the uniform Na+ distribution at 300 K but fails at 200 K.
The non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation, which predicts exponential decay toward the droplet center at 300 K, cannot describe the distribution of multiple ions at 200 K.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study uses molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the spatial distribution of Na+ ions within supercooled aqueous nanodroplets containing 100 to 1100 water molecules at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. The authors report direct computational evidence that supercooled nanodroplets develop a heterogeneous solvent structure: a low-density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water molecules surrounded by a higher-density, more disordered subsurface. At supercooling, a single Na+ ion is expelled from the low-density core and peaks within approximately 0.1 nm of the subsurface density maximum, whereas at room temperature, the ion distribution is nearly uniform across the droplet interior. 

To analyze the single-ion distribution, the authors introduce a reference analytical model of "electrostatic confinement" (EC), which expresses the droplet energy as the sum of electrostatic and surface energies of a deformable dielectric droplet. The model predicts that an ion is subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, with a spring constant K(ε) that peaks at a relative dielectric constant of ε ≈ 2.73. The model predictions agree with the simulation findings at room temperature but not at supercooling, where the heterogeneous water structure dominates. For multiple ions, the subsurface localization persists at 200 K, and the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann (NPB) equation—which predicts exponential decay toward the center at 300 K—cannot describe the distribution at supercooling. 

The authors note that for the smallest system (N = 100 H2O), the low-density core is absent due to large relative shape fluctuations and immediate ion solvation of the Na+ ion. The study anticipates serving as a starting point for investigating supercooled electrosprayed droplets used to preserve macromolecule conformations in native mass spectrometry. Key results include: the EC model predicts r^2 < 12 Å excursions for a single charge at N = 1000; NPB fits at 300 K yield λPB ≈ 1.2 nm for 776 H2O and 1.3 nm for 1100 H2O, compared to a theoretical λPB ≈ 0.8; and for 8 Na+ ions in 1100 H2O at 200 K, two peaks appear at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm, indicating subsurface localization.

Research Context
The spatial distribution of ions in droplets determines chemical reactivity in atmospheric and man-made aerosols, with applications in spray-based ionization for native mass spectrometry and droplets as microreactors for chemical synthesis. Aerosol droplets in the lower atmosphere carry small charges of few excess ions, while droplets in thunderclouds and electrosprays are highly charged. Experiments have detected an abundance of "magic" cluster sizes associated with clathrate structures and have studied reactivity relevant to atmospheric chemistry. FT-ICR mass spectrometry of clusters with 50–70 H2O molecules yields estimated temperatures of 130–150 K due to evaporative cooling dominating black body radiation heating. Supercooled droplets serve as preservation environments for peptide conformations sprayed from bulk solution using variable-temperature electrospray ionization coupled with IMS and MS. Most computational studies have focused on clusters at room or elevated temperatures, while relatively few address supercooled clusters due to equilibration challenges. Voth and co-workers previously investigated a single Na+, Cl-, and H+ in clusters of 100 H2O at 100–450 K, finding ions excluded from the interior below freezing and located near the surface. Prior atomistic simulations of multiple ions in aqueous nanodroplets (diameter ≈ 2–16 nm, 300–450 K) showed almost uniform radial distribution for N ≈ 1000 H2O with a distinct maximum in outer layers. The solution of the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation for spherical geometry serves as a reference model for comparing atomistic simulations with continuum theory. The distribution of multiple ions and biological molecules such as peptides at supercooling remains completely unknown. Prior supercooled water cluster simulations (N ≥ 200) revealed an anomalous, inverted radial density profile with a low-density tetrahedrally ordered core surrounded by a high-density subsurface. The authors previously reported multiple-ion atomistic simulations at 300–450 K for nanodroplets with diameters of 2–16 nm.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question asks how the heterogeneous solvent structure—a low-density tetrahedrally ordered core surrounded by a high-density disordered subsurface—in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets differentiates the ion distribution from that observed at room temperature. The authors hypothesize that the low-density water core in supercooled droplets will differentiate the ion distribution from that at room temperature, a contrast not observed in their previous studies at higher temperatures. This hypothesis could not be explored in earlier research because the small cluster sizes of fewer than 100 water molecules precluded the formation of the low-density core. The authors also seek to establish a reference analytical model for a single ion's location in a fluctuating droplet, which the authors note is still missing from the literature. The predicted outcome is that at supercooling, the single Na+ ion will be expelled from the low-density core to the more disordered subsurface, in contrast to the uniform room-temperature distribution. The multiple-ion question extends whether the subsurface localization persists for multiple ions and how it relates to the NPB prediction of exponential decay toward the droplet center.

Methodological Details
The study uses molecular dynamics simulations of Na+ ions in aqueous nanodroplets at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K, representing standard and supercooled conditions. Nanodroplet sizes range from N = 100 water molecules (diameter ≈ 1.8 nm) to N = 1100 (diameter ≈ 4.0 nm), with intermediate sizes of N = 360 and 776 also studied. Water molecules are modeled using the TIP4P/2005 transferable intermolecular potential with four points. Na+ parameters are taken from OPLS-AA, with the ion having a charge of +1e and bound charge. Simulations are performed by GROMACS v4.6.1 using a periodic cubic box with length L (from Table 1) large enough to avoid interaction between the droplet and its periodic images. The cutoff for Coulomb and Lennard-Jones interactions is at L/2, much larger than the droplet's diameter to reproduce long-range electrostatic interactions. Simulations are carried out in the canonical ensemble (NVT) with temperature controlled by the Nosé-Hoover thermostat with a time constant of 0.1 ps. Equations of motion are integrated with the leap-frog algorithm using a time step of 2 fs. The Na+ ion is placed at the surface for the majority of single-ion runs and at the center for two runs each at N = 360 and 776 at T = 200 K. All multiple-ion runs start with ions near the droplet's center of mass. The mean number of molecules N d forming the connected cluster and relaxation time τ are determined from the neighbor correlation function, with N d and τ values reported in Table 1. Evaporation within the simulation box is negligible at the temperatures of interest. To ensure equilibration at 200 K, the authors run two simulations for each N = 360 and 776 nanodroplet: one with the ion at the center quenched through conjugate-gradient minimization and one with the ion initially on the surface. Equilibration is confirmed when ion density profiles from both starting conditions converge, which occurs after 400 ns for N = 776 at 200 K. For N = 1100, equilibration time is assumed longer by a factor of τ 1100 / τ 776 ≈ 2. Relaxation times for multiple ions are presumed shorter, and single-ion simulations provide upper bounds. Additional structural quantities are reported as a function of radial distance from the pure water droplet COM, including water density ρ(r), Voronoi-based density ρv(r), tetrahedral order parameter qT(r), and distance to the fifth O neighbor d5(r). Voronoi cells are computed for O sites with H sites ignored, using the same procedure as in the authors' previous study. The tetrahedral order parameter is defined at the particle level with cut-off r = 0.35 nm, and radial averaging uses a bin size of ∆r = 0.05 nm.

Procedures And Architectures
The reference analytical model considers a charged dielectric droplet that may undergo shape fluctuations, with the energy expressed as the sum of electrostatic and surface energy. The ion is subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, and the effect is termed "electrostatic confinement" (EC). The energy related to the ion's distance from the droplet's COM (∆E 1) has the functional form of a harmonic potential, with spring constant K(ε) defined by the model's algebraic derivation. The maximum of K(ε) is attained at ε = 1 + √ 3 ≈ 2.73, where ε is the relative dielectric constant. Limiting cases of ε = 1 (no droplet perturbation) and ε = ∞ (localized field) are noted where electrostatic interaction with the surface vanishes. The model predicts that EC is more pronounced at low temperature, high charge, small radius, and intermediate dielectric constant values. Small droplets with high charge may undergo Rayleigh instability leading to "star"-shaped droplets, necessitating an increased radius while keeping the Rayleigh parameter Q^2/R^3 constant. High charges are modeled by creating charged cyclic peptides, DNA, or RNA strand configurations to illustrate EC effects. The minimal dimensions of ion excursions from the center are estimated at r^2 < 12 Å for a single charge Q = 1e in a droplet of 1000 water molecules. At room temperature, the diffusion coefficient D is ∼ 10^-9 m^2/s, so simulation times of 10–100 ns are sufficient to resolve ion positions. The droplet's equimolecular radius is 3.8 nm and the charge is +8e in the peptide example; the distribution tapers off before reaching the surface. For comparison with atomistic simulations, the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation for a rigid spherical geometry predicts an exponential decay of ion distribution toward the center. The theoretical λPB value, calculated with water dielectric constant of 75 and the assumption that all charge is at the surface, is approximately 0.8. For droplets of a few thousands of water molecules, shape fluctuations are significant, so the value of λPB is interpreted only qualitatively. At 300 K, the fitting function for 776 H2O with 5 Na+ is 0.42 exp(-(1.14-x)/1.2), yielding λPB ≈ 1.2 nm. For 1100 H2O with 8 Na+ at 300 K, the fitting function is 0.40 exp(-(1.37-x)/1.3), yielding λPB ≈ 1.3 nm. At 200 K, the multiple-ion distribution cannot be analyzed using the NPB exponential decay form.

Key Results
For pure water nanodroplets at high temperature (300 K for N ≥ 200, 260 K for N ≤ 200), ρ(r) is that of a typical liquid droplet with a flat interior decaying sigmoidally to near-zero over approximately an intermolecular distance. At low temperature (200 K), significant layering exists for all nanodroplet sizes, with density increasing as r approaches the surface. The Voronoi-based density ρv(r) is monotonically decreasing or flat with r for all nanodroplet sizes at high temperature, but shows a monotonic increase toward a subsurface peak at low temperature. ρv(r) begins to decay to zero approximately 0.3 nm before ρ(r), identifying molecules within the high ρv(r) region as completely surrounded and not on the surface. At T = 300 K, the single Na+ radial distribution ρNa(r) is approximately constant in the droplet interior, consistent with the EC model. The Na+ distribution does not distinctly peak at the droplet's COM because the geometric confinement effect dominates over the force toward the COM due to low charge. At T = 200 K, the peak of ρNa(r) is located within 0.1 nm of the peak in ρv(r), meaning the ion resides in the highest density subsurface environment rather than the center. The dielectric constant increases with density at constant temperature and polarization factor, making the subsurface a better solvation environment than the surface. For N = 100 at 200 K, ρNa(r) is peaked just below 0.3 nm, and the peak coincides with a local minimum in ρ(r), suggesting layering plays a role in locating the ion in small droplets. For N = 776 at 200 K, the tetrahedrality parameter qT(r) shows a significant decrease coinciding with the subsurface density peak. The distance to the fifth neighbor d5(r) shows a more disordered structure in the vicinity of the subsurface density peak at low temperature. qT(r) begins to increase beyond its minimum at 1.6 nm in the surface layer, but this increase is not indicative of increased tetrahedral order. For N = 100 at 200 K, the cluster does not form a tetrahedrally organized core because the central H2O molecules participate in immediate ion solvation and large shape fluctuations occur. For N = 100, direct visual inspection reveals the Na+ lies one or two layers in from the cluster surface, and the outer water molecules participate in immediate solvation. In droplets of 1100 H2O with 8 Na+ at 200 K, two peaks are observed in the radial distribution at distances of 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm. The lower intensity peak at 0.52 nm corresponds to one ion that can exchange with the ions giving rise to the outer peak, so two peaks do not indicate a metastable state. At T = 300 K, multiple-ion distributions are almost uniform with an incipient broad maximum appearing in the outer layers. The exponential decay from the NPB equation manifests more clearly in larger droplets at lower temperature, but at 200 K it cannot be applied to multiple ions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The electrostatic confinement effect exerts a force towards the droplet COM, but at low charges (Q = 1e) the geometric confinement dominates, preventing a central peak in the ion distribution at 300 K. At supercooling, the hetero-structured solvent—low-density tetrahedral core, disordered high-density subsurface—expels Na+ ions from the center, overriding the EC model prediction. The subsurface preference of the ion is consistent with the fact that the dielectric constant increases with density at constant temperature and polarization. The surface layer, while at high ρ(r), does not provide a good solvation environment for the ion, so the ion peaks in the subsurface where ρv(r) is high but ρ(r) has decayed. The EC model, while providing the only known reference for single-ion location in a fluctuating droplet, may deviate from simulations at supercooling when the low-density core affects ion position. The EC model can be extended by including ion size and hydrophobic effects to further refine predictions. The evaporative cooling of droplets is a process that may be important in a droplet's lifetime during ionization methods used in native mass spectrometry. A conical deformation is a key component in the mechanism of ion emission, and whether the low-density core at supercooling hinders this conical deformation is an open question. The study anticipates providing a starting point for investigating the structure of supercooled electrosprayed droplets containing unstructured peptides and ion complexes. These studies will assist in interpreting ion mobility-mass spectrometry data on the detection of macromolecule conformations in bulk solution. The distribution of multiple ions at supercooling in electrosprayed droplets has implications for Rayleigh fission and ion evaporation mechanisms in aerosol science.

Contradictions And Limitations
The N = 100 nanodroplet at 200 K does not form a tetrahedrally organized core because the central H2O molecules participate in immediate ion solvation and the system is subject to large relative shape fluctuations. The EC model predictions may deviate from simulated ion distributions at supercooling when the low-density core affects the location of the ions. For N = 1100 at 200 K, the authors assume equilibration time is longer by a factor of τ 1100 / τ 776 ≈ 2 without direct confirmation. The relaxation times for multiple-ion simulations are presumed to be shorter based on single-ion simulations, but this is not formally quantified. Sampling of the ion distribution in such systems is a challenge; simulation times must be much longer than the time for a molecule to diffuse the width of the droplet. The interpretation of the NPB λPB value is only qualitative because shape fluctuations are significant in droplets of a few thousand water molecules. For N = 100 at 200 K, the peak in ρNa(r) coincides with a local minimum in ρ(r), suggesting layering rather than the predicted EC-driven localization is primary. The Voronoi cell computation ignores H sites, which may affect the density calculation and tetrahedral order parameter. No random seed is reported for the MD simulations, limiting exact reproducibility of stochastic trajectories. The authors do not explicitly report the train-test split or validation protocol as the study is a molecular dynamics simulation, not a machine learning application. There are no demographic or human participant data, making ethical considerations inapplicable to the study design.

Claims
A low-density, tetrahedrally ordered core forms in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets and expels single and multiple Na+ ions to a more disordered, higher-density subsurface. At T = 200 K, the peak of ρNa(r) is located within 0.1 nm of the peak in ρv(r), placing the ion in the subsurface. The tetrahedral order parameter qT(r) shows a significant decrease at low temperature coinciding with the subsurface density peak. The Voronoi-based density ρv(r) shows a monotonic increase toward a subsurface peak at 200 K, absent at 300 K. For N = 100, the cluster lacks a tetrahedrally organized core due to large relative shape fluctuations and immediate ion solvation. For N = 100 at 200 K, the peak in ρNa(r) coincides with a local minimum in ρ(r), suggesting layering may play a role rather than just the density-driven EC effect. The EC model, which explains the uniform distribution at 300 K, predicts a harmonic potential towards the center, a prediction that the simulations refute at 200 K. This mechanism may hinder the formation of conical deformations required for ion emission in supercooled electrosprayed droplets. The ion distribution at supercooling in electrosprayed droplets has implications for Rayleigh fission and ion evaporation mechanisms.
The electrostatic confinement model, predicting a harmonic potential for a single ion in a flexible droplet, explains the uniform Na+ distribution at 300 K but fails at 200 K. At T = 300 K, the Na+ radial distribution is consistent with the EC effect, appearing almost uniform in the interior. The geometric confinement effect dominates over the force towards the droplet's COM at low charge Q = 1e, explaining the lack of a central peak. The EC model is more pronounced at intermediate dielectric constant ε ≈ 2.73. At T = 200 K, the model predictions deviate because the low-density core affects the ion location, a factor not accounted for in the dielectric droplet model. For N = 100 at 200 K, the peak coincides with a local minimum in ρ(r), suggesting layering overrides the EC prediction. The model serves as the first reference for a single-ion in a flexible droplet, providing a baseline for future model extensions including ion size and hydrophobic effects.
The non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation, which predicts exponential decay toward the droplet center at 300 K, cannot describe the distribution of multiple ions at 200 K. The NPB exponential decay fits at 300 K with λPB values of 1.2 nm and 1.3 nm, but at 200 K the distribution cannot be analyzed using the NPB form. At 200 K, the multiple ions are expelled from the core and show a maximum at the same location as the single ion. The authors note that for droplets of a few thousand water molecules, shape fluctuations make the λPB value only qualitative, complicating comparison. At 300 K, the NPB prediction of exponential decay toward the COM is approximately in qualitative agreement with simulations for larger droplets. The failure of the NPB model at supercooling highlights that the continuum dielectric approximation cannot capture the effects of the heterogeneous tetrahedral solvent structure.

Data And Code Availability
The authors report that simulations were performed by GROMACS v4.6.1 and the water model is TIP4P/2005, but no specific data repository or code link is provided in the text. Voronoi volumes for all O sites and qT(r) values are reported as functions of radial distance, with data taken from the authors' previous study (Ref. 31). The fitting parameters for the NPB exponential decays at 300 K (0.42 exp(-(1.14-x)/1.2) and 0.40 exp(-(1.37-x)/1.3)) and the spring constant K(ε) values are explicitly reported.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Two simulations per N = 360 and 776 nanodroplet at 200 K—one starting with the ion at the center and one on the surface—confirm equilibration after 400 ns. The convergence of the trajectories for Na+ starting on the surface and at the COM is shown in Figure S3 of the supplementary information. For N = 1100, equilibration is assumed to be longer by a factor of approximately 2, a heuristic based on the relaxation time ratio τ 1100 / τ 776. The Voronoi-based density ρv(r) is used instead of number density ρ(r) to reduce the effect of undulations and layering, making the density trend easier to characterize. For multiple ions, the relaxation times are presumed shorter and the single-ion simulations provide upper bounds on the relaxation times. The Rayleigh instability is avoided by increasing the droplet radius while keeping the Rayleigh parameter Q^2/R^3 constant for high-charge models.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 plots the spring constant K(ε) as a function of the relative dielectric constant, showing the maximum at ε ≈ 2.73. Figure 2 plots the distribution of the distance of the peptide center of mass relative to the droplet COM for a 3.8 nm droplet with +8e charge. Figure 3 shows ρ(r), ρv(r), and ρNa(r) for all studied nanodroplet sizes at 200 K and 300 K, including qT(r) and d5(r) for N = 776 at 200 K. Figure 4 compares the radial distributions of single and multiple Na+ ions in 776 H2O nanodroplets at 200 K and 300 K, including the tetrahedrality parameter and d5. Figure 5 shows the radial distributions of multiple Na+ ions in 1100 H2O nanodroplets at 200 K and 300 K, revealing two peaks for the 8-ion system. Table 1 reports the mean number of molecules N d in the connected cluster, the relaxation time τ, and simulation times for each N and T. Figure S2 in the supplementary information shows the "star"-shaped droplets that arise when the Rayleigh limit is exceeded.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first direct computational evidence that a low-density tetrahedrally ordered core in supercooled nanodroplets expels single and multiple Na+ ions to the disordered, high-density subsurface, a behavior not observed at room temperature. 2. The strongest evidence is the single Na+ radial distribution peaking within 0.1 nm of the subsurface density maximum at 200 K, coinciding with a significant decrease in qT(r) and a more disordered d5(r), in contrast to the nearly uniform distribution at 300 K. 3. The future path involves extending the electrostatic confinement model with ion size and hydrophobic effects, investigating the impact of supercooling on conical deformations in electrosprayed droplets, and applying these findings to supercooled nanodroplets containing peptides and macromolecules for native mass spectrometry.

summary.title: Learning design rules for selective oxidation catalysts from high-throughput experimentation and artificial intelligence
summary.authors: Lucas Foppa, Christopher Sutton, Luca M Ghiringhelli, Sandip De, Patricia Löser, Stephan A Schunk, Ansgar Schäfer, Matthias Scheffler
summary.field_subfield: Heterogeneous catalysis; materials science; subgroup-discovery artificial intelligence
summary.type_of_paper: Research article - Experimental and computational catalysis with machine learning
summary.executive_summary: This study demonstrates how a subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach can be applied to a hybrid dataset of high-throughput experimentation (HTE) and density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations to identify key physicochemical parameters and constraints—so-called SG rules—that exclusively describe materials and reaction conditions with outstanding catalytic performance for the selective oxidation of propylene. The researchers synthesized and tested 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus (three-component systems) across various reaction temperatures (200–400ºC). Ten composition-related parameters derived from calculated free-atom properties, plus temperature, were used as candidate descriptive parameters. SGD identified three key parameters: temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity (VY), whose specific rules defined a subgroup of 15 data points (1.2% of the dataset) with an average oxygenate yield of 24.15%, five times higher than the global average of 4.83%. The highest yield in the training set was 26.85%. These SG rules were then used to guide the design of four-component (ruthenium, tungsten, phosphorus + one additional element) and five-component catalysts. The four-component catalysts achieved oxygenate yields up to 60.19%, and the five-component catalyst reached 59.60%, both more than twice the highest yield from the training set. A second SGD analysis on the four- and five-component HTE data (746 data points) yielded different rules reflecting higher temperatures and different composition-dependent parameters (L and VH instead of JK and VY). The study shows that SG rules not only reflect underlying physical processes associated with exceptional performance but also generalize to more complex systems, enabling the identification of catalysts with yields far exceeding those in the training data.
