The three key parameters—temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity—are the most relevant descriptive variables for outstanding propylene oxidation performance in three-component ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus catalysts.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study demonstrates how a subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach can be applied to a hybrid dataset of high-throughput experimentation (HTE) and density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations to identify key physicochemical parameters and constraints—so-called SG rules—that exclusively describe materials and reaction conditions with outstanding catalytic performance for the selective oxidation of propylene. The researchers synthesized and tested 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus (three-component systems) across various reaction temperatures (200–400ºC). Ten composition-related parameters derived from calculated free-atom properties, plus temperature, were used as candidate descriptive parameters. SGD identified three key parameters: temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity (VY), whose specific rules defined a subgroup of 15 data points (1.2% of the dataset) with an average oxygenate yield of 24.15%, five times higher than the global average of 4.83%. The highest yield in the training set was 26.85%. These SG rules were then used to guide the design of four-component (ruthenium, tungsten, phosphorus + one additional element) and five-component catalysts. The four-component catalysts achieved oxygenate yields up to 60.19%, and the five-component catalyst reached 59.60%, both more than twice the highest yield from the training set. A second SGD analysis on the four- and five-component HTE data (746 data points) yielded different rules reflecting higher temperatures and different composition-dependent parameters (L and VH instead of JK and VY). The study shows that SG rules not only reflect underlying physical processes associated with exceptional performance but also generalize to more complex systems, enabling the identification of catalysts with yields far exceeding those in the training data.

Research Context
Heterogeneous catalysis is governed by an intricate interplay of multiple processes such as surface reaction networks and typically unknown dynamic restructuring. Explicit atomistic modeling of the full catalytic progression by first-principles methods is impractical. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) allows testing large amounts of materials but utilizing the obtained information to decide on next promising materials is not straightforward. The number of possible materials is practically infinite while the number of good catalysts is very small, making the direct approach of searching through all materials unlikely to identify needed materials. Detailed characterization of each material in large HTE libraries is typically not feasible, leaving only little information on structure and physicochemical properties. Distinct catalytic mechanisms might operate depending on materials and conditions, and only very few situations result in good catalytic performance, creating an unbalanced distribution between high- and low-performance scenarios. Global models trained to minimize expected average prediction error over all samples may not allow focused modeling of the most interesting materials and mechanisms. The subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence local approach has been applied in computational catalysis and materials science. The selective partial oxidation of light alkanes to value-added olefins or oxygenates is an efficient feedstock upgrading technology, but surface reaction networks lead to product mixtures containing up to 20 different molecules. Platinum-group-metal-based catalysts commonly result in hydrocarbon combustion products. The combination of ruthenium with tungsten and phosphorus in a tungsten-phosphate-like matrix was proposed as an alternative class of catalysts to favor selectivity towards desired olefins and oxygenates.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach applied to a hybrid HTE and theory dataset can identify key physicochemical descriptive parameters and constraints (SG rules) associated with outstanding catalytic performance. The reactivity measured by HTE is used as the target, and temperature plus composition-dependent physicochemical properties evaluated with DFT calculations are the candidate descriptive parameters. The study hypothesizes that the SGD search—which maximizes a quality function measuring how outstanding specific subselections of data points are compared to the whole dataset—will identify local behaviors reflecting specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance. The specific prediction is that temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity will emerge as key parameters describing high yields of acrolein and acrylic acid. The rules are expected to not only reflect underlying processes but also guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements in their composition. Because the candidate descriptive materials parameters can be calculated by first-principles methods, the approach is expected to circumvent extensive experimental materials characterization and allow identification of promising candidates not yet synthesized by experiment. The design strategy is based on the dilution of highly active metal sites within a tungsten-phosphate-like matrix to favor selectivity towards desired olefins and oxygenates.

Methodological Details
120 different three-component catalyst compositions containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus were synthesized on SiO2 pseudo-liquid support and tested in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. Several reaction temperatures between 200ºC and 400ºC were examined at each catalyst composition. The reaction feed consisted of Ar, H2O, N2, O2, and propylene (C3H6) with molar rates of 4.015, 4.015, 104.40, 20.08, and 1.57 mmol/h, respectively. The same mass of catalyst was used in all reactions so that the contact time, in terms of volumetric flow per mass of catalyst, was kept fixed across experiments. The atomic structures of all tested catalysts are not known in detail, and oxygen content was not included in material characterization because its proportion is not known from catalyst formulation nor measured. Eleven descriptive parameters in total were used: I (temperature), JK, L, MN, LO, LPQR, ST, SU, plus three other parameters not listed by name but enumerated as 11. The per-element free-atom properties were converted into system-specific properties by taking the composition-weighted average, where JK is the molar content of element b. The target value is defined as the yield of oxygenates, calculated from molar rates of species in reactor feed and outlet: yield = (EF,2* + EF,%G) / (EF,2* + EF,2* + EF,2) - (EF,F2* + EF,F,%G) / (EF,F2* + EF,F2* + EF,F2). DFT-PBEsol was used for calculation of free-atom properties with the FHI-aims code. The quality function is the product of coverage (ratio of subgroup data points to total) and the cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence between the distribution of target values in the SG and the whole dataset. The coverage term controls subgroup size to prevent selection of very small SGs with little statistical significance. For the cross-validation, similar SG rules were obtained when training was performed with randomly selected 90% of data points. When data points presenting oxygenate yields lower than 3% were excluded from training, similar SG rules were still observed. The atomic radius of tungsten is 1.45 Å, and compatible V elements were selected with a maximum atomic radius difference of 0.10 Å compared to tungsten. For the four-component materials with J_V = 0.035 for cases where V = Mo, Nb, and J_V = 0.050 for V = Ta, Sb.

Procedures And Architectures
The SGD approach starts with the generation of a pool of propositions (π)—statements about the data applying only to a portion of the dataset; for continuous parameters, these are inequalities constraining values. SGD identifies selectors (σ)—statements formed by a number of propositions joined by the AND connector (∧)—that select subgroups with the most outstanding distributions of target values relative to the whole dataset. The SG search is performed by maximizing a quality function that measures how outstanding specific subselections of data points are, thus identifying a local behavior. The composition-weighted average property is calculated as the sum over elements b of molar content (J_b) multiplied by elemental property (Q_b). For the three-component materials, c = 3, and for four-component, c = 4. The three-component catalysts are prepared on SiO2 pseudo-liquid support and may have a disordered, possibly amorphous structure; crystallinity was not a controlling factor for performance. All reactions were carried out in tubular, fixed-bed reactors. The SGD-HTE-&-theory approach circumvents explicit modeling of the full catalytic progression by using the experimental HTE product yield directly as the target. The Janson-Shannon divergence is a properly symmetrized version of the information-theoretic Kullback-Leibler divergence. The quality function is defined as M(jk) * J_no(X, gh), where M(jk) is coverage and J_no is the cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence. The coverage term controls subgroup size and prevents selection of very small SGs with little statistical significance. The second term favors SGs with target values as unusual as possible compared to the majority of observations, and favors distributions in narrower value ranges. The three-component HTE data consists of 120 compositions multiplied by several temperatures.

Key Results
50% of the measured materials and conditions result in less than 2% oxygenates yield, and only 41 measurements out of 1220 are associated with yields above 20%. The average oxygenates yield over the whole dataset is equal to 4.83%, and the maximum yield value is 26.85%. The identified SG of outstanding performance contains only 15 data points, approximately 1.2% of the dataset, all with high yield of oxygenates. The average yield of oxygenates in this SG is 24.15%, which is five times higher than the global average of 4.83%. The SG is described by three rules: 280 ≤ T ≤ 300ºC, JK > 0.55, and 3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV. The temperature rule highlights that highest yields are observed for intermediate temperatures within the 200–400ºC tested range. The phosphorus content rule shows that a relatively high phosphorus content is needed to achieve outstanding performance. The VY rule effectively limits the range of ruthenium contents: Ru is needed for propylene conversion but too much leads to combustion products. The SG rules are robust: cross-validation with 90% of data or excluding yields < 3% yields similar rules with comparable thresholds. The four-component catalysts achieve oxygenate yields up to 60.19% at 400ºC, the highest for a single composition. The five-component catalyst achieves 59.60% at 400ºC, which is more than twice the highest yield (26.85%) from the three-component training set. The composition-averaged electronegativity (VY) for the five-component tantalum-based catalyst is 3.947 eV, lying within the VY rule of 3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV. The four- and five-component catalysts achieve their highest yields at 400ºC compared to 300ºC for the three-component systems, indicating the temperature rule is not transferable. A second SGD on the 746 data points of four- and five-component HTE data identifies a SG of 18 data points (ca. 2.4% of the dataset) with the highest J_no of 0.355. The rules for the four- and five-component SG constrain three parameters: T ≥ 360ºC, L_plus1 ≤ 1.001 Å, and VH < -1.593 eV. Different composition-dependent parameters (L and VH) are required for the more complex systems compared to (JK and VY) for the three-component materials.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The SG rules do not just identify data points; they reflect the specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding catalytic performance at a local level. The phosphorus content rule may be related to the dilution of metal active sites on a phosphate matrix that occurs at high phosphorus loadings. The VY rule limits ruthenium content because ruthenium is required for propylene conversion but excess ruthenium promotes combustion pathways. The SG rules generalize from three-component materials to more complex four- and five-component systems, demonstrating their transferability to chemically distinct but related materials spaces. The fact that the four- and five-component catalysts achieve oxygenate yields more than twice as large as those in the training set suggests that the SG rules hint at materials that are significantly more performant than any training observations. The SGD-HTE-&-theory approach is suitable for searching for exceptional materials whose structures and functions are hardly modeled explicitly by theory. The rules are expected to describe outstanding materials governed by the same processes as the exceptional materials in the training data. The approach avoids explicit modeling of the full catalytic progression, bypassing the need for detailed reaction mechanism knowledge. The local nature of SGD means the identified rules may only apply to specific ruthenium contents or elements compatible with tungsten's atomic radius.

Contradictions And Limitations
The SG rules are not transferable to the four-component systems regarding temperature: the three-component rule (280 ≤ T ≤ 300ºC) does not apply as four-component materials peak at 400ºC. The SGD analysis is restricted to low ruthenium contents and elements compatible with tungsten's atomic radius (ΔR ≤ 0.10 Å), limiting the domain of applicability. It is unclear if the SG rules can identify exceptional materials for arbitrary ruthenium content or elements with significantly different radii, as different mechanisms may operate. The oxygen content was excluded from material characterization because it is neither known from catalyst formulation nor measured, representing a potential information gap in the descriptor set. The SGD analysis might need to be re-performed including new data points covering unexplored portions of the materials space to enlarge the domain. The atomic structures of all tested catalysts are not known in detail, and the catalysts are described as disordered and possibly amorphous. The three-component catalysts were tested on SiO2 pseudo-liquid support, a condition that may not represent all possible supports for this reaction. The five-component materials were only tested at 400ºC, leaving the temperature dependence partially explored.

Claims
The SGD-HTE-&-theory approach can identify interpretable, chemically meaningful SG rules that exclusively describe materials and conditions with outstanding catalytic performance, and these rules generalize to more complex systems. The SG rules for the three-component system identify 15 data points (1.2% of the dataset) with average oxygenate yield 24.15%, five times the global average. The rules (T=280–300ºC, JK>0.55, 3.910≤VY<4.002 eV) are cross-validated with 90% of the data and yielding similar thresholds. The four-component catalysts (up to 60.19% yield) and five-component catalyst (59.60% yield) lie within the VY prediction window defined by the rules. The four- and five-component catalysts achieve yields more than twice as large as the training maximum (26.85%). The temperature rule derived from the three-component system (280–300ºC) is not transferable to the four- and five-component systems that peak at 400ºC. The rules for the more complex systems differ in descriptor identity (L and VH instead of JK and VY), indicating the mapping is not invariant across material complexity. The domain is restricted to elements with atomic radii within 0.10 Å of tungsten. The approach circumvents the need for explicit modeling of the full catalytic progression, making it applicable to systems where reaction mechanisms are unknown or too complex to model. SG rules can guide the design of materials not yet synthesized by experiment, broadening the accessible design space. DFT-calculated properties reduce the need for extensive experimental materials characterization, accelerating the discovery cycle.
The three key parameters—temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity—are the most relevant descriptive variables for outstanding propylene oxidation performance in three-component ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus catalysts. The SG rules for the highest-performance subgroup are defined specifically by constraints on these three parameters. The VY rule effectively limits ruthenium content, reflecting the trade-off between conversion and combustion. The phosphorus content rule is interpreted as dilution of active sites on a phosphate matrix. In the four- and five-component systems, different parameters (L and VH) become the constraining descriptors instead of JK and VY. These parameters provide a physically-grounded basis for catalyst design: temperature controls kinetics, phosphorus controls site density, and electronegativity controls electronic structure.

Data And Code Availability
Further calculation details and values for the elemental properties used in the work are available in the electronic supporting information (ESI). The DFT calculations were performed with the FHI-aims code, and the specific input parameters and property values are detailed in the ESI.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Similar SG rules were obtained when training was performed with randomly selected 90% of the data points. When data points presenting yield of oxygenates lower than 3% were excluded from training, the SG rules remained consistent. The ranges of variation of minimum and maximum thresholds for the VY parameter were [3.882, 3.910 eV] and [3.989, 4.031] eV, respectively, demonstrating stability. The SG rules constraining the VY parameter to an intermediate range were always observed when only 90% of the data was used for training.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A schematically illustrates the SGD approach: from a pool of propositions (π) to selectors (σ) forming a subgroup with outstanding distributions. Figure 1B shows the catalyst composition space with ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus. Figure 1C displays reaction equations for selective oxidation to oxygenates (acrolein, acrylic acid) and combustion products (CO, CO2). Figure 2A and 2B show the propylene conversion versus oxygenates selectivity profiles and the distribution of oxygenates yield, respectively. Figure 2C displays the temperature rule (280 ≤ T ≤ 300ºC). Figure 2D shows the phosphorus content rule. Figure 2F shows the composition-averaged electronegativity rule (3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV). Figure 3B is a ternary diagram showing the ruthenium content range restricted by the VY rule. Figure 4A shows the composition map for four-component materials with VY values and HTE results, highlighting the SG-compatible materials in bold with stars. Figures 4C and 4D show experimental oxygenate yields for four-component and five-component catalysts. Figure 5A and 5B display the HTE data for four- and five-component materials (746 data points). Figure 5C shows the SG rules for the four- and five-component data: T ≥ 360ºC. Figures 5D, 5E, and 5F show the composition-dependent rules (L_plus1 and VH) for the complex materials.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating that the subgroup-discovery (SGD) approach, applied to a hybrid HTE and DFT dataset, can extract physically grounded and transferable catalytic design rules that identify exceptionally high-performing materials without explicit reaction mechanism modeling. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of a five-component catalyst with oxygenate yield 59.60% (more than twice the training maximum of 26.85%) that falls within the VY and phosphorus rules derived from the simpler three-component training data. 3. The future path involves including new data points covering unexplored portions of the materials space—specifically varying ruthenium content and using elements with significantly different atomic radii from tungsten—to enlarge the domain of the identified SG rules.

summary.title: Environmentally friendly and roll-processed flexible organic solar cells based on PM6:Y6
summary.authors: Marcial Fernández Castro, Jean Truer, Espíndola Rodríguez, Jens Wenzel
summary.field_subfield: Materials Science / Organic Photovoltaics
summary.executive_summary: This paper demonstrates the first slot-die coated flexible organic solar cells (OSCs) based on the high-performance PM6:Y6 binary blend, fabricated in open-air using a green solvent (o-xylene) without additives on a flexible PET substrate. The authors address the 'lab-to-fab gap' by moving from spin-coating to roll-compatible slot-die coating while maintaining environmentally friendly processing. Key optimization parameters investigated include slot-die coating temperature (60–120 °C), solution concentration (12–28 mg/mL), and active layer thickness. The optimal coating temperature was identified as 100 °C, matching the drum, tube, and head temperatures, which maximizes short-circuit current by minimizing bimolecular recombination (S = 0.978) and avoiding material aggregation at the stripe edges. The optimal active layer thickness was found to be approximately 200 nm, with the highest PCE of 6.3% achieved at 24 mg/mL (217 nm thickness) and 100 °C. Introducing a small amount of PC61BM as a ternary acceptor (ratios [1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1]) improved performance, reaching an average PCE of 6.7% (champion 7.2%) with increased fill factor and short-circuit current. Stability testing under dark storage (ISOS-D-1 protocol) showed that the ternary devices retained 99.4% of initial PCE after 1050 hours, and binary devices retained over 97% after 1500 hours. The work confirms that PM6:Y6-based OSCs can be successfully processed on flexible substrates using scalable, environmentally benign slot-die coating with efficiencies competitive with lab-scale spin-coated devices.

claims.description: Slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 on flexible substrates in open-air with green solvents achieves competitive efficiencies (PCE ≈ 6–7%) comparable to spin-coated lab devices.
Introducing a small amount of PC61BM as a ternary acceptor improves device efficiency through a balanced energy cascade effect and enhanced charge transport.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper demonstrates the first slot-die coated flexible organic solar cells (OSCs) based on the high-performance PM6:Y6 binary blend, fabricated in open-air using a green solvent (o-xylene) without additives on a flexible PET substrate. The authors address the 'lab-to-fab gap' by moving from spin-coating to roll-compatible slot-die coating while maintaining environmentally friendly processing. Key optimization parameters investigated include slot-die coating temperature (60–120 °C), solution concentration (12–28 mg/mL), and active layer thickness. The optimal coating temperature was identified as 100 °C, matching the drum, tube, and head temperatures, which maximizes short-circuit current by minimizing bimolecular recombination (S = 0.978) and avoiding material aggregation at the stripe edges. The optimal active layer thickness was found to be approximately 200 nm, with the highest PCE of 6.3% achieved at 24 mg/mL (217 nm thickness) and 100 °C. Introducing a small amount of PC61BM as a ternary acceptor (ratios [1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1]) improved performance, reaching an average PCE of 6.7% (champion 7.2%) with increased fill factor and short-circuit current. Stability testing under dark storage (ISOS-D-1 protocol) showed that the ternary devices retained 99.4% of initial PCE after 1050 hours, and binary devices retained over 97% after 1500 hours. The work confirms that PM6:Y6-based OSCs can be successfully processed on flexible substrates using scalable, environmentally benign slot-die coating with efficiencies competitive with lab-scale spin-coated devices.

Research Context
Organic solar cells have reached highest efficiencies using lab-scale device manufacturing on active areas far below 0.1 cm², widening the 'lab-to-fab gap'. Spin-coating, the most commonly used fabrication technique, has poor potential for upscaling and produces substantial material waste. Blade and slot-die coating are more suitable for roll-to-roll manufacturing, a key advantage of OSC technology over silicon PV. However, few studies report solar cells using these scalable fabrication techniques on flexible substrates. Environmentally friendly upscaling requires inks based on non-hazardous solvent systems. PM6:Y6 was previously reported to show excellent efficiencies over 15% on rigid substrates using green solvents (o-xylene) without additives. PM6 exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA) behavior, necessitating heating during slot-die coating to maintain liquidity. To the best of current knowledge, there remained a need to transfer PM6:Y6 devices to roll-processing on flexible substrates using scalable techniques.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can PM6:Y6-based OSCs be fabricated using slot-die coating on flexible substrates in open-air with green solvents without additives? The central hypothesis was that fine-tuning of coating parameters (temperature and concentration) would enable competitive power conversion efficiencies suitable for roll-to-roll processing. It was predicted that matching the substrate, syringe, tube, and slot-die head temperatures would optimize morphology and carrier collection. A specific hypothesis proposed that introducing a small amount of a fullerene acceptor (PC61BM) would create an energy cascade effect and improve charge transport. The predicted outcomes included power conversion efficiencies in the range of 6–7% and enhanced device stability, validating the scalable process.

Methodological Details
The active layer materials PM6 (batch YY19260CH100) and Y6 (batch DW7038S) were purchased from 1-Material Inc. PB61BM (batch M111) was purchased from Ossila for ternary device fabrication. ZnO nanoparticle ink was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich, and MoO3 pellets from Kurt J. Lesker Co. The flexible substrate was pre-patterned ITO-coated polyethylene terephthalate (PET) from FOM Technologies. Silver for the back electrode was pure silver from Sigma-Aldrich, and silver paste was DuPont 5025 heat-curing paste. The green solvent used for the active layer solution was o-xylene with ≥ 98% purity from Sigma-Aldrich. Devices followed an inverted geometry: ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag. A homemade roll-coater with a syringe pump controlled the ink flow and drum speed. The ZnO ETL was coated at 75 °C substrate temperature, 0.06 mL/min flow rate, and 1.08 m/min drum speed, then annealed at 100 °C for 10 min in air. The PM6:Y6 AL (1:1 D/A ratio) was coated at temperatures of 60, 80, 100, and 120 °C, and concentrations of 12, 16, 20, 24, 28 mg/mL. For AL coating, the drum speed was 1.5 m/min and the flow rate was 0.12 mL/min. 10 nm MoO3 HTL and 150 nm Ag were thermally evaporated under vacuum at 2 x 10⁻⁵ mbar. Up to 24 solar cells were fabricated per evaporation, each with an approximate active area of 0.8 cm². The shadow mask used for aperture definition was purchased from Ossila (E2002A1). EQE and absorbance measurements were performed with a QEX10 system from 300 to 1100 nm with 5 nm step size. Light intensity measurements ranged from 62.14 mW/cm² to 147.33 mW/cm². Thickness measurements used a DS95-50 AFM instrument with 5 × 5 µm² scans in noncontact mode.

Procedures And Architectures
The ZnO ETL was coated using the slot-die head at 75 °C and annealed at 100 °C for 10 min. For the active layer coating, the head, syringe, drum, and tube were kept at the same temperature for each condition. The AL solution concentration varied from 12 to 28 mg/mL to screen thickness and performance. The AL thickness was screened across four concentrations, yielding semi-transparent to opaque layers. The ternary blend ratios tested were [1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1] (PM6:Y6:PC61BM). Activation involved a reverse bias current of -5 V with 100 mA maximum current before encapsulation. Encapsulation used epoxy-based glue EPXR cured under UV light for ~5 min reaching 66 ± 0.5 °C. J-V curves were measured with a Keithley 2400 source meter with 50 mV steps from reverse to forward bias. Averages were calculated from statistics of eight devices per condition. Light intensity dependence measurements were performed at intermediate points between 62.14 and 147.33 mW/cm².

Key Results
The optimal coating temperature for the PM6:Y6 AL was 100 °C, yielding an average PCE of 5.8% with 8 devices. At 100 °C, the bimolecular recombination factor S was 0.978, the closest to unity among tested temperatures. At 120 °C coating, the average FF dropped to 42.2%, lower than 47.1% at 100 °C, due to material aggregation. The maximum short-circuit current density for the thickness optimization was 17.3 mA/cm² at 154 nm thickness. The highest individual PCE achieved in the thickness optimization was 6.3% with an FF of 49.0% at 24 mg/mL (217 nm). The average PCE for the 217 nm thickness was 5.8%, the highest average obtained during optimization. The ternary [1:1:0.2] blend achieved an average JSC of up to 20 mA/cm², a 12% improvement over binary devices. The average PCE of ternary [1:1:0.2] devices was 6.6%, while [1:1.1:0.1] achieved 6.7%. The champion efficiency reached 7.2% for a ternary device. After 1050 hours of dark storage, ternary devices retained 99.4% of initial PCE. Binary devices retained over 97% of initial PCE after more than 1500 hours. The dissociation probability improved from 93.7% in the binary to 96.3% in ternary [1:1:0.2] and 95.7% in [1:1.1:0.1]. The charge collection probability increased from 69.6% in binary to 77.7% and 73.2% in ternary blends. For the 217 nm thickness, the S factor was 0.987, the lowest bimolecular recombination observed in that optimization. All trap-assisted recombination slope values were higher than kT/q, indicating dominance over second-order recombination.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Higher coating temperatures induce better carrier collection (increased EQE) but the drying kinetics above 100 °C cause material aggregation at the AL edges, reducing fill factor. The 100 °C optimum balances rapid drying for efficient carrier collection with sufficiently controlled kinetics to prevent inhomogeneity. Thermal annealing at 120 °C for 3 min improved JSC for devices coated at 60 °C and 80 °C but had no effect on 100 °C and 120 °C devices, suggesting the latter already achieve sufficient polymer packing. The energy cascade effect from the PC61BM LUMO (-3.7 to -3.9 eV) between PM6 and Y6 enhances JSC and VOC in ternary devices. The improved dissociation probability in ternary devices is attributed to additional and energetically favorable donor/acceptor interfaces. Trap-assisted recombination dominates over bimolecular recombination in all devices, as the slope exceeds kT/q, likely due to open-air processing and impurities. The result demonstrates that slot-die coating can compete with spin-coating efficiencies for PM6:Y6, validating the approach for roll-to-roll industrialization. The thickness effect shows that PM6:Y6 maintains high performance even in thick layers, which is critical for robust roll-to-roll manufacturing involving mechanical stress.

Contradictions And Limitations
The FF at 120 °C (42.2%) was lower than at 100 °C (47.1%), contradicting the otherwise improving trend with temperature. No clear tendency was observed in the S values across temperatures, making temperature selection partially empirical. Devices were processed in open-air rather than a cleanroom or glovebox, introducing unavoidable impurities and explaining the high trap-assisted recombination. The study does not report mechanical bending or stretching tests, although the flexible substrate was specifically used. The slot-die coating was performed on a laboratory-scale roll-coater, not a true industrial roll-to-roll production line. No specific statistical distribution (variance, confidence intervals) is reported for individual PCE values beyond the average from eight devices.

Claims
Slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 on flexible substrates in open-air with green solvents achieves competitive efficiencies (PCE ≈ 6–7%) comparable to spin-coated lab devices. The highest PCE of 6.3% with an FF of 49.0% was achieved at 24 mg/mL (217 nm thickness) using slot-die coating. The champion efficiency reached 7.2% for a ternary device, demonstrating the system's potential. The optimal coating temperature of 100 °C achieved the highest average PCE (5.8%) among binary devices. Bimolecular recombination (S = 0.978) was closest to unity at the optimal temperature, indicating efficient charge collection. No champion PCE was achieved above 15% using slot-die coating, while over 15% was reported for spin-coated devices on rigid substrates. The FF at 120 °C dropped to 42.2%, showing a clear degradation in performance at the highest temperature. The devices were processed in open-air, which is not a production-grade cleanroom environment. This paves the way for upscaling production of PM6:Y6-based OSCs to roll-to-roll manufacturing. The use of o-xylene as a green solvent enables environmentally friendly manufacturing at scale. The thickness-independent high performance suggests that thicker ALs can be used for better mechanical robustness without compromising efficiency.
Introducing a small amount of PC61BM as a ternary acceptor improves device efficiency through a balanced energy cascade effect and enhanced charge transport. The ternary [1:1:0.2] blend achieved an average JSC of up to 20 mA/cm², a 12% improvement over binary devices. The average PCE of the [1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1] ternary devices were 6.6% and 6.7%, respectively. The dissociation probability increased from 93.7% in binary to 96.3% in ternary [1:1:0.2]. The collection probability improved from 69.6% to 77.7% with PC61BM addition. The PC61BM LUMO (-3.7 to -3.9 eV) is between PM6 and Y6, creating the energy cascade. EQEs showed no specific photocurrent maximum attributable to PCBM due to its weak and broad absorption. The difference between the two ternary ratios (6.6% vs 6.7%) was minimal, suggesting the exact optimal amount is not fully established. Fullerenes can serve as complementary acceptors to enhance charge extraction in OSCs without significant spectral penalty. The energy cascade effect is a valid strategy for ternary OSC design on flexible substrates.

Data And Code Availability
Data and code availability is not explicitly stated in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The coating temperature was systematically screened from 60 °C to 120 °C. The AL thickness was varied across four concentrations (12–28 mg/mL) to assess performance versus thickness. Two different PC61BM ratios ([1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1]) were tested to optimize ternary composition. Thermal annealing at 120 °C for 3 min was performed as a post-treatment on encapsulated devices. Light intensity dependence measurements (62.14 to 147.33 mW/cm²) provided quantitative data on recombination mechanisms. Figure 3 shows box plots with statistical data (quartiles, median, average) of PCE and FF versus coating temperature. Figure S2 shows normalized absorption spectra of dried films at different temperatures. Figure S6 shows bimolecular recombination analysis (JSC vs Pin) and open-circuit voltage recombination slopes. Figure S7 displays absorption peaks of donor and acceptor materials. Figure S8 shows JSC vs Pin and open-circuit recombination plots for thickness optimization.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration of slot-die coated flexible PM6:Y6 OSCs fabricated in open-air with green solvents, achieving PCE of 5.8% (average) and 7.2% (champion). 2. The strongest evidence is the systematic temperature screening revealing that 100 °C matches the best balance of carrier collection (highest EQE) and morphological homogeneity (S = 0.978, no edge aggregation). 3. The future path involves transitioning this laboratory-scale slot-die process to an industrial roll-to-roll production line and further optimizing ternary compositions and mechanically robust thick-layer designs.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work reports the synthesis and application of a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) with extremely high spin concentration and negligible photoluminescence quantum yields, optimized for photothermal conversion. Four radical materials (TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8) were prepared via facile demethylation and consequent oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. The ANARs exhibit high thermal, electrochemical, and photostability, with negligible change after 15 CV cycles and excellent ten-cycle laser stability. ESR measurements confirm high spin concentration, and UV-Vis-NIR spectra show absorption extending from 300 to 2000 nm in powder state. TPA-TPA-O6 exhibits the highest performance: under 808 nm laser irradiation at 0.8 W/cm², temperature rises from 25 °C to 210 °C within 60 s; at 1.0 W/cm², it reaches 250 °C. For solar-driven water evaporation under 1 sun irradiation, TPA-TPA-O6 achieves 89.41% efficiency and a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg/m² h⁻¹, representing top performance among pure organic small molecule photothermal materials. The material was also applied to seawater desalination, reducing concentrations of Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, and K⁺ below membrane-based method values. This work provides a novel strategy for designing stable high-spin radical photothermal materials with minimal cost and easy synthesis.

Research Context
Open-shell organic radicals have attracted tremendous attention in recent years due to their potential applications in optoelectronics, organic magnets, photothermal, thermoelectric, and spintronic materials. Narrow optical band gap can be relatively readily achieved through reasonable chemical modification and structural control. Comparing with other widely reported photothermal conversion materials such as inorganic materials, two-dimensional framework and conjugated polymer materials, organic small molecules are relatively overlooked by researchers in this field. Inorganic materials contain highly precious and nondegradable metal, while two-dimensional framework and conjugated polymers suffer from poor synthesis reproducibility and high cost. The previous organic small molecules represented by porphyrin and cyanine dyes limit their large-scale application due to cumbersome synthesis procedure and poor photothermal stability. Among the small molecules, the open-shell radicals with high photothermal conversion efficiency and thermal/electrochemical stability are rarely reported in previous work. It is very challenging to prepare airstable organic conjugated radicals due to their intrinsic high reactivity with oxygen. The preparation of stable neutral radicals is not only the basis for in-depth study of radical chemistry theory but also the prerequisite for the realization of multifunctional application. Therefore, photothermal materials based on organic stable radicals, bearing their unique physical and optical properties, can be applied in solar-driven water evaporation, photothermal therapy and photothermal catalysis field by converting near-infrared (NIR) light into heat via nonradiative decay. Based on previous research on stable radicals, the authors designed a series of aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) without steric hindrance group based protecting groups. Compared with traditional triarylamine radical cations, these neutral conjugated nitrogen oxide radicals can be readily prepared, purified and exhibit high thermal, electrochemical, and photostability.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether stable neutral aromatic nitric acid radicals can be prepared in air without steric hindrance groups and whether they exhibit high spin concentration and enhanced nonradiative decay for efficient photothermal conversion. The authors hypothesize that these ANARs, bearing unique physical and optical properties from their rich resonance structures including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide structures, will exhibit extremely high spin concentration and highly enhanced nonradiative decay. It was predicted that TPA-TPA-O6, among the four synthesized ANAR materials, would exhibit the highest photothermal conversion performance due to its more obvious radical character and lower bandgap compared to counterparts with triazine and pyrene cores. The hypothesis further posited that the high concentration of radical spin would boost nonradiative decay, thereby efficiently enhancing the photothermal conversion of the radical in the solid state. The predicted outcome was that these radical materials would achieve competitive solar thermal conversion performance among organic materials, and their excellent solubility in green solvents would confer advantages over inorganic and high-performance polymer photothermal materials.

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANAR materials (TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8) were synthesized by introducing different cores: triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, and spiro fluorene, respectively. The synthesis proceeds via facile demethylation and consequent oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. Methoxy substituted precursors were dissolved in dichloromethane at a concentration of 5 mg/mL for the electrochemical measurements. Target radical compounds were coated on carbon-glass electrodes to form films for cyclic voltammetry measurements. All CV curves were measured for 15 cycles in dichloromethane containing 0.1 M nBu4NPF6 as supporting electrolyte with a scan rate of 0.1 V/s. Potential values are reported with a saturated calomel electrode as reference, using the Fc⁺/Fc couple (0.27 V) as an internal standard. For ESR characterization, a constant test amount of 0.02 mmol was used for both precursors and demethylated radicals. Photothermal properties were evaluated by monitoring temperature increment under 808 nm laser irradiation with an IR thermal camera. The water evaporation system used a commercially available white polyurethane (PU) porous foam as support, with the TPA-TPA-O6 loaded inside by impregnating pure PU foam in solution and drying at 80 °C. The foam sample had a 2.0 cm diameter and was loaded with 30 mg of TPA-TPA-O6. Seawater desalination performance was verified by measuring ion concentrations of Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, and K⁺ after floating the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam on seawater.

Procedures And Architectures
The four ANAR materials were synthesized in two steps from methoxy-substituted precursors via demethylation and subsequent oxidation, yielding products whose detailed synthetic schemes and characterizations are provided in the supporting information. UV-Vis-NIR absorption spectra were recorded in DMSO solution and as films, revealing consistent spectra for TPA-TPA-OMe with absorption at 305 nm and 380 nm. The TPA-TPA-O6 radical film exhibited a clear and long absorption tail in the range of 400-825 nm, indicating radical character in the solid state. For pyrene and triazine cores, TPA-PY-O8 showed an absorption edge around 1000 nm and TPA-TPZ-O6 around 800 nm in film. Cyclic voltammetry was conducted in dichloromethane solution and on carbon-glass electrodes, measuring 15 cycles with 0.1 V/s scan rate, showing negligible change in redox curves. HOMO and LUMO energy levels were calculated from CV curves, with the Fc⁺/Fc internal standard at 0.27 V. ESR spectra were obtained at the same test amount (0.02 mmol) to characterize radical spin signal and concentration. Photoluminescence and PLQY tests were performed in dichloromethane solution and as films, with fluorescence emission between 450 and 570 nm. For photothermal conversion, TPA-TPA-O6 was irradiated by an 808 nm laser with energy power of 0.8 W/cm² and 1.0 W/cm². The water evaporation system was established by floating the loaded PU foam on water, with solar irradiation at 1.0 W/cm² (1 sun).

Key Results
For TPA-TPA-O6, the HOMO energy level of the demethylated radical is recorded as -4.90 eV, with PLQY in film measured at 0.1%. The demethylated counterparts TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8 have HOMO levels of -4.81, -4.97, and -4.84 eV, respectively, with PLQYs of 0.9%, 1.0%, and 0.3%. ESR measurements confirmed that TPA-TPA-O6 and Spiro-O8 showed significantly enhanced ESR signal intensities compared to triazine and pyrene cores, indicating higher radical concentration. The radical powder of TPA-TPA-O6 is totally black, consistent with wide absorption covering the whole visible region, and its absorption extends from 300 to 2000 nm in powder state. Under 808 nm laser at 0.8 W/cm², TPA-TPA-O6 temperature increased rapidly from 25 °C to 210 °C within 60 s, while TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 only rose to about 40 °C. Increasing laser power to 1.0 W/cm² raised TPA-TPA-O6 temperature to about 250 °C within 60 s, with excellent stability for ten cycles of laser irradiation. For the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam (2.0 cm diameter, 30 mg loading), equilibrium temperature reached 81.2 °C under 600 s continuous irradiation, compared to 36 °C for the pure PU foam. After 1 hour of 1 sun illumination (1 kW/m²), the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam temperature was 45 °C, about 10 °C higher than the pure PU foam. The water evaporation rate is 1.293 kg/m² h⁻¹ and the solar-driven water evaporation efficiency (η) is 89.41% under 1 sun illumination. All demethylated counterparts showed highly reversible CV curves under oxidation and negligible change after scanning for 15 cycles, indicating unexpected electrochemical stability. Precursors showed fluorescent emission between 450 and 570 nm with moderate PLQY (Table S1), while the corresponding radical products exhibited no fluorescence in film and PLQYs lower than 1%.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The high spin concentration of the ANARs, confirmed by ESR, leads to highly nonradiative decay and enhanced photothermal conversion efficiency. The strong donor-acceptor conjugation effect simultaneously reduces the optical bandgap and determines the paramagnetic property of the radical materials. The rich resonance structures, including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide structures with unpaired electrons delocalized in conjugated backbones, provide the basis for chemical and electrochemical stability. The radical-promoted nonradiative decay mechanism explains the superior photothermal conversion of TPA-TPA-O6 compared to conventional photothermal materials. The design without steric hindrance groups allows for efficient radical generation upon phenolic hydroxyl oxidation in air, bypassing traditional protecting-group strategies. The excellent solubility of the ANARs in green solvents like ethanol and DMSO contrasts with high-performance inorganic and polymer photothermal materials, offering reproducibility advantages.

Contradictions And Limitations
TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 showed lower ESR signal intensities and poorer photothermal conversion, which the authors suggest might be due to lower radical concentration and partial protonation to form hydroxyl groups. The lower bandgap of triazine and pyrene cores made it more difficult to be oxidized by O2, resulting in weaker ESR signals and reduced photothermal performance, highlighting that lower bandgap alone does not guarantee superior photothermal conversion. The seawater desalination performance was only verified for the TPA-TPA-O6 based system, and comparison with the membrane-based method is qualitative rather than quantitative. The water evaporation measurement was performed under a single irradiation condition (1.0 W/cm²), limiting conclusions about performance under varying solar intensities. The paper does not report the random seed used for any computational calculations, nor the specific train/test split for any quantitative comparisons. The supporting information is mentioned but not included in the main text, limiting accessibility to complete synthetic routes and characterization data.

Claims
TPA-TPA-O6 is one of the most efficient photothermal conversion materials among pure organic small molecules, achieving 89.41% solar-to-vapor efficiency. The water evaporation rate reached 1.293 kg/m² h⁻¹ under 1 sun irradiation. TPA-TPA-O6 achieved 89.41% efficiency, representing top performance in pure organic small molecule photothermal materials. The seawater desalination ion reduction is qualitative and only compared to a generic membrane-based method without specific quantitative benchmarks. Other star-shaped ANARs (TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, Spiro-O8) exhibited significantly poorer photothermal conversion, limiting the claim's generality to the entire ANAR series. This establishes a new benchmark for pure organic small molecule photothermal materials and demonstrates a practical path for solar water harvesting. The strategy of using stable radicals without steric hindrance provides a general framework for designing low-cost, high-efficiency photothermal materials.
Stable neutral open-shell nitric acid radicals can be synthesized in air without steric hindrance groups, retaining high thermal, electrochemical, and photostability. All demethylated ANARs showed highly reversible CV curves and negligible change after 15 cycles. TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited excellent stability for ten cycles of laser irradiation on and off. The radicals showed comparable electrochemical and air stability with their methoxy precursors. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 showed weaker ESR signals due to lower oxidation susceptibility, suggesting the stability is core-dependent. The synthesis without steric hindrance groups simplifies preparation and purification, enabling large-scale application and further structural optimization. The demonstration of stable radicals in air is a fundamental advance for radical chemistry and multifunctional applications.
The high spin concentration of ANARs drives photothermal conversion via a nonradiative decay mechanism, surpassing radiative decay pathways. The PLQYs of radical products were lower than 1%, indicating restricted radiative decay. The powder absorption extends from 300 to 2000 nm, facilitating efficient sunlight harvesting. Nonradiative decay will be largely boosted due to the high concentration of radical spin, enhancing photothermal conversion. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 still exhibited some PLQY (0.9% and 1.0%), indicating not complete quenching. This mechanism validates the use of open-shell radicals for NIR-to-heat conversion, with applications in photothermal therapy and catalysis. Future work can explore even more planar structures to further enhance conductivity and nonradiative decay.

Data And Code Availability
The supporting information containing detailed synthetic schemes (Figure S1-S9), characterization data (Table S1), and detailed photothermal and seawater desalination data is available free of charge at http://pubs.acs.org. No specific code repository or supplementary data files are cited beyond the supporting information package.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors compared four different core structures (TPA, TPZ, PY, Spiro) to identify the optimal design for ANAR photothermal materials. A ten-cycle laser irradiation stability test confirmed the photothermal durability of TPA-TPA-O6. Temperature response was tested at two laser power levels (0.8 W/cm² and 1.0 W/cm²) to demonstrate consistent behavior with increasing power. The comparison between TPA-TPA-O6 (89.41% η) and its counterparts (TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, Spiro-O8) served as an in-material ablation study identifying the optimal structural combination.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A, B, C presents the synthetic schemes and core structures of the four star-shaped ANAR materials. Figure 2A and 2B show the UV-Vis-NIR absorption spectra of precursors and radical products in solution and film, highlighting the 300-2000 nm absorption of TPA-TPA-O6. Figure 3 displays the CV curves for all eight samples measured over 15 cycles, showing highly reversible oxidation behavior. Figure 4A shows ESR spectra of precursors and radical products (0.02 mmol), revealing significantly enhanced spin signals upon demethylation. Figure 4B shows PLQY measurements demonstrating quenched fluorescence in the radical products. Figure 4D shows PLQY and temperature increment under 808 nm laser irradiation for all four radical materials. Figure 5A shows the rapid temperature increase of TPA-TPA-O6 from 25 °C to 210 °C within 60 s under 0.8 W/cm². Figure 5B shows an IR thermal camera image of the TPA-TPA-O6 powder during photothermal conversion. Figure 5C shows the temperature of TPA-TPA-O6 as a function of laser power, reaching 250 °C at 1.0 W/cm². Figure 6A shows the broadband absorption of TPA-TPA-O6 from 300 to 2000 nm. Figure 6B shows the water evaporation efficiency and rate measurements under 1 sun illumination. Figure 6C shows the ten-cycle laser stability test. Figure 6D shows the absorption spectrum of TPA-TPA-O6 in powder and dispersed state in PU foam. Figure 6E shows the surface temperature comparison between PU+TPA-TPA-O6 and pure PU foam under 1 sun irradiation. Figure 6F shows the water mass change curves for the evaporation efficiency determination. Figure 14 shows the equilibrium temperature of PU+TPA-TPA-O6 (81.2 °C) under 600 s irradiation. Figure 17 and Table S2 report water evaporation efficiencies and rates for the TPA-TPA-O6 and other reported photothermal materials. Figure 18 shows the ion concentration reduction of seawater after desalination by PU+TPA-TPA-O6. Table S1 lists CV-derived HOMO and LUMO energy levels for all precursors and radical products, along with PLQY values.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of stable neutral aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) without steric hindrance groups, prepared in air, exhibiting extremely high spin concentration and negligible photoluminescence, enabling efficient NIR-to-heat photothermal conversion. 2. The strongest evidence is the 89.41% solar water evaporation efficiency and 1.293 kg/m² h⁻¹ evaporation rate of TPA-TPA-O6, coupled with temperature increases from 25 °C to 210 °C in 60 s and ten-cycle photothermal stability. 3. The future path involves further development of ANAR materials with enhanced planarity to exploit their restricted radiative decay and potential high conductivity for photothermal conversion, organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics performed at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles under ambient air conditions, achieving yields up to 100% and 100% selectivity with a broad substrate scope. The approach utilizes Eosin Y (EY) as a low-cost organic photocatalyst at only 0.6 mole% loading, K3PO4 as the base, and 40 mM CTAB as the micellar scaffold. The micellar surface acts as an efficient scaffold to host both the photocatalyst and arylamine substrates, enabling a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with a 0.3 ps time constant. The reaction proceeds under green light (525 nm) within 4 hours, significantly outperforming previously reported Ir-based photocatalytic methodologies which required 24 hours for only 64% conversion at a much higher catalyst dose. The enhanced catalytic efficacy is attributed to the non-diffusive PET mechanism and the modulation of redox potentials at the CAI, where the micellar Stern layer provides a microenvironment that solubilizes both hydrophilic and hydrophobic probes at distinct locations, bringing the photocatalyst and substrates into close proximity. The broad substrate scope includes electron-rich and electron-deficient amine centers, with electron-rich arylamines giving 100% conversion in 4 hours. Atmospheric oxygen serves as a sacrificial oxidant, regenerating the photocatalyst via hydrogen peroxide formation. Fluorescence quenching, lifetime, and up-conversion measurements confirm the excited-state quenching by p-anisidine and the ultrafast PET. Radical trap experiments with BHT validate the amine radical intermediate, with a characteristic adduct detected at 342.2399 g/mol. This work represents the first report on aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds under ambient conditions, opening new opportunities for green synthesis of azoaromatics.

Research Context
Developing efficient protocols for synthesizing azoaromatics in aqueous media under ambient conditions is highly desirable from a green and sustainable chemistry perspective. Azoaromatics are an important class of organic molecules with tremendous potential in optical storage, molecular switches, and industrial applications. The traditional diazotization method produces unstable diazonium intermediates and unwanted waste, with applicability limited by the nature of the counterions. Metal nanoparticle-catalyzed synthesis of azo compounds from anilines and nitroaromatics has been reported but suffers from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, high temperature, and inert atmosphere requirements. Photocatalytic reductive coupling of nitrobenzenes suffers from poor product selectivity due to simultaneous generation of azoxyaromatics or nitrosobenzene and requires an inert atmosphere, limiting large-scale practical applicability. Photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) of arylamines to azoaromatics using Ir-based photocatalysts has been demonstrated but suffers from slow reaction kinetics, moderate yields, high catalyst dose, and limited substrate scope under ambient atmosphere. All earlier reports utilized organic solvents for azo synthesis due to the low solubility of amine substrates in aqueous medium, leaving a gap for efficient green catalytic routes in water. Charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles provide a unique microenvironment that can modulate chemical and photochemical reactions otherwise inefficient in bulk medium. CAIs provide unique electric fields that align probe dipoles with respect to the interface and facilitate product selectivity, while the micellar scaffold solubilizes hydrophilic and hydrophobic probes at distinct locations, bringing the PC and substrates in close proximity. Interfacial surface charges dictate the interaction with charged molecules, making the micellar environment critical for bimolecular reactions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a metal-free, organic photocatalytic system operating at charged aqueous interfaces can achieve efficient oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics in water under ambient air conditions. The study hypothesizes that the micellar CAI will act as an efficient scaffold to host both Eosin Y and arylamine substrates at the Stern layer, enabling non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer and modulating redox potentials to facilitate the coupling. The authors predict that the combination of CAI-induced confinement, redox potential modulation, and proximity enhancement will yield superior kinetics and selectivity compared to previous Ir-catalyzed or metal-mediated methodologies in organic solvents. The hypothesis further implies that atmospheric oxygen will serve as a sacrificial oxidant to regenerate the photocatalyst via hydrogen peroxide formation, making the process sustainable and metal-free. The predicted outcome is 100% conversion and 100% selectivity of azo products under ambient atmosphere using a minimum photocatalyst dose, achievable within hours rather than days. The broad substrate scope hypothesis extends to electron-rich and electron-deficient amine centers, predicted to be thermodynamically feasible at the micellar surface irrespective of substituents.

Methodological Details
The photocatalyst employed is Eosin Y (EY), a common and low-cost organic dye selected for its red-shifted absorption and photoactive properties. The base used for the reaction is K3PO4 (2 equivalents) in water, though KOH and DABCO were also tested. The surfactant CTAB forms spherical micelles at the optimized concentration of 40 mM, as confirmed by HR-TEM measurements. Photophysical behavior of EY was probed in the presence of CTAB, SDS, and triton X-100 to identify micellar association. EY bears two negative charges at pH 7, enabling electrostatic interaction with the positively charged CTAB micelles. The absorption peak of EY in water at 516 nm exhibits a bathochromic shift of 9 nm with CTAB and 16 nm with TX-100 micelles, indicating micellar association. EY exhibits fluorescence quenching in the presence of premicellar concentrations of CTAB and TX-100, but shows enhanced fluorescence (2.4-fold) only at and near (0.75-1.0 mM) the CMC of CTAB. No spectral changes were observed in the presence of SDS, signifying lack of interaction with the anionic surfactant. EY undergoes CTAB-induced aggregation at premicellar concentrations due to ion-pair formation, with aggregates dissociating at or near the CMC due to entrapment at the micellar Stern layer. The fluorescence lifetime of EY increases from 1.17 ns in water to 2.74 ns upon micellization of CTAB, confirming micellar association. EY@CTAB was found stable in the presence of K3PO4, whereas EY@TX-100 suffers disassembly, leading to the choice of EY@CTAB for subsequent studies. K3PO4 neither interferes with EY-CTAB specific association nor interacts with the excited state of EY@CTAB, as revealed from the unperturbed fluorescence lifetime. The optimized reaction conditions for p-anisidine conversion involve a green light source at 525 nm, 0.6 mole% Eosin Y, 2 equiv. K3PO4, 40 mM CTAB, in water under ambient air for 4 hours. Substrates screened include electron-rich arylamines (1-7), aniline (8), and halides p-chloroaniline (9) and p-bromoaniline (10), along with p-nitroaniline as a control. Reaction products were characterized by GC-MS and NMR measurements, with HR-MS and HR-TEM used for additional structural and morphological verification. The fluorescence of EY@CTAB at 545 nm was monitored for quenching upon addition of substrates, analyzed via Stern-Volmer plots. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements were employed to determine the time constant of the excited-state quenching. Radical trap experiments involved irradiating with green light for 5 min, adding 1 equivalent of 2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol (BHT) for 5 min, and further irradiating for 4 hours. H2O2 sensing strips were used to detect the formation of hydrogen peroxide in the reaction mixture during light irradiation. The mapped redox potentials indicated thermodynamic feasibility of arylamine oxidation by EY* at the micellar surface regardless of substituents. No random seed, exact replicate numbers, or instrument models for GC-MS and NMR are reported in the paper. No specific train/test split or demographic data is applicable to this chemistry experiment.

Procedures And Architectures
The reaction is initiated by green light irradiation at λ = 525 nm in an aqueous solution containing 40 mM CTAB micelles, 0.6 mole% Eosin Y, and 2 equivalents of K3PO4. The CTAB surfactant forms spherical micelles at 40 mM, verified by HR-TEM measurements, providing a micellar scaffold for the reaction. The photocatalytic cycle proceeds via the absorption of green light by EY, formation of an excited state, and subsequent electron transfer from the arylamine substrate. The electron-rich arylamine undergoes oxidation at the micellar Stern layer, generating an amine radical that couples with another radical or molecule to form the azo product. Proton abstraction is a critical step for the POC of amine substrates, catalyzed by K3PO4; both K3PO4 and KOH, as well as organic DABCO, are effective as bases. The conversion yields are slightly lower with DABCO as a base compared to inorganic bases. The PET quenching of EY* by p-anisidine is instantaneous, occurring in a few picoseconds at the micellar surface. The quenching rate constant kq = 6.3 × 10 12 M -1 s -1 was derived from a linear Stern-Volmer plot, indicating non-diffusive bimolecular quenching. The presence of K3PO4 has no noticeable effect on the SV plots and quenching rate constant, signifying that PET precedes the proton abstraction step by base. Atmospheric oxygen serves as a sacrificial oxidant, accepting electrons and transforming to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), which regenerates the photocatalytic cycle. The distinct color change of H2O2 sensing strips before and after light irradiation confirms the reduction of aerial O2 to H2O2 in the reaction mixture. The blue light condition (previously reported) requires 6 hours for 100% conversion under standard conditions, whereas the green light at 525 nm achieves 100% conversion in 4 hours. The reaction was performed under ambient air atmosphere without requiring any inert gas. For radical trap experiments, the mixture was irradiated for 5 min, 1 equivalent of BHT was added, then further irradiated for 4 h, with HR-MS and GC-MS used for analysis. The radical trap experiment used p-anisidine as substrate, and HR-MS revealed a characteristic peak at 342.2399 g/mol for the p-anisidine-BHT adduct. The micellar Stern layer is identified as the location where both the photocatalyst and substrate are solubilized, as arylamines prefer the hydrocarbon/aqueous interface over the bulk aqueous medium.

Key Results
The optimized reaction for p-anisidine to 1,2-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene achieves 100% conversion to the desired azo product in 4 h under standard conditions. The selectivity to the azo product is 100%, with no other byproducts detected by GC-MS and NMR. The required photocatalyst dose is only 0.6 mole% EY, and 40 mM CTAB is utilized as the surfactant. The reaction is triggered by green light at 525 nm under ambient air atmosphere. The method outperforms previous Ir-based reports by an 8.3-fold reduction in photocatalyst dose. Previous reports required 24 h for 64% conversion in acetonitrile; the present method achieves 100% conversion in 4 h in water. Electron-rich arylamines (substrates 1-7) all show 100% conversion within 4 hours of reaction. Aniline (substrate 8) under standard conditions also shows 100% conversion to the azo product. p-Chloroaniline (substrate 9) shows a conversion yield of 98%, and p-bromoaniline shows 95%. The fluorescence quenching experiments with p-anisidine yield a Stern-Volmer quenching rate constant kq = 6.3 × 10 12 M -1 s -1, indicating a non-diffusive bimolecular quenching process. Fluorescence up-conversion measurements reveal an ultrafast PET with a time constant of 0.3 ps in the presence of p-anisidine. EY exhibits fluorescence quenching with p-nitroaniline, suggesting a lack of electron transfer to EY* at the micellar surface. The radical trap experiment with BHT shows negligible conversion (~5.0%) to the desired azo product even after 4 h of irradiation, confirming the radical mechanism. A characteristic HR-MS peak at 342.2399 g/mol confirms the formation of p-anisidine-BHT adducts, validating the amine radical intermediate. The fluorescence lifetime of EY@CTAB decreases significantly upon substrate addition, authenticating excited-state quenching by p-anisidine. The mapped redox potentials indicate the oxidation of arylamines by EY* is thermodynamically feasible at the micellar surface irrespective of substituents. The presence of K3PO4 has no noticeable effect on the SV plots and quenching rate constant, signifying that PET precedes proton abstraction. The fluorescence enhancement of 2.4-fold only near the CMC of CTAB supports micellar association and the role of the CMC in the catalytic mechanism. CTAB forms spherical micelles at 40 mM, confirmed by HR-TEM measurements, providing the necessary micellar geometry for the reaction. The reaction is feasible with blue light but requires 6 h for 100% conversion under standard conditions, compared to 4 h with green light. The H2O2 sensing strips show distinct color change before and after light irradiation, confirming O2 as a sacrificial oxidant.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The primary mechanism is non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) between the arylamine substrate and the excited-state photocatalyst at the micellar Stern layer. The 0.3 ps time constant for PET confirms an ultrafast, direct electron transfer rather than a diffusion-controlled process. The charged aqueous interface (CAI) of the micelle modulates redox potentials, bringing the substrate and photocatalyst to thermodynamically compatible conditions at the interface. Confinement at the micellar Stern layer increases the local concentration of both the photocatalyst and the substrate, facilitating bimolecular coupling. The micelle acts as an electrochemical scaffold, with interfacial surface charges aligning probe dipoles and dictating substrate-catalyst interactions. The broad substrate scope, including electron-rich and electron-deficient amines, demonstrates the generality of the CAI-mediated oxidative coupling. Atmospheric oxygen serves as a sacrificial electron acceptor, closing the photocatalytic cycle through hydrogen peroxide formation, enabling a sustainable metal-free process. The PET mechanism precedes proton abstraction by the base, decoupling the electron transfer and deprotonation steps, which contributes to the observed selectivity. The work represents the first report on aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds using a photocatalytic oxidative coupling methodology under ambient conditions.

Contradictions And Limitations
p-Chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline show slightly lower conversion yields (98% and 95%, respectively) than the 100% achieved with electron-rich substrates, suggesting substituent effects on the coupling kinetics. The radical trap experiment with BHT only reduces conversion to ~5.0% rather than complete inhibition, indicating some residual conversion or imperfect radical trapping. No fluorescence quenching was observed with p-nitroaniline, indicating that the PET mechanism is not applicable to electron-deficient substrates at this interface. The paper does not report exact replicate numbers, statistical significance, or confidence intervals for the conversion and selectivity measurements. No random seed, instrument models (GC-MS, NMR), or specific experimental controls (e.g., photocatalyst-free, light-free) are explicitly reported. The substrate concentrations (initial molarity of arylamines) are not specified in the text or tables, limiting reproducibility of exact reaction kinetics. The bibliography is not provided in the source text, so the exact references and their roles cannot be independently verified.

Claims
The micellar CAI enables metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics in water under ambient conditions with 100% yield and selectivity. The reaction achieves 100% conversion and 100% selectivity within 4 hours under ambient air. The method uses a sustainable metal-free photocatalyst (EY at 0.6 mole%) and aqueous conditions. Broad substrate scope (1-7) gives 100% conversion in 4 hours. GC-MS and NMR confirm azo product formation and 100% selectivity. p-Chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline yield 98% and 95% conversion, respectively, not 100%. The BHT radical trap does not completely inhibit conversion, leaving ~5.0% conversion. p-Nitroaniline shows no PET quenching, limiting the scope to substrates capable of electron transfer to EY*. The method is the first aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds via photocatalytic oxidative coupling, opening new green synthetic pathways. The 8.3-fold reduction in photocatalyst dose compared to Ir-based methods makes the approach more sustainable and economically viable. The non-diffusive PET mechanism at CAIs could be applied to other oxidative coupling reactions in aqueous media.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The EY@CTAB composite was chosen over EY@TX-100 because the latter suffers disassembly in the presence of K3PO4. Base comparison showed K3PO4 and KOH are effective; DABCO gives slightly lower yields. The fluorescence lifetime of EY@CTAB is unperturbed by K3PO4, confirming no direct interaction with the base. The reaction is feasible under both green (525 nm) and blue light, but blue light requires 6 hours instead of 4 hours for 100% conversion. No spectral changes were observed with SDS, ruling out micellar association with anionic surfactants.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 tabulates optimized reaction conditions, showing 100% conversion in 4 h with 0.6 mole% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB under 525 nm green light. Figure 1a shows the bathochromic shift of EY in water (516 nm) with CTAB and TX-100 micelles. Figure 1b and Figure S1 show fluorescence quenching of EY with premicellar CTAB and TX-100. Figure 1c shows CTAB-induced EY aggregation at premicellar concentrations and dissociation near the CMC. Figure 1d and Table S2 show fluorescence lifetime enhancement of EY from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns upon CTAB micellization. Figures S2 and S3 show stability of EY@CTAB versus disassembly of EY@TX-100 in the presence of K3PO4. Figure S4 shows HR-TEM images confirming CTAB forms spherical micelles at 40 mM. Figure S5 shows blue light reaction kinetics requiring 6 h for 100% conversion. Figure S6 shows H2O2 sensing strips detecting peroxide formation under light irradiation. Figure S13 shows the gradual decrease in EY@CTAB fluorescence intensity with increasing p-anisidine concentration. Figure 2b shows the SV plot with kq = 6.3 × 10 12 M -1 s -1 and SV plots for other arylamines. Figure S14 shows that K3PO4 has no noticeable effect on SV plots. Figure 2c shows the SV plot with the addition of K3PO4. Figure 2d shows fluorescence up-conversion and the 0.3 ps time constant with p-anisidine. Figure S15 shows HR-MS of the p-anisidine-BHT adduct at 342.2399 g/mol.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics in water under ambient air, achieving 100% yields and selectivity at a 0.6 mole% photocatalyst loading in 4 hours at the micellar CAI. 2. The strongest evidence is the ultrafast 0.3 ps PET time constant combined with SV quenching (kq = 6.3 × 10 12 M -1 s -1), the radical trap BHT adduct at 342.2399 g/mol, and the 8.3-fold reduction in catalyst dose compared to Ir-based Ir-based methods. 3. The future path lies in extending the CAI-based oxidative coupling approach to other oxidative couplings, using different photocatalysts and surfactants, and potentially scaling up the synthesis of complex azoaromatics in water.
