summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, WS2, and WSe2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara (Osaka Metropolitan University); Takashi Kobayashi (Chuo University); Tetsuji Dohi (Chuo University); Takeshi Yoshimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Norifumi Fujimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Daisuke Kiriya (Osaka Metropolitan University)
summary.field_subfield: 2D Materials / Transition Metal Dichalcogenides / Photoluminescence Spectroscopy
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a universal postpreparation method for enhancing photoluminescence (PL) intensity in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), applicable to both sulfur-based (MoS2, WS2) and selenium-based (MoSe2, WSe2) compounds, achieved through spontaneous crystal fluctuation induced by coating with paraffin. The key finding is a dramatic PL enhancement relative to as-exfoliated flakes: MoS2 shows a 215-fold increase, WS2 a 55-fold increase, MoSe2 a 50-fold increase, and WSe2 a 9-fold increase. The mechanism involves paraffin (melting point 42–45 °C) deposited onto a spin coater from a melt at 80 °C, with a heat blower maintaining the liquid state during coating. The large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin generates mechanical stress at the paraffin-TMDC interface, driving gradual spontaneous fluctuation and eventual desorption of the monolayer from the underlying substrate. In cases where the monolayer is not constrained by surrounding bulk flakes, the desorption produces a shrunk bundled structure. The substrate effect, identified as a key limiter of PL intensity, is removed through the penetration of paraffin between the monolayer and substrate, which reduces electron doping from the substrate and decreases carrier concentration. Raman spectroscopy of 30 monolayer MoS2 samples confirms this, with an average E' peak shift of -0.72 cm⁻¹ indicating strain and an A' peak shift of +1.03 cm⁻¹ indicating reduced carrier concentration. PL mapping reveals nonuniform PL enhancement, with intensity approximately 2.3 times greater at the center than at the rim for a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes, attributed to in-plane wrinkles and a funnel effect. The approach is universal, contrasting with prior methods such as p-doping (F4TCNQ) or superacid treatment (TFSI) restricted to sulfur-based TMDCs. Furthermore, paraffin’s transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility make it suitable for packaging flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells. The spin-coated film is transparent, enabling optical microscopy and in-situ PL measurement, while a thick cast film is opaque.

claims.description: Paraffin coating provides a universal postpreparation method for remarkable PL enhancement in both sulfur- and selenium-based monolayer TMDCs.
The substrate effect is the key limiter of PL intensity, and its removal via paraffin penetration at the monolayer-substrate interface is the mechanism of enhancement.
Paraffin is a viable packaging and functional material for flexible TMDC optoelectronics due to its transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a universal postpreparation method for enhancing photoluminescence (PL) intensity in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), applicable to both sulfur-based (MoS2, WS2) and selenium-based (MoSe2, WSe2) compounds, achieved through spontaneous crystal fluctuation induced by coating with paraffin. The key finding is a dramatic PL enhancement relative to as-exfoliated flakes: MoS2 shows a 215-fold increase, WS2 a 55-fold increase, MoSe2 a 50-fold increase, and WSe2 a 9-fold increase. The mechanism involves paraffin (melting point 42–45 °C) deposited onto a spin coater from a melt at 80 °C, with a heat blower maintaining the liquid state during coating. The large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin generates mechanical stress at the paraffin-TMDC interface, driving gradual spontaneous fluctuation and eventual desorption of the monolayer from the underlying substrate. In cases where the monolayer is not constrained by surrounding bulk flakes, the desorption produces a shrunk bundled structure. The substrate effect, identified as a key limiter of PL intensity, is removed through the penetration of paraffin between the monolayer and substrate, which reduces electron doping from the substrate and decreases carrier concentration. Raman spectroscopy of 30 monolayer MoS2 samples confirms this, with an average E' peak shift of -0.72 cm⁻¹ indicating strain and an A' peak shift of +1.03 cm⁻¹ indicating reduced carrier concentration. PL mapping reveals nonuniform PL enhancement, with intensity approximately 2.3 times greater at the center than at the rim for a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes, attributed to in-plane wrinkles and a funnel effect. The approach is universal, contrasting with prior methods such as p-doping (F4TCNQ) or superacid treatment (TFSI) restricted to sulfur-based TMDCs. Furthermore, paraffin’s transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility make it suitable for packaging flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells. The spin-coated film is transparent, enabling optical microscopy and in-situ PL measurement, while a thick cast film is opaque.

Research Context
Transition metal dichalcogenides (MX2, M=Mo,W X=S,Se) attract attention for optical transistors, LEDs, and solar cells due to their three-atom thin crystal structure and direct band gap at K points. However, the poor photoluminescence (PL) intensity of monolayer TMDCs limits their optical performance, caused by over-carrier concentrations, strains, and crystalline defects. For n-type materials MoS2 and WS2, p-type doping with p-dopants such as F4TCNQ or tetrafluoro-1,4-benzoquinone successfully enhances PL intensity. Treatment with a superacid molecule, bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI), produces PL enhancement of hundreds of times in sulfur-based compounds. In contrast, the above methods are not effective for the selenium-based TMDCs of MoSe2 and WSe2, with limited strategies such as oleic acid or hydrohalic acid treatment. For WSe2, reported methods separate a monolayer from substrates by floating or inserting ions to remove the substrate effect. As shown, there are different strategies for improving the optical property of different TMDCs, and no universal strategy has been found for a large variety of 2D semiconductor materials. One potential strategy for improving PL intensity in all compounds is removing the substrate effect by mechanical floating of the monolayers from the underneath substrate material. However, floating the monolayer is difficult and a postpreparation method for this has not been established.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a universal method can enhance PL intensity in both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs through a single treatment. The hypothesis is that coating with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin, leverages its large thermal expansion coefficient to induce spontaneous fluctuation and desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. The predicted outcome is that substrate effect removal will increase PL intensity in MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, and WSe2, demonstrating a universal strategy for TMDCs. The authors hypothesize that the deformation to a shrunk bundled structure occurs when the monolayer is not surrounded by bulk flakes due to stress at the interface with paraffin. PL mapping is expected to reveal nonuniform PL enhancement in the monolayer plane, dependent on the state of the fluctuation. The paraffin coating is further hypothesized to serve as a packaging material for flexible optoelectronics due to its transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility. The expected Raman signature includes negative E' peak shift indicating strain and positive A' peak shift indicating decreased carrier concentration.

Methodological Details
Four monolayer TMDCs were examined: MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, and WSe2, with different band gaps and emission wavelengths. The paraffin used has a melting point of 42-45 °C and was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C in advance. For paraffin coating, the paraffin was dropped onto a sample placed on a spin coater. A heat blower (hair dryer) was applied during spin coating to keep the paraffin in a melted state. A thick film of paraffin achieved by simple casting resulted in a glassy appearance that was not transparent. The spin-coated paraffin film was transparent, enabling optical microscope observation and PL measurement through the film. WS2 was measured on a Si/SiO 2 substrate for PL spectra. PL enhancement on monolayer WS2 was also observed on a quartz substrate. Raman spectra of 30 samples of monolayer MoS2 were collected before and after paraffin coating. The E' peak represents vibrations in the in-plane direction sensitive to strain, while the A' peak represents vibrations in the out-of-plane direction sensitive to carrier concentration. PL spectra and PL mapping images were collected from each sample. Time-resolved measurements were performed immediately after coating, after 2 hours at room temperature, and after a further 1 hour at room temperature. Optical microscope images were obtained for as-exfoliated and paraffined samples.

Procedures And Architectures
Paraffin melted at 80 °C was dropped onto samples on a spin coater with the heat blower applied. Paraffin penetrates underneath each monolayer TMDC during the coating process. The paraffin removes the substrate effect from the TMDCs by penetrating at the interface between substrate and monolayer. The strain is induced by the large thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin. The monolayer shows gradual spontaneous fluctuation and eventual desorption from the substrate over time. Deformation to a shrunk bundled structure occurs when the monolayer is not surrounded by bulk flakes. Time-resolved optical microscopy tracked deformation over 3 hours at room temperature. PL and Raman spectra were collected before and after paraffin coating for each sample. Raman spectra were analyzed for both E' and A' peak positions. PL mapping confirmed nonuniform enhancement in the whole plane.

Key Results
The factor of PL enhancement for MoS2 was 215-fold relative to as-exfoliated flakes. WS2 showed a PL enhancement of 55-fold from as-exfoliated flakes, with a specific sample showing about 36 times enhancement in Fig. 1b. MoSe2 achieved a PL enhancement of 50-fold, and WSe2 achieved a 9-fold enhancement. For the specific WS2 sample in Fig. 1b, the normalized PL spectrum showed a decrease in the shoulder at the low-energy side, suggesting decreased trion-derived PL signal. Optical microscopy confirmed paraffin covers the entire monolayer, with PL mapping showing PL enhancement across the whole plane but nonuniformity. Raman spectroscopy of 30 MoS2 samples showed the E' peak shifted in the negative direction by about -0.72 cm -1 on average, indicating strain. The A' peak shifted in the positive direction by 1.03 cm -1, indicating a decrease in the carrier concentration. In the bulk-surrounded MoS2 sample, PL mapping revealed nonuniform high PL intensity, with intensity about 2.3 times greater at the center than at the rim. The PL peak position at the center of the bulk-surrounded monolayer shifted 5-10 meV lower in energy than at the rim. FWHM decrease and the upshift of the peak after paraffin coating in sulfur-based TMDCs suggest the PL is dominated by exciton-derived emission.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The substrate effect is identified as the key factor in enhancing PL intensity, removed by paraffin penetration. Strain induced by the volume change from the high thermal expansion coefficient of paraffin drives the fluctuation and desorption. The removal of electron doping from the substrate reduces electron concentration in the monolayer TMDCs. In the bulk-surrounded case, in-plane mechanical stress induces fluctuation, forming a wrinkle that traps excitons via a funnel effect. The wrinkled area decreases the band gap, concentrating excitons and increasing PL intensity. Paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent, making it suitable for packaging flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells. The underlying science is applicable to other 2D layered materials due to the thermal expansion coefficient mechanism. The spin-coated paraffin film enables in-situ optical microscopy and PL measurement through the film.

Contradictions And Limitations
The WSe2 PL enhancement of only 9-fold is substantially lower than the 215-fold of MoS2, indicating a less efficient mechanism for selenium-based TMDCs. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the catalytic challenge of methane partial oxidation (POM) to methanol and acetic acid, a process traditionally requiring harsh high-pressure conditions. The authors report a bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst supported on hydrophobic silica (HS) synthesized via a modified deposition precipitation method. The key achievement is the continuous flow conversion of methane to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure and mild temperatures using 15% w/v H2O2 as the oxidant. In the continuous flow process, the Au-Fe catalyst produced methanol with a yield of 224 mmol per gram of combined Au+Fe at atmospheric pressure, and co-feeding CO yielded acetic acid with a yield of 92 mmol per gram. In the batch process at 10 bar, the catalyst achieved a remarkable yield of 1666 mmol methanol per gram with 95% selectivity. The design leverages the synergistic effects of low-valent Fe3-δ+ species generated by Au, the hydrophobicity of the silica support to prevent active site blocking by moisture and facilitate product desorption, and the Lewis acidic sites on the silica matrix for C-H activation. Characterization via ICP-OES confirmed an optimal loading of 0.46 wt% Fe and 0.23 wt% Au. XPS revealed both Fe3+ and Fe3-δ+ species, and EXAFS confirmed single-atomic Fe and elemental Au with some charge transfer. HRTEM showed Fe atomic clusters and Au nanoparticles of 1.3-3.0 nm. The hydrophobic support exhibited a contact angle of 118°. CD4 isotope labeling confirmed that methanol originated from methane, not support ligands. The work demonstrates that tuning bimetallic compositions on a tailored hydrophobic support can achieve methane valorization under benign conditions, potentially opening a pathway for commercial methane-to-oxygenate technologies.

Research Context
Methane is a major global warming contributor and is difficult to activate due to its non-polar C-H bonds. Direct partial oxidation of methane to methanol is considered a 'holy grail' problem in catalysis. Traditional reports suffer from low product yields and require high temperature, high-pressure conditions. Methane is often converted indirectly via syngas (CO+H2) because direct oxidation to methanol is thermodynamically challenging. Existing high-pressure continuous process reports using H2O2 yield only 0.081 mol per kg catalyst per hour at 20 bar. Previous batch oxidation over oxo dicopper anchored on carbon nitride produced 129.7 mmol per gram per hour with low methanol selectivity. Single-atom catalysts have emerged as promising for methane activation but still face challenges with stability and selectivity. Hydrophobic versus hydrophilic supports significantly affect peroxide activation and catalyst longevity in H2O2-based oxidation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can methane be partially oxidized to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure in a continuous flow process? Will a bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst supported on hydrophobic silica exhibit synergistic effects that activate methane under mild conditions? Can co-feeding CO with methane induce a selectivity switch from methanol to acetic acid? The authors hypothesized that low-valent Fe3-δ+ species stabilized by Au would serve as the active sites for both CH4 activation and H2O2 cleavage. The hydrophobic environment was expected to prevent active site blocking by moisture and facilitate methanol desorption, thereby suppressing over-oxidation. The Lewis acid sites on the silica matrix would facilitate C-H sigma complex formation for methane activation. The continuous flow performance would surpass the high-pressure batch performance in terms of per-gram catalyst productivity.

Methodological Details
A modified deposition precipitation (DP) method was used to disperse atomic clusters of Fe onto hydrophobic silica (HS) support. The optimum catalyst loading was determined via ICP-OES to be 0.46 wt% Fe and 0.23 wt% Au. The silica support hydrophobicity was confirmed by contact angle analysis showing an angle of 118°. The FeHS catalyst was synthesized by depositing Fe using NaOH, which incorporated Na into the silica matrix. The specific surface area of the AuFeHS catalyst was measured at 392 m²/g. XPS characterization used an electron flood gun and required no charge correction. Au nanoparticle size distribution ranged from 1.4 to 2.8 nm. The 29Si NMR confirmed Q2, Q3, Q4, and T2, T3 states in the HS support. In-situ IR spectroscopy with CO adsorption probed isolated metal atoms, showing signals at 2105 and 2175 cm⁻¹. A specific surface area measurement was performed using the present synthesis method.

Procedures And Architectures
The catalyst was supported on hydrophobic silica modified with NaOH to introduce Na-O-Si framework sites. For batch reactions, H2O2 (15% w/v) served as the oxidant, with initial screening at 10 bar methane pressure. The optimum batch conditions were established at 50 °C and 10 bar methane pressure. For continuous flow, a fixed-bed reactor was used at atmospheric pressure for up to 7 hours. The temperature was optimized for continuous flow, finding 80 °C to be the best condition. Product analysis was performed by gas chromatography (GC) using standard calibrations for yield quantification. NMR spectroscopy confirmed the product structure; a representative spectrum was attached as supplementary information. Isotope labeling experiments used CD4 as feed to confirm that the methyl group originated from methane. A control experiment used N2 gas instead of methane to confirm no side-product formation from the catalyst or support. The continuous flow scheme is described as a fixed-bed reactor at atmospheric pressure.

Key Results
In the batch process at 10 bar, the AuFeHS catalyst achieved a yield of 1666 mmol per gram (Au+Fe) with 95% selectivity for methanol. Under co-fed CO conditions in the batch reactor at 50 °C and 20 bar, acetic acid was the main product with a yield of 3403 μmol per gram within 1 hour. In the continuous flow process at atmospheric pressure, the AuFeHS catalyst yielded 224 mmol methanol per gram of Fe+Au over 4 hours. Co-feeding CO in continuous flow produced acetic acid with an overall yield of 92 mmol per gram of Fe+Au. The continuous flow methanol yield of 422 μmol·h⁻¹ per gram catalyst (0.42 mol per kg per hour) outperformed previous O2 and H2O2 reports. The FeHS catalyst produced 24.2 mmol methanol per gram Fe in continuous flow, while the Fe loading alone gave 285 mmol in batch. The AuHS catalyst produced only 12 mmol per gram Au of methanol in continuous flow. The CO2 selectivity was 10% when CO was added to the feed, versus 5–6% with methane alone under standardized conditions. The AuFeHS catalyst achieved 95% selectivity in batch, which is noted as one of the highest selectivity reported. The specific surface area was 392 m²/g, with a contact angle of 118°, confirming successful hydrophobic functionalization.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The low-valent Fe3-δ+ species, identified at 709.5 eV, are established as critical sites for both CH4 activation and H2O2 activation. The Au nanoparticles, acting as excellent CO oxidation catalysts, provide low-energy activation sites for CO adsorption. The intimate interaction between Fe and Au was visualized via STEM line analysis, supporting the bimetallic synergy model. Charge transfer from Au to Fe stabilizes the low-valent Fe species, preventing deactivation by reacting oxidants. The C-H sigma complex mechanism on Lewis acid sites initiates methane activation, with subsequent conversion to CH3 radicals on Fe3-δ+ sites. Once CH3 and OH radicals are formed, methanol formation, facile CO insertion, and acetic acid generation proceed sequentially. The Na-modified silica provides an environment that favors peroxide radical proximity to active metal sites while maintaining low physisorbed water content. The role of Na and Lewis acid sites in the POM reaction is acknowledged but noted as beyond the scope of this study. The authors conclude that tuning active Fe species through bimetallic modulation opens a scope for commercial methane-to-oxygenate technologies.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper notes that the role of Na and Lewis acid sites remains unexplored and is beyond the scope of this study. FeHS images from HRTEM showed no contrast difference characteristic of Fe particles, leaving the exact atomic structure of Fe unconfirmed by direct imaging. The XPS binding energies were reported as recorded without charge correction, though an electron flood gun was used. The author notes that even though catalysts were optimized, the role of Na and Lewis acid sites warrants further exploration. The paper does not specify the exact feed rate of methane in the continuous flow reactor, only the duration. The specific concentration of H2O2 in the continuous flow feed is not explicitly quantified beyond the 15% w/v description. The paper does not report a random seed or explicit temperature control mechanism for the reactor. The authors acknowledge that the hydrophobic support preparation requires care to keep peroxide radicals close to active metal sites. The paper mentions that Au particle size increases in aqueous conditions, but does not quantify this effect on the specific catalyst. The data is presented as a ChemRxiv preprint and has not been peer-reviewed.

Claims
The AuFeHS catalyst achieves continuous methane oxidation to methanol at atmospheric pressure with a yield surpassing all previous reports. The continuous flow methanol yield of 0.42 mol per kg per hour outperforms reported values using O2 as an oxidant. The H2O2-based 20 bar batch report produced only 0.081 mol per kg per hour, significantly lower than the present work. The continuous flow yield of 224 mmol per gram Fe+Au is presented as the best reported for these conditions. The paper acknowledges that the Au-Pd colloidal particles report higher yields, though with lower selectivity and higher pressures. The Cu2@C3N4 supported catalyst also reports better yields but suffers from poor selectivity. Successful methane valorization at atmospheric pressure significantly reduces the energy and capital requirements for industrial methane conversion. The bimetallic approach provides a tunable strategy for producing multiple oxygenates from a single methane feed.
Co-feeding CO with methane selectively produces acetic acid with high yield from the AuFeHS catalyst. In the batch process with CO, acetic acid was the main product with a yield of 3403 μmol per gram within 1 hour. In continuous flow, co-feeding CO yielded 92 mmol acetic acid per gram Fe+Au. The selectivity switch was confirmed by GC and NMR, with only 166 μmol methanol formed alongside acetic acid. The CO2 selectivity increased from 5–6% to 10% when CO was added, indicating a trade-off with over-oxidation. This co-reactant strategy enables the simultaneous production of methanol and acetic acid from a single methane feed. The approach could be adapted for other co-reactants to access different C1/C2 oxygenates.

Data And Code Availability
The supplementary information contains material characterization methods, catalytic procedures, product calculations, and XAS calculations. A DOI is provided for the ChemRxiv preprint: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2023-h00ht. The supporting information includes GC product data, NMR spectra, and XAS analysis details.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A control experiment without methane flow showed no product formation, confirming methane as the source. A control experiment without oxidant showed no product formation, confirming H2O2 as the source. A control experiment without catalyst showed no product formation, confirming the catalytic role of the metal species. The N2 gas feed control showed no products, confirming that support-derived organic groups do not contribute to oxygenate formation. CD4 isotope labeling confirmed the methyl group in methanol originated from methane, not support ligands. Support comparison: Au and Fe on SBA-15 yielded significantly lower methanol production than on HS. The Fe concentration screening established 0.5 wt% as optimum for methane activation. Au loading was varied to find the optimal 0.23 wt% loading.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: HRTEM images showing Fe atomic dispersion (a) and Au nanoparticles of 1.3–3.0 nm (b, c) with elemental mapping (d). Figure 2: XPS spectra showing Fe2p (a) with Fe3+ and Fe3-δ+ peaks, Au4f (b) showing Au0 and Auδ+, and Fe K-edge XANES (c). Figure 3: Catalytic activity plots for batch oxidation: methanol yield (a, b), CO-co-fed acetic acid (d), and support comparison (c). Figure 4: Continuous flow performance plots showing methanol yield over 7 hours for HS, FeHS, AuFeHS, and AuHS catalysts. Figure 5: 29Si NMR spectra showing Q2, Q3, Q4, and T2, T3 states before and after NaOH and Au deposition. Table S4: Detailed catalytic activity data comparing AuFeHS with FeHS, AuHS, and SBA-15 supported catalysts. Table S6: Comparison of the AuFeHS catalyst performance with the best reported methanol POM results in the literature. Fig. S1-2: Contact angle measurement of 118° for the hydrophobic silica.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first report of continuous methane oxidation to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure using an H2O2-based bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst on hydrophobic silica, with yields of 224 mmol methanol per gram (Fe+Au) and 92 mmol acetic acid per gram. 2. The strongest evidence is the isotope labeling (CD4) confirming the methyl group originates from methane, combined with the CD4/CH3 and CD3/CH2 NMR analysis that rules out support decomposition as the product source. 3. The future path involves exploring the role of Na and Lewis acidic sites, optimizing catalyst for other C-H bond-activated molecules, and pursuing commercialization of methane-to-oxygenate technologies.

summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris

summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the critical problem of identifying the ground-state configuration of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a prominent fast-ion conducting solid electrolyte for lithium batteries. To date, experimental and theoretical efforts have failed to reach a consensus on the Li occupancy (24d:96h ratio), with various computational and experimental values coexisting in the literature. The authors develop a systematic workflow to generate all crystallographically permitted c-LLZO structures and energetically order them. The workflow proceeds in three main stages: first, eliminating structures with overlapping Li atoms (Li-Li distance < 1.7 Å), which geometrically restricts the possible 24d:96h ratios; second, eliminating symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH), reducing the configuration space from ~2.3×10^8 to ~2×10^6 structures; and third, energetically ordering the structures using a multiple linear regression (MLR) model trained on 1235 single-point DFT calculations. The DFT calculations use the ONETEP code, PBE GGA functional, and 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff. The MLR model, trained on Li-Li interaction frequency distributions, achieved a test-set correlation of 0.9996. The analysis reveals that 19 out of the 20 lowest-energy structures have an 8:48 ratio, with four structures within 0.026 eV of the ground state, characterized by similar 24d configurations and slight 96h variations. Geometry optimizations of these four structures show the energy gap narrows further. A key finding is that a large portion of previously reported structures in the literature violate the geometric Li-Li exclusion constraint and are thus non-physical. The method is generalized for crystals with partially occupied sites. All generated structures are published in a freely accessible database. The authors acknowledge that the workflow neglects entropic contributions, assumes retention of ordering upon relaxation, and that COMPASSIII forcefield predictions significantly diverge in inter-ratio ordering. This work provides a rigorous foundation for future c-LLZO research, aiming to improve accuracy and reproducibility in computational studies.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the critical problem of identifying the ground-state configuration of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a prominent fast-ion conducting solid electrolyte for lithium batteries. To date, experimental and theoretical efforts have failed to reach a consensus on the Li occupancy (24d:96h ratio), with various computational and experimental values coexisting in the literature. The authors develop a systematic workflow to generate all crystallographically permitted c-LLZO structures and energetically order them. The workflow proceeds in three main stages: first, eliminating structures with overlapping Li atoms (Li-Li distance < 1.7 Å), which geometrically restricts the possible 24d:96h ratios; second, eliminating symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH), reducing the configuration space from ~2.3×10^8 to ~2×10^6 structures; and third, energetically ordering the structures using a multiple linear regression (MLR) model trained on 1235 single-point DFT calculations. The DFT calculations use the ONETEP code, PBE GGA functional, and 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff. The MLR model, trained on Li-Li interaction frequency distributions, achieved a test-set correlation of 0.9996. The analysis reveals that 19 out of the 20 lowest-energy structures have an 8:48 ratio, with four structures within 0.026 eV of the ground state, characterized by similar 24d configurations and slight 96h variations. Geometry optimizations of these four structures show the energy gap narrows further. A key finding is that a large portion of previously reported structures in the literature violate the geometric Li-Li exclusion constraint and are thus non-physical. The method is generalized for crystals with partially occupied sites. All generated structures are published in a freely accessible database. The authors acknowledge that the workflow neglects entropic contributions, assumes retention of ordering upon relaxation, and that COMPASSIII forcefield predictions significantly diverge in inter-ratio ordering. This work provides a rigorous foundation for future c-LLZO research, aiming to improve accuracy and reproducibility in computational studies.

Research Context
C-LLZO is a leading cubic polymorph of LLZO with high ionic conductivity, but the 24d:96h Li occupancy remains unresolved. Previous computational studies adopt one experimental value as a reference, and the resulting structure disagreement undermines calculated thermodynamic and observable properties. The total combinatorial space for 120 sites with 56 Li is ~7.4×10^34, making brute-force enumeration impossible. A 1.7 Å Li-Li cutoff is established, constrained by the ionic radius and t-LLZO minimum distance (2.56 Å). The 48g site is excluded from the study as it is not reported in most refinements.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to systematically find and energetically rank all possible Li site occupancies in the c-LLZO unit cell. The authors hypothesize that a significant energy difference exists between different 24d:96h ratios and that structural properties can predict energy. The specific hypothesis is that the 24d:96h ratio will be energetically detectable and that a geometric Li-Li exclusion constraint invalidates many reported structures. The predicted outcome is that most previously reported structures may be geometrically infeasible or unstable. The workflow is hypothesized to generalize to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Methodological Details
The framework uses the c-LLZO crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al. (19). A minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å is imposed for structural filtering. Two geometric consequences of the 1.7 Å constraint are derived: max 48 out of 96h sites occupied, and each 24d occupancy eliminates 4 of 96h sites. Approximately 2.3×10^8 structures including symmetry-equivalent duplicates are initially generated. The upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice is constructed for each structure, flattened, and sorted. Local sensitive hashing (LSH) is used for fast approximate similarity searches, reducing pairwise comparison complexity from O(N^2) to O(N). Symmetry validation was performed on the 12:44 and 13:43 ratios comparing LSH against ASE's rigorous symmetry check. Only approximately 1% of structures were identified as symmetrically unique, allowing a reduction by a factor of 100. The configuration space was further reduced to around 2×10^6 unique structures. 1235 single-point DFT calculations were performed in total. The DFT subset consists of 200 energetically lowest structures by COMPASSIII and ~1000 random structures. Data were split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio. 20 geometry optimization calculations were performed to assess relaxation effects.

Procedures And Architectures
ONETEP code with PBE GGA exchange correlation functional and 830 eV kinetic energy cutoff was used for DFT. CASTEP on-the-fly generated pseudopotentials were employed. The structures were represented by a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interactions, a reformulation of the connectivity matrix. A multiple linear regression (MLR) model fitted the DFT energies to the interaction frequency descriptors. COMPASSIII forcefield was used on the Li-sublattice only for initial ordering, achieving 0.991 correlation for 13:43. A Li-dimer energy curve (30 single-point calculations) showed minimum at ~2.7 Å with large penalty at 1.7 Å. ASE's symmetry equivalence check validated the LSH-based reduction. The MLR model tested for symmetry inclusion found it made negligible difference. BFGS geometry optimization used site-specific moves (96h to 96h, 96h to 48g, 96h to 24d) in order of frequency. The MLR model was validated with a test-set correlation of 0.9996.

Key Results
The MLR model predicted structure energies within a range of 5.8 eV of the lowest energy structure. 19 out of the 20 lowest-energy structures identified by MLR have a 24d:96h ratio of 8:48. The 19th lowest-energy structure has a ratio of 9:47. Four structures, all 8:48, fall within 0.026 eV (approximately 1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest energy structure. The average energy of all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground state structures. Average energy per ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy, showing energetic preference against 24d occupation. COMPASSIII on the Li-sublattice alone predicted a more pronounced inter-ratio energy separation than ONETEP (Figure S3). A 96h to 24d transition during geometry optimization in one instance yielded a 0.58 eV energy drop, moving the ratio from 9:47 to 10:46. The 96h to 24d transition was observed only once. A negative correlation exists between mean Li displacement distance and final optimized energy, and a weaker one with distance to crystallographic site. The LSH reduction reduced the configuration space by approximately a factor of 100.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The geometric Li-Li exclusion reveals that many experimentally and theoretically reported c-LLZO structures are non-physical. The 8:48 ratio is identified as the energetically preferred 24d:96h configuration, with four nearly degenerate ground states. The method provides a fast, scalable alternative to exhaustive DFT, usable for any partially occupied crystal system. The 96h to 24d transition during relaxation suggests that the crystallographic site boundaries are flexible under geometric optimization. The absence of entropic contributions means the energetic ordering assumes frozen configurational entropy.

Contradictions And Limitations
The MLR ordering procedure neglects entropic contributions and assumes retention of ordering upon relaxation. COMPASSIII over-predicted the energy separation between different 24d:96h ratios compared to ONETEP (Figure S3). The geometric Li-Li exclusion is a necessary but not sufficient condition for physical realizability. LSH is limited to comparison of monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions and is sensitive to method specificity. The 48g site was excluded as it is not typically reported, which might bias the search space. The authors state they did not perform large-scale energy prediction of geometry optimized structures.

Claims
A large proportion of experimentally and theoretically reported c-LLZO structures violate the 1.7 Å Li-Li geometric exclusion constraint. The 1.7 Å cutoff is less than 2× the Li ionic radius and smaller than t-LLZO's 2.56 Å minimum distance. The Li-dimer energy calculation shows a large penalty for Li atoms at 1.7 Å. The geometric constraint restricts possible 24d:96h ratios and eliminates non-physical configurations. The paper does not explicitly count how many literature structures were eliminated, only references to Figure 1 as a general indicator. The geometric exclusion is a necessary condition, but the paper acknowledges coulombic forces also matter. Future LLZO research must use valid, geometrically feasible structures as starting points for DFT and experimental assignment. Experimental assignments using x-ray diffraction may be less reliable than those using neutron diffraction for Li occupancy.
The 8:48 24d:96h ratio is the energetically preferred configuration for c-LLZO, with four nearly-degenerate ground states. 19 out of the 20 lowest-energy structures predicted by MLR have an 8:48 ratio. The four lowest-energy structures are within 0.026 eV of each other. The average energy per ratio increases with 24d occupancy. The four structures have identical 24d configurations with only 96h variations. The entropic contribution to the free energy is not accounted for, and the 96h-to-24d relaxation transition suggests the ratio could shift. The MLR model is trained on only 1235 points, and geometry optimization shows energy narrowing. The experimental Li occupancy should target 8:48 when performing refinements. The narrow energy gap suggests experimental measurement precision must be very high to distinguish these four structures.

Data And Code Availability
The generated database of all possible c-LLZO structures is published freely in the supporting information. The database includes unique identities for each structure. The symmetry validation scripts are provided in the supporting information. The paper does not explicitly state a repository for the MLR model or the DFT input files beyond referencing SI.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The MLR model was tested with a 1:3 train/test split and achieved 0.9996 correlation on the test set. The LSH symmetry reduction was validated against ASE's rigorous symmetry check on the two smallest ratios. COMPASSIII forcefield validation on the Li-sublattice showed a correlation of 0.991 for the 13:43 ratio. Symmetry was tested as an MLR feature but had negligible effect. A small dataset of 20 structures was used to test the effect of geometry relaxation. The COMPASSIII-ONETEP comparison showed systematic inter-ratio energy bias in the forcefield.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the Li-Li interaction distance scale, the geometrical constraint region, and the experimental occupancy plot. Figure 2b shows the ordering of the lowest-energy structures by energy with ratio and identity. Figure 3 illustrates the workflow from occupancies to the 4 final structures. Figure S3 compares 1235 DFT relative energies to COMPASSIII predictions. Table S1 lists all experimental papers reporting 24d:96h site occupancies. Table S2 lists all theoretical studies reporting 24d:96h ratios and generation methods. Table 1 provides the number of unique structures for each 24d:96h ratio. Figure S4 shows the Li-dimer energy curve used to justify the 1.7 Å cutoff.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a scalable workflow using geometric exclusion, LSH symmetry reduction, and MLR energy ordering to identify the 8:48 ground state of c-LLZO. 2. The strongest evidence is the MLR model achieving 0.9996 correlation with 19/20 lowest-energy structures sharing the 8:48 ratio, validated by a 1.7 Å geometric constraint derived from ab initio dimer calculations. 3. The future path includes extending the workflow to other partially occupied crystals, including entropic contributions, and performing full-scale relaxation of the lowest-energy candidates.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This feature article presents a comprehensive review and overview of recent advances in bioinspired supramolecular materials that mimic the dynamic contact events at cellular bio-interfaces. The authors argue that the construction of artificial extracellular matrices and membrane-deforming supramolecular materials, functionalized with dynamic properties, offers a powerful approach for regenerative medicine and drug delivery systems. The article is organized into four main sections, each addressing a different bio-interface: the extracellular matrix, phospholipid bilayers, redox-responsive peptides, and membrane-expanding molecular machines. For the extracellular matrix, self-assembling peptide hydrogels are developed with tunable stiffness via point mutations (RADA16 vs. A16G). A16G-N-cadherin conjugated hydrogels are shown to promote neuroblast migration in an in vivo neonatal neocortex injury model. For the phospholipid bilayer, JigSAP-tagged growth factors (VEGF) exhibit high incorporation efficiency (93 mol% vs. 3 mol% untagged) and sustained release profiles, enabling angiogenesis in an ischaemic stroke mouse model. JigSAP also incorporates a redox-active methionine residue (JigSAP-IMI/MII) allowing for stimulus-responsive gel-sol transition controlled by hydrogen peroxide. For membrane stabilization, Chol-MBP peptide-stabilized DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets show extended blood circulation compared to spherical vesicles. Finally, the photo-responsive molecular machine AzoMEx enables endocytosis-like membrane fission, allowing efficient encapsulation and blood-circulation-stable delivery of M13 phages, with retained infectivity across multiple organs. The article concludes that while these supramolecular approaches hold great promise for regenerative medicine and drug delivery, the field of biomimetic bio-interface engineering is still in its infancy and requires further development toward practical biomedical applications.

Research Context
Bio-interfaces are field of contact between molecules, cells, and tissues where dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies (ECM, phospholipid bilayers, membrane proteins) govern cellular activities. Typical dynamic functions at these interfaces include adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation, with the extracellular matrix (ECM) adhering to membrane protein receptors like cadherin to regulate migration and releasing signaling factors for cell differentiation. Phospholipid bilayers, as the major component of cellular and organelle membranes, mediate substance transportation via exocytosis and endocytosis, with membrane-embedded proteins performing signal transduction by sensing external signals. Recent progress in supramolecular chemistry and nanotechnology has made it possible to create dynamic materials that functionalize and control bio-interfaces, but a molecular approach enabling endocytosis-like transport where membrane deformation is synchronized with substance transport remains critically unexplored.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how self-assembling supramolecular materials can be designed and functionalized to mimic the dynamic actions and architectural properties of natural bio-interfaces for applications in tissue regeneration and cargo delivery. Hypothesis 1: Tuning the conformational flexibility of self-assembling peptide fibres via point mutations can control the macroscopic stiffness of the resulting hydrogel, thereby modulating neuroblast migration. Hypothesis 2: Jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces in peptide-based materials (JigSAP) can enable efficient incorporation and sustained release of full-length proteins, overcoming the incompatibility between protein binding and release in conventional ECM materials. Hypothesis 3: Redox-active methionine residues can be introduced to supramolecular peptide gels to enable stimulus-responsive gel-sol transitions for kinetics-controlled cargo release. Hypothesis 4: Peptide-stabilized phospholipid nanosheets can maintain their bicelle structure and enable extended blood circulation compared to spherical vesicles, suitable for systemic drug delivery. Hypothesis 5: A photo-responsive molecular machine can induce membrane-expanding outside-in fission in liposomes, enabling efficient encapsulation and protective transport of micrometer-size substances like phage viruses.

Methodological Details
The peptide hydrogel platform utilizes self-assembling peptide fibres with repeating sequences of RADA (Arg-Ala-Asp-Ala) forming nanofibres through beta-sheet-type hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interaction. Peptides consisting of RADA16 form nanofibres in aqueous media, while A8G (alanine-to-glycine mutant) and A16G (terminal-alanine-to-glycine mutant) were used to tune conformational flexibility and hydrogel stiffness. A16G-tagged N-cadherin (A16G-Ncad) was expressed via an E. coli expression system for conjugate protein display on the peptide scaffold. JigSAP is a fibre-forming peptide with the sequence Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2, possessing AXXXA and GXXXG motifs derived from glycophorin A that generate a jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surface. Protein incorporation assays were conducted by covalently conjugating full-length EGFP, EGFP-5V, and EGFP-RADA16 at the C-terminus of JigSAP, 5V, and RADA16, respectively. Rheological analysis of JigSAP hydrogels measured the storage modulus (G') and loss modulus (G'') as a function of increasing shear strain to characterize the strain thinning profile. Circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy monitored the conformational transition of 1 wt% JigSAP from helix/coil to beta-sheet over 100 hours in DMEM. For the stroke model, a distal middle cerebral artery occlusion was used to produce ischaemic stroke in mice, and 1.0 wt% JigSAP, 1.6 ng VEGF, or VEGF-JigSAP conjugates were injected into the injured cortex. Phospholipid nanosheets were formed by mixing DPPC with Chol-MBP (PHGGGPHGG peptide) at a ratio of 5/1, with a total peptide concentration of 5.0 wt%. Copper crosslinking was achieved by adding 2.0 equivalents of Cu 2+ ions to the DPPC/Chol-MBP dispersion. Fluorescent Cy5-labeled DPPC vesicles and DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets (5.0 wt% total) were administered via tail vein injection for IV-CLSM observation. For the phage delivery system, GUVDOPC/AzoMEx liposomes ([DOPC] = 180 µM, [AzoMEx] = 20 µM) were used with 22.6 × 10^11 M13 phage virions per mL. M13 phages encapsulated into GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp (pAsp = poly(aspartic acid), PEG = poly(ethylene glycol)) were administered via tail vein for organ distribution analysis. Plaque assays were performed on homogenized organ samples 15 minutes after 100 μL IV injection to quantify retained M13 phage infectivity. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) were used to visualize self-assembled morphologies.

Procedures And Architectures
The peptide hydrogel architecture relies on RADA-based repeating sequences forming beta-sheet-type networks; conformational flexibility is tuned by alanine-to-glycine mutations, with A8G forming bundled nanofibres and A16G forming curved fibres. MD simulations visualized that the conformal flexibility of A16G decreases hydrogel stiffness compared to RADA16, while A16G-Ncad hydrogels provide the necessary ligands for neuroblast migration. Time-lapse imaging of ventricular-subventricular zone neuroblasts on culture dishes coated with A16G or A16G/A16G-Ncad mixtures assessed migration rate. In vivo stroke experiments involved injecting hydrogel mixtures into the neonatal neocortex at low temperature after distal middle cerebral artery occlusion, with Dcx+ staining identifying migrating neuroblasts. JigSAP hydrogel formation proceeds via a 100-hour CD-monitored helix-to-beta-sheet transition, yielding nanofibres with an average width of 3.2 nm and length of several µm. The JigSAP hydrogel exhibits a high rigidity of 1.1 x 10 4 Pa, and rheological measurements confirmed a strain-thinning profile characteristic of covalent-like robustness. Redox-responsive gels are formed by substituting methionine at different positions (IMI vs MII) in JigSAP, where oxidized forms JigSAP-IMI-Ox and JigSAP-MII-Ox remain dispersed at pH 7.4 and 1.0 wt% peptide in DMEM. Nanofibre formation is further investigated by adding 30% H2O2 aq. to the top of the hydrogels to trigger oxidation-mediated gel-sol transition. Phospholipid nanosheets are assembled by mixing DPPC and Chol-MBP, with PHGGG motifs binding Cu 2+ ions at the membrane edge to prevent dissociation. Stability testing involved diluting the DPPC/Chol-MBP dispersion to 0.2 wt%, at which point spherical aggregates of less than 100 nm appear without Cu 2+ crosslinking. For endocytosis-like fission, the AzoMEx molecular machine (diazocine core) undergoes photoisomerization-triggered opening/closing motion, expanding the DOPC liposomal membrane. AzoMEx-GUV membranes interact with 1-µm-long anionic M13 phage viruses, which accumulate in the deforming membrane area and are incorporated via outside-in fission. The encapsulated M13 phages are coated with a block polymer of poly(aspartic acid) and poly(ethylene glycol) before tail vein administration to mice. Blood circulation is monitored by IV-CLSM of the earlobe 15 minutes post-injection, comparing unencapsulated M13 phageCy5 (dashed line) and encapsulated M13 phageCy5 (solid line). The final delivery assessment uses plaque assays on homogenized spleen, liver, kidney, heart, lung, and brain samples, with spleen and liver diluted 10-fold before assay.

Key Results
A16G hydrogel, which forms curved fibres as visualized by TEM and MD simulations, exhibits lower stiffness than RADA16 hydrogel, providing enhanced mobility and thixotropic properties for injectable applications. Time-lapse imaging showed that the migration rate of neuroblasts was significantly higher on A16G-Ncad hydrogels than on A16G alone. In vivo stroke model revealed that Dcx+ neuroblasts were abundantly observed in A16G/A16G-Ncad mixture hydrogels, whereas they were seen sparsely in A16G alone or A16G/Ncad mixtures. JigSAP-tagged EGFP protein exhibited an incorporation efficiency of 93 mol%, compared to only 3 mol% for untagged EGFP. EGFP proteins tagged with 5V showed 66 mol% incorporation, and EGFP-RADA16 showed 55 mol% incorporation, both significantly higher than untagged. The protein release profile from JigSAP hydrogel showed 21 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP released after 24-hour incubation at 37 °C, increasing to 39 mol% after 168 hours. In contrast, EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 release stagnated after 48 hours, with only 5 mol% and 8 mol%, respectively, released even after 168 hours. In the ischaemic stroke mouse model, the number of double-positive cells (laminin+/EdU+) increased in the injured area when VEGF-JigSAP or VEGF+JigSAP was injected, indicating promoted angiogenesis. DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets maintained their structure at 0.2 wt% dilution upon addition of 2.0 equivalents of Cu 2+ ions, whereas untreated nanosheets showed spherical aggregates. IV-CLSM revealed FL DPPC vesicles were aggregated and clogged in the blood vessels, while FL DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed, demonstrating extended circulation. GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp encapsulated M13 phages showed higher stability in blood than bare M13 phageCy5, as observed by IV-CLSM. Plaque assays quantified retained M13 phage infectivity post-distribution: spleen [25.6 ± 13.2] × 10^9 virions/mg; liver [18.3 ± 3.2] × 10^9 virions/mg; kidney [1.3 ± 0.6] × 10^9 virions/mg; heart [1.1 ± 0.5] × 10^9 virions/mg; lung [0.5 ± 0.3] × 10^9 virions/mg; brain [0.2 ± 0.1] × 10^9 virions/mg. JigSAP hydrogel exhibits remarkably high rigidity (1.1 x 10 4 Pa) and a strain-thinning profile, demonstrating that supramolecular nanofibres are robust like covalently polymerized materials.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The ECM mimicking strategy demonstrates that fibrous self-assembly of peptide motifs (RADA16, A16G, JigSAP) can reconstruct tissue-specific interfacial structures that regulate cell adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation. Membrane-deforming materials using self-assembling peptides control phospholipid bilayer morphology and deformation, which directly relates to the dynamic interfacial functions of substance transportation and signal sensing. Jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces provide a bottom-up methodology for integrating full-length proteins into supramolecular scaffolds without compromising their biological activity, enabling sustained-release growth factor delivery for tissue regeneration. The AzoMEx molecular machine enables a biomimetic outside-in vesicle fission that synchronizes membrane deformation with cargo uptake, offering a synthetic analog to endocytic biomolecular machines. These supramolecular approaches present powerful ways to develop unprecedented regenerative medicines and drug delivery systems by manipulating the fundamental contact events between molecules, cells, and tissues.

Contradictions And Limitations
The in vitro time-lapse imaging of neuroblasts on coated culture dishes may not fully capture the spatiotemporal complexity of actual in vivo neurogenesis in the developing cortex. The neonatal neocortex injury model, while useful for proof-of-concept, may not translate to regenerative strategies for adult brain injury where the regenerative environment is more compromised. Blood circulation stability of Chol-MBP nanosheets was tested at 5.0 wt% total content, but long-term systemic clearance kinetics and eventual biodegradation pathways were not fully characterized. The M13 phage delivery system was evaluated in mice but not in a relevant pathological model, and long-term infectivity or host immune response to the encapsulated virus was not reported. The paper is a review highlighting recent advances and does not present comprehensive head-to-head comparisons with established clinical benchmarks for any of the proposed strategies. The strain thinning of JigSAP hydrogels was noted as typically observed in covalently polymerized materials, but the ultimate durability under repetitive cycles was not explicitly quantified.

Claims
Self-assembling peptide fibres can be engineered with tunable stiffness through conformational control, providing biomimetic scaffolds for neuro-regenerative therapy. A16G (alanine-to-glycine mutant) forms curved fibres visualized by TEM and MD simulations, leading to lower hydrogel stiffness compared to RADA16. A16G-Ncad hydrogels demonstrated significantly higher neuroblast migration rates than A16G alone in time-lapse imaging. In vivo neonatal neocortex injury model with A16G/A16G-Ncad injections produced abundant Dcx+ neuroblasts in the injured area. The in vivo stroke model was conducted in the neonatal neocortex, not an adult brain injury model. This fibrous self-assembly mimics the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells, offering a novel strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy. Future work could explore other adhesion molecules beyond N-cadherin for multi-modal ECM reconstruction.
JigSAP-tagged growth factors achieve exceptionally high incorporation and sustained release from self-assembling peptide nanofibres, enabling angiogenesis in ischaemic stroke models. EGFP-JigSAP showed 93 mol% incorporation vs. 3 mol% for untagged EGFP. Protein release reached 39 mol% after 168 hours for EGFP-JigSAP, while only 5% and 8% were released for 5V and RADA16 counterparts. VEGF-JigSAP and VEGF+JigSAP injections in the ischaemic stroke model increased double-positive laminin/EdU cells in the injured area. The VEGF release was evaluated in a mouse stroke model without cell transplantation, but the long-term regenerative outcome beyond 15 minutes of blood circulation was not fully tracked. The jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic dimerization mechanism generalizes to controlled sustained release of various full-length growth factors for tissue regeneration. Future applications could include delivery of different growth factors tailored to specific tissue regeneration targets.
Phospholipid nanosheets stabilized by self-assembling metal-chelating peptides enable extended blood circulation of bicelle carriers for systemic drug delivery. DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets maintained structure at 0.2 wt% dilution with 2.0 equivalents of Cu 2+ crosslinking. IV-CLSM showed FL DPPC vesicles aggregated and clogged in blood vessels, while FL DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed. The Chol-MBP design enables the bicelle morphology to persist under dilution and blood flow conditions. The stability was demonstrated at 5.0 wt% total content; lower concentrations or higher shear conditions were not systematically evaluated. The self-assembling approach of Chol-MBP demonstrates a suitable carrier for the whole body by blood administration. Future work could optimize surface decoration of nanosheets for specific organ targeting.
A photo-responsive molecular machine can trigger membrane-expanding outside-in fission in liposomes, enabling efficient encapsulation and protective transport of phage viruses. GUVDOPC/AzoMEx with 22.6 × 10^11 M13 phage virions/mL achieved efficient encapsulation via outside-in fission. M13 phages encapsulated in GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp showed higher stability in blood than bare M13 phageCy5. Plaque assays confirmed retained infectivity of M13 phages in spleen [25.6 ± 13.2], liver [18.3 ± 3.2], kidney [1.3 ± 0.6], heart [1.1 ± 0.5], lung [0.5 ± 0.3], and brain [0.2 ± 0.1] × 10^9 virions/mg. The phage delivery was evaluated in wild-type mice, and the long-term infectivity or host immune response to the encapsulated virus was not reported. The AzoMEx-GUV technology for M13 phage encapsulation could be applied to an in vivo phage display method for selecting peptides binding to target ligands in living bodies. This synthetic endocytosis-like transport mechanism is applicable to other micrometer-size cargo.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Conformational flexibility ablation: alanine-to-glycine point mutations in the RADA peptide backbone (A8G vs A16G) demonstrated contrasting hydrogel stiffness and fibre morphology confirmed by TEM and MD simulations. Protein tagging ablation: EGFP incorporation was compared between JigSAP-tagged, 5V-tagged, and RADA16-tagged versions versus untagged EGFP, showing 93%, 66%, and 55% incorporation efficiencies, respectively. Copper crosslinking ablation: DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets diluted to 0.2 wt% showed spherical aggregates without Cu 2+, but maintained nanosheet structure with 2.0 equivalents of Cu 2+. Redox ablation: JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII (methionine at different positions) showed contrasting macroscopic properties upon oxidation, with oxidized forms remaining dispersed under physiological conditions. Coating ablation: M13 phages were compared between bare and GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp encapsulated forms for blood circulation stability.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Schematic representation of bio-interfaces in cellular activities, illustrating the dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies at cellular interfaces. Figure 2: Morphological characterization of A8G and A16G peptide nanofibres by TEM, MD simulations, and corresponding hydrogel stiffness properties (a-f). Figure 3: Time-lapse imaging of neuroblast migration on A16G and A16G/A16G-Ncad hydrogels (a), and in vivo Dcx+ staining in the injured neonate neocortex (b). Figure 4: JigSAP characterization including CD spectra (a-b), nanofibre morphology (c), hydrogel formation (d), rheology (e-f), protein incorporation efficiencies (g-j), and protein release profiles (k) for stroke model and neuronal regeneration (l-r). Figure 5: Redox-responsive JigSAP hydrogels, including gel-sol transitions of JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII upon H2O2 addition (a-h). Figure 6: Phospholipid nanosheet characterization including morphology by TEM (a-d), IV-CLSM circulation in earlobes of mice (e-g). Figure 7: AzoMEx-enabled endocytosis-like fission and M13 phage delivery including light-triggered membrane deformation, encapsulation, IV-CLSM circulation (e-n), and plaque assays of homogenized organ samples (o-t).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of supramolecular materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces, including artificial ECMs with tunable stiffness, JigSAP with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces for growth factor incorporation and sustained release, redox-switchable peptide gels, phospholipid nanosheets stabilized by metal-chelating peptides, and photo-responsive molecular machines enabling endocytosis-like membrane fission. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of in vitro morphological characterization (TEM, CD, MD simulations) with in vivo functional assays, including a neonatal neocortex stroke model for neuroblast migration, IV-CLSM for blood circulation, and plaque assays for M13 phage infectivity across multiple organs. 3. The future path involves further development of biomimetic interfaces with dynamic nature toward practical biomedical applications, extending the M13 phage encapsulation technology to in vivo phage display, and exploring broader classes of growth factors and tissue regeneration targets.

summary.title: GUIDEMOL: a Python graphical user interface for molecular descriptors based on RDKit
summary.authors: Joao Aires (NOVA School of Science and Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Chemoinformatics; Computational Chemistry
summary.executive_summary:
GUIDEMOL is a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) developed using the tkinter package, built on top of the RDKit chemoinformatics software, designed to process molecular structures and calculate molecular descriptors. The application targets chemoinformatics users, including scientists and students with no programming skills, providing easy access to RDKit's descriptor calculation tools. It supports both established RDKit descriptors and grid representations of 3D molecular structures using electrostatic potential (EP) or voxel encoding. For 3D structure generation, GUIDEMOL uses RDKit's MMFFOptimizeMolecule with mmffVariant='MMFF94' and maxIters=5000, with options to remove metals using the MetalDisconnector class, keep the largest fragment with LargestFragmentChooser(preferOrganic=True), or neutralize using Uncharger. The 3D descriptors available via the RDKit rdMolDescriptors module include RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA, along with exact molecular weight.

For EP grid calculation, the GUI allows users to choose between Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges calculated via AllChem.ComputeGasteigerCharges() or GetMMFFPartialCharge(), specify grid center coordinates, side length, cube size, and a cutoff distance. The voxelization option uses an atomic property (atomic number, partial charge, molecular refractivity contribution, or logP contribution via Wildman-Crippen) in a user-defined 3D grid, with a parameter σ controlling the contribution decay. A command-line interface (CLI) is also provided for grid representation calculations. The software is released under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license and is hosted on GitHub. A key observation reported is that for some molecules and certain descriptors (GETAWAY, MORSE, WHIM), inconsistent values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or different operating systems, exemplified by the molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. The paper positions GUIDEMOL as a minimalist interface for routine chemoinformatics tasks, emphasizing reproducibility and ease of use for QSPR/QSAR workflows. The source code is available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
GUIDEMOL is a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) developed using the tkinter package, built on top of the RDKit chemoinformatics software, designed to process molecular structures and calculate molecular descriptors. The application targets chemoinformatics users, including scientists and students with no programming skills, providing easy access to RDKit's descriptor calculation tools. It supports both established RDKit descriptors and grid representations of 3D molecular structures using electrostatic potential (EP) or voxel encoding. For 3D structure generation, GUIDEMOL uses RDKit's MMFFOptimizeMolecule with mmffVariant='MMFF94' and maxIters=5000, with options to remove metals using the MetalDisconnector class, keep the largest fragment with LargestFragmentChooser(preferOrganic=True), or neutralize using Uncharger. The 3D descriptors available via the RDKit rdMolDescriptors module include RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA, along with exact molecular weight.

For EP grid calculation, the GUI allows users to choose between Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges calculated via AllChem.ComputeGasteigerCharges() or GetMMFFPartialCharge(), specify grid center coordinates, side length, cube size, and a cutoff distance. The voxelization option uses an atomic property (atomic number, partial charge, molecular refractivity contribution, or logP contribution via Wildman-Crippen) in a user-defined 3D grid, with a parameter σ controlling the contribution decay. A command-line interface (CLI) is also provided for grid representation calculations. The software is released under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license and is hosted on GitHub. A key observation reported is that for some molecules and certain descriptors (GETAWAY, MORSE, WHIM), inconsistent values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) in different runs or different operating systems, exemplified by the molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. The paper positions GUIDEMOL as a minimalist interface for routine chemoinformatics tasks, emphasizing reproducibility and ease of use for QSPR/QSAR workflows. The source code is available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol.

Research Context
Molecular descriptors lie at the core of the QSPR/QSAR methodology, used by scientists across disciplines with varying computer proficiency. Chemoinformatics is increasingly integrated into chemistry, biology, and material science curricula, creating a demand for accessible teaching software. Several existing programs calculate molecular descriptors across platforms: CDK (PaDEL, CDK Descriptor Calculator) uses Java libraries; BlueDesc is a command-line tool providing up to 174 descriptors using CDK and JOELib2; OCHEM integrates thousands of descriptors from various groups; and ChemDes provides 3679 molecular descriptors and 59 fingerprint types. Proprietary software such as MOE, VolSurf+, CORINA Symphony, ChemAxon Calculator Plugins, and alvaDesc also offer descriptor calculation capabilities. The open-source RDKit software implements a wide range of chemoinformatics tools, including molecular descriptor calculation, and is extensively used in machine learning projects. The Mordred package, a Python-based tool, calculates molecular descriptors using RDKit wrappers and original implementations, available as command-line or web application. Python's tkinter package, the standard Tcl/Tk interface bundled with Python, enables easy GUI development for chemoinformatics tools. Shi and Borchardt combined RDKit and tkinter to develop JRgui for Joback and Reid group contribution molecular descriptors. 3D grid representations of molecules encoding atoms in voxels have recently attracted attention for processing by deep learning neural networks. Electrostatic potentials generated by point charges at atom centers have long been used in 3D-QSAR and molecular similarity assessment. Direct 3D representations can be used for pre-aligned structures (e.g., relative to a reference or after docking) or processed by convolutional neural networks. The motivation for this work is to provide a minimalist interface to routine chemoinformatics tasks and well-established descriptor calculations.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central objective is to develop a Python GUI built on RDKit that requires no programming skills from the user. The application aims to provide easy access to RDKit's existing molecular descriptor calculation tools for chemoinformatics users. The software is designed to calculate not only established RDKit descriptors but also grid representations of 3D molecular structures based on electrostatic potential or voxel encoding. The GUI is intended to enable users to specify parameters such as atomic properties, grid coordinates, cube size, and cutoff distances. The authors hypothesize that a minimalist tkinter-based interface can serve as an adaptable template for other chemoinformatics tasks and molecular descriptors. A secondary objective is to provide a command-line interface for grid representation calculations to ensure reproducibility and programmatic access. The authors anticipate that the open-source BSD license release will facilitate bug detection, fixing, and extension by the community.

Methodological Details
The GUI was built using various tkinter widgets managed by the grid geometry manager: Buttons for calculations, Checkbuttons for YES/NO options, Radiobuttons for mutually exclusive choices, Entries for numeric input, Labels for text display, and a Scrollbar. File/directory selection is implemented via the tkinter.filedialog module, enabling users to choose input and output files. A log file is automatically created in the output directory to record successful molecule processing and failures. The software is released under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license, allowing both commercial and non-commercial use. The source code is hosted at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol, with the repository identifier jairesdesousa. The RDKit version used is 2022.9.5, specified in the software notes. The software is written in Python and utilizes the RDKit cheminformatics library for all structural processing and descriptor calculation. There is no formal evaluation study with a participant pool, validation dataset, or benchmarking against other descriptor calculation tools reported. The method is the software architecture itself, described as a minimalist interface to routine chemoinformatics tasks. The software supports both the tkinter GUI and a standalone command-line interface for the same 3D grid calculation functionalities.

Procedures And Architectures
3D molecular models are generated using the RDKit function MMFFOptimizeMolecule with mmffVariant='MMFF94' and maxIters=5000. Pre-generation options include: remove metals using the MetalDisconnector class, keep the largest fragment with LargestFragmentChooser(preferOrganic=True), or neutralize structures with Uncharger. Hydrogen atoms are added using the Chem.AddHs() function. The rdMolDescriptors module in RDKit provides the seven available 3D descriptors: RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA. The exact molecular weight can also be selected as a descriptor. EP grids are generated using Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges calculated via AllChem.ComputeGasteigerCharges() or GetMMFFPartialCharge(). The EP at each cube c is computed as the sum of partial charges q_i multiplied by the distance r_ic between atom i and cube center. The sum excludes atoms within 1 Å of the cube center (contributing their partial charge directly) and atoms beyond the user-defined cutoff distance. Voxelization uses a user-defined 3D grid based on an atomic property selected from: atomic number, partial atomic charge (Gasteiger or MMFF), molecular refractivity contribution, or logP contribution via _CalcCrippenContribs(). The voxel value VoxG_c at each cube c is computed as the sum over atoms of the property p_i multiplied by exp(-r_ic^2/σ^2), where σ controls contribution decay. Missing hydrogen atoms can be added with the argument addCoords=True, ensuring 3D coordinates are calculated without moving other atoms. The CLI supports flags: -i (input), -o (output), -g {pot,vox}, -p {Gasteiger,MMFF,MR,LogP,AtomicNumber}, -cx/-cy/-cz (center coordinates), -r (cube size), -w (EP cutoff), -sx/-sy/-sz (grid dimensions). An example CLI command calculates an EP grid with Gasteiger charges, centered at (0,0,0), size 5 Å, resolution 0.5 Å, cutoff 3 Å, output to outfile.csv. The molecular descriptors are saved in a CSV output file with the molecule name and ID as the final columns.

Key Results
GUIDEMOL provides a functional GUI for RDKit molecular descriptor calculation and 3D grid representation of molecules. The software also provides a CLI for generating EP and voxel grid representations, ensuring reproducibility. A key technical observation: for some molecules and descriptors (GETAWAY, MORSE, WHIM), inconsistent descriptor values were obtained with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5) across different runs or operating systems. The specific example molecule exhibiting this inconsistency is COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. The RDKit version specified is 2022.9.5, indicating the software was tested and validated on this release. The 7 RDKit 3D descriptors (RDF through SMR_VSA) are all available via the GUI. The grid representation parameters (center coordinates, size, resolution, atomic property) are fully configurable by the user through the graphical interface. No quantitative performance metrics, accuracy measurements, or head-to-head comparisons with other descriptor software are reported.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 3D voxel and EP representations are positioned as inputs for complex AI algorithms and convolutional neural networks, aligning with recent trends in structure-based deep learning. The software is described as a minimalist interface to routine chemoinformatics tasks, lowering the barrier to entry for non-programmers. The BSD license release facilitates community adoption, bug fixing, and extension to other molecular descriptors or chemoinformatics tasks. The dual GUI and CLI architecture addresses both user accessibility and programmatic reproducibility requirements in QSPR/QSAR workflows. The observation of inconsistent descriptor values across runs/OS highlights an underlying reproducibility challenge in some RDKit descriptor implementations.

Contradictions And Limitations
For some molecules and descriptors (GETAWAY, MORSE, WHIM), different values were obtained with the same RDKit version in different runs or operating systems, undermining reproducibility. The example molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br demonstrates the inconsistency, though no quantitative delta between runs is specified. The software is a technical note, so no formal validation, usability testing, or benchmark comparisons against competing software are provided. No formal evaluation of computational efficiency, memory usage, or user satisfaction is reported. The paper does not specify any randomized testing procedure or systematic validation beyond the noted reproducibility issue.

Claims
GUIDEMOL provides a graphical user interface requiring no programming skills for RDKit-based molecular descriptor calculation and 3D grid representation. The application is built on tkinter, the standard Python GUI package, accessible to non-programmers. It implements the seven RDKit 3D descriptors (RDF through SMR_VSA) via the rdMolDescriptors module. The CLI also provides a programmatic entry point for grid calculations. Inconsistent descriptor values were observed for some molecules across different runs/OS using the same RDKit version. No formal usability evaluation or validation study is presented. The software democratizes RDKit descriptor tools for chemists, biologists, and students without programming expertise. The BSD license and open-source nature facilitate community-driven extension and maintenance.
GUIDEMOL enables calculation of 3D grid representations based on electrostatic potential or voxel encoding, with fully configurable user parameters. The GUI allows selection of atomic properties (atomic number, partial charge, refractivity, logP) for voxel grids. EP grids use Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges calculated with RDKit. The CLI provides identical grid calculation parameters to the GUI. No empirical validation of the grid representation quality or comparison to established 3D-QSAR benchmarks is reported. These 3D representations are compatible with deep learning neural networks and convolutional neural networks. The dual GUI/CLI approach addresses both interactive exploration and batch processing needs.

Data And Code Availability
The source code is available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol under the three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license. The repository is hosted on GitHub with the handle jairesdesousa.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors report that for some molecules and descriptors (GETAWAY, MORSE, WHIM), different values were obtained with the same RDKit version in different runs or operating systems. No formal ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, or error analyses are performed or reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the GUIDEMOL graphical user interface with tkinter widgets (Buttons, Checkbuttons, Radiobuttons, Entries, Labels, Scrollbar).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a tkinter-based Python GUI and CLI that makes RDKit molecular descriptor calculation and 3D grid representation (EP/voxels) accessible to users with no programming skills, under a BSD license for open use. 2. The strongest evidence is the implementation of all seven RDKit 3D descriptors (RDF through SMR_VSA) plus the dual GUI/CLI architecture, though a reported reproducibility issue with some descriptors across runs/OS highlights a practical limitation. 3. The future path is defined by the minimalist, extensible design, the open-source BSD license, and the capability to extend the software for other molecular descriptors or different chemoinformatics tasks.
