summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang; Tianzuo Li; Jiyeon Lee; Dahye Lim; Lianjie Xu; Yajie Liu; Jongcheol Seo; Wen-Bin Zhang
summary.field_subfield: Protein Engineering; Topological Protein Design
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports the first design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), where two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings fold synergistically into a compact, integrated structure. Unlike prior artificial topological proteins that typically contain multiple domains, cat-DHFR is a single-domain protein whose topology was generated entirely by rewiring the internal connectivity of the wild-type DHFR fold through a split-and-rejoin strategy. The design utilized the fact that DHFR and GFP tolerate rethreading, enabling the creation of a topology where the original fold itself serves as the entangling template. The wild-type DHFR (PDB: 4KJJ) backbone was virtually cleaved at a position between α-helix-C and β-sheet-5 (residues 88 and 89), generating two intertwined segments with a Gaussian linking number (GLN) of +0.726. Upon cyclization using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs, the catenane formed with a GLN of +1.120. The synthetic strategy employed circular permutation to place cyclization motifs on opposite sides of the fold, with the most efficient ring closure occurring between residues 23 and 24 using 16residues-long loops. The gene cassette contained two DHFR segments as the entangling template, two mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs, and a TEV protease recognition site. The construct was expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3) at 16°C for 20 hours, purified by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography and size exclusion chromatography, and further characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, far-UV CD, near-UV CD, ion mobility mass spectrometry (IMS), collision-induced dissociation (CID), and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). The catenane retained approximately 36% of wild-type catalytic activity (~5 U/mg vs ~14 U/mg), with a 5-fold increase in Km and a 38% reduction in kcat. Binding affinities were significantly reduced (KD for DHF ~173-fold higher; NADPH ~14-fold higher), but the catenane showed improved tolerance to 5% DMSO (87% vs 74%). An unambiguous proof of topology via crystallography was not achieved, so topology was confirmed indirectly by TEV protease cleavage yielding linear and cyclic fragments, and by IMS-MS and CID. The authors conclude that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability, establishing a new horizon in protein science.

claims.description: The first single-domain protein catenane was successfully designed and synthesized by rewiring the connectivity of a single protein fold.
The catenane topology preserves catalytic function and enhances chemical stability of the enzyme.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper reports the first design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), where two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings fold synergistically into a compact, integrated structure. Unlike prior artificial topological proteins that typically contain multiple domains, cat-DHFR is a single-domain protein whose topology was generated entirely by rewiring the internal connectivity of the wild-type DHFR fold through a split-and-rejoin strategy. The design utilized the fact that DHFR and GFP tolerate rethreading, enabling the creation of a topology where the original fold itself serves as the entangling template. The wild-type DHFR (PDB: 4KJJ) backbone was virtually cleaved at a position between α-helix-C and β-sheet-5 (residues 88 and 89), generating two intertwined segments with a Gaussian linking number (GLN) of +0.726. Upon cyclization using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation pairs, the catenane formed with a GLN of +1.120. The synthetic strategy employed circular permutation to place cyclization motifs on opposite sides of the fold, with the most efficient ring closure occurring between residues 23 and 24 using 16residues-long loops. The gene cassette contained two DHFR segments as the entangling template, two mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs, and a TEV protease recognition site. The construct was expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3) at 16°C for 20 hours, purified by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography and size exclusion chromatography, and further characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, far-UV CD, near-UV CD, ion mobility mass spectrometry (IMS), collision-induced dissociation (CID), and isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). The catenane retained approximately 36% of wild-type catalytic activity (~5 U/mg vs ~14 U/mg), with a 5-fold increase in Km and a 38% reduction in kcat. Binding affinities were significantly reduced (KD for DHF ~173-fold higher; NADPH ~14-fold higher), but the catenane showed improved tolerance to 5% DMSO (87% vs 74%). An unambiguous proof of topology via crystallography was not achieved, so topology was confirmed indirectly by TEV protease cleavage yielding linear and cyclic fragments, and by IMS-MS and CID. The authors conclude that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability, establishing a new horizon in protein science.

Research Context
Natural protein domains fold as independent linear polypeptide chains with limited topological diversity. Unconventional chemical topology has been recognized as a unique dimension for protein engineering. Artificial topological proteins synthesized to date usually contain multiple domains, complicating the study of topological effects on structure-property relationships. The most profound impact of chemical topology should be studied in single-domain topological proteins. DHFR and GFP have been shown to tolerate rethreading, producing linear variants with preserved function. None of the prior works on DHFR engineering go beyond the linear backbone defined by the cellular ribosomal template.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a single-domain protein be converted into a mechanically interlocked catenane without collapsing the fold? The central research question asks whether rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs can introduce artificial entanglement while preserving catalytic function. The hypothesis is that the original fold itself can serve as the entangling template, eliminating the need for an exogenous entangling motif. The authors predict that cat-DHFR will retain catalytic capability and exhibit enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation. The design assumes that circular permutation can position cyclization motifs to minimize steric hindrance between bulky split-intein pairs.

Methodological Details
The host organism for protein expression was E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. Genes for cat-DHFR and l-DHFR were sub-cloned into pMCSG19 and pET21a vectors, respectively. Protein expression was carried out at 16°C for 20 hours to ensure proper folding and complete ligation reactions. Proteins were purified under native conditions using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. Eluted products were further purified by size exclusion chromatography (SEC). LC-MS spectra confirmed the identities of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR by accurate molecular weight measurements. Far-UV CD spectra and near-UV CD spectra were used to assess the folding status and secondary structure. Ion mobility spectrometry (IMS) and collision-induced dissociation (CID) provided indirect evidence of topology. Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) was used to determine dissociation constants for DHF, NADPH, and THF. The wild-type DHFR structure from PDB: 4KJJ served as the template for virtual cleavage. SDS-PAGE analysis of purified products showed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR. cat-DHFR exhibited a major band at less than 20 kDa on SDS-PAGE.

Procedures And Architectures
The design algorithm calculated a total of N!/[(N-M)!*M!] ways of splitting M loops from N total loops to produce two rings. The Gaussian linking number (GLN) matrix of wt-DHFR was used to identify the splitting position. Cleavage was performed between residues 88 and 89, yielding two intertwined segments with GLN +0.726. Residues 1-88 and residues 89-159 formed the two rings of the catenane. The design produced a catenane with a GLN of +1.120, compared to +0.726 for the split intermediate. Two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs were used for ring closure. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24. Rewired loops were designed to be 16residues long to bridge the split structural motifs. A TEV protease recognition sequence was embedded in the first ring for proteolytic cleavage. A linear DHFR control (l-DHFR) was designed with extra N- and C-terminal amino acids but identical internal composition. Kinetic assays monitored dihydrofolate reduction at 25°C by measuring absorbance at 340 nm.

Key Results
cat-DHFR retained ~5 U/mg activity compared to ~14 U/mg for the linear control, representing 36% retention. The previously reported rethreaded DHFR showed no reducing activity at all, making cat-DHFR activity significant. The reconstituted physical complex of two DHFR fragments retained only 15% of enzymatic activity. The Km of cat-DHFR was approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR. The kcat of cat-DHFR was approximately 38% of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) was reduced by an order of magnitude. The KD for DHF increased approximately 173-fold, and KD for NADPH increased ~14-fold. The KD for the product THF increased by ~3.6-fold, facilitating product release. cat-DHFR showed 87% residual activity in 5% DMSO, compared to 74% for l-DHFR. SDS-PAGE showed a major band for cat-DHFR at less than 20 kDa, with faster mobility than l-DHFR. SEC overlay showed cat-DHFR eluting at a slightly larger retention volume with a broader peak. Far-UV CD spectra of cat-DHFR showed reduced positive ellipticity at ~200 nm and negative ellipticity between 210 and 230 nm. The design with same-side split-inteins produced only ~33% catenane form, with considerable single-ring side products. The shortest linker yielded only about one-fifth the output of the longest linker (~12 mg/L).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The retention of ~36% activity suggests that rewiring and catenation do not collapse the hydrophobic core or disrupt the active site. The circular permutation-induced CD spectral changes matched previously reported effects in circularly permutated DHFR, indicating only minor local disturbances. The presence of a folded structure in cat-DHFR is consistent with the requirement that folding precedes template-directed catenane formation. The reduced Km and kcat reflect the compromised binding affinity of the mechanically interlocked architecture toward substrates and cofactors. The improved DMSO tolerance suggests that mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal resilience of the enzyme. The authors envision that directed evolution could restore or surpass the linear control activity. The results suggest linear proteins may be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition.

Contradictions And Limitations
Crystallography of cat-DHFR was attempted but failed, precluding unambiguous structural confirmation. Possible reasons for crystallization failure include unsatisfactory purity, disordered linkers, or reduced binding affinity. The catenane retains only 36% of wild-type activity, which is substantial but incomplete. The SEC peak for cat-DHFR is broader, suggesting a more dynamic structure due to coupled movement of two interlocked rings. Same-side split-intein orientation produced only ~33% catenane, showing that steric hindrance of bulky split-inteins is critical. The shortest linker yielded only one-fifth the output of the longest linker, limiting the viable linker space.

Claims
The first single-domain protein catenane was successfully designed and synthesized by rewiring the connectivity of a single protein fold. The design rewrote the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement. GLN increased from +0.726 in the split intermediate to +1.120 in the catenane. Cat-DHFR was characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and IMS. Crystallography failed, so the exact atomistic structure remains unverified. Activity is only ~36% of wild-type. Linear proteins can be converted to concatenated counterparts with identical composition. A new horizon in protein science opens for designing single-domain topological proteins.
The catenane topology preserves catalytic function and enhances chemical stability of the enzyme. cat-DHFR retained 5 U/mg activity vs 14 U/mg for l-DHFR. cat-DHFR retained 87% activity in 5% DMSO vs 74% for l-DHFR. The previously reported rethreaded DHFR had no reducing activity at all. The Km increased 5-fold and kcat decreased to 38%, reducing catalytic efficiency by an order of magnitude. Mechanical interlocking enhances thermal resilience of enzymes. The reduced activity can be optimized further by directed evolution.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A control using split-intein ligation on the same side of DHFR produced only ~33% catenane form with considerable single-ring side products. The site between residues 23 and 24 was found to be the most efficient for ring closure. Linker length tests showed that as L2 became shorter, split-inteins could not efficiently reconstitute, reducing yield to ~12 mg/L. The method was generally robust before the linker became too short.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the design of cat-DHFR, including the virtual cleavage site, GLN matrices, the gene cassette design, and the retrosynthetic analysis. Figure 2 presents SDS-PAGE, SEC overlay, LC-MS spectra, far-UV CD spectra, and TEV protease cleavage results confirming catenane topology. Figure 4 shows the catalytic activity curves at 340 nm and the comparison between cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Figure S1 presents the GLN matrices of split DHFR and cat-DHFR. Table 1 reports kinetic parameters (Km, kcat) and dissociation constants (KD) for both enzymes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the design and synthesis of the first single-domain protein catenane, achieved by rewiring the connectivity of a single fold to generate artificial entanglement without exogenous motifs. 2. The strongest evidence includes the GLN increase from +0.726 to +1.120, 36% catalytic activity retention compared to zero activity for rethreaded variants, and 87% DMSO tolerance. 3. The future path involves directed evolution to fully restore activity and the expansion of this single-domain topological strategy to other protein families.

summary.title: Non-idealities in CO2 electroreduction mechanisms revealed by automation-assisted kinetic analysis
summary.authors: Joy S Zeng; Vineet Padia; Joseph H Maalouf; Aditya M Limaye; Alexander H Liu; Michael A Yusov; Ian W Hunter; Karthish Manthiram
summary.field_subfield: Electrochemistry / CO2 reduction reaction kinetics
summary.type_of_paper: Research article reporting a robotic platform and mechanistic study
summary.executive_summary: This work introduces a robotic platform designed to automate electrochemical kinetic analysis of CO2 reduction to CO at immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts. Unlike previous automation strategies tailored for high-throughput screening, this system enables sequential testing where each individual experiment can employ a different working electrode, electrolyte composition, gas-phase reactant, and applied voltage. The authors used the robot to collect large-scale rate data over wide operating ranges for cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc), and applied cohesive kinetic analysis (quantitative model fitting) rather than simple linearization (Tafel plots). They report non-idealities in reaction rate data: both bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences are non-linear and change with applied potential across all three catalysts. Specifically, CoPc and CoTPP exhibit an apparent bicarbonate order that becomes less negative (less inhibitory) at more reductive potentials, while FePc shows stronger bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. These behaviors are attributed to electrolyte poisoning via bicarbonate adsorption and potential-dependent mixed rate control. The study demonstrates that common linearization strategies fail to capture these complexities and that cohesive kinetic analysis coupled with automation provides a more robust strategy for mechanistic interrogation in electrocatalysis. The authors also report that their measured rates for CoPc were up to ten times lower than previously reported literature values, and that incomplete Faradaic efficiency (c.a. 60%) was observed, likely due to parasitic oxygen reduction at the counter electrode. The work sets a precedent for using automation-assisted kinetic analysis to reveal non-ideal reaction mechanisms that are prevalent but often missed by traditional electrocatalytic analysis methods.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work introduces a robotic platform designed to automate electrochemical kinetic analysis of CO2 reduction to CO at immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts. Unlike previous automation strategies tailored for high-throughput screening, this system enables sequential testing where each individual experiment can employ a different working electrode, electrolyte composition, gas-phase reactant, and applied voltage. The authors used the robot to collect large-scale rate data over wide operating ranges for cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc), and applied cohesive kinetic analysis (quantitative model fitting) rather than simple linearization (Tafel plots). They report non-idealities in reaction rate data: both bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences are non-linear and change with applied potential across all three catalysts. Specifically, CoPc and CoTPP exhibit an apparent bicarbonate order that becomes less negative (less inhibitory) at more reductive potentials, while FePc shows stronger bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. These behaviors are attributed to electrolyte poisoning via bicarbonate adsorption and potential-dependent mixed rate control. The study demonstrates that common linearization strategies fail to capture these complexities and that cohesive kinetic analysis coupled with automation provides a more robust strategy for mechanistic interrogation in electrocatalysis. The authors also report that their measured rates for CoPc were up to ten times lower than previously reported literature values, and that incomplete Faradaic efficiency (c.a. 60%) was observed, likely due to parasitic oxygen reduction at the counter electrode. The work sets a precedent for using automation-assisted kinetic analysis to reveal non-ideal reaction mechanisms that are prevalent but often missed by traditional electrocatalytic analysis methods.

Research Context
Electrocatalytic mechanistic analysis traditionally relies on linearization of simple rate equations, forming the basis for Tafel and reactant order analyses. This approach assumes dependences on voltage and concentration can be factored separately on log-log or semi-log graphs. However, linearization requires highly simplifying assumptions that fail to account for surface coverage effects, mixed rate control, and side reactions. Given the 59 mV/dec scaling of electrochemical equilibrium constants, surface coverages can drastically change within a few hundred millivolts. Cohesive kinetic analyses, more common in thermocatalysis, allow consideration of these complexities by fitting large data volumes to general rate equations. A meta-analysis of reported Tafel data showed that Tafel slopes do not show a strong preference for commonly interpretable values like 120, 60, or 40 mV/dec. This pointed to the prevalence of additional mechanistic phenomena not captured by traditional Tafel analysis. The heavy data requirement of cohesive kinetic analysis means manual collection can entail months of intensive experimentation. To date, most electrocatalytic automation strategies are tailored toward high-throughput catalyst or condition screening. Miniaturized scanning droplet cells use microliter electrolyte volumes and cannot be used for kinetic analysis without 100% Faradaic efficiency. Parallel arrays allow simultaneous testing but typically require aggregated effluent quantification or manual work-up. An automated kinetic analysis workflow would ideally involve sequential testing with online product quantification within well-defined reactors.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether non-linearizable reaction mechanisms are prevalent across common immobilized metal tetrapyrrole CO2RR catalysts. The authors hypothesize that complex phenomena such as electrolyte poisoning, mixed rate control, and surface coverage effects explain the observed kinetic behaviors. The specific research system targets cobalt phthalocyanine, cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin, and iron phthalocyanine. The hypothesis predicts that bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences will change with applied potential, revealing non-ideal kinetics. The authors expect that CoPc and CoTPP share a similar reaction mechanism. The FePc mechanism is predicted to involve a species later in the catalytic cycle as the most abundant reactive intermediate. The study aims to show that non-idealities are prevalent across this class of catalysts and that cohesive kinetic analysis reveals them. The automation concept is expected to accelerate and standardize the data collection workflow for kinetic analysis. A critical question is whether the newly measured kinetic trends preserve the previously reported ones while revealing new complexities.

Methodological Details
CoPc catalysts were dissolved in N,N-dimethylformamide and drop-casted onto calcined Toray060 carbon paper electrodes at loadings of 5.98 x 10^-11 mol/cm^2. CoTPP and FePc catalysts were dissolved in carbon black-containing DMF solutions and drop-casted at loadings of 5.11 x 10^-10 mol/cm^2 and 8.04 x 10^-10 mol/cm^2 respectively. Carbon black was used for less active catalysts to increase catalyst loading while avoiding aggregation. All catalysts were tested at low loadings where aggregation was not expected to be an issue. Electrolytes were prepared by mixing stock solutions of 0.5 mol/L Na2CO3 and 1 mol/L NaClO4. The stock solutions were bubbled overnight with CO2 and stored before mixing to achieve desired bicarbonate concentrations. Electrolyte solutions had an overall ionic strength of 1 mol/L. The robot automates sequential testing of up to ten electrochemical cells. Each cell in a queue can have a different electrode, electrolyte, gas-phase reactant composition, and applied voltage. The cell assembly is a three-electrode, undivided compartment cell. The working electrode is a carbon paper disk clamped between top and bottom cell pans, exposing a 10 mm diameter circle. A leak-free Ag/AgCl reference electrode was inserted on the side of the cell body. A 0.25 mm diameter platinum wire counter electrode was inserted on the opposite side. The Pt counter electrode was chosen over carbon-based to preclude adventitious anode oxidation products. The Ag/AgCl reference electrode was calibrated against a saturated calomel electrode daily and swapped every 1-3 days. The cell body moves horizontally to sequentially perform electrochemistry on each cell pan, and vertically to open and close. Electrolyte is pumped through the electrolyte in port, and CO2 is bubbled into the electrolyte. A gas chromatograph connected to the gas out port provides online detection of CO and H2. The robot cleans the cell body by moving onto a wash station and pumping milliQ water for several cycles. The data is processed via an SQL database; a Python script calculates average current, partial CO current, and partial H2 current as a function of operating condition to an Excel document.

Procedures And Architectures
The robot design consists of a single cell body housing the reference and counter electrodes, plus a line of ten cell pan pairs. Two electrolyte configurations: each cell pan can have an individual electrolyte in a local vial, or a common reservoir. In this work, the common reservoir configuration was employed so the electrolyte could be freshly bubbled with CO2. For each electrolysis, the robot closes the cell body, pumps electrolyte, initiates gas flow, waits a few minutes, applies voltage, and initiates online quantification. Electrolysis is performed in batches of ten, with all ten runs using the same electrolyte composition. Upon completion of each experiment, the robot uploads run information and associated data files to an SQL database. The cell body is rinsed after the completion of a full set of ten electrolyses using the common reservoir electrolyte. The cell washing sequence executes after the ten runs, followed by manual washing of the cell pans. Data analysis uses cohesive kinetic analysis: quantitative statistical model fitting over wide reaction conditions. Models include bicarbonate poisoning, mixed control between bicarbonate-dependent and bicarbonate-independent pathways, and on-cycle poisoning species. Models are fitted with statistical goodness-of-fit metrics to compare against experimental data. The current is below the theoretical mass transport limited current density. The cell uses the same electrode form factor as conventional electrochemical sandwich cell testing.

Key Results
For CoPc, the CO2 order dependence appears quite ideal: a simple first-order dependence is within error for both potentials shown. For CoTPP, the apparent CO2 order is slightly below one and decreases at more reductive potentials, characteristic of surface saturation effects. For FePc, the CO2 order dependence is most attenuated at less reductive potentials, and curves for two potentials intersect. At low CO2 partial pressures, voltage inhibits the reaction for FePc, but this does not occur at higher CO2 partial pressures. CoPc and CoTPP show an apparent bicarbonate order that is most negative at less reductive potentials and becomes positive at more reductive potentials. FePc shows greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. The measured partial CO rates for CoPc were up to ten times lower than previously reported in literature. Faradaic efficiencies toward CO were typically under 30% for CoPc. Across all runs, an average of only c.a. 60% was attributable to CO and H2 formation. The remaining Faradaic efficiency was presumably lost to oxygen reduction at the counter electrode. Faradaic efficiencies toward HER were typically around 30 to 60%. Previously reported kinetic trends in CO production were preserved despite the rate magnitude discrepancy. The newly collected data was well-correlated with that of the previous work. Hallmarks of non-ideal reaction mechanisms, such as curvature and potential-dependent changes in bicarbonate order, were clearly evident.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The bicarbonate poisoning mechanism involves adsorption of bicarbonate onto an unoccupied catalyst site, forming a bicarbonate-poisoned surface species. This poisoning has a positive electrosorption valency: less bicarbonate adsorption at more reductive potentials due to negative charge repulsion. The micro-intuition is that the negative charge on bicarbonate is more repelled as the electrode becomes more negatively charged during reductive polarization. For CoPc and CoTPP, the attenuation of bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials is explained by mixed control between bicarbonate-dependent and bicarbonate-independent pathways. The bicarbonate-dependent pathway attains a greater degree of rate control at more reductive potentials, leading to an apparent positive bicarbonate dependence. For FePc, the stronger inhibition at more reductive potentials is explained by the most abundant reactive intermediate (MARI) being a species prior to the unoccupied site. Alternatively, apparent bicarbonate inhibition can be explained by mixed control between two catalytic pathways where high coverage of a bicarbonate-dependent intermediate diverts flux. A bicarbonate-dependent surface intermediate can function as an on-cycle poisoning species. The mechanism for FePc likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the most abundant reactive intermediate. The results suggest that ostensibly opposing kinetic observations in the literature might be reconciled by differences in operating conditions, where limited-range measurements see only one part of a more complicated whole. The study highlights that kinetic phenomena like electrolyte poisoning, coverage effects, and mixed control are important considerations for CO2RR at metal tetrapyrroles. The work demonstrates how automation can assist with cohesive kinetic analysis and sets forth general mechanistic considerations for interpreting complex rate data.

Contradictions And Limitations
The cell is a single-compartment undivided cell, allowing crosstalk between anode and cathode, leading to parasitic oxygen reduction. Incomplete Faradaic efficiency (c.a. 60%) was observed across all runs, and the remaining FE was presumably lost to oxygen reduction. The measured rates for CoPc were up to ten times lower than previously reported literature values. Faradaic efficiencies toward CO were lower than expected, typically under 30% for CoPc. The robot washing procedure is only a rinse, not a full cleaning; the authors note this may not cause contamination issues but it is a potential limitation. Cell pans are washed manually, which is not fully automated and could introduce human variability. The mechanism models only qualitatively capture the observed trends and do not quantitatively fit all experimental data via statistical goodness-of-fit metrics. The current is below the theoretical mass transport limited current density, but the authors acknowledge flow configuration can have unexpected influence. The reference electrode calibration and swapping (every 1-3 days) are manual tasks within the automated workflow. The robot does not currently have a membrane to separate anode and cathode, which is identified as a future engineering extension.

Claims
The robotic system enables flexible and automated reaction rate data collection for electrocatalysis, accelerating and standardizing the workflow. The robot automatically performs sequential testing of up to ten cells with independent electrode, electrolyte, reactant, and voltage. The resulting workflow was more time- and labor-efficient than manual data collection. All data files were automatically uploaded to an SQL database with automated Python processing. Cell pan washing is manual, and reference electrode calibration/swapping are manual steps. The system is configured for sequential testing, not true parallel operation of ten independent cells. The approach can be extended to other electrocatalytic reactions beyond CO2RR. Software development could automatically enumerate mechanisms and suggest most informative experimental conditions.
Non-linear and voltage-dependent CO2 and bicarbonate order dependences are prevalent across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc catalysts. CoPc and CoTPP show bicarbonate order most negative at less reductive potentials and positive at more reductive potentials. FePc shows greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. CO2 order for CoTPP is slightly below one and decreases at more reductive potentials. FePc CO2 order is more attenuated at less reductive potentials and curves intersect. For CoPc, the CO2 order dependence appears quite ideal with first-order dependence within error. The models only qualitatively capture the trends and do not quantitatively fit all data. Traditional Tafel and order dependence analyses are insufficient for capturing these complexities. Mechanistic debates at these catalysts should include coverage effects, mixed control, and poisoning.
CoPc and CoTPP share a similar reaction mechanism, while FePc likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the MARI. CoPc and CoTPP bicarbonate trends are explained by the same poisoning and mixed control model. FePc bicarbonate trend requires the MARI to be a species prior to the unoccupied site. The mechanism for FePc was invoked separately from CoPc and CoTPP. No definitive mechanistic assignment was made; the discussion is conceptual and generalized. The mechanistic debates at these catalysts remain a topic of debate with multiple competing theories. The MARI at FePc is hypothesized to be a species before CO2 activation, unlike CoPc/CoTPP.

Data And Code Availability
All experimental data reported in this work are available in xlsx format. Supporting information including reagent information, detailed experimental protocols, supplemental data, and additional discussion are available in PDF. The work is posted on ChemRxiv with DOI 10.26434/chemrxiv-2023-h0zh1 and license CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. ORCID for corresponding author is provided as https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3443-3504.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors evaluated data robustness by comparing newly measured CoPc rates against previously reported literature values. The newly measured rates toward CO production were up to ten times lower than previously reported. CO Faradaic efficiencies were typically under 30%, lower than expected from literature. Despite rate magnitude discrepancies, previously reported kinetic trends in CO production were preserved. The newly collected data was well-correlated with that of the previous work. Hallmarks of non-ideal reaction mechanisms were clearly evident in the new data.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the overall robot design with the cell body and ten cell pan pairs. Figure 1B illustrates the cell body, cell pan, electrolyte and gas connections. Figure 1B also shows the gas chromatograph connected to the gas out port. Figure S2A shows the individual cell pan electrolyte configuration; Figure S2B shows the common reservoir configuration. Figure S3 shows the cell body wash station. Figure 2A-C show the apparent bicarbonate orders for CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. Figure 2D and 2E show generalized representations of the poisoning models for CoPc/CoTPP and FePc. Figure 2F and 2G show on-cycle poisoning models. Figure 3A-C show the CO2 order dependences for all three catalysts. Figure 3D and 3E show surface saturation and on-cycle poisoning models for CO2 dependence. Figure S5 shows the incomplete Faradaic efficiency data. Figure S7 and S8 compare newly measured CoPc rates against literature. Figure S9 provides aggregated rates for all three catalysts. Figure S10 shows selectivities towards CO and H2 for all three catalysts. Figure S10A specifically shows Faradaic efficiencies toward CO. Figure S7 shows preservation of kinetic trends. Figure S8 shows correlation between new and old data.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a robotic platform that automates sequential electrochemical kinetic analysis over a wide range of conditions, enabling cohesive kinetic modeling of complex reaction mechanisms. 2. The strongest evidence is the observation of voltage-dependent, non-linear bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc, interpreted by bicarbonate poisoning and mixed rate control models. 3. The future path includes incorporating a membrane for anode/cathode separation, alternative gas flow configurations, and software for automated mechanism enumeration.

summary.title: Visualization of π-hole in molecules by means of Kelvin probe force microscopy
summary.authors: B Mallada, M Ondráček, M Lamanec, A Gallardo, A Jiménez-Martín, B De La Torre, P Hobza, P Jelínek
summary.field_subfield: Physical Chemistry; Surface Science; Scanning Probe Microscopy
summary.type_of_paper: Original research article reporting direct experimental visualization of a π-hole system
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the first direct experimental visualization of a π-electron-deficient cavity (π-hole) on a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The π-hole was observed in 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) on an Au(111) surface, while its absence was confirmed in the parent anthracene (An) molecule. The authors employed a combination of scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM), noncontact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM) with a CO-functionalized tip, KPFM, and DFT-based simulations to unambiguously resolve the submolecular charge distribution. The supramolecular assembly of FCl-An and An on Au(111) was imaged, showing a rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules per unit cell, a configuration dictated by attractive intermolecular electrostatic interactions between fluorine atoms, σ-holes on chlorine, and positively charged hydrogen atoms. KPFM mapping at short tip-sample distances revealed a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the LCPD signal of FCl-An, corresponding to the calculated electrostatic potential of a free-standing molecule. Specific-site force-distance spectroscopy determined the adsorption heights of An and FCl-An at 330 pm and 360 pm, respectively, a 30 pm difference attributable to the π-hole increasing the ionization potential and suppressing charge density induction at the molecule-metal interface. SAPT0 energy decomposition confirmed that dispersion dominates adsorption, but induction energy is larger for An than FCl-An. The work demonstrates that KPFM with functionalized probes is a powerful tool for resolving internal charge distributions in molecules, expanding on previous results that resolved the σ-hole on individual atoms. This expands the understanding of π-hole systems and opens new avenues for studying submolecular charge distribution's role in chemical and physical properties of molecular systems.

claims.description: The KPFM method with a CO-functionalized tip can directly visualize a submolecular π-hole on a single molecule.
The π-hole in FCl-An increases its ionization potential and suppresses charge induction at the molecule-metal interface.

Executive Summary
This study reports the first direct experimental visualization of a π-electron-deficient cavity (π-hole) on a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The π-hole was observed in 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) on an Au(111) surface, while its absence was confirmed in the parent anthracene (An) molecule. The authors employed a combination of scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM), noncontact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM) with a CO-functionalized tip, KPFM, and DFT-based simulations to unambiguously resolve the submolecular charge distribution. The supramolecular assembly of FCl-An and An on Au(111) was imaged, showing a rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules per unit cell, a configuration dictated by attractive intermolecular electrostatic interactions between fluorine atoms, σ-holes on chlorine, and positively charged hydrogen atoms. KPFM mapping at short tip-sample distances revealed a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the LCPD signal of FCl-An, corresponding to the calculated electrostatic potential of a free-standing molecule. Specific-site force-distance spectroscopy determined the adsorption heights of An and FCl-An at 330 pm and 360 pm, respectively, a 30 pm difference attributable to the π-hole increasing the ionization potential and suppressing charge density induction at the molecule-metal interface. SAPT0 energy decomposition confirmed that dispersion dominates adsorption, but induction energy is larger for An than FCl-An. The work demonstrates that KPFM with functionalized probes is a powerful tool for resolving internal charge distributions in molecules, expanding on previous results that resolved the σ-hole on individual atoms. This expands the understanding of π-hole systems and opens new avenues for studying submolecular charge distribution's role in chemical and physical properties of molecular systems.

Research Context
Submolecular charge distribution is fundamental for predicting physical-chemical properties and non-covalent interactions of molecules. In polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, carbon's electronegativity compared to hydrogen accumulates electron density in delocalized π-bonds. Substituting hydrogen with more electronegative substituents like fluorine or chlorine reverses this population, making the π-bond system electron-deficient. The resulting π-electron-deficient cavity in the molecule's central part is called a π-hole. So far, the π-hole concept has been developed exclusively on a theoretical basis using quantum calculations. Experimentally, the existence of π-holes has only been proven indirectly from measured data that could only explain their presence. A direct experimental observation clearly proving the π-hole's existence has been lacking until this work. Scanning probe microscopy with functionalized probes has recently enabled unprecedented spatial resolution of chemical and spin structure, atomic charge, and σ-holes. The Kelvin probe force microscopy method, which enabled σ-hole resolution, is presented as the ideal tool for real-space observation of π-holes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the KPFM method can directly visualize the π-hole in a single molecule, confirming the theoretical prediction. The authors test this by comparing 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An), predicted to harbor a π-hole, with its unsubstituted parent anthracene (An). The hypothesis is that FCl-An will exhibit submolecular LCPD variation characteristic of a π-hole, while An will not. A second question is how the presence of a π-hole affects the adsorption energy and height of molecules on a metallic substrate. The authors predict the π-hole will increase the ionization potential, suppressing charge density induction and increasing the adsorption height. These effects were to be tested on an Au(111) surface, using both experimental KPFM/AFM measurements and DFT-based SAPT0 energy decomposition.

Methodological Details
The study employed Au(111) as the substrate, prepared by repeated cycles of Ar+ sputtering at 1 keV and annealing at 800 K. STM topography was acquired in constant current mode with bias voltage applied to the sample. For nc-AFM, a qPlus sensor with resonant frequency ≈ 30 kHz and stiffness ≈ 1800 N/m was operated in frequency modulation mode. The oscillation amplitude was set to 200 pm, and both nc-AFM and KPFM images were captured in constant height mode. Pt/Ir tips were sharpened by focused ion beam (FIB) and further cleaned by gentle indentation (~1 nm) in the bare substrate. FCl-An and An molecules were sublimated simultaneously with two Knudsen cells under UHV conditions at room temperature for 15 s. KPFM LCPD maps were obtained by fitting a parabolic expression to Δf(V, x, y) data at every point of a 64 x 80 pixels grid. The grid covered 3 nm x 5 nm, with each data point acquired in approximately 3 seconds and each parabola containing 600 points. The bias range for parabolic fitting was (-150, 400) mV, and the acquisition height was chosen in the attractive regime to maximize electrostatic contribution. The STM/nc-AFM/KPFM images were processed using WSxM software. DFT calculations used FHI-AIMS with the PBE functional and light default basis sets, with no k-grid for surface calculations. The Au(111) slab consisted of 4 atomic layers and the surface supercell was a 6x6 unit cell of the unreconstructed surface. For free-standing molecules, calculations used hybrid PBE0 with tight basis without substantial changes in geometry or charge distribution. Van der Waals correction was applied via Tkatchenko-Scheffler method with Hirshfeld partitioning, excluding direct Au-Au interaction. The supramolecular supercell was √39×√39 and deformed: 1.20% stretch, 1.06% compression, and angle reduced from 60° to 56.3° to match 2 optimal unit cells. During geometry optimization, free-standing molecules were constrained to planar while surface molecules allowed all but bottom Au atoms to relax. Geometries were considered fully optimized when all forces except constraints were under 2 meV/Å. For individual molecules, MP2/cc-pVTZ optimized geometries were used for molecular orbitals and electrostatic potential maps. SAPT0 cluster calculations used a 38-atom gold layer with (111) orientation, optimized at PBE0 level with Grimme's D3 dispersion and def2-TZVPP basis. All DFT calculations were carried out by ORCA, and SAPT0 was performed by PSI4 in cc-pVDZ basis.

Procedures And Architectures
The molecular assembly was grown by simultaneous sublimation of An and FCl-An on an atomically clean Au(111) surface at room temperature under UHV. STM images acquired at a base temperature of 4.8 K revealed ordered molecular islands of alternating species. nc-AFM with a CO-functionalized tip in constant height mode was used to resolve the chemical identity and arrangement of each molecule. DFT calculations of the supramolecular structure agreed perfectly with nc-AFM images, revealing a rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules per unit cell. The assembly arrangement was attributed to attractive electrostatic interactions between negatively charged F atoms, σ-holes on Cl, and positively charged H atoms. The mere deposition of An alone produced no self-organized structures, confirming the assembly was driven by intermolecular interactions. KPFM LCPD maps were generated by extracting the parabolic vertex (LCPD) and maximum frequency shift (Δf*) at each grid point. Simulated KPFM images were generated using the Probe Particle model adapted to a CO-terminated tip. The CO elastic deflection was modeled using the lateral spring constant of 0.25 N/m. DFT-calculated electron densities were used for Pauli repulsion, and electrostatic potential/polarizability maps were employed for KPFM simulation. The CO tip was modeled with a dz²-like charge quadrupole of -0.2 e/ Å². Specific-site force-distance spectroscopy was carried out above the central benzene unit of both molecules to compare adsorption heights. The difference between the minima of two Δf-z curves (30 pm) directly related to the difference in adsorption height. SAPT0 analysis was performed on a cluster model consisting of one molecule and a 38-atom Au layer. DFT and SAPT0 gave very similar adsorption energies, and SAPT0 provided the interaction energy decomposition into dispersion, electrostatic, and induction terms.

Key Results
KPFM images of FCl-An revealed a characteristic bow-tie pattern of submolecular LCPD variation in its central part, which was absent in An. This internal variation matched the calculated electrostatic potential distribution of a free-standing FCl-An molecule. The effect was attributed to the heterogeneous charge distribution of the π-hole due to different electronegativity of F and Cl modulating charge transfer from the π-system. The simulated KPFM images, calculated using the PP model, showed excellent agreement with experimental data. Force-distance spectroscopy revealed the adsorption heights of An and FCl-An on Au(111) to be 330 pm and 360 pm, respectively. This 30 pm difference in adsorption height directly confirmed the effect of the π-hole on the molecule-surface interaction. DFT slab calculations also predicted adsorption heights of 325 and 360 pm, showing the role of Cl atoms does not influence height. Induced electron density between the molecule and Au surface was found to be more significant for An than for FCl-An. The HOMO orbital of An was found close to the Fermi level, facilitating charge induction, whereas the π-hole in FCl-An increased the ionization potential and suppressed induction. SAPT0 energy decomposition showed attractive interaction dominated over dispersion energy in all cases. The induction energy was larger for An than for FCl-An, confirming that the π-hole weakens the electrostatic coupling to the surface. DFT and SAPT0 gave very similar results for adsorption energies, validating the cluster model approach. The presence of the π-hole was explicitly confirmed by comparing FCl-An, which exhibited the submolecular contrast, with An, which did not.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The π-hole, identified as a π-electron-deficient cavity, creates a positive electrostatic region that modifies all electrostatic interactions. The increased ionization potential of FCl-An due to the π-hole suppresses charge induction at the molecule-metal interface. This weakened electrostatic interaction leads to larger adsorption height and smaller induced charge, explaining the experimentally observed 30 pm difference. The work demonstrates that scanning probe microscopy with functionalized tips can resolve submolecular charge distributions within single molecules. This advances the study of non-covalent interactions from a theoretical concept to a direct experimental observation, opening new possibilities for probing molecular chemical properties via submolecular charge distribution. The combination of KPFM and DFT/SAPT0 provides a complete picture linking submolecular charge distribution, adsorption energetics, and spectroscopic signatures.

Contradictions And Limitations
High-resolution AFM images showed similar carbon skeleton contrast for both FCl-An and An, providing no direct evidence of a π-hole. FCl-An molecules were systematically imaged brighter than An due to a topographic effect, which could be mistaken for charge contrast without KPFM. AFM images alone could not distinguish the two species unambiguously without the complementary nc-AFM structural analysis. The KPFM contrast is highly dependent on tip-sample distance, with submolecular features disappearing at larger distances. At short tip-sample distances, tip relaxations can noticeably influence the KPFM signal, generating measurement artifacts. Tip relaxations cause noticeable deviation in the LCPD signal from its parabolic shape, unlike in nc-AFM where they improve resolution. The data was not shown for distances outside the parabolic regime, and tip-sample distance was chosen based on Δf minima rather than a systematically varied set. The KPFM simulations assume a specific dz²-like charge quadrupole for the CO tip, which might introduce model dependency. The SAPT0 calculations used a cluster model with a 38-atom Au layer, and while similar to slab calculations, the exact representation may differ from a macroscopic surface. The number of Au atoms in the cluster model was fixed at 38, which may limit transferability to other geometries. The paper does not report random seeds for DFT/SAPT0 or specific details of the WSxM image processing steps. The exact stoichiometry of the FCl-An/An ratio in the supramolecular assembly was not systematically quantified. The KPFM grid size of 3 nm x 5 nm may limit observation of features outside this area.

Claims
The KPFM method with a CO-functionalized tip can directly visualize a submolecular π-hole on a single molecule. FCl-An exhibited a characteristic bow-tie LCPD pattern, while An showed no such feature. Simulated KPFM images matched the experimental data very well. The LCPD signal matched the calculated electrostatic potential of a free-standing molecule. The 30 pm adsorption height difference confirmed the π-hole's electrostatic effect. DFT calculated electron densities showed reduced induction for FCl-An. AFM images showed similar carbon skeleton contrast for both species, providing no direct π-hole evidence. Tip relaxations at short distances can generate artifacts in the LCPD signal. KPFM contrast is highly distance-dependent, with no submolecular features at large distances. Scanning probe microscopy can be used to probe submolecular charge distributions in isolated molecules. The π-hole concept can now be tested against other molecular systems with different substituents. The method extends beyond σ-holes to π-hole systems, broadening the scope of SPM applications.
The π-hole in FCl-An increases its ionization potential and suppresses charge induction at the molecule-metal interface. DFT showed the HOMO of An close to the Fermi level, facilitating charge induction. SAPT0 induction energy was larger for An than for FCl-An, consistent with suppressed induction. The 360 pm adsorption height for FCl-An (vs 330 pm for An) confirmed the reduced binding. DFT slab calculations predicted 325 and 360 pm for An and FCl-An. The SAPT0 cluster model gave only very similar results, not identical, to the DFT slab model. Cl atoms were found not to influence the adsorption height, meaning only the π-hole contributes. Submolecular charge distribution dictates the molecule-surface interaction energetics. The electrostatic contribution can be systematically engineered by modulating π-hole systems.

Data And Code Availability
The paper does not explicitly state data or code availability; the WSxM software was used for image processing, and FHI-AIMS, ORCA, and PSI4 were used for theoretical calculations.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The presence of the π-hole was tested by comparison with the parent anthracene molecule, which lacked the π-hole and showed no submolecular LCPD contrast. The electrostatic effect was further checked by comparing KPFM images with calculated electrostatic potential maps of the free-standing molecule. The simulation used the Probe Particle model adapted to a CO-terminated tip, with the elastic deflection modeled at 0.25 N/m. The parabolic fit showed no significant distortion or deviation from expected behavior across the (-150, 400) mV bias range for both molecules and tip. DFT and SAPT0 gave very similar results of adsorption energies on Au(111), validating the cluster model approach. Submolecular resolution was absent in Δf* images (compensated LCPD) for both molecules, supporting the choice of acquisition height. The effect was cross-validated using DFT-calculated electron densities in the induced charge density maps.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the electrostatic quadrupole moment of PAH molecules and its reversal with electronegative substituents, illustrating the π-hole concept. Figure 2a and 2b display STM and nc-AFM images of the FCl-An/An molecular assembly on Au(111) at 4.8 K, showing the rhombic periodic structure. Figure 2c and 2d show the unit cell arrangement with one An and two FCl-An molecules, and a diagram of the electrostatic interactions. Figure 3a shows the calculated electrostatic potential of free-standing FCl-An, and 3b shows the calculated induced electron density between molecule and Au(111). Figure 3c shows the simulated KPFM image for FCl-An, and 3d shows the experimental KPFM map revealing the bow-tie pattern. Figure 3f shows the simulated KPFM image for An, showing no submolecular features. Figure 3a, d shows the LCPD map with the bow-tie pattern in the central part of FCl-An. Figure 4a shows Δf-z spectroscopy curves above the central benzene unit of both molecules, revealing a 30 pm difference in minima. Figure 4b and 4c display calculated induced electron densities at the molecule-metal interface for An and FCl-An. Figure 6 displays constant height AFM images showing submolecular contrast emerging on FCl-An molecules. Table S2 reports adsorption energies from DFT and SAPT0, and the dispersion energy decomposition. Table S3 presents the SAPT0 energy decomposition for all three molecules, including dispersion, electrostatic, and induction terms. Figure S1 displays selected occupied orbitals of An and FCl-An, revealing different shapes and charge localization. Figure S4 shows the KPFM contrast dependence on tip-sample distance, with the parabolic fit parameters. Figure S5 shows the absence of submolecular resolution in Δf* images at Δf minima.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole on a single molecule using KPFM, confirming the theoretical prediction through the bow-tie pattern in FCl-An and its absence in An. 2. The strongest evidence is the 30 pm difference in adsorption height between An (330 pm) and FCl-An (360 pm), combined with KPFM submolecular contrast, DFT-calculated electrostatic potentials, and SAPT0 energy decomposition. 3. The future path lies in expanding the KPFM-based approach to other π-hole and σ-hole systems, and using submolecular charge distribution to predict and design non-covalent interactions in chemical and biological processes.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy using a multitask QRNN machine learning force field trained on combined density functional theory (DFT) data from both periodic and non-periodic systems. The Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in Li-ion batteries is a complex, redox-reactive material formed by the reaction of organic electrolytes with lithium anodes, and no single simulation method can fully capture its formation over the required time and length scales. Standard DFT methods are too slow, and hybrid functionals with improved barrier heights fail to scale for periodic systems. The authors use a QRNN architecture with multitask learning, training on four output heads: GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and a SPICE-specific wB97X-D3BJ head, alongside a dedicated SPICE general organic chemistry dataset for latent space broadening. Active learning using AFIR and NEB reaction sampling was employed to sample relevant reactive geometries. Each initial SEI candidate system consisted of 700 EC molecules, 52 Li+ ions, and 52 PF6- ions (7416 total atoms) in a 1M LiPF6/EC solution, with four added Li+ ion levels (5, 12, 23, 33). Candidates were annealed via NPT MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each, and ranked by mean potential energy from a 20 ps MD trajectory at 300 K and 1 atm. Validation was conducted against the best available surface reaction energy barrier calculations, showing the model captures stabilizing P-F and Li-O bonds versus destabilizing C-O and Li-F bonds. The authors note that while the ranking provides a first-of-its-kind quantitative comparison, experimental validation of SEI density, diffusivity, or mechanical properties is currently unavailable. Future work is proposed to extend the methodology to multiple electrolyte formulations, other MLFF architectures (Nequip, MACE), and partial-charge-enabled models (CHGNet). The work serves as a proof-of-concept that multitask MLFFs can model the most complex redox-reactive systems simulated thus far, laying a foundation for quantitative SEI design and optimization.

Research Context
During battery discharge, the anode must be unstable with respect to the cathode but stable with respect to the electrolyte, necessitating a passivating SEI layer. Key questions about whether SEIs are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them remain unanswered, limiting next-generation battery development. No existing simulation method is fully applicable to the SEI due to its complex chemical structure spanning conductors, insulators, and redox reactions across large length and time scales. Standard pure density functionals work well for metallic systems but badly underestimate reaction barriers, making them unsuitable for accurate SEI description. Hybrid functionals like wB97X yield improved barrier heights but struggle with metals and have very poor computational scaling for periodic systems. MLFFs promise atomistic simulation with DFT accuracy and classical force field sampling speed, but traditional fixed-functional forms are difficult to fit for complex systems like the SEI. Prior QRNN models used GFN2-xTB or DFT dipole labels for electronegativity networks, which the authors tested against GFN0-, GFN1-, and GFN2-xTB reference charges.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a multitask QRNN MLFF trained on combined periodic and non-periodic DFT data, augmented with a general organic chemistry dataset, produce the first quantitatively ranked set of SEI candidate structures? The central hypothesis was that multitask learning with QRNN could capture the complex redox reactions characteristic of the SEI by leveraging data from disparate chemical systems simultaneously. It was predicted that the SEI would form as a mixture of organic and inorganic components, and that specific bond types would correlate with structural stability. The authors predicted that P-F and Li-O bonds would be associated with more stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds would be less stable. The SPICE general organic chemistry dataset was hypothesized to shape the model's latent space without imposing heavy cost on the primary SEI prediction capacity. The model was expected to produce stable dynamics under extreme annealing conditions (400 K, 1000 atm), surpassing traditional MLFF performance.

Methodological Details
The reference theory for non-periodic systems was selected as wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, while PBE-D3 in a plane wave basis served as the periodic reference. A random subset of non-periodic systems was also labeled with PBE-D3 to improve information exchange between output heads in the multitask scheme. The SPICE dataset added to the training included the element subset H, Li, C, O, F, and P, with GFN1-xTB atomic partial charge labels. Each initial SEI system contained 700 EC molecules, 52 Li+ ions, and 52 PF6- ions in a 1M LiPF6/EC solution, totaling 7416 atoms per box. Four candidate sets were defined with 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box, levels derived from 40 MD iterations with reaction templates. The lithium slab was initialized as a BCC lattice with lattice constant optimized by the model, placed next to equilibrated EC at 2 Å separation. Lithium oxide, lithium carbonate, lithium fluoride, and lithium hydroxide were added to the training set in both periodic and cluster geometries. Crystal geometries were augmented with non-equilibrium structures generated by adding Gaussian noise to Cartesian coordinates. Amorphous sampling was pursued using Schrodinger Disordered System Builder with a Van der Waals radius factor of 0.5 to produce steric clashes that overcame reaction barriers. No DFT-generated MD, AFIR, or NEB geometries were used as training inputs, only single-point DFT on geometries generated by non-DFT means. Periodic DFT was performed with Quantum Espresso in Schrodinger Materials Science Suite 2022-3 using GGA PBE with D3 dispersion and 40 Ry cutoff. The Brillouin zone was integrated with a 3x3x3 k-point mesh for bulk supercells and a 3x3x1 k-point mesh for surface supercells. Gas-phase wB97X-D3BJ DFT used Psi4 v1.6 with SCF type MEM_DF, basis tolerance 1e-10, ints tolerance 1e-10, maxiter 200, robust pruning, partialcholesky orthogonalization, and 1e-6 cholesky tolerance. NEB used lithium surfaces with 54 atoms (6 layers of 9 atoms each) topped with a single EC molecule, focusing on known EC decomposition reactions. Non-periodic clusters were extracted from reactive data by choosing a radius around each central atom from a uniform distribution of 3.0 to 5.2 Å. All cut bonds in clusters were capped with hydrogen atoms, with a 1.2 Å buffer for hydrogen-containing atoms. Validation was performed against surface reaction energy barriers, with the SEI simulator generating candidates via OPLS4 MD with reaction templates. Energy and gradient RMSEs were reported in kcal/mol and kcal/mol/Å for energies and gradients, respectively.

Procedures And Architectures
The model architecture was a QRNN with multitask output heads for GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and a SPICE-specific wB97X-D3BJ head. The loss function comprised energy and atomic force mean squared error for each theory level, plus charge mean squared error. Charges were not separated into distinct output heads, all levels used consistent charge labels from GFN1-xTB. The first and last output heads (GFN1-xTB and SPICE-wB97X) were used only to shape the latent space during training, not for SEI prediction. The Adamax optimizer with decoupled weight decay was used; the final model used a learning rate of 2e-3. One percent of data, selected uniformly at random, served as the validation set, as the model lacked sufficient capacity to overfit. Hidden layer sizes were 256, 224, and 192 for all elements, with a batch size of 64. A high weight decay of 3e-3 per batch was found helpful for geometry optimization but reduced reaction barrier heights, so the final model used 1e-3. The final model was an exponential moving average of training parameters, averaging every 10 batches with alpha = 0.001. Candidate generation used a SEI Simulator method with OPLS4 MD, starting with 700 EC molecules and 52 ions of Li+ and PF6- per box. Reaction templates involved adding electrons, balanced by inserting Li+ ions to replicate Li+ reduction to Li0. Initial geometries were annealed using reactive QRNN MD under NPT conditions at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each. Ranking was performed by calculating the mean potential energy over a 20 ps MD trajectory at 300 K and 1 atm. Bonding analysis was performed by recalculating the Lewis structure for the entire system using Schrödinger Materials Science Suite. Each system was run with a unique random seed for packing and MD, ensuring sampling of diverse configurations. The SPICE data addition resulted in no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE but an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. The width of the hidden layers was doubled when adding more disparate data to maintain model capacity.

Key Results
The multitask QRNN produced stable dynamics under NPT conditions at 400 K and 1000 atm, unlike traditional MLFFs that typically fail under such extreme conditions. The QRNN model was validated against the best available surface reaction energy barrier calculations, enabling the first plausible ranking of SEI candidate structures. The model correctly identified P-F and Li-O bonds as associated with more stable SEI structures, confirmed by bond count vs. total system energy analysis. C-O and Li-F bonds were identified as associated with less stable structures in the SEI candidate set. The validation analysis showed that the SPICE data addition caused no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE but led to an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. The Fig. 4 plot of bond counts versus total system energy (zero = most stable) showed the strongest correlation for P-F and Li-O bonds. The model identified the lowest-energy SEI candidate structure out of the most lithiated subgroup (33 added Li atoms) predicted by the wB97X-D3BJ output head as the best candidate. The QRNN model successfully sampled and relaxed geometries that spanned the relevant reactive chemical space of EC decomposition on lithium surfaces. The active learning approach used AFIR and NEB on the QRNN potential energy surface to identify and sample reaction-relevant configurations. The latent space of the multitask MLFF was shown to contain unused capacity capable of broadening chemical applicability via SPICE data inclusion. The model achieved stability during annealing at 400 K and 1000 atm, which is often not the case for MLFFs, demonstrating robustness of the QRNN architecture for extreme conditions. The SPICE data inclusion demonstrated that a supplemental general organic chemistry dataset can shape MLFF latent space without compromising primary prediction performance.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The QRNN's multitask structure, training on both periodic and non-periodic DFT data, allows the model to simultaneously capture metallic surface reactions and cluster-based organic chemical space. The latent space broadening demonstrated by SPICE data suggests that MLFFs can generalize across disparate chemical domains, opening the door to universal MLFFs for battery materials. The identification of P-F and Li-O as stabilizing bonds, versus C-O and Li-F as destabilizing, provides a chemical rationale for SEI stability that can guide experimental design. The QRNN's ability to maintain stability under extreme annealing conditions suggests the architecture and training scheme robustly capture the physics of reactive surfaces. The model demonstrates that multitask MLFFs can simulate the most complex redox-reactive system to date, combining metal-organic surfaces with liquid electrolyte dynamics. The work establishes a precedent for generating quantitatively comparable SEI structure rankings from a single electrolyte formulation, enabling future optimization via multiple formulation comparison. The authors suggest that the full power of the technique will materialize when comparing multiple electrolyte formulations, allowing calculation of Li+ diffusivity and mechanical properties. The results imply that the MLFF approach can serve as a screening tool, pre-selecting promising SEI candidate structures before expensive experimental validation.

Contradictions And Limitations
The most significant limitation is the lack of experimental validation; no experiments exist for any SEI composition, precluding comparison of density, diffusivity, viscosity, or elastic modulus. The model was validated against surface reaction energy barriers, not the actual thermodynamic stability of the fully equilibrated SEI, which may differ. The SEI candidates were generated using only a single electrolyte formulation (1M LiPF6 in EC), and the authors acknowledge that the full power comes from comparing multiple formulations. The reaction sampling focused on known EC decomposition reactions on lithium surfaces and did not sample reactions on lithium oxide or lithium carbonate. The model scope is still small compared to what is required for full SEI characterization, and the authors do not regard it as a final model. The high weight decay used during initial geometry optimization (3e-3) reduced reaction barrier heights, necessitating a drop to 1e-3 for the final model at the cost of convergence. The model was validated against the best available calculations, which themselves may have systematic errors not quantified in the paper. The probability of being proven wrong by future experiments is high, as the model operates in an environment where theoretical and experimental references are limited.

Claims
Multitask training with a QRNN MLFF, combined with enhanced reaction sampling, enables the first quantitative ranking of SEI candidate structures. The QRNN model produced stable dynamics under NPT at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps, which is often not the case for MLFFs. Validation against the best available surface reaction energy barriers confirmed the model captured stabilizing and destabilizing bond types. The SPICE data addition caused no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE, showing the multitask approach is capacity-efficient. Active learning with AFIR and NEB successfully sampled relevant reactive geometries for SEI formation. There is no direct experimental validation; density, diffusivity, and mechanical property measurements for SEI do not exist. The model was validated against reaction barriers, not directly on the thermodynamics of the fully relaxed SEI. The SPICE data did increase hybrid-head RMSE by 8%, indicating some cost for expanding the latent space. Future work can extend this to multiple electrolyte formulations and calculate Li+ diffusivity and mechanical properties. The methodology can be applied to other SEI chemistries and different MLFF architectures like Nequip and MACE.
P-F and Li-O bonds stabilize SEI structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds destabilize them. Figure 4 showed bond counts versus total system energy with P-F and Li-O associated with lower energy structures. The bonding analysis recalculation confirmed the correlation between bond type and structural stability. The bonding analysis was performed on a single lithiated subgroup (33 added Li+) rather than across all candidate levels. The correlations were identified from the model output (wB97X-D3BJ head), not independently validated. These bond-level insights can guide experimental SEI design, focusing on structural motifs that promote stability.

Data And Code Availability
The list of SEI candidate structures (seed*.pdb), energies (energies.csv), the original 1M LiPF6 in EC solution (initial_EC_1M_LiPF6.pdb), and plotting scripts (*.py) are available at figshare.com/s/e842ae88023902700e12.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Adding the SPICE general organic chemistry dataset (H, Li, C, O, F, P) caused no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE but an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. The hidden layer width was doubled to maintain model capacity when adding the SPICE dataset. A high weight decay of 3e-3 per batch was found helpful for convergence but reduced reaction barrier heights; the final model used 1e-3. The authors recommended testing models trained on subsets of the dataset to determine which parts are most critical to accuracy and stability.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the initial SEI geometry, starting with 700 EC molecules and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6- in a 1 M solution. Table 1 presents the surface reaction energy barrier validation against the best available DFT calculations. Figure 4 displays bond counts with respect to total system energy (zero = most stable) for the most lithiated SEI candidate set (33 added Li+) using the wB97X-D3BJ model output.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first quantitatively comparable ranking of SEI candidate structures using a multitask QRNN MLFF trained on combined periodic and non-periodic DFT data, demonstrating that MLFFs can capture complex redox reactions on metal-organic surfaces. 2. The strongest evidence is the model's stability under NPT conditions at 400 K and 1000 atm, coupled with validation of stabilizing (P-F, Li-O) and destabilizing (C-O, Li-F) bond motifs against reaction barrier calculations. 3. The future path involves extending to multiple electrolyte formulations, other architectures (Nequip, MACE, CHGNet), and computing Li+ diffusivity and mechanical properties, ultimately enabling detailed optimization of SEI chemistry.

summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the biological activity of crude leaf extract from Ajuga iva, containing phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes, against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis. Phytoecdysteroids, plant-produced steroids that mimic insect molting hormones, affect a wide range of insects at very low concentrations while remaining non-toxic to mammals due to structural differences. The authors tested three concentrations (50, 100, and 250 µg/µl) of A. iva crude leaf extract on first and third instar S. littoralis larvae reared on castor bean leaves. First instar larvae showed significant dose-dependent mortality of 25%, 65%, and 85% at the three concentrations, compared to 5% in the water-treated control. Third instar larvae fed on the 250 µg/µl treatment exhibited significantly reduced larval weight gain (LWG: F3.104 = 20.334, 17.246, 13.007; p < 0.001) and decreased relative growth rate (RGR), with the highest concentration causing a reduction of 0.05 g/g day on day 6 and 0.20 g/g day on day 8 compared to controls (p < 0.001). Histological analysis of the larval gut revealed smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei, reduced actin fibers, and massive deterioration of the gut epithelium consistent with apoptosis. Larvae failed to reach the threshold weight for pupation and died without completing development. The authors conclude that A. iva extracts represent a promising green pesticide alternative for managing S. littoralis, reducing risks to human health and the environment.
