judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the biological activity of crude leaf extract from Ajuga iva, containing phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes, against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis. Phytoecdysteroids, plant-produced steroids that mimic insect molting hormones, affect a wide range of insects at very low concentrations while remaining non-toxic to mammals due to structural differences. The authors tested three concentrations (50, 100, and 250 µg/µl) of A. iva crude leaf extract on first and third instar S. littoralis larvae reared on castor bean leaves. First instar larvae showed significant dose-dependent mortality of 25%, 65%, and 85% at the three concentrations, compared to 5% in the water-treated control. Third instar larvae fed on the 250 µg/µl treatment exhibited significantly reduced larval weight gain (LWG: F3.104 = 20.334, 17.246, 13.007; p < 0.001) and decreased relative growth rate (RGR), with the highest concentration causing a reduction of 0.05 g/g day on day 6 and 0.20 g/g day on day 8 compared to controls (p < 0.001). All third instars exposed to any concentration died after 11 days of feeding, with none surviving beyond 8 days at the highest dose. Reciprocal feeding experiments confirmed that the extract affected RGR regardless of whether it was fed before or after control leaves. The purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (ecdysterone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) at 250 µg/µl produced similar effects to the crude extract, while commercial standards at 100 ppm each showed no significant activity, confirming the high concentration requirement. Histological analysis of the larval gut revealed smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei, reduced actin fibers, and massive deterioration of the gut epithelium consistent with apoptosis. Larvae failed to reach the threshold weight for pupation and died without completing development. The authors conclude that A. iva extracts represent a promising green pesticide alternative for managing S. littoralis, reducing risks to human health and the environment.

Research Context
Spodoptera littoralis is a major pest affecting cotton, maize, rice, alfalfa, potato, tomato, ornamentals, and orchard trees. Insect control currently relies primarily on insecticides, which pose risks to human health and the environment. Phytoecdysteroids, with a cholest-7-en-6-one carbon skeleton (C27), are plant-produced steroids analogous to arthropod molting hormones. They are present in 5-6% of plant species and synthesized through the mevalonic acid pathway. Phytoecdysteroids mimic insect 20-hydroxyecdysteroid, binding ecdysone receptors and eliciting the same developmental responses. Ecdysteroids are not toxic to mammals because their structure differs significantly from mammalian steroids. Previous studies showed Ajuga remota extracts inhibited ecdysis in Bombyx mori and Ajuga reptans killed greenhouse whiteflies. A 5 μg/ml dose of pure Ajuga iva ecdysterone significantly reduced fecundity, fertility, and survival of Oligonychus perseae, outperforming commercial ecdysterone. The authors previously identified and quantified high contents of three phytoecdysteroids and two clerodanes in A. iva growing in Israel.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central hypothesis was that crude A. iva leaf extract, including 20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone, might be a promising pest-control agent. The authors hypothesized that these phytoecdysteroids, which interfere by controlling molting and are responsible for metamorphosis and antifeedant activities, would reduce damage caused by S. littoralis larvae. The first research question addressed whether A. iva crude leaf extract affects S. littoralis larvae. The second question asked whether phytoecdysteroids isolated from the crude leaf extract and commercial standards have different effects on the larvae. The third question investigated whether phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut. The authors predicted a dose-dependent reduction in larval growth, survival, and development throughout all larval stages. The study was designed to compare crude extract, purified phytoecdysteroid mixture, and commercial standards across different larval instars and feeding sequences.

Methodological Details
First and third instar S. littoralis larvae were obtained from Murad Ghanim's laboratory at the Agricultural Research Organization and reared on castor bean leaves. Young and mature leaves and stems of fresh plants were collected after blooming (July-November), oven-dried at 55 °C for 3-4 days, and homogenized to a fine powder. For crude extract preparation, 24 g of pooled leaf and stem powder were soaked in 240 ml of 100% MeOH, homogenized at 2500 rpm for 1 h, centrifuged at 112 g for 10 min, filtered, concentrated under vacuum, and dried in a chemical vaporizer for 5 days. Phytoecdysteroids were purified from 100 g of leaf and stem powder in 300 ml methanol, treated with H2O to give 30% aqueous methanol, and extracted as previously described. LC-TOF-MS analysis used an Agilent 1290 Infinity Series liquid chromatograph coupled with an Agilent 1290 Infinity DAD and Agilent 6224 Accurate Mass TOF mass spectrometer. TLC used silica gel GF-254 plates with 0.25 mm thickness and 20 × 20 cm dimensions for component separation. For first instar bioassays, 10 larvae per treated leaf in 11 replicates were allowed to feed for 3 days in a climate-controlled room at 25 °C on mature castor bean leaves smeared with aqueous extract (1:10 dilution) and Tween 20 (1.5 mg). Control leaves were smeared with double-distilled water and Tween 20. Extract concentrations of 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl were prepared by dissolving 1.2 g dried extract in 4.8 ml ddH2O and Tween 20 (0.5 mg/ml) for the 250 µg/µl, and subsequent serial dilution. For third instar bioassays, 1 or 10 larvae were fed on 1 treated castor bean leaf for 4 or 8 days at 25 °C, with four different treatment permutations. In an additional third instar experiment, n = 20 replicates were exposed to three concentrations (50, 100, 250 µg/µl) for 4 days, with pupation monitored for an additional 15 days. Gut morphology was examined using DAPI and phalloidin staining, with guts fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min, washed in 0.1% Triton X-100, and incubated in 0.1% phalloidin and 0.1% DAPI. Confocal microscopy used a Leica SP8 and Olympus IX 81 confocal laser scanning microscope. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS software v.20 for Windows. Data were analyzed using t-test for first instar, mixed-model ANOVA (repeated measures) for RGR, Friedman test for survival, and repeated measures ANOVA for LWG, with significance reported at p < 0.05.

Procedures And Architectures
Larvae were fed on mature castor bean leaves smeared with aqueous crude extract or ddH2O + Tween 20 and dried in a chemical hood for 2 h prior to exposure. First instar experiment used 3 days of feeding; third instar experiments used 4 or 8 days, with additional fresh leaves provided after 4 days. The four third-instar treatment conditions compared: (1) 250 µg/µl crude extract for 4 days + 4 days fresh, (2) 250 µg/µl crude extract + 250 µg/µl phytoecdysteroid mixture for 4 days, (3) 4 days crude extract + 4 days ddH2O control, and (4) 4 days ddH2O control + 4 days crude extract. RGR was calculated as (ln W2 - ln W1) / (t2 - t1), where W are weights at times t1 and t2. Pupation rate was evaluated for an additional 15 days after the 8-day feeding period. For the gut histology, larvae were tested after 7 days of treatment, and guts were dissected in phosphate buffered saline (1X PBS). Guts were incubated in 0.1% phalloidin in PBST for 30 min, washed three times with PBST, and mounted in 0.1% DAPI in hybridization buffer. The hybridization buffer contained 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 0.9 M NaCl, 0.01% w/v sodium dodecyl sulfate, and 30% v/v formamide. Actin fibers and nuclei were visualized under the Leica SP8 and Olympus IX 81 confocal laser scanning microscope. Commercial standards ecdysterone, makisterone A, and cyasterone at a maximum concentration of 100 ppm each were used for a separate control treatment.

Key Results
Flash chromatography of A. iva crude leaf extract yielded three individual isolated compounds (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) with Rf values similar to commercial standards. First instar S. littoralis larvae showed significant dose-dependent mortality of 25%, 65%, and 85% at the three concentrations (50, 100, 250 µg/µl), respectively, compared to 5% in the control. Third instar larvae fed on the three concentrations showed significantly reduced LWG (F3.104 = 20.334, 17.246, and 13.007, respectively; p < 0.001) compared to control. All concentrations of crude leaf extract significantly decreased (p < 0.001) larval RGR, with the effect appearing as early as 2 days. At the highest concentration, RGR decreased by 0.05 g/g day on day 6 and 0.20 g/g day on day 8 compared to control (F3.16,18 = 12.641, p < 0.001). All concentrations significantly reduced third instar larval survival after 11 days (X2-3 = 6.221, p = 0.038), with none of the treated larvae surviving more than 8 days at 250 µg/µl and 10 days at other concentrations. In reciprocal feeding experiments, RGR was affected by crude extract feeding after day 5 (F3.16,18 = 7.310, p < 0.001), with no surviving larvae (X2-3 = 9.282, p = 0.021). When the treatment order was reversed, significant RGR decrease was obtained on days 2-4 (F3.16,18 = 4.595, 3.608, and 8.113; p = 0.034, 0.02, 0.001). 250 µg/µl of the purified phytoecdysteroid mixture significantly reduced RGR (F2.20,18 = 6.172, p = 0.001) and few larvae survived (X2-3 = 11.305, p = 0.04). Larvae fed on 250 µg/µl crude extract or phytoecdysteroid mixture lost weight, stopped growing, and ultimately died. Larvae fed on 100 ppm mixture of commercial standards for 8 days showed no significant effect on S. littoralis. Guts of larvae treated with 250 µg/µl crude extract or the phytoecdysteroid fraction showed smaller nuclei that were abnormally shaped, moved to the edges of the cell, and were thinner than normal. In contrast to control guts with normal actin-filament organization, treated guts showed smaller actin filaments and reduced amount. Larvae exposed to crude extract or phytoecdysteroid fraction had less actin fibers and smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei throughout the gut. Larvae fed 250 µg/µl of crude extract or phytoecdysteroid fraction for 8 days were unable to complete development and pupate after 15 days. Incomplete pupae had short limbs, small heads, decreased weight, and only stomach and chest pupated, considered nonpupation; none completed development to adult moths.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The effects were pronounced throughout all larval developmental stages, including pupation, as predicted by previous work. Phytoecdysteroids from A. iva have been found to reduce fertility and fecundity of Bemisia tabaci and Oligonychus perseae, consistent with the current S. littoralis findings. The dose-dependent effect of A. iva crude leaf extract is in agreement with other studies showing phytoecdysteroids act in a concentration-dependent manner. S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg, indicating that the current treatment levels are above the known threshold for deterrence. Larvae did not reach the threshold weight for pupation and died because they could not complete their life cycle, suggesting the effect on pupation is a consequence of reduced growth. Gut cell histolysis with clear signs of apoptosis, massive deterioration of the gut epithelium, destruction of microvilli, and formation of vacuoles were observed in treated larvae. The effect on pupation could be a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance affecting internal levels of ecdysone. Disruptions in S. littoralis gut morphology and disappearance of actin microfilament structures could be a consequence of the phytoecdysteroid titers in the A. iva crude leaf extract. Phytoecdysteroids may affect insects by interfering with their developmental stages, especially during metamorphosis. Abnormal gut development can lead to reduced LWG, which in turn causes mortality. The results support the notion that phytoecdysteroids may be useful for managing economically important insect pests while reducing risks to human health and the environment.

Contradictions And Limitations
No fractionation of clerodanes from A. iva crude leaf extract was performed due to difficulty calibrating the protocol and high cost of commercial standards. Only a few commercial standards were used because they were expensive and not feasible as control treatment at the treatment concentrations. The commercial standard mixture was at 100 ppm each (total 300 ppm), much lower than the 250,000 ppm of the crude extract treatments, limiting direct comparability. S. littoralis was not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg in previous studies, contrasting with the current study's dose-dependent deterrence. Larvae were fed on castor bean leaves; the effect might differ on other host plants. The study used larvae from a single colony at one laboratory, potentially limiting generalizability across different pest populations. The paper was a preprint (bioRxiv) and not yet subjected to formal peer review at the time of posting. The authors state they could not use commercial standards at the same concentrations as the applied treatment, introducing a concentration gap.

Claims
Ajuga iva crude leaf extract and its phytoecdysteroid fraction are effective biopesticides against Spodoptera littoralis, causing dose-dependent mortality and developmental arrest. First instar larvae showed mortality of 25%, 65%, and 85% at the three concentrations compared to 5% in control. Third instar RGR decreased by 0.05 g/g day on day 6 and 0.20 g/g day on day 8 at 250 µg/µl. None of the treated larvae survived more than 8 days at 250 µg/µl. The purified phytoecdysteroid mixture at 250 µg/µl produced similar mortality and growth effects. Commercial standards at 100 ppm each showed no significant effect, indicating the crude extract's activity is concentration-dependent. S. littoralis was previously not deterred from feeding by 20-hydroxyecdysone at 50-70 mg/kg. Phytoecdysteroids could be incorporated into IPM programs as green insect control agents. The dose-dependent response suggests optimization of application concentration is possible for field use. The multi-modal effect (growth, survival, gut damage) supports a dual mechanism of action.
The phytoecdysteroid fraction (ecdysterone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) alone is sufficient to induce mortality and developmental arrest in S. littoralis. The fraction at 250 µg/µl reduced RGR significantly (F2.20,18 = 6.172, p = 0.001). Few larvae survived on the fraction-treated leaves (X2-3 = 11.305, p = 0.04). Histological damage was identical between crude extract and fraction treatments. The fraction was not tested at all three concentrations, only at 250 µg/µl. The fraction test was a single experiment (n = 20) compared to multiple experiments for the crude extract. Targeting specific phytoecdysteroids rather than crude extract might reduce off-target effects. The purified fraction could serve as a lead compound for more focused pesticide development.
A. iva extracts cause irreversible gut histolysis and apoptosis through destruction of the epithelium and microvilli, contributing to reduced growth and death. Gut cells showed histolysis with clear signs of apoptosis, massive deterioration of epithelium, and destruction of microvilli. Actin fibers were smaller and reduced in amount in treated guts. Larvae were unable to complete development and pupate after 15 days. Incomplete pupae showed short limbs, small heads, and decreased weight. The histological damage continued until the insects died, so the causal sequence of gut damage vs. hormonal disruption is not fully established. No time-course histology was performed to see if gut damage preceded or followed growth reduction. Gut tissue damage may be a primary mechanism of action rather than just a consequence of hormonal imbalance. The histolytic effect provides a pathological basis for the observed mortality that complements the endocrinological explanation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Reciprocal feeding experiments (feeding on extract then control, and vice versa) confirmed the dose-dependent effect is persistent regardless of exposure order. A purified fraction (ecdysterone, makisterone A, cyasterone) was compared against the crude extract at the same concentration (250 µg/µl), yielding similar growth and survival effects. A commercial standard mixture at 100 ppm each (300 ppm total) showed no effect, contrasting with the crude extract and fraction at 250,000 ppm, demonstrating a high concentration threshold. Sensitivity was assessed in both first and third instar larvae, with dose-dependent responses confirmed in both life stages. Larval weight gain and RGR were assessed in n = 20 replicates for the third instar experiment, providing adequate statistical power. Pupation was monitored for an additional 15 days post-treatment, providing comprehensive developmental assessment. Statistical significance was reported at p < 0.05 across all experiments, using multiple comparison methods.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: TLC comparison of phytoecdysteroid spots from A. iva crude leaf extract with commercial ecdysteroids. Figure 2a: First instar S. littoralis mortality percentages at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl of crude extract versus water control. Figure 2b: Third instar larval weight gain across three treatment concentrations, showing significant reduction at all doses. Figure 3a: Time-course RGR decrease from day 2 through day 8 at the highest concentration (0.20 g/g day reduction on day 8). Figure 3b: Third instar survival rates after 11 days, with no survivors at 250 µg/µl beyond day 8 and none at other doses beyond day 10. Figure 4a: RGR decrease in larvae fed on crude extract then control, showing effect onset after day 5. Figure 4b: No surviving larvae in the reversed feeding sequence experiment. Figure 4c: RGR decrease on days 2-4 when larvae were fed on control then crude extract. Figure 5a: RGR reduction and weight loss for 250 µg/µl crude extract versus phytoecdysteroid mixture, with larvae depicted showing growth arrest and death. Figure 5b: Few larvae survived on the fraction-treated leaves, confirming the sufficiency of the purified phytoecdysteroids. Figure 6: Confocal microscopy of larval guts showing smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and reduced actin filaments in treated vs. control. Figure 7: Incomplete pupae following 250 µg/µl crude extract or fraction treatment for 8 days, showing developmental arrest.

Three Takeaways
1. Core: A. iva crude leaf extract and its purified phytoecdysteroid fraction induce dose-dependent mortality, reduced growth (LWG, RGR), and gut histolysis in S. littoralis, with no larvae surviving beyond 8-10 days at 250 µg/µl. 2. Strongest evidence: First instar mortality of 85% at 250 µg/µl and 100% mortality of third instars within 8 days, combined with histological confirmation of gut cell apoptosis (histolysis, thinner nuclei, reduced actin). 3. Future path: The study identifies A. iva as a potential IPM agent; next steps should include testing on diverse host plants, fractionating clerodanes, and developing field-applicable application protocols.

The study addressed: (1) Does *A. iva* crude leaf extract affect *S. littoralis* larvae? (2) Do phytoecdysteroids isolated from the crude leaf extract and commercial standards have different effects? (3) Do phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut? The authors predicted that the extract and purified phytoecdysteroid mixture would reduce damage caused by *S. littoralis* larvae, impair development, and reduce survival in a dose-dependent manner.

    *   **Methodological Details (~500 words):**
        Larvae: First and third instars from Murad Ghanim's laboratory, reared on castor bean leaves.
        Extract prep: 24 g leaf and stem powder, 240 ml 100% MeOH, homogenized at 2500 rpm for 1 h, centrifuged at 112 g for 10 min, filtered, concentrated under vacuum, dried in chemical vaporizer for 5 days.
        Phytoecdysteroid purification: 100 g powder in 300 ml MeOH, vacuum-concentrated, H2O treated to 30% aqueous methanol, extracted as previously described.
        Identification: LC-TOF-MS (Agilent 1290 Infinity Series), TLC (silica gel GF-254, 0.25 mm; 20 × 20 cm).
        Bioassay: Mature castor bean leaves smeared with aqueous crude extract (1:10 dilution) and Tween 20 (1.5 mg). Dried in chemical hood for 2 h.
        First instar: 10 larvae per treated leaf, 11 replicates, 3 days feeding, 25 °C, ddH2O + Tween 20 control.
        Third instar: 1 or 10 larvae per leaf, 4 or 8 days feeding, 25 °C. Treatments: (1) 250 µg/µl crude extract 4 days + 4 days fresh, (2) same + 250 µg/µl phytoecdysteroid mixture, (3) crude extract 4 days + control 4 days, (4) control 4 days + crude extract 4 days.
        Additional third instar experiment: Three concentrations (50, 100, 250 µg/µl) for 4 days, n = 20 replicates. Pupation monitored for additional 15 days.
        Gut: 7 days treatment, DAPI and phalloidin staining, 4% paraformaldehyde fixation, 0.1% Triton X-100 washing, 0.1% phalloidin, 0.1% DAPI, confocal microscopy.
        Statistics: IBM SPSS v.20. t-test for first instar, mixed-model ANOVA (repeated measures) for RGR, Friedman test for survival, repeated measures ANOVA for LWG, p < 0.05.

    *   **Procedures & Architectures (~400 words):**
        LC-TOF-MS configuration: Agilent 1290 Infinity Series liquid chromatograph coupled with Agilent 1290 Infinity DAD and Agilent 6224 Accurate Mass TOF mass spectrometer.
        Extracting phytoecdysteroids: 30% aqueous methanol solution extracted.
        TLC plates: silica gel GF-254, 0.25 mm thickness, 20 × 20 cm dimensions.
        Concentrations: 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl.
        Dose preparation: 1.2 g dried extract powder in 4.8 ml ddH2O and Tween 20 (0.5 mg/ml) for 250 µg/µl; 0.83 ml of 250 µg/µl diluted in 3 ml ddH2O to 100 µg/µl; 0.67 ml of 100 µg/µl diluted in 3 ml ddH2O to 50 µg/µl.
        Staining: DAPI (0.1%) in hybridization buffer, phalloidin (0.1%) in PBST.
        Microscopy: Leica SP8 and Olympus IX 81 confocal laser scanning microscope.
        Stat tests: t-test, mixed-model ANOVA, Friedman test, repeated measures ANOVA.
        Software: IBM SPSS software v.20.

    *   **Key Results (~500 words):**
        1. TLC: Three individual compounds isolated (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, cyasterone). Rf values similar to commercial standards (Fig. 1).
        2. First instar mortality: 25%, 65%, 85% at 50, 100, 250 µg/µl; control 5% (Fig. 2a).
        3. Third instar LWG: F3.104 = 20.334 (50 µg/µl), 17.246 (100 µg/µl), 13.007 (250 µg/µl); p < 0.001 (Fig. 2b).
        4. RGR: Significantly reduced at all concentrations (Fig. 3a). At 250 µg/µl: -0.05 g/g day on day 6, -0.20 g/g day on day 8; F3.16,18 = 12.641, p < 0.001.
        5. Survival: All concentrations significantly reduced third instar survival after 11 days (X2-3 = 6.221, p = 0.038, Fig. 3b). None survived more than 8 days at 250 µg/µl, 10 days at others.
        6. Reciprocal feeding: RGR affected by extract feeding after day 5 (F3.16,18 = 7.310, p < 0.001, Fig. 4a). No surviving larvae (X2-3 = 9.282, p = 0.021, Fig. 4b).
        7. Reversed order: Significant decrease in RGR days 2-4 (F3.16,18 = 4.595, 3.608, 8.113; p = 0.034, 0.02, 0.001; Fig. 4c).
        8. Phytoecdysteroid mixture: 250 µg/µl reduced RGR (F2.20,18 = 6.172, p = 0.001) (Fig. 5a). Few larvae survived (X2-3 = 11.305, p = 0.04, Fig. 5b).
        9. Commercial standards: 100 ppm mixture (ecdysterone, makisterone A, cyasterone) for 8 days showed no significant effect.
        10. Gut: Smaller nuclei, abnormal shape (moved to cell edges, thinner), reduced actin fibers and amount (Fig. 6d-i).
        11. Pupation: Larvae unable to complete development/pupate after 15 days. Incomplete pupae had short limbs, small heads, decreased weight, only stomach and chest pupated.

    *   **Interpretation & Theoretical Implications (~200 words):**
        Phytoecdysteroids interfere by controlling molting, responsible for metamorphosis and antifeedant activities. S. littoralis is very sensitive to A. iva crude leaf extract and the three fractionated phytoecdysteroids. The reduced growth rate (LWG, RGR) suggests another mode of action besides molting interference. The larval gut cells showed histolysis with clear signs of apoptosis; gut epithelium showed massive deterioration, destruction of microvilli, and formation of vacuoles. Reduced LWG led to larvae not reaching the threshold weight for pupation, causing death. The effect on pupation could be a consequence of disruptions in hormonal balance affecting internal ecdysone levels. Actin microfilament disappearance (Fig. 6) could be a consequence of phytoecdysteroid titers.

summary.title: Sorry, we're open: Golden Open Access and inequality in the natural sciences
summary.authors: Russell J Gray
summary.field_subfield: Science policy, academic publishing, natural sciences, inequalities in science
summary.type_of_paper: Original research with statistical analysis and discussion
summary.executive_summary:
This study by Russell J. Gray investigates the structural inequality inherent in Golden Open Access (GOA) publishing within the natural sciences. The author analyzes metadata from 237 open-access natural science journals, examining the relationships between Article Processing Charges (APC), Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), citability, and the country of publisher. Using data from the Directory of Open Access Journals (n = 14,275 initially, with a biological sciences subset of 1,047, and a final deeply vetted dataset of 237 journals) and R statistical analysis, the study finds that APC is significantly positively correlated with IF (r = 0.391, p < 0.001), EF (r = 0.303, p < 0.001), and citability (r = 0.323, p < 0.001). Furthermore, publishers from developed countries exhibit higher APCs, IFs, EFs, and citability compared to those from developing countries.

The discussion extends beyond quantitative findings to qualitative implications: the author argues that high APCs in prestigious journals do not inherently guarantee research reliability (Brembs, 2018) and that the IF system creates false perceptions of credibility (Brembs, 2013). The study highlights a structural inequality where higher-ranking institutions have greater access to high-impact journals, while researchers from developing countries or independent individuals are marginalized. The author shares a personal anecdote about a paper on the Sumatran elephant where Research4Life financial assistance was denied due to US-based co-authorship, illustrating how funding eligibility criteria create exclusionary barriers for important research. The study concludes by calling for systemic reform in academic publishing to create a more inclusive and equitable global scientific environment, arguing that prestige and cost should not be equated with reliable science.

claims.description: APC is positively correlated with IF, EF, and citability in natural science journals.
Publishers from developed countries hold disproportionate share of high-impact, high-APC natural science journals.

Executive Summary
This study by Russell J. Gray investigates the structural inequality inherent in Golden Open Access (GOA) publishing within the natural sciences. The author analyzes metadata from 237 open-access natural science journals, examining the relationships between Article Processing Charges (APC), Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), citability, and the country of publisher. Using data from the Directory of Open Access Journals (n = 14,275 initially, with a biological sciences subset of 1,047, and a final deeply vetted dataset of 237 journals) and R statistical analysis, the study finds that APC is significantly positively correlated with IF (r = 0.391, p < 0.001), EF (r = 0.303, p < 0.001), and citability (r = 0.323, p < 0.001). Furthermore, publishers from developed countries exhibit higher APCs, IFs, EFs, and citability compared to those from developing countries.

The discussion extends beyond quantitative findings to qualitative implications: the author argues that high APCs in prestigious journals do not inherently guarantee research reliability (Brembs, 2018) and that the IF system creates false perceptions of credibility (Brembs, 2013). The study highlights a structural inequality where higher-ranking institutions have greater access to high-impact journals, while researchers from developing countries or independent individuals are marginalized. The author shares a personal anecdote about a paper on the Sumatran elephant where Research4Life financial assistance was denied due to US-based co-authorship, illustrating how funding eligibility criteria create exclusionary barriers for important research. The study concludes by calling for systemic reform in academic publishing to create a more inclusive and equitable global scientific environment, arguing that prestige and cost should not be equated with reliable science.

Research Context
The rise of Sci-Hub and ResearchGate has increased journal accessibility and nullified the previous paywall system. Many high-impact journals have transitioned to mandatory open access, known as Golden Open Access. The cost associated with publishing in open-access journals creates a problematic system of perceived reliability. Researchers from institutions in developing countries still pay full price for western nation high-impact Mega-Journals. The publication process can be incredibly stressful and time-consuming for researchers. High-impact journals generate exposure through increased citations and a reputation of credibility. Prices of high-impact GOA journals become problematic for researchers without available funding. The previous paywall system's ability to create capital for journals has been nullified.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study analyzes metadata to determine links between publication costs, impact factor, eigen factor, and citability for natural science journals. The analysis then discusses implications of inequality among the global scientific community in the open-access framework. The implicit hypothesis is that IF, EF, and citability all increase as APC increases. Another hypothesis is that each metric is higher in publishers from developed countries in comparison to developing countries. The study examines potential trends between country of publisher and APC, IF, EF, and citability. The question probes whether publishers from developed countries are more likely to have higher APC and impact metrics. The study addresses how these trends implicate inequality within the global scientific community.

Methodological Details
Data was acquired from the Directory of Open Access Journals. The initial dataset contained journal name, APC, country of publisher, and currency records for 14,275 journals. R statistical software was used for all data analyses. The scholar package was used to generate impact factors using journal name strings. The quantmod package converted all currencies to USD for standardization. The dplyr and reshape2 packages were used to clean and select specific data. The ggplot2 package was used for data visualizations. A subset of 1,047 journals was queried using keyword data for biological sciences. Keywords included ecology, conservation, agriculture, species, and forest. Journals with an IF greater than 40 were excluded to reduce disparities between natural and medical sciences. Excluded journals were checked to ensure none were related to natural sciences; they related to oncology, medical, and engineering. The final analyses were performed on a deeply vetted dataset of 237 open-access natural science journals. APC was examined in relation to citability, IF, and Eigen Factor. The country of each journal publisher was examined against cost, citability, IF, and EF. The ggpubr package was used to perform correlation analysis. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to analyze potential correlations between APC, IF, EF, and citability.

Procedures And Architectures
Currency standardization involved converting all APC values to USD using the quantmod package. Impact factors were generated from journal name strings using the scholar package. The biological science subset was created by keyword filtering of the original DOAJ dataset. Excluded journals with IF >40 were verified via keyword check to remove non-natural science topics. The data cleaning pipeline used dplyr and reshape2 for selecting specific data and cleaning. Data visualizations were generated using the ggplot2 package. APC correlations were tested against IF, EF, and citability using Pearson's correlation coefficient. Country of publisher was examined to determine trends between country and APC, IF, EF, and citability. The analysis was a single-author descriptive and correlational study using R. Pearson correlations were reported with sample size n=237 and p-values.

A linear trend was found between IF, EF, and citability in relation to APC. Mean APC of the open-access journals analyzed was $1,344.27 USD. Mean Impact Factor (IF) was 2.855. Mean Eigen Factor (EF) was 0.017. Mean total citation count (citability) was 5,925.92. APC was significantly positively correlated with IF (Pearson correlation: r(237) = 0.391, p < 0.001). There was a highly significant positive correlation between APC and EF (Pearson correlation: r(237) = 0.303, p < 0.001). There was a highly significant positive correlation between APC and citability (Pearson correlation: r(237) = 0.323, p < 0.001). Publishers from developed countries were more likely to have higher APC, IF, EF, and citability. Figure 1 visualizes the trends between these metrics across publisher countries.

With increasing publishing costs, impact, importance, and overall citations increase in open-access natural science journals. The majority of journal publishers with the highest APC, IF, EF, and citability are from developed countries. Research published in journals from developing countries is less likely to gain exposure. Journals from developing countries are less likely to generate profit and credibility. Expensive APC in prestigious journals are not linked to reliability of research (Brembs, 2018). The impact factor of prestigious journals creates a false perception of reliability in published research (Brembs, 2013). The GOA system is inherently flawed: more manuscripts published mean more capital generated. This gives rise to predatory journals and editorial complacency. GOA journals may create an environment where publisher profit is prioritized over scientific integrity. Higher-ranking institutions have more access to expensive, high-impact journals. Lower-ranking institutions are forced to publish in less expensive or closed-access journals. Authors from developing countries pay the prices of developed countries for high-impact journals. Individual researchers with no institutional affiliation face even narrower options. Independent researchers with no institutional affiliation have been on the rise over the past decade. Biodiversity hotspots are in the tropics, so most conservation research is conducted there. Tropical nations meet Research4Life criteria, but the majority of research includes authors from developed countries. Foreign authors from developed countries nullify Research4Life eligibility, forcing authors to seek other journal types. The author concludes that journal publications, research impact, and citations are the academic currency of career scientists.

The sample of 237 journals is relatively small for generalizing across all of natural sciences. The analysis is restricted to natural sciences, excluding medical and engineering journals. No information is provided about data quality control or validation beyond keyword vetting. The exclusion criterion of IF >40 is arbitrary and may exclude relevant natural science journals. No information is given about specific currency conversion rates used by the quantmod package. The study is a single-author analysis, which may limit diversity of interpretation. The reduction from 1,047 biological science journals to 237 natural science journals is not detailed.

1. The core contribution is establishing quantitative correlations between APC, IF, EF, and citability in GOA natural science journals, showing that higher publishing costs track with higher impact metrics, while publisher country status creates structural inequality. 2. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study develops a multiplex PCR-based assay comprising 343 primer pairs (two pools of 172 pairs each) that provides full-genome coverage of SARS-CoV-2, overcoming the sensitivity limitations of standard RT-PCR which detects only 4-8 viral copies at 95% confidence. The multiplex strategy targets hundreds of regions simultaneously, allowing detection of SARS-CoV-2 at low copy numbers, including below 1.1 copies (mathematically predicted) and experimentally verified down to 0.6 copies with 37% amplicon recovery. Using two plasmids spiked into human total RNA cDNA, the authors demonstrated electrophoretic visualization of clean characteristic target peaks from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies, with a 56% detection probability at 1.1 copies (exceeding the predicted 12% based on conservative efficiency estimates). For clinical validation, 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens with viral loads from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL were sequenced on Illumina MiSeq, achieving 95-99% genome coverage at 100X depth. Mutations were detected by two independent algorithms with a 60% frequency threshold for true positives, revealing seven key mutation loci and identifying the D614G mutation in 11 of 13 specimens. Furthermore, the authors developed a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method using random hexamer-adapters and background removal, which recovered 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome from 4,500 copies spiked into 10 ng human gDNA with only ~0.6M total reads per library, without host depletion. The method achieved 0% cross-reactivity with other human coronaviruses (MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, OC43, NL63, HKU1), validating high specificity. The work establishes a highly sensitive diagnostic platform capable of both specific SARS-CoV-2 detection and metagenomic surveillance of novel or emerging pathogens.

Research Context
While RT-PCR is the gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis due to ease of use and high sensitivity, its clinical utility is limited by low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or mutations in primer binding sites. Standard RT-PCR methods have been reported to detect only 4-8 copies of virus at 95% confidence intervals, yet only 47-59% of true positive cases are identified, and 75% of negative results are later found positive. Heat inactivation of clinical samples causes loss of viral particles, further hindering diagnostic efficiency, and the urgent need for robust surveillance is underlined by the wide and rapid spreading of SARS-CoV-2. Prior methods such as RT-PCR, serological testing, and RT-LAMP have been used, but they cannot distinguish SARS-CoV-2 from other respiratory pathogens like influenza, parainfluenza, adenovirus, RSV, rhinovirus, and bacterial pneumonia causes. Obtaining full-length viral genome sequence through NGS is essential for surveillance of evolution and community spread containment, and phylogenetic studies have guided policy-making. Multiplex PCR has been shown as an efficient, low-cost method to detect Hantaan orthohantavirus and Plasmodium falciparum with 99% median coverage and 99.8% specificity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a multiplex PCR approach, by simultaneously targeting and amplifying hundreds of viral targets, achieve higher sensitivity than standard RT-PCR and detect degraded viral fragments or mutations? The authors hypothesized that a panel of 172 multiplex PCR primers with 99bp average amplicon length spanning the entire 29,903bp genome could detect SARS-CoV-2 at low copy numbers. A secondary pool of 171 primers overlapping gaps from the first pool was designed to provide full genome coverage and further lower the detection limit. The mathematical model predicted that 172 amplicons at 6% amplification efficiency could detect 1.15 copies at 95% probability, and the two combined pools would reach 0.29 copies. A parallel hypothesis proposed that a random-hexamer-based multiplex PCR method could enable metagenomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 and novel pathogens with modest sequencing depth. The metagenomic approach was predicted to identify SARS-CoV-2 at ~1 million reads depth without additional host depletion.

Methodological Details
Two plasmids containing the full sequence of the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2 were used for initial validation. A total of 28 targets are expected to be amplified within the 172-amplicon panel. The plasmids were spiked into cDNA generated from human total RNA to simulate real clinical samples. Copy numbers were precisely determined by droplet-based digital PCR (ddPCR) using a QX200 system from Bio-Rad. The two plasmids were diluted from approximately 9,000 copies down to below one copy. 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens previously diagnosed positive by RT-PCR were used for clinical validation. Viral loads ranged from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL, measured by quantification. The multiplex PCR products were first analyzed by electrophoresis to visualize positive peaks. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina MiSeq platform. For metagenomic validation, 4,500 copies of N and S gene-containing plasmids were spiked into 10 ng of human gDNA. Mutations were detected by two independently developed algorithms, and mutations with frequency >60% were considered true. For intra-host mutation analysis, mutations with 20% to 60% frequency were retained, with a 20% cutoff based on synthetic controls from Twist Bioscience.

Procedures And Architectures
The multiplex PCR panel consisted of 172 primer pairs (average amplicon length 99bp) with 76±10bp average gaps between adjacent amplicons. A second pool of 171 primer pairs was designed whose target regions overlapped with gaps from the first pool. The workflow included a secondary PCR step to add sample indexes and NGS sequencing primers, followed by electrophoresis analysis of raw PCR products. A mathematical model used 100bp amplicon length and 30kb genome size, assuming 99% RT-PCR efficiency. Multiplex PCR amplification efficiency was estimated at 6% for single-strand cDNA, based on the observed 26% efficiency for four DNA strands of human chromosomes. The metagenomic method used random hexamer-adapters for multiplex PCR and a background removal reagent for non-specific product removal. For RNA samples, Paragon Genomics' reverse transcription reagents were used to convert RNA to cDNA, reducing human ribosomal RNA. Two independent algorithms were used for mutation detection; only mutations confirmed by both were reported. Sub-sampling experiments reduced data to 150,000 and 100,000 total reads per library for coverage verification.

Key Results
With 28 amplicons from one plasmid, the theoretical prediction gave a 16% chance to detect one copy of the virus. The mathematical model predicted a 66% probability to sample 1.1 copies, and a 12% chance to detect them at 6% efficiency. Experimentally, the authors observed a 56% probability to detect 1.1 copies with one copy of plasmid in multiplex PCR, exceeding the predicted 12%. Library peaks were obtained from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies, with quantification showing a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies. The yield of libraries started to saturate when the copy number reached 1,700. In contrast, a single target amplified by RT-PCR rapidly dropped at 2.85 copies, while the multiplex retained signal. Approximately 96% of amplicons were recovered with 14 copies, 77% with 2.8 copies, and 37% with 0.6 copies. About 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus, and 98-99% at 100X for 22 to 675,885 copies at 5,000 reads per amplicon. At 150,000 total reads (437 reads/amplicon), at least 93% of the genome was covered at 100X. At 100,000 total reads (291 reads/amplicon), 86% of the genome was covered at 100X. Even at 50,000 total reads per library, at least 58% of the genome was covered at 100X. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of the 13 specimens. In the metagenomic assay, 16% of recovered bases and 13% of recovered reads were within the viral N and S genes. 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were covered in the metagenomic assay, while only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified. After optimization, 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered in the metagenomic assay. Zero percent of sequencing reads from each of the 13 samples aligned to the genome sequence of MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, OC43, NL63, or HKU1.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Simultaneously targeting multiple regions increases the frequency of detection events in the mathematical model and enables detection of degraded nucleotide fragments. The experimental 56% detection probability at 1.1 copies suggests that the true multiplex PCR efficiency for single-stranded cDNA is substantially higher than the 6% assumed in the initial model. The 47-56% detection rate of SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR can be explained partly by the predicted 26% detection probability per single amplicon in the mathematical model. The seven mutation loci and D614G prevalence suggest these specimens were collected in close communities or represent transmission chains. Low %AF intra-host mutations in low copy/low depth samples are likely artifacts of PCR amplification noise rather than true intra-host heterogeneity. The 10-fold depth variation across amplicons is a routine characteristic of the multiplex technology and cannot be overcome by simply increasing sequencing depth. The random hexamer strategy favors regions with 'random' base composition, preferentially amplifying exonic regions and mitochondrial DNA over repetitive human genomic sequences.

Contradictions And Limitations
One genome from the sample with 5,000 estimated viral copies had 96% coverage at 100X instead of the expected 98-99%, attributed to poor sample quality from processing. The authors caution that without UMI labeling, intra-host mutations (≥20% AF) could still be contaminated with PCR amplification noise, especially at low viral inputs. The 56% detection probability at 1.1 copies exceeds the predicted 12% from the 6% efficiency model, indicating the model was over-conservative regarding single-strand amplification. The saturation point of 1,700 copies for library yield may be even lower in clinical samples, limiting the upper dynamic range of the assay. Metagenomic detection still requires verification and validation for other coronaviruses and respiratory viruses before practical application.

Claims
The multiplex PCR assay achieves superior sensitivity to RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 detection, capable of amplifying multiple targets simultaneously to tolerate mutations and detect degraded genomes. The experimental detection of 56% probability at 1.1 copies exceeds the predicted 12%, demonstrating sensitivity below the RT-PCR limit. Electrophoretic visualization of clean peaks was maintained down to 2.8 copies, whereas RT-PCR signal vanished at 2.85 copies. The two-pool design provides full genome coverage with 96% recovery at 0.6 copies in the validation experiments. One clinical sample with 5,000 copies showed unexpectedly lower (96%) coverage, suggesting potential variability in real-world performance. The assay could replace RT-PCR for diagnostics where viral load is low or primer-binding site mutations are suspected. High-resolution electrophoresis is necessary to differentiate target amplicons from primer dimers, limiting the assay to equipped laboratories.
The random-hexamer-based multiplex PCR metagenomic method can recover >96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome from human gDNA at modest sequencing depth (~0.6M reads) without host depletion. After optimization, 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered in the metagenomic experiment. 13% of recovered reads mapped to N and S genes, while only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified. The 96% coverage exceeds the 50% threshold recommended for genome drafting. The 10-fold coverage difference across amplicons is a persistent limitation that sequencing depth alone cannot remedy. The method has not been independently validated for other coronaviruses or respiratory viruses. The method could enable low-cost metagenomic surveillance of novel pathogens with standard sequencing infrastructure.
The SARS-CoV-2 panel demonstrates zero cross-reactivity with other human coronaviruses (MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, OC43, NL63, HKU1), establishing high diagnostic specificity. Zero percent of sequencing reads from all 13 samples aligned to any of the five other human coronavirus genomes. The D614G mutation and seven key loci were identified consistently across specimens, confirming target specificity. The authors note that some primer dimers are produced in negative samples, requiring electrophoresis for definitive negative identification. The panel could be expanded to include simultaneous detection of influenza and other respiratory viruses.

Data And Code Availability
The paper does not explicitly state whether the sequencing data or specific bioinformatic pipelines are publicly available. The mathematical models were described in the text with key parameter values provided.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sensitivity was tested by subsampling data to 150,000 and 100,000 total reads per library to verify coverage at reduced depth. The metagenomic method was optimized iteratively, with final 96% recovery achieved after refinement of the random-hexamer strategy. The 10-fold coverage difference was noted as a routine feature of the multiplex technology, validated with Supplemental Figure 4.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents the mathematical models of RT-PCR (A), the multiplex PCR panel design (B), the estimated detection limits (C), and the workflow including secondary PCR and electrophoresis (D). Figure 2 shows library peaks from 8,900 to 2.8 plasmid copies (A), quantification with 1-1,000 copies range (B), experimental detection at 1.1 copies (C), and read distribution (D) and amplicon recovery percentages (E). Figure 3 displays genome coverage versus viral copy number (A), sub-sampling coverage results (B), amplicon uniformity (C), log10 distance from mean (D), and the mutation landscape across 13 specimens (E). Figure 4 illustrates the metagenomic method results: N and S gene coverage (A), viral versus mitochondrial versus human coverage (B, C), human exonic region preference (D), coverage gaps in chromosomes (E), SARS-CoV-2 gap distribution (F), and final 96% recovery after optimization (G). Supplemental Figure 1 shows the predicted RT-PCR detection probability per copy (26%). Supplemental Figure 2 and Supplemental Table 1 provide UMI-labeled primer amplification efficiency estimates. Supplemental Figure 3 shows RT-PCR signal drop at 2.85 copies. Supplemental Table 2 lists viral loads for all 13 specimens. Supplemental Table 3 details mutation frequencies for the 13 genomes. Supplemental Table 4 shows base and read counts in the metagenomic assay. Supplemental Table 5 lists coverage metrics for amplicons in the metagenomic assay.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a multiplex PCR method that combines hundreds of specific primers to achieve full-genome coverage of SARS-CoV-2, enabling detection at low copy numbers (down to 0.6 copies with 37% recovery) and providing both diagnostic specificity and metagenomic surveillance capabilities. 2. The strongest evidence is the experimental detection of 56% probability at 1.1 viral copies, which substantially exceeds the model-predicted 12% (at 6% efficiency), demonstrating that the multiplex strategy's true operational sensitivity outperforms conservative theoretical estimates. 3. The future path involves validating the metagenomic multiplex method for detection of other coronaviruses and respiratory viruses, expanding the panel to include influenza, and standardizing the workflow for routine diagnostic and surveillance use in variable laboratory settings.

summary.title: Translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome
summary.authors: Celine Fabret (CNRS); Olivier Namy (CNRS)
summary.field_subfield: Molecular biology / Structural biology - Ribosome translation fidelity
summary.executive_summary:
This study investigates the translational properties of Ribo-T, a tethered ribosome in Escherichia coli whose two ribosomal subunits are covalently linked via short RNA linkers to form a single entity. Ribo-T was previously engineered and demonstrated the ability to sustain cell growth, although with slower doubling times (107 min for Ribo-T vs. 35 min for wild-type) and a protein synthesis rate that was 50% that of wild-type ribosomes. The authors characterize Ribo-T's translational accuracy at three key checkpoints using the bacterial pCL99 dual reporter system (lacZ-luc fusion) in an Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) background. Using three -1 frameshifting sites (IS911, IS3, dnaX) and one +1 frameshifting site (prfB), stop codon readthrough reporters at UAG, UGA, and UAA codons, and the lacZ-lacY intergenic region for translation initiation, the authors quantify the impact of subunit tethering on translation fidelity.

Key findings: 1) Ribo-T ribosomes perform -1 programmed frameshifting at efficiencies comparable to wild-type (13-45% across all three sites, p ≥ 0.54), while +1 frameshifting is severely impaired (2% for Ribo-T vs. 33% for WT; 1.8% with Ribo-T SD vs. 0.6% with WT, p ≤ 1.6×10⁻⁵), confirming that Ribo-T cannot use SD sequences as stimulatory elements for +1 frameshifting. 2) Ribo-T ribosomes initiate translation from SD sequences inefficiently, with a 4-fold reduction in luciferase activity compared to WT (p = 4.7×10⁻⁴), though they can use orthogonal SD sequences. 3) Ribo-T ribosomes exhibit a slight but measurable impairment in stop codon recognition, with readthrough rates 2-5 times higher than wild-type at all three stop codons (UAG: 0.07% vs. 0.013%; UGA: 0.26% vs. 0.11%; UAA: 0.04% vs. 0.01%), with p-values ranging from 2.5×10⁻⁴ to 4.7×10⁻⁷. The authors conclude that subunit tethering selectively disrupts SD-mediated processes (initiation and +1 frameshifting) and stop codon recognition, likely due to structural constraints at helix 44 where the ASD sequence resides, while -1 frameshifting remains unaffected. The slow-growth phenotype is attributed to slower rRNA biogenesis rather than translational defects, highlighting the greater-than-expected flexibility of the ribosome in supporting viability even when tethered.

Ribo-T ribosomes cannot use SD sequences as stimulatory elements for either translation initiation or +1 programmed frameshifting.
Ribo-T ribosomes terminate translation less efficiently at stop codons, exhibiting slightly elevated readthrough rates.

Research Context
Ribosomes are evolutionary conserved ribonucleoprotein complexes that function as two separate subunits in all kingdoms. During translation, the two subunits associate during initiation, rotate during elongation, and dissociate after protein release. This organization is thought to be essential for biogenesis, successful protein synthesis and cell viability. A ribosome with tethered subunits, in which the two subunits were covalently linked in a single entity, was recently engineered in Escherichia coli. The hybrid ribosomal RNA consisting of small and large subunit sequences was shown to be functional and to sustain cell growth. Ribo-T doubling times were 107 min compared to 35 min for wild-type, with protein synthesis at 50% of wild-type levels. The slow growth phenotype was attributed to Ribo-T biogenesis being slower than wild-type biogenesis, rather than impaired Ribo-T activity. Cell viability depends on a balance between rapid protein synthesis and accurate decoding of genetic information. Recoding events such as frameshifting and stop codon readthrough serve as powerful tools for investigating the translation accuracy of Ribo-T ribosomes. Translational fidelity remains low throughout all steps, but signals in specific mRNAs can program high rates of errors at defined locations. Prior to this study, the translational properties of Ribo-T had not been characterized, leaving the impact of subunit tethering on accuracy unresolved.

The central research question is: do Ribo-T ribosomes maintain the correct reading frame as faithfully as wild-type ribosomes during programmed frameshifting? The second question is: do Ribo-T ribosomes terminate translation accurately at stop codons, or do they exhibit impaired stop codon recognition? The third question addresses whether Ribo-T ribosomes translate messenger RNA accurately, specifically focusing on SD sequence-dependent translation initiation at the lacZ-lacY intergenic region. The authors also investigate the preferential mode of translation used by Ribo-T ribosomes to express adjacent open reading frames, given that the two subunits were inseparable. The implicit hypothesis is that subunit tethering restricts the mutual mobility of the two ribosomal subunits, which is thought to be essential for the translocation mechanism. Specifically, the authors predict that processes requiring subunit association and dissociation—namely SD-mediated initiation, SD-dependent frameshifting, and stop codon recognition—will be impaired. Conversely, processes less dependent on subunit mobility, such as -1 frameshifting, are predicted to be unaffected by subunit tethering. The expected outcome is that Ribo-T will show altered frameshifting and termination profiles compared to wild-type ribosomes, confirming that subunit tethering has translational consequences. The study hypothesizes that the tethering at helix 44 (H44) modifies the orientation of the ASD sequence, preventing Ribo-T from using SD sequences in a normal manner. The predicted slow-growth phenotype is expected to stem from slower rRNA processing rather than impaired translational activity.

Methodological Details
Experiments were performed with the Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) strain from Invitrogen. The bacterial strains were transformed with the poRibo-T2 vector carrying the Ribo-T ribosomal DNA for expression of Ribo-T ribosomes. The ASD sequence of the Ribo-T 16S rRNA was altered from the wildtype sequence 5'-UCACCUCCUUA-3' to an orthogonal sequence. A bacterial pCL99 dual reporter system was used, carrying the lacZ-luc fusion gene under the T7 promoter. The fusion gene encodes the β-galactosidase and luciferase enzymes. The plasmid carries a streptomycin resistance gene and the CloDF13-derived CDF replicon. Target sequences for translation accuracy were inserted by oligocloning into the MscI restriction site of pCL99. Double-stranded oligonucleotides were obtained by hybridizing complementary oligonucleotides in ligation buffer after heating for 5 min at 100°C and incubation at room temperature. All constructs were verified by sequencing, and in-frame controls were constructed for each target sequence. Translational efficiency was calculated as the ratio of luciferase activity to β-galactosidase activity for the target, divided by the same ratio for the in-frame construct. The median value was calculated for at least six independent experiments. Significance of differences was determined by Student's t-tests. For wild-type ribosome analysis, constructs carried a wild-type SD sequence AGGAGG upstream from lacZ. For Ribo-T ribosome assessment, constructs carried a mutated SD sequence CACCAC upstream from lacZ, complementary to the Ribo-T 16S rRNA 3' end. Both wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes were present in strains containing the Ribo-T vector, but only Ribo-T could initiate lacZ translation due to the mutated SD sequence. Crosstalk between wild-type ribosomes and orthogonal mRNA was checked and found too low to affect results; with WT ribosomes alone, mutated SD constructs generated too little β-galactosidase for measurement. The mtmB1 gene stop codon from Methanosarcina barkeri, allowing pyrrolysine insertion, was used to quantify stop codon readthrough. The text references 7 for cell extract volumes but the values appear truncated in the source (µl and 20 µl). The ASD sequence in the text (5'-UCAUUGUGGUA-) is truncated in this preprint version, leaving the full orthogonal sequence unreported.

Procedures And Architectures
The Ribo-T was engineered by linking the small and large subunit rRNA sequences via short RNA linkers to form a single hybrid entity. Three programmed -1 frameshifting sites were selected from the IS911, IS3, and dnaX insertion sequence elements and E. coli dnaX gene. Frameshifting was triggered by a slippery sequence and stimulatory elements, either an RNA structure (stem-loop for IS911 and dnaX, pseudoknot for IS3) or an SD sequence upstream. The combination gave -1 frameshifting efficiencies of approximately 13%, 8%, and 60% for IS911, IS3, and dnaX, respectively, with WT ribosomes. For +1 frameshifting, the site from the E. coli prfB gene was selected. The +1 frameshifting process depends on a poor termination context (UGA C) and a stimulatory SD sequence upstream. The wild-type SD sequence was replaced with a Ribo-T-recognized SD sequence for the reverse experiment in -1 frameshifting. For translation initiation analysis, the 46-nucleotide intergenic lacZ-lacY sequence with its SD sequence promoting initiation at lacY was used. The SD sequence was either deleted or replaced with the Ribo-T SD sequence for analysis. A stable stem loop structure was inserted immediately downstream from lacZ as a roadblock for potential scanning ribosomes. For stop codon readthrough, the mtmB1 stop codon sequence was inserted into the reporter plasmid. All experiments were performed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) using the poRibo-T2 vector carrying the Ribo-T ribosomal DNA. The tethering occurs via helix 44 (H44) in the 16S rRNA, which contains the ASD sequence. The Ribo-T was produced by engineering a hybrid ribosomal RNA consisting of small and large subunit rRNA sequences.

Key Results
Ribo-T ribosomes performed -1 frameshifting at efficiencies comparable to wild-type: 13% for IS911 (13% WT vs 14% Ribo-T, p=0.54), 33% for IS3 (33% vs 33%, p=0.77), and 43-45% for dnaX (43% WT vs 45% Ribo-T, p=0.77). Replacing the dnaX SD with a Ribo-T-recognized SD decreased WT frameshifting to 11% (vs 43%, p=1.7×10⁻³) but had no effect on Ribo-T frameshifting (45% vs 44%, p=0.85), confirming Ribo-T frameshifting is SD-independent. Wild-type ribosomes achieved +1 frameshifting at 33% on the prfB sequence, but Ribo-T ribosomes frameshifted at only 2% (p=8.9×10⁻⁹ versus wild-type). Replacing the +1 frameshifting SD with a Ribo-T SD maintained Ribo-T efficiency at 1.8% (p=0.56), while WT activity dropped to 0.6% (versus 33%, p=1.6×10⁻⁵), confirming Ribo-T cannot use SD as a stimulatory element for +1 frameshifting. In the absence of Ribo-T, no luciferase activity was observed when the SD upstream of luc was removed; with WT SD, high luciferase activity was obtained, validating SD dependence of translation initiation. With the Ribo-T SD sequence, luciferase induction was increased by a factor of four (p=4.7×10⁻⁴) in Ribo-T strains, indicating Ribo-T can use this orthogonal SD albeit inefficiently relative to WT with WT SD. Expression of luciferase was four times stronger when the Ribo-T SD was upstream of lacZ than in the absence of an SD sequence (p=9.8×10⁻⁶), a magnitude similar to WT SD. The stem-loop roadblock downstream of lacZ had no effect on luc translation (p=0.22), strongly suggesting the initiation of luc translation occurred through internal loading of Ribo-T ribosomes rather than a scanning process. Ribo-T ribosomes terminated translation less efficiently than wild-type at all three stop codons: UAG 0.07% vs 0.013% (p=4.7×10⁻⁷), UGA 0.26% vs 0.11% (p=5×10⁻³), and UAA 0.04% vs 0.01% (p=2.5×10⁻⁴). These readthrough rates are 2-5 times higher for Ribo-T than for wild-type at each codon, indicating a slight impairment of stop codon recognition. Doubling times for Ribo-T were 107 min compared to 35 min for wild-type ribosomes. The rate of protein synthesis with Ribo-T catalysis was 50% that with wild-type ribosomes. Ribosome profiling in Ribo-T-expressing cells revealed increased ribosome density at start codons and near the 3' ends of genes.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The findings indicate that subunit tethering selectively disrupts SD-ASD interactions necessary for both SD-dependent frameshifting and translation initiation, while -1 frameshifting, which is less SD-dependent, remains unaffected. The +1 frameshifting defect (Ribo-T 2-1.8% vs WT 33%) likely reflects the different roles of SD-ASD interaction in the two frameshifting types, where +1 frameshifting requires SD-mediated release of the deacylated E-site tRNA to destabilize the ribosome complex. The initiation defect—4-fold reduced SD-dependent luciferase induction—suggests that the altered orientation of the ASD sequence on helix 44 prevents Ribo-T from using SD sequences in a normal manner during initiation and elongation. The stop codon readthrough impairment (2-5 fold higher rates) suggests that the covalently linked structure may be less dynamic, impairing the A-site's ability to bind termination factors. The slow-growth phenotype (107 min doubling time) is attributed to slower rRNA processing during biogenesis rather than translational defects, as evidenced by relatively maintained frameshifting and ~50% translation rate. These results challenge the view that subunit mobility is strictly essential for all translocation events, as Ribo-T remains functional even when tethered. The work suggests that while sufficient translation for cell viability can be maintained with tethered subunits, structural consequences for helix 44 and ASD orientation emerge. A high-resolution structural determination of Ribo-T ribosomes would help resolve the structural basis of the SD-recognition defect. The question of whether tethered ribosomes would be efficient in eukaryotes, where translation initiation does not involve SD-ASD interaction, remains open.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a bioRxiv preprint (March 12, 2020) and has not been certified by peer review, limiting the definitive nature of the conclusions. The ASD sequence in the text (5'-UCAUUGUGGUA-) is truncated in this preprint version, and the full orthogonal sequence is not reported in the provided source. The cell extract volumes appear truncated in the source (µl and 20 µl), preventing full experimental reproducibility. The Ribo-T was engineered independently by two groups, and the structural differences between the two constructs were not examined. The study is limited to Escherichia coli; the applicability to other bacteria or eukaryotes is speculative. No structural data (X-ray, cryo-EM) of Ribo-T were reported, and the mechanism of reduced SD recognition remains purely speculative. The stop codon readthrough was measured using the mtmB1 sequence from Methanosarcina barkeri, which may not reflect endogenous stop codon readthrough in Escherichia coli. Crosstalk between wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes was described as 'too low to affect the results,' but no quantitative measurement of crosstalk is provided. The paper does not report the number of replicates or the specific SD sequence used for the +1 frameshifting reverse experiment, beyond 'a sequence recognized by Ribo-T ribosomes.' The study was limited to three -1 frameshifting sites and one +1 frameshifting site, and the generalizability across all recoding signals is untested.

Ribo-T ribosomes perform -1 programmed frameshifting independently of the SD sequence at efficiencies comparable to wild-type ribosomes. Ribo-T performed -1 frameshifting at 13% (IS911), 33% (IS3), and 43-45% (dnaX), matching WT (13-43%) with p ≥ 0.54 for all comparisons. Replacing the dnaX SD with a Ribo-T-recognized SD decreased WT frameshifting to 11% but did not affect Ribo-T frameshifting (45% vs 44%, p=0.85). Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to the presence of an SD sequence even though they maintain high levels of -1 frameshifting. The Ribo-T ribosomes still exhibit a slightly higher -1 frameshifting efficiency at the dnaX site (45% vs 43%) compared to WT, though the difference is not statistically significant (p=0.77). The SD-ASD interaction is not essential for -1 frameshifting, which suggests a mechanism that does not require SD-directed E-site tRNA release. This contrasts with the +1 frameshifting defect, implying different molecular requirements for the two frameshifting types.
Ribo-T ribosomes cannot use SD sequences as stimulatory elements for either translation initiation or +1 programmed frameshifting. +1 frameshifting was 2% for Ribo-T vs 33% for WT (p=8.9×10⁻⁹), and remained at 1.8% with Ribo-T SD versus 0.6% with WT SD (p=1.6×10⁻⁵). Luciferase induction was four-fold reduced in the presence of the Ribo-T SD compared to WT SD (p=4.7×10⁻⁴), indicating inefficient SD use during initiation. The stem-loop roadblock control (p=0.22) showed no effect on luc translation, supporting the conclusion that Ribo-T ribosomes use internal loading rather than scanning. Ribo-T ribosomes are unable to sense SD sequences and use them as stimulatory elements for frameshifting to either the -1 or +1 frame. Ribo-T was still able to use the orthogonal Ribo-T SD sequence to produce four-fold more luciferase than no SD (p=9.8×10⁻⁶), albeit at much lower levels than WT with WT SD. The Ribo-T SD-dependent initiation signal was of a similar magnitude to the WT SD signal, just 4-fold reduced. Subunit tethering restricts the normal SD-ASD interaction, likely due to structural constraints at helix 44 where the ASD sequence resides. The initiation defect may contribute to the reduced protein synthesis rate (50% of WT) in Ribo-T cells.
Ribo-T ribosomes terminate translation less efficiently at stop codons, exhibiting slightly elevated readthrough rates. Stop codon readthrough was 0.07% vs 0.013% for UAG (p=4.7×10⁻⁷), 0.26% vs 0.11% for UGA (p=5×10⁻³), and 0.04% vs 0.01% for UAA (p=2.5×10⁻⁴). Ribo-T ribosomes display a slight impairment of stop codon recognition, with readthrough rates consistently 2-5 times higher than wild-type at each codon. The readthrough levels remain very low (0.04-0.26%), meaning the defect is slight rather than severe. The covalently linked structure may reduce conformational dynamics at the A-site, impairing termination factor binding. This is consistent with increased ribosome density near 3' ends seen in Ribo-T ribosome profiling.

In-frame controls were constructed for each target sequence to verify that observed effects were not due to artifacts in the ORF. Crosstalk between wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes was checked and found too low to affect results; with WT ribosomes alone, mutated SD constructs generated too little β-galactosidase for measurement. Replacing WT SD with Ribo-T SD for +1 frameshifting confirmed Ribo-T retained defect (1.8%) while WT activity was abolished (0.6%, p=1.6×10⁻⁵). All constructs were verified by sequencing to ensure correct sequence integrity. The median value was calculated for at least six independent experiments, ensuring reproducibility.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is demonstrating that subunit tethering selectively impairs SD-mediated translation initiation and +1 frameshifting while -1 frameshifting and general protein synthesis at ~50% WT levels remain intact. The strongest evidence is the +1 frameshifting defect (2% vs 33%, p=8.9×10⁻⁹) and the 4-fold reduced SD-dependent luciferase induction (p=4.7×10⁻⁴), both showing highly significant impairments of SD-mediated processes. summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces BATI (Bayesian rare variant Association Test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation), a novel statistical framework for identifying disease-associated rare variants. The method leverages the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) to perform full Bayesian inference on generalized linear mixed models, allowing for the simultaneous integration of multiple categorical and numerical variant-specific characteristics (functional annotations, damage scores) as covariates. Unlike existing score-based methods that rely on pre-computed burden statistics or restricted variance-component tests, BATI performs full model estimation, overcoming computational bottlenecks while maintaining flexibility. The authors benchmark BATI against five established RVAS tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR) on semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing cohorts combining thousands of real WES datasets with ClinVar-identified breast cancer risk variants. In scenarios where risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance (VE < 0.5%), BATI achieves power above 75% (median 55% across three genes) while competing methods fail. The method is integrated into the 'rvGWAS' framework, which encompasses quality control, data stratification detection, and functional annotation integration. Application to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The key innovation lies in the ability to combine biological context with full Bayesian inference without the computational burden of MCMC, making the approach suitable for genome-wide scans.
