judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces BATI (Bayesian rare variant Association Test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation), a novel statistical framework for identifying disease-associated rare variants. The method leverages the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) to perform full Bayesian inference on generalized linear mixed models, allowing for the simultaneous integration of multiple categorical and numerical variant-specific characteristics (functional annotations, damage scores) as covariates. Unlike existing score-based methods that rely on pre-computed burden statistics or restricted variance-component tests, BATI performs full model estimation, overcoming computational bottlenecks while maintaining flexibility. The authors benchmark BATI against five established RVAS tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR) on semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing cohorts combining thousands of real WES datasets with ClinVar-identified breast cancer risk variants. In scenarios where risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance (VE < 0.5%), BATI achieves power above 75% (median 55% across three genes) while competing methods fail. The method is integrated into the 'rvGWAS' framework, which encompasses quality control, data stratification detection, and functional annotation integration. Application to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The key innovation lies in the ability to combine biological context with full Bayesian inference without the computational burden of MCMC, making the approach suitable for genome-wide scans.

Research Context
Rare variant association studies (RVAS) are necessary because rare variants (RV) are more likely to affect protein structure, stability, or function than common variants. Traditional GWAS-style single-variant tests lack power due to low allele frequencies, necessitating aggregated analysis within biological units like genes or pathways. Existing RVAS methods fall into two main categories: score-based burden tests that pool alleles into a single measure, and variance-component tests (SKAT, C-alpha) that handle heterogeneous variant effects. The hierarchical Bayesian multiple regression model (HBMR) accounts for genotype misclassification but requires MCMC sampling, which is computationally intensive for genome-wide applications. The mixed-effects test (MiST) incorporates variant characteristics into a GLMM but uses a score test rather than full model inference, limiting its flexibility. Previous benchmark studies relied on pure simulations based on HapMap statistics, creating artificial cohorts that do not represent realistic noise levels or functional variant architectures.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a Bayesian approach using INLA can perform full model inference for RVAS while flexibly integrating multiple variant-specific covariates without the computational cost of MCMC. The authors hypothesize that BATI will outperform existing RVAS tests on realistic, semi-synthetic WES cohorts, particularly when meaningful biological context like functional annotation is used. A secondary hypothesis is that BATI will successfully cope with complex population structure and other confounders in realistic cohorts. The authors predict that BATI will achieve power above 75% in scenarios where competing tests fail, specifically when risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. The test of the hypothesis involves comparing BATI against Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, and HBMR across 100 simulations per gene for both 1000GP and Iberian WES cohorts. The model selection criterion is tested via a difference in deviance information criterion (ΔDIC) approach proposed by Holand et al., with threshold estimation from 10 randomized case-control splits.

Methodological Details
The study utilizes two large WES datasets: the 1000GP cohort and the Iberian cohort as the basis for the semi-synthetic simulations. From 1000GP, half of the samples were randomly assigned as cases and the other half as controls. From the Iberian cohort, one third were selected as cases and two thirds as controls, totaling 1,810 individuals. The breast cancer risk cohort was augmented by querying ClinVar for breast cancer variants annotated as exonic or splicing. Variants with MAF higher than 0.01 in any ancestry population across EVS, 1000GP, or ExAC were removed. The simulator randomly assigns WES samples to cases or controls and introduces predisposition variants into the VCF files of cases. Ten random cohort splits were performed, and the median ΔDIC threshold from these splits was used for model selection. For BATI and HBMR, thresholds were calculated for Bayes factor and translated to ΔDIC TIER levels. At 0.01% TIER, only 2 genes (out of ~20,000) are expected to be significant by chance, serving as the false discovery benchmark. Eight breast cancer risk gene architectures were tested: BRCA2 (missense and LoF), BARD1, CHEK2, PALB2, and others. For the real-world application, a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) study was analyzed using rvGWAS.

Procedures And Architectures
BATI is implemented as part of the rvGWAS framework, which includes quality control, interactive filtering, data stratification detection, and functional annotation integration. The model is a hierarchical Bayesian GLMM for the association of rare variants with phenotypes in case-control studies. The INLA implementation uses the R package INLA version 17.06.20. BATI integrates categorical and numeric characteristics of genetic variants as covariates, including functional annotations and damage estimates. The model selection uses a difference in deviance information criterion (ΔDIC) approach: ΔDIC = DIC(H0) - DIC(H1). For threshold estimation, 10 datasets were generated by randomly shuffling cases and controls, and the median ΔDIC was used. BATI uses the Laplace approximation to produce numerical approximations of the posterior distributions. The phenotype Y follows an exponential family distribution with a linear predictor containing fixed and random effects. Random effects include variant-specific effects treated as the random part of the model, while patient and variant characteristics are fixed. Four existing RVAS tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST) and two Bayesian alternatives (HBMR, BATI) are implemented in rvGWAS.

Key Results
For the Iberian cohort (1,167 individuals), all methods except BATI show power close to 0 when VE = 0.5% and TIER = 0.01%. BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes at VE = 0.5%, with a median power of 55% across the 100 simulations. At VE = 1% and TIER = 0.1%, BATI calls all risk genes with >80% power. Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently fail to call BRCA2 (both missense and LoF versions) at 0.5% VE. HBMR fails to call BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2 at TIER 0.1% at VE = 0.5%. Power plots at 0.5% VE for Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O look very similar, indicating shared strengths and weaknesses across these three methods. MiST fails to identify any risk gene at low VE or low TIER thresholds in the realistic WES cohorts. In the Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study, rvGWAS identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. At 0.01% TIER, only 2 genes out of approximately 20,000 are expected significant by chance. Estimated thresholds were highly similar across all 10 randomized case-control splits, as confirmed by Supplementary S6 Figure.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
BATI demonstrates that integrating both categorical and numerical variant characteristics as covariates in a full Bayesian model significantly increases power compared to score-based or score-test approaches. The significant gain in power when risk genes contain mostly LoF variants suggests that the model captures the functional impact profile of causal disease variants more effectively than competing methods. BATI performs at least as well as other methods when testing genes containing mostly missense variants, indicating the model's flexibility across different genetic architectures. The success of BATI in the CLL application validates the framework for real-world data analysis beyond benchmarking environments. The finding that Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O share similar performance patterns suggests that these burden-and SKAT-type methods should be combined with completely different approaches to compensate for specific weaknesses. The ability to integrate large numbers of covariates makes BATI a flexible testing approach that can be extended to other biological units or genomic contexts.

Contradictions And Limitations
MiST performed favorably on purely artificial benchmark sets but failed on realistic WES cohorts, likely due to zero-inflated p-values from inappropriate handling of low variant counts. The Iberian cohort (1,167 individuals) is smaller than the 1000GP cohort (1,810 individuals), causing most tests to perform slightly worse. The semi-synthetic simulator combines real WES datasets with ClinVar risk variants, but it is still a controlled experimental design that may not capture all real-world epidemiological complexities. The study reports that random 'causal' variants in previous simulations hampered benchmarking of methods leveraging specific functional characteristics of causal disease variants. No random seed or specific data splitting procedure for the real CLL data is reported, limiting reproducibility of the clinical application. The paper notes that INLA is based on numerical approaches, but its accuracy relative to MCMC was only demonstrated for 'several models,' not all applicable RVAS model structures. The sample size for the real-world CLL study is not specified, making it difficult to assess generalizability beyond this single cohort.

Claims
BATI outperforms existing RVAS methods on realistic, semi-synthetic WES cohorts when meaningful biological context such as functional annotation is used. BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes at VE = 0.5%, while all other methods show power close to 0. BATI calls all genes at TIER 0.1% with >80% power even at VE = 0.5%, whereas Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O fail to call BRCA2. BATI maintains stable performance across both 1000GP and Iberian cohorts despite different cohort sizes and structures. For genes with mostly missense variants, BATI performs 'at least as good' rather than strictly better than competing methods. MiST, which is a score-based method, shows relatively small differences from BATI and HBMR in some performance patterns. The inclusion of functional annotations as covariates in a full Bayesian model can compensate for low variance explained by risk variants. rvGWAS can be deployed as a general-purpose framework for rare variant association analysis using WES or WGS data.
BATI successfully copes with complex population structure and other confounders in realistic WES cohorts. The paper explicitly states BATI successfully copes with complex population structure and other confounders. The Iberian cohort, with its distinct population structure, showed similar performance patterns for BATI as the 1000GP cohort. No quantitative metrics (e.g., ΔAIC, correlation analyses) are provided to formally quantify the correction of population structure. The method can be applied to non-homogeneous cohorts without explicit, time-consuming adjustment for ancestry.

Data And Code Availability
BATI is implemented as part of the 'rvGWAS' framework, which integrates multiple RVAS tests, quality control, filtering, and functional annotation. The software uses the R-INLA package (version 17.06.20). The semi-synthetic cohorts were built by combining real WES datasets with ClinVar variants, but the specific datasets used are not listed.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The model selection threshold was validated across 10 randomized case-control splits to ensure robustness of ΔDIC as a selection criterion. The power was assessed across 100 simulations per risk gene to quantify variability in individual gene detection. The 1000GP (1,810 individuals) and Iberian (1,167 individuals) cohorts were benchmarked to assess sensitivity to sample size. No formal ablation study comparing BATI with and without specific covariates (e.g., functional annotation vs. damage scores) is reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 and Table 2 present gene-wise power plots for the 1000GP cohort, showing risk gene identification across 100 simulations at 5%, 0.1%, and 0.01% TIER. Supplementary S6 Figure shows the estimated significance thresholds are highly similar across all 10 randomized case-control splits. Supplementary S8 Figure shows power results for the Iberian cohort, with the right panel depicting VE = 0.5% and TIER = 0.01%. Supplementary S9 Figure presents the gene-wise power plots for the Iberian cohort. Supplementary S4 Table and Table 1 list the specific ΔDIC TIER thresholds for each method.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is BATI, a Bayesian RVAS test using INLA that performs full model inference while integrating multiple categorical and numerical variant characteristics as covariates. 2. The strongest evidence is that BATI achieves power above 75% (median 55% across three genes) at VE = 0.5%, where all competing score-based and variance-component tests show power close to zero. 3. The future path involves extending BATI to other biological units, improving the rvGWAS framework for broader genomic applications, and validating the method in more diverse real-world clinical cohorts.

summary.executive_summary: Nipah virus (NiV), an infectious negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus of the genus henipavirus, causes severe disease with a case fatality rate exceeding 75%. The lack of approved treatments has confined management to isolation and surveillance, and WHO has designated it a priority for accelerated R&D. This paper reports a two-pronged combined evidence strategy to systematically curate, evaluate, and prioritize Nipah virus inhibitors (NVIs). A thorough literature search (yielding 838 papers) combined with a crowdsourcing curation model produced a well-curated knowledgebase of 182 NVIs, 125 of which are small-molecule inhibitors. The study computed over 1800 physicochemical descriptors using PaDel and performed comparative analysis against FDA-approved drugs (2346 compounds) and antivirals from the Enamine library (4644 compounds). A diversity analysis revealed 90 clusters among 98 unique small-molecule NVIs, with 93.3% (84 clusters) as singletons, indicating high chemical diversity. Of the 125 small-molecule entries, 98 are unique inhibitors, and EC50/IC50 values were obtained for 70 compounds, ranging from 0.47 to 7562710 nM. Structural similarity analysis identified 34 NVIs related to 76 FDA-approved drugs. Drug-likeness evaluation via DruLito (8 filters) found only two of 91 compounds passed all filters except CMC. A separate prioritization based solely on assay robustness identified 11 NVIs. Three compounds—NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048—passed 6 DruLito filters; NVIC0048 exhibited high overlap with all six FDA-approved physicochemical parameter ranges, while NVIC0032 demonstrated the best activity among the three. The NVIK platform is hosted on a LAMP server with search tools (simple, query builder, structure), visualization (CIRCOS, Cytoscape), and a submission form for community contributions. The platform includes mapping to Pubchem/ChemSpider, DrugBank, and ZINC. No clinical-stage drugs are currently in trial for NiV. The study highlights the combination of druglike property evaluation and assay robustness as a more comprehensive prioritization strategy than either alone. The platform is designed to be a living, crowdsourced resource for the Nipah inhibitor community.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Nipah virus (NiV), an infectious negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus of the genus henipavirus, causes severe disease with a case fatality rate exceeding 75%. The lack of approved treatments has confined management to isolation and surveillance, and WHO has designated it a priority for accelerated R&D. This paper reports a two-pronged combined evidence strategy to systematically curate, evaluate, and prioritize Nipah virus inhibitors (NVIs). A thorough literature search (yielding 838 papers) combined with a crowdsourcing curation model produced a well-curated knowledgebase of 182 NVIs, 125 of which are small-molecule inhibitors. The study computed over 1800 physicochemical descriptors using PaDel and performed comparative analysis against FDA-approved drugs (2346 compounds) and antivirals from the Enamine library (4644 compounds). A diversity analysis revealed 90 clusters among 98 unique small-molecule NVIs, with 93.3% (84 clusters) as singletons, indicating high chemical diversity. Of the 125 small-molecule entries, 98 are unique inhibitors, and EC50/IC50 values were obtained for 70 compounds, ranging from 0.47 to 7562710 nM. Structural similarity analysis identified 34 NVIs related to 76 FDA-approved drugs. Drug-likeness evaluation via DruLito (8 filters) found only two of 91 compounds passed all filters except CMC. A separate prioritization based solely on assay robustness identified 11 NVIs. Three compounds—NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048—passed 6 DruLito filters; NVIC0048 exhibited high overlap with all six FDA-approved physicochemical parameter ranges, while NVIC0032 demonstrated the best activity among the three. The NVIK platform is hosted on a LAMP server with search tools (simple, query builder, structure), visualization (CIRCOS, Cytoscape), and a submission form for community contributions. The platform includes mapping to Pubchem/ChemSpider, DrugBank, and ZINC. No clinical-stage drugs are currently in trial for NiV. The study highlights the combination of druglike property evaluation and assay robustness as a more comprehensive prioritization strategy than either alone. The platform is designed to be a living, crowdsourced resource for the Nipah inhibitor community.

Research Context
Nipah virus (NiV) is an infectious negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus of the Paramyxoviridae family causing severe disease with >75% fatality. The lack of treatment has forced NiV management to be restricted to isolation and surveillance. WHO's R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases (2018) indicates an urgent need for accelerated Nipah research. Prior outbreaks occurred in Malaysia (1998-1999) and Bangladesh (2001), with mortality rates ranging from 50-100%. Recent outbreaks occurred in Kerala, India (May 2018; 19 cases) and Ernakulam district in 2019. NiV causes cell-to-cell fusion forming multinucleated cells (syncytia), which drives pathogenicity without viral budding. The virus has a high mutation rate, human-to-human transmission, and survival time up to 4 days under various environmental conditions. No known treatment exists; broad-spectrum ribavirin shows contradictory results with mortality reduction below 50%. Experimental drugs like Favipiravir and Remdesivir have shown some protection in animal models (Syrian hamster; African green monkeys). Existing antiviral inhibitor databases (IRD, ViPR, Enamine) contain very limited or no information specific to Nipah virus inhibitors. Previously reported NVIs are scattered across different datasets with no systematic evaluation as starting points for drug discovery.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to systematically curate and prioritize Nipah virus inhibitors (NVIs) from literature-reported bioactivity datasets. The study hypothesizes that a two-pronged combined evidence strategy—evaluating both assay robustness and drug-likeness—will provide a more reliable prioritization than a single-metric approach. The authors posit that systematic evaluation of NVIs against FDA-approved drug and antiviral library benchmarks will identify druglike, non-toxic scaffolds. The expected outcome was a curated knowledgebase (NVIK) and a ranked list of top NVIs suitable for further drug development. The study predicted that NVIs would exhibit diverse structural features and that a subset would show structural similarity to existing FDA drugs. A predicted mechanism was that common structural features across compounds with different molecular weights could reveal important pharmacophore elements for NiV inhibition. The hypothesis was that the NVIK platform would facilitate community engagement and continuous dataset updates via a crowdsourcing model. The expected result was that the majority of NVIs would show physicochemical properties similar to FDA-approved drugs, enabling drug repurposing or scaffold identification.

Methodological Details
The study used PubMed and Google as primary sources to collect Nipah virus-related research papers. Papers were identified using the query 'Nipah' and screened for the keyword in their abstract or title. At the time of curation, 838 papers with the Nipah keyword were shortlisted for data-mining. A scoring system assigned values of 10 (confirmed inhibitor info), 5 (possible info), 4 (peptide inhibitors), and 0 (no relevant info). Papers with scores of 10, 5, and 4 were manually curated to create a Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK) sheet. The curation was conducted using a crowdsourcing model with data made publicly available since May 2018. A separate team of curators re-performed the curation independent of the initial team for data quality control. Errors were marked in 'Red' in the curation sheet and marked 'Green' once verified by both teams. Each entry in the NVIK-Open resource Sheet was tagged with the contributor's email ID for provenance. Data was stored in a shared sheet serving as the crowdsourcing platform. The NVIK platform was developed using open-source LAMP (Linux-Apache-Mysql-PHP) server technology. The web interface used PHP, HTML, JavaScript, AJAX, and CSS for text, structure, and complex query-based search. Search tools included Simple Search (text-based), Query Builder (logical AND/OR), and Structure Search (SMILES, SDF, MOL formats). A JSME browser allowed users to draw compounds directly for searching in NVIK. Physicochemical properties browsable included molecular weight, XLogP, polar surface area (PSA), hydrogen bond donor (HBD), hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), and rotatable bonds. Near neighbors (NNs) were identified using NNeib (version 5.12.0) and clusters were generated via Jarp (version 6.0.2). A dissimilarity threshold of 0.15 (based on 1 - Tanimoto coefficient) was used for clustering. A total of 1875 descriptors were calculated for all compounds using PaDel software. CIRCOS was customized to represent relationships among physicochemical properties, with 98 inhibitors defined and a band width of 1000. Cytoscape was used to generate compound network diagrams (CND) for visualizing clusters. NVIK contained 182 total entries, of which 125 were small-molecule inhibitors and 57 were peptides or incomplete. Of the 125 small-molecule entries, 98 were unique inhibitors; 98 inhibitors had structures available. EC50/IC50 values were obtained for 70 of the 98 unique inhibitors. EC50/IC50 values ranged from 0.25 nM to 7562710 nM for 182 entries and 0.47 nM to 7562710 nM for 125 small-molecule entries. Compounds were mapped to DrugBank, Pubchem/Chemspider, and ZINC databases. Drug-likeness was assessed using DruLito, which screened all compounds against eight filters: Lipinski, MDDR-like, Veber, Ghose, BBB, CMC-50 like, and weighted/unweighted QED. PAINS filter was applied to assess compounds' toxicity profiles. Comparison was made with 2346 FDA-approved compounds and 4644 antivirals from the Enamine library. Enamine was specified as a library of nucleoside-like antiviral compounds.

Procedures And Architectures
The data collection procedure started with identifying 838 papers via the Nipah keyword, followed by manual curation and validation. The two-pronged prioritization strategy comprised: (i) prioritization based on assay robustness and (ii) estimation of drug-likeness parameters. Drug-likeness analysis included diversity analysis, similarity to FDA-approved compounds (for repurposing) and antivirals (for new scaffolds), PAINS and DruLito profiling, and comparison to ZINC lead-like libraries. Assay robustness was evaluated by assessing the strength and type of the assay used to identify each inhibitor. The LAMP server architecture enabled concurrent access and community submissions to the NVIK platform. The Query Builder allowed complex logical queries, enabling users to retrieve targeted results, such as compounds tested in specific cell lines with different IC50 values. Clustering was performed using the dissimilarity threshold of 0.15, which is based on (1 - Tanimoto coefficient). The customized CIRCOS visualization represented the relationship among physicochemical properties with 98 inhibitors defined, forming a baseline for cyclic and aliphatic compounds. The compound network diagrams (CND) and CIRCOS plots visualized clusters and near neighbors, revealing common structural features across different molecular weight ranges. The DruLito screening applied eight filters in sequence to each compound. Only two of 91 compounds passed all DruLito filters except the CMC-50 filter. Independent evaluation based on assay robustness was conducted separately from DruLito filtering. The platform includes a submission form for new compounds, providing database statistics and physicochemical properties automatically upon entry. The NVIK database provides browsing by major fields including molecular weight, XLogP, polar surface area, HBD, HBA, and rotatable bonds. The platform has a provision to submit new inhibitors as and when reported by the community for further enhancement.

Key Results
NVIK contains 182 total entries, with 125 small-molecule entries and 57 peptide or incomplete entries. Of the 125 small-molecule entries, 98 are unique inhibitors, with structures available for all 98. EC50/IC50 values were obtained for 70 of the 98 inhibitors, ranging from 0.25 to 7562710 nM across all entries. For small-molecule entries, IC50/EC50 values range from 0.47 to 7562710 nM. Clustering of 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters, with 84 clusters (93.3%) as singletons and 14 clusters (15.5%) as non-singletons. The high percentage of singletons indicates the NVIK library is chemically diverse. Near neighbor analysis revealed that compounds with different molecular weight ranges can be near neighbors, e.g., GS-441524 (531.202 g/mol) and GS-441524 (NUC) (291.267 g/mol). In structural similarity analysis, 34 NVIs were found similar to 76 FDA-approved drugs. For example, 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine (NVIC0097) showed structural similarity to four FDA molecules: Adenosine, Vidarabine, Fludarabine, and Ademetionine. Comparison with FDA-approved compounds (2346) and Enamine antiviral compounds (4644) showed that for the majority of NVIs, distribution of all six physicochemical properties was similar to FDA drugs. DruLito screening revealed that only two of 91 compounds passed all filters except the CMC-50 like rule. Independent prioritization based solely on assay robustness identified 11 NVIs. Three prioritized NVIs—NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048—passed 6 DruLito filters and were accepted in FDA drugs analysis. NVIC0048 displayed a high degree of overlap with all six physicochemical parameter ranges of FDA-approved drugs. NVIC0032 demonstrated the best activity among the three prioritized compounds and had considerable overlap with FDA drug properties. A total of 1875 descriptors were computed for the inhibitors using PaDel. The Enamine library comprises 4644 nucleoside-like antiviral compounds. FDA-approved comparison group included 2346 compounds.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The high chemical diversity (93.3% singletons) suggests the NVIK library covers a broad structural space, enabling multiple avenues for further development. The finding that compounds with different molecular weights can be near neighbors points toward common structural pharmacophores responsible for antiviral activity, regardless of overall size. Structural similarity to FDA drugs (34 NVIs similar to 76 drugs) suggests drug repurposing potential and provides scaffolds for scaffold hopping into new antiviral space. The combined strategy of DruLito filtering plus assay robustness-based prioritization provides a more stringent and comprehensive screening funnel than a single-parameter approach. The NVIK platform establishes a decentralized, crowdsourced infrastructure for NiV inhibitor data, addressing the fragmentation of existing datasets. The platform's design for ongoing community submission creates a living dataset capable of absorbing new compounds as they are reported. The data can also be utilized beyond Nipah for other viruses due to the broad antiviral potential of the identified compounds.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not report the specific assay types used for each inhibitor, limiting reproducibility of the assay-robustness prioritization. The 838-paper initial set is based on keyword searching alone, which may miss relevant papers not explicitly using the term 'Nipah'. The 5-point scoring system (10, 5, 4, 0) introduces subjective judgment into the data curation process. The 125 small-molecule entries contain only 98 unique inhibitors, indicating data redundancy and the need for deduplication in future efforts. Only 70 of 98 inhibitors have EC50/IC50 values, leaving 30 with unquantified bioactivity. The paper does not report the specific DruLito filter weights or the exact CMC-50 cutoff value used. No random seed or reproducibility controls are mentioned for the Jarp clustering or NNeib neighbor identification. The crowdsourcing model relies on community-reported data with varying quality, making comprehensive validation of all entries challenging. The authors note that for the small-molecule entries, 57 compounds were excluded because they were peptides or lacked complete information, limiting the scope. The paper does not explicitly state whether compounds screened through the PAINS filter were also subjected to additional toxicity or in vivo assays. The Enamine antiviral library was used for comparison but the specific criteria for including these nucleoside-like compounds are not detailed.

Claims
The NVIK platform provides a well-curated knowledgebase of 182 NVIs (98 unique small-molecule inhibitors) with diverse structural features and mapped to major chemical databases. NVIK has 182 total entries, 125 of which are small-molecule inhibitors with 98 unique compounds. Structures are available for all 98 inhibitors and 70 have EC50/IC50 values. Compounds are mapped to DrugBank, Pubchem/Chemspider, and ZINC. The knowledgebase includes physicochemical descriptors, assay robustness data, and structural similarity metrics. Only 70 of 98 inhibitors have quantitated bioactivity, leaving 30 without EC50/IC50 values. The dataset remains incomplete, as 57 entries were peptides or had incomplete information. The platform becomes a centralized hub for the Nipah inhibitor community to submit and access curated data. Community engagement can lead to a living dataset that evolves with new research.
A combined evidence strategy prioritizing NVIs by both assay robustness and DruLito drug-likeness filters is more effective than a single-metric approach. DruLito screening alone only let two of 91 compounds pass all filters except CMC. Independent assay robustness prioritization identified 11 NVIs suitable for further study. The top three prioritized compounds (NVIC0025, NVIC0032, NVIC0048) all passed 6 DruLito filters and showed FDA drug-likeness. NVIC0048 displayed high overlap with all six FDA physicochemical parameter ranges. The paper does not explicitly perform a head-to-head comparison between single-metric and combined-metric prioritization outputs. The prioritization of 11 NVIs was based on subjective assay robustness assessment without reported scoring criteria. Drug discovery efforts can use this prioritized list as high-confidence starting points for in vitro and in vivo validation. This strategy reduces false positive rates compared to single-metric prioritization.
The NVIK library is chemically diverse, with 90 clusters (84 singletons) indicating broad structural coverage. Clustering of 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters. 84 clusters (93.3% of NVIs) were singletons. 14 clusters (15.5% of NVIs) were non-singletons. Near neighbor analysis confirmed that compounds with different molecular weights can be clustered together. The high singleton rate could also reflect low-quality or sparse data for individual compounds, not necessarily true chemical diversity. The clustering was performed at a fixed dissimilarity threshold of 0.15 without sensitivity analysis. The diversity supports multiple development routes, from drug repurposing to novel scaffold exploration. Near neighbor analysis can identify pharmacophore features common to disparate scaffolds.

Data And Code Availability
The NVIK platform is publicly available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah, which has been active since May 2018. The data is hosted on the NVIK-Open resource Sheet, which serves as the crowdsourcing platform. The web interface includes a submission form for community contributions, and the database provides physicochemical properties and statistics upon compound submission. The platform has provision to submit new inhibitors as and when reported by the community for further enhancement. Compounds are mapped to Pubchem/Chemspider IDs wherever possible.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The data quality check involved a separate team of curators re-performing the curation independently of the initial team. Errors were marked in 'Red' and verified in 'Green' by both teams. The crowdsourcing model included contributor email ID tagging for provenance. Data curation and quality check were performed manually, not by automated pipelines. No random seeds, train/test splits, or hyperparameter sensitivity analyses are reported; the study is a curation and prioritization effort. The paper does not report the specific PAINS filter settings or toxicity metrics used for toxicity profiling. The authors mention that the 1875 descriptors were computed for all entries but do not report a validation step for descriptor accuracy. No calibration checks or internal validation of the NNeib and Jarp outputs are described. The paper does not report an ablation comparing prioritization with and without each individual filter (DruLito, PAINS, assay robustness).

Ethical Considerations
The study is a literature-based data curation and computational prioritization effort with no human subjects involved. The NVIK is a crowdsourcing platform where community contributions are aggregated and validated by curators. All data curated from literature was credited to the original contributors, and the platform tracks contributor email IDs for provenance. The paper does not explicitly discuss IRB approval or ethics review, as no human subjects or animal data were directly collected or used.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 shows the predefined data structure used by curators to organize NVIK entries. Figure 1 shows the unique fields in the NVIK database, including physicochemical properties and search options. Figure 2 depicts the overall distribution of important physicochemical properties of NVIs, including a CIRCOS visualization. Figure 3 compares NVIs with FDA-approved compounds and antivirals based on six physicochemical properties. Figure 4 shows only two of 91 compounds passing all DruLito filters except the CMC-50 like filter. Table 2 presents prioritized NVIs, their DruLito filter passes, and overlap with FDA drug physicochemical parameter ranges. Compound network diagrams (CND) were made using Cytoscape to visualize clusters and near neighbors. The NVIK web interface includes search, browsing, and submission tools visualized in Figures 1 and the browsing interface description.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the NVIK platform, a crowd-sourced knowledgebase of 182 NVIs (98 unique small-molecule inhibitors) with a combined prioritization strategy integrating DruLito drug-likeness, PAINS toxicity filtering, and assay robustness evaluation. 2. The strongest evidence is the structural diversity analysis showing 90 clusters among 98 NVIs, with 34 NVIs sharing structural similarity to 76 FDA-approved drugs, and the identification of three prioritized compounds (NVIC0025, NVIC0032, NVIC0048) that passed 6 DruLito filters with high FDA-drug overlap. 3. The future path is for the scientific community to continuously curate and submit new compounds to the NVIK platform, using the prioritized NVIs as high-confidence starting points for further in vitro and in vivo validation.

summary.title: 3D Genome Analysis Identifies Enhancer Hijacking Mechanism for High-Risk Factors in Human T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
summary.authors: Lu Yang; Fengling Chen; Haichuan Zhu; Yang Chen; Bingjie Dong; Minglei Shi; Weitao Wang; Qian Jiang; Leping Zhang; Xiaojun Huang; Michael Q Zhang; Hong Wu
summary.field_subfield: Hematology; 3D Genome Architecture; Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
summary.type_of_paper: Integrated 3D genome and RNA-seq study with clinical outcome analysis
summary.executive_summary:
This study provides the first integrated 3D genome and RNA-seq analysis of 18 newly diagnosed T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) patients and 4 healthy T cell controls, revealing that 3D genome alterations—encompassing compartment switches, TAD-level changes, and loop reorganizations—serve as a biological readout for functional transcriptomic changes and contribute to the etiology and prognosis of T-ALL.

Approximately 29% of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were associated with 3D genome structural alterations, with nearly 45% of upregulated genes showing links to 3D changes when controlling for transcription factor effects. The authors identified 34 previously unrecognized translocations and 44 new translocation-mediated loops, with 47% of breakpoints in noncoding regions and 66% in the stable A compartment. A central mechanism identified is translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking: in the ETP, TLX, and TAL subtypes, translocated enhancers from genes normally expressed during T cell development (e.g., BCL11B, TRB) drive ectopic activation of T-ALL-associated transcription factors, blocking differentiation.

The HOXA cluster, a hallmark of T-ALL, was found to be partitioned into two TADs with different boundary configurations. Different translocation-mediated fusions (PSIP1-NUP98 vs. KMT2A-MLLT1) preferentially alter interactions within the 3' and 5' TADs, respectively, controlling specific HOXA gene expression patterns. For the three HOXA-translocation cases, breakpoints upstream of HOXA13 mediated new loops between the HOXA 5' TAD and active enhancers from BCL11B, CDK6, and ERG, leading to ectopic HOXA13 (case 076) or HOXA11-A13 (case 108) expression.

Clinical correlation revealed that HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity (but not HOXA9) is associated with poor overall and event-free survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALL, and HOXA13+ status is an independent survival predictor. The findings implicate 3D genome alterations as critical determinants of T-ALL development and prognosis, suggesting anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit patients with ectopic HOXA11-A13.

The study demonstrates that T-ALL subtypes can be hierarchically classified by 3D genome organization at multiple levels and that ETP and non-ETP ALLs represent different "frozen stages" of T cell development, with 3D alterations serving as a functional readout of transcriptional and developmental arrest.

claims.description: 3D genome alterations provide a functional readout for transcriptome changes and contribute to nearly half of the upregulated genes in T-ALL.
ETP and non-ETP ALL represent different frozen stages of T cell development detectable by 3D genome organization.
Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and fusion events drive ectopic activation of HOXA cluster and other transcription factors.
Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is associated with poor survival and can be targeted by anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study provides the first integrated 3D genome and RNA-seq analysis of 18 newly diagnosed T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) patients and 4 healthy T cell controls, revealing that 3D genome alterations—encompassing compartment switches, TAD-level changes, and loop reorganizations—serve as a biological readout for functional transcriptomic changes and contribute to the etiology and prognosis of T-ALL.

Approximately 29% of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were associated with 3D genome structural alterations, with nearly 45% of upregulated genes showing links to 3D changes when controlling for transcription factor effects. The authors identified 34 previously unrecognized translocations and 44 new translocation-mediated loops, with 47% of breakpoints in noncoding regions and 66% in the stable A compartment. A central mechanism identified is translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking: in the ETP, TLX, and TAL subtypes, translocated enhancers from genes normally expressed during T cell development (e.g., BCL11B, TRB) drive ectopic activation of T-ALL-associated transcription factors, blocking differentiation.

The HOXA cluster, a hallmark of T-ALL, was found to be partitioned into two TADs with different boundary configurations. Different translocation-mediated fusions (PSIP1-NUP98 vs. KMT2A-MLLT1) preferentially alter interactions within the 3' and 5' TADs, respectively, controlling specific HOXA gene expression patterns. For the three HOXA-translocation cases, breakpoints upstream of HOXA13 mediated new loops between the HOXA 5' TAD and active enhancers from BCL11B, CDK6, and ERG, leading to ectopic HOXA13 (case 076) or HOXA11-A13 (case 108) expression.

Clinical correlation revealed that HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity (but not HOXA9) is associated with poor overall and event-free survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALL, and HOXA13+ status is an independent survival predictor. The findings implicate 3D genome alterations as critical determinants of T-ALL development and prognosis, suggesting anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit patients with ectopic HOXA11-A13.

The study demonstrates that T-ALL subtypes can be hierarchically classified by 3D genome organization at multiple levels and that ETP and non-ETP ALLs represent different "frozen stages" of T cell development, with 3D alterations serving as a functional readout of transcriptional and developmental arrest.

Research Context
Recent studies demonstrated that 3D genome alterations play important roles in tumorigenesis, including hematological malignancies. However, how such alterations may provide key insights into T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia patients is largely unknown. The T-ALL genome has not been integrated with RNA-seq to characterize the functional impact of 3D structural changes. Previous work did not identify novel translocations or translocation-mediated loops in T-ALL patient samples. The mechanism linking 3D genome reorganization to HOXA cluster dysregulation in T-ALL remained uncharacterized.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question was whether 3D genome alterations in T-ALL provide functional insights into disease etiology and differentiation arrest. A secondary question was whether 3D genome structural changes correlate with transcriptome perturbations and differential gene expression. The authors also investigated whether chromosomal translocations generate novel loops that mediate enhancer hijacking of T-ALL-associated transcription factors. The working hypothesis was that 3D genome organization, including compartment, TAD, and loop levels, could hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes along the T cell differentiation trajectory. Another hypothesis proposed that ETP and non-ETP ALL represent different frozen stages of T cell development detectable by 3D genome landscapes. The specific hypothesis tested was that translocation-mediated loops anchor at pre-existing CTCF binding sites and mediate convergent CTCF interactions via loop extrusion. A final hypothesis stated that ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression would associate with poorer clinical outcomes in T-ALL patients.

Methodological Details
Eighteen T-ALL patient samples were collected under a protocol approved by the ethics committee of the Peking University Institute of Hematology. Leukemia blast cells were prepared by density-gradient centrifugation and purified for CD19- CD14- CD235- CD45+ CD7+ by FACS analysis. Peripheral blood samples were obtained from four healthy donors under approval of the Peking University ethics committee. T cells were purified from healthy donors using the EasySep Direct Human T Cell Isolation Kit. RNA-seq libraries were prepared with the TruSeq RNA Library Prep Kit v2 and sequenced to an average depth of 15 million read pairs per sample. Reads were aligned to the hg19 genome using TopHat (v2.1.0) and FPKM normalization was performed. DESeq2 was applied to identify differentially expressed genes with FDR <0.01 and fold change >2, excluding genes with fewer than 5 reads in 20% of samples. ChIP-seq reads were mapped to hg19 with Bowtie2 (v2.3.5), and ATAC-seq reads were mapped with Bowtie2 using the -X 2000 parameter. Hi-C was performed on one million cells per sample according to the BL-Hi-C protocol. Average depth of patient Hi-C samples was 486 million read pairs with a read length of 150 bp. Hi-C raw data were treated as single ends for breakpoint refinement to single base-pair resolution. HiCpipe integrated ChIA-PET2 for bridge linker trimming, HiC-Pro for alignment and artifact removal, and Juicer for contact matrix generation. Compartments were calculated at 100 kb resolution using Juicer, defining compartments by the over 70% sample majority rule. TAD boundaries were calculated using the Insulation score method on pooled 40 kb Hi-C matrices of all samples. Differential TAD boundaries were defined with t-test FDR <0.01 and a difference higher than the 50% quantile of the overall difference. Loops were called using HiCCUPS with differential loop detection adapted from Douglas et al., split into distance ranges (> or < 150 kb). Differential loops were called within each range at FDR < 0.1 and then combined. Aggregate peak analysis plots were generated using Juicer APA at 5 kb resolution. hic_breakfinder was adapted to detect translocations, followed by manual assessment and single base-pair breakpoint determination. Translocations were confirmed when exact locations supported by more than 3 chimeric reads were identified. RcisTarget was used to predict key transcription factors regulating upregulated genes. GREAT (v3.0.0) was used for loop anchor functional analysis, and DAVID (v6.8) for KEGG pathway enrichment. Hi-C heatmaps and Visual 4C plots were generated by MATLAB code. FIMO was used to detect 20 bp CTCF motifs in Loucy and Jurkat CTCF peaks.

Procedures And Architectures
BL-Hi-C data underwent Knight-Ruiz normalization to generate compartment and TAD analyses. The compartment eigenvector command of Juicer was used under 100 kb resolution. A TAD was defined only when boundaries were detected in at least two conditions among normal T cells, ETPs and non-ETPs. Domain scores were calculated by dividing intra-TAD interactions by all interactions connected to the corresponding TAD. Differential domain scores required t-test FDR <0.01 and fold change higher than 70% quantile. Loops were split into two distance ranges at 150 kb to minimize bias. Translocation-mediated loops were manually recorded on interchromosome Hi-C maps using Juicebox. Known translocations were collected from references and ChimerPub; a translocation was novel if any breakpoint was not near a known breakpoint within 100 kb. Chimeric reads overlapped with translocations at 5–20 kb resolution; breakpoints were called where more than 3 chimeric reads supported the location. Hi-C maps were normalized by cis interaction pairs for visualization. A visual 4C (V4C) plot was generated at 10 kb resolution for specific loci. The translocation partner breakpoints were mapped to BCL11B and CDK6 on chromosome 14 and chromosome 7, and ERG on chromosome 21. Breakpoints within the 5' TAD upstream of HOXA13 were mapped to the 5' TAD boundary. ChIP-seq analysis of the HOXA+ Loucy cell line detected increased interactions correlated with H3K27ac gains. The 11 HOXA genes were partitioned between 2 TADs, with C11/13 as the 3' boundary of the 5' TAD. C7/9 served as the 5' boundary for most HOXA− and all 5'HOXA+ samples. C10/11 served as the 5' boundary for most 3'HOXA+ samples. Six enhancer regions E1–E12 were identified in each TAD for HOXA interaction analysis. The loop anchors were analyzed by GREAT using the nearest gene within 100 kb. Genes related to loops were determined if their promoter (5 kb around TSS) overlapped the loop anchors. Loop extrusion was inferred from loops anchored at convergent CTCF motifs. The 5'HOXA+ and HOXA-T cases in Hi-C were associated with double negative and ETP phenotypes. Translocation-mediated fusion events could be detected in 5/7 HOXA+ samples. T-ALL samples were projected onto the T cell developmental trajectory defined by RNA-seq. PCA revealed most ETP ALL samples arrested at LMPP to Thy1 stages, and non-ETP at Thy2 to Thy4 stages. ETP and non-ETP ALLs were better separated at the loop level than at the compartment level. Approximately 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops were identified in ETP. Gene expression changes between ETP and non-ETP ALL were plotted against the combined p-value of loop strength and D-score changes. Approximately 20% of upregulated genes in ETP and 16% in non-ETP ALL harbored chromatin structure changes. A strong positive correlation (Pearson's correlation coefficient 0.685) was found between expression and chromatin structural changes. Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expressions were associated with immature phenotypes and poor outcomes. The HOXA genes are transcriptionally repressed in normal T cells but transactivated in T-ALL by fusion proteins recruiting DOT1L to the HOXA locus. Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking in ETP, TLX and TAL subtypes involved ectopic expression of genes such as TLX3. The cis mechanism included BCL11B-TLX3, TRB-TAL2, and 3 novel HOXA translocations. The trans mechanism involved translocation-mediated gene fusions such as PSIP1-NUP98, SET-NUP214, and MLL. HOXAcluster contains 11 genes and is a common feature of T-ALL. HOXA+ T-ALLs separated into 3'HOXA+ or 5'HOXA+ subgroups based on HOXA gene expression. The 5'HOXA+ subgroup was characterized by ectopic HOXA11-A13 expressions. Significantly enhanced interactions between E2-E6 and genes in the 3'HOXA subgroup were detected. Significantly enhanced interactions between E8, E9, E11, E12 and genes in the 5'HOXA subgroups were detected. ChIP-seq confirmed increased interactions correlated with gains in the H3K27ac histone mark. KMT2A-MLLT1, PICALM-MLLT10, DDX3X-MLLT10, and SET-NUP214 fusions were associated with interaction dynamics and HOXA1-A10 expression in the 3'HOXA subgroup. PSIP1-NUP98 fusion was associated with the 5'HOXA subgroup. Inter-TAD inversion led to the adoption of active CDK6 enhancers and new loop formation. CTF binding sites C11/13 insulated genes in the 3' TAD from the hijacked enhancers. Ectopic expression of HOXA13 in case 076 and HOXA9-A13 in case 077 was driven by new loops. Ectopic expression of HOXA11-A13 in case 108 was driven by new loop formation. HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity, alone or in combination, was associated with poor overall and event-free survivals. T-ALLs with TAL1/2 positivity were associated with better overall survival. TLX positivity had no association with the outcome. HOXA11-A13+ cases were characterized by DN and ETP phenotypes, higher JAK-STAT pathway mutations, and HOXA13+ as independent predictor.

Key Results
Approximately 29% (996 of 3392) of the DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. Among the DEGs associated with B-to-A compartment switches, increased D-scores, and enhanced loops, genes were mostly upregulated and enriched in hematopoietic cell lineage, transcriptional misregulation in cancer, and cell cycle pathways. Genes associated with A-to-B compartment switches, decreased D-scores, and reduced loops were mostly downregulated and enriched in cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and T cell receptor signaling pathways. Approximately 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL could be associated with 3D genome alterations, of which 56% were directly related to structural alterations and the remainder due to TF dysregulation. CDK6 locus exhibited a strong intra-TAD interaction and its expression was upregulated in all T-ALL samples, and CDK6 was identified as a potential target for T-ALL treatment. Several upregulated oncogenic driver genes and T-ALL-associated transcription factors, including MYB, MYCN, BCL11A, SOX4 and WT1, had increased D-scores. Transcription factors SOX4, WT1, and TFDP2 had structural alterations at all three levels, and were among top-ranking candidates regulating approximately 28% of upregulated genes. Most ETP ALL samples were arrested at the immature LMPP to Thy1 stages, while non-ETP samples were arrested at Thy2 to Thy4 stages on the developmental trajectory. Approximately 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops were identified in ETP, and a strong positive correlation (Pearson's 0.685) linked gene expression changes to the combined p-value of loop strength and D-score changes. Approximately 20% of upregulated genes in ETP and 16% in non-ETP ALL harbored chromatin structure changes, including key transcription factors or oncogenes like CEBPA, MYCN, LYL1 for ETP, and LEF1, TCF12, PAX9 for non-ETP ALL. ETP ALL enhanced loops genes were enriched in immune response-activating signal transduction, myeloid cell differentiation, and regulation of B cell activation. Non-ETP ALL enhanced loops genes were enriched in positive regulation of RNA metabolism, transcription, and TCR V(D)J recombination. The lack of TCR rearrangement in most ETP ALL samples and different rearrangements in individual non-ETP samples could be observed from Hi-C maps. Lack of RAG1 and PTCRA expression in most ETP ALL samples, essential for TCR V(D)J rearrangements, was also observed. Subtype-specific loops and expression patterns were detected in the MEF2C locus in ETP and the PAX9 locus in non-ETP ALL, associated with H3K27ac and CTCF marks in KE37 and Jurkat. Forty-six translocations were identified in 14 out of 18 T-ALL samples, including 34 novel events and 26 interchromosomal events. Among 78 unique breakpoints, 47% were located in noncoding regions and 66% in the stable A compartment. The translocations resulted in the formation of 44 new translocation-mediated loops, and their ends tended to anchor at pre-existing loop anchors and CTCF binding sites. Nearly 78% of translocation-mediated loops with CTCF motifs were linked to pairs of convergently orientated CTCF motifs, suggesting mediation by loop extrusion. A complete match existed between loop-based hierarchical clustering and T-ALL clinical subtypes, signified by chromosomal translocation-mediated dysregulation of T-ALL-associated transcription factors. Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking in the ETP, TLX, and TAL subtypes involved genes such as TLX3 hijacking enhancers from the translocated BCL11B gene via translocation-mediated loops. The cis mechanism included BCL11B-TLX3, TRB-TAL2, and 3 novel HOXA translocations, with most hijacked enhancers from genes normally expressed during T cell development. The trans mechanism involved translocation-mediated gene fusions including PSIP1-NUP98, SET-NUP214, and MLL events that could epigenetically activate HOXA cluster gene expressions. Fifteen T-ALL samples without HOXA translocation were separated into HOXA-negative and HOXA-positive expression groups based on HOXA gene expression, with translocation-mediated fusion events detected in 5 out of 7 HOXA-positive samples. The HOXA+ T-ALLs separated into 3'HOXA+ or 5'HOXA+ subgroups with respect to the location of HOXA genes within the cluster. The three HOXA-T cases had expression patterns closer to the 5'HOXA+ subgroup, characterized by ectopic HOXA11-A13 expressions. The 5'HOXA+ and HOXA-T cases were associated with double negative and ETP phenotypes. The 11 HOXA genes were partitioned between 2 TADs, with C11/13 as the 3' boundary of the 5' TAD in all samples. C7/9 served as the 5' boundary for most HOXA- and all 5'HOXA+ samples, while C10/11 was used by most 3'HOXA+ samples. Significantly enhanced interactions between E2-E6 and genes in the 3'HOXA subgroup, and between E8, E9, E11, E12 and genes in the 5'HOXA subgroups, were detected either as a group average or individually. KMT2A-MLLT1, PICALM-MLLT10, DDX3X-MLLT10, and SET-NUP214 fusions were associated with interaction dynamics and HOXA1-A10 expression in the 3'HOXA subgroup. The PSIP1-NUP98 fusion was associated with the 5'HOXA subgroup. These translocations mediated new loop formations between the 5' of the HOXA cluster and active enhancers associated with BCL11B, CDK6, and ERG genes. New loops led to ectopic expression of HOXA13 in case 076, HOXA9-A13 in case 077, and HOXA11-A13 in case 108. The inter-TAD inversion in case 108 led to the adoption of active CDK6 enhancers and new loop formation, causing ectopic expression of HOXA11-A13. CTF binding sites C11/13 in case 076, C7/9 in case 077, and C10/11 in case 108 insulated genes in the 3' TAD from the influence of the hijacked enhancers. HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity, alone or in combination, but not HOXA9 expression, was associated with poor overall and event-free survivals in young adult and pediatric T-ALLs. T-ALLs with TAL1/2 positivity, mutually exclusive from HOXA positivity, were associated with better overall survival. TLX positivity had no association with the outcome. HOXA11-A13+ cases were characterized by DN and ETP phenotypes, higher JAK-STAT pathway mutations, and HOXA13+ status as independent predictor for overall survival. HOXA11-A13+ cases also had a higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations compared to HOXA1-A10+, TAL+, and TLX+ samples.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
3D genome alterations serve as a biological readout of the functional impact of structural changes on gene expression in T-ALL development. T-ALL samples represent different frozen stages of T cell development, with 3D genome landscapes capturing developmental arrest at specific checkpoints. The strong correlation between loop-D-score changes and gene expression changes supports the functional relevance of 3D alterations in T-ALL pathogenesis. The association of nearly 45% of upregulated genes with 3D changes, with over half directly linked to structural alterations, underscores the central role of 3D genome architecture in oncogene activation. Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking provides a structural mechanism for the ectopic activation of T-ALL transcription factors, explaining how non-coding rearrangements drive disease. The partition of HOXA genes into two TADs with different boundary configurations, and the differential loop patterns driven by different fusion proteins, reveal a complex 3D regulatory control of HOXA expression. The convergence of CTCF motifs at translocation-mediated loops suggests loop extrusion as a fundamental mechanism for structural rearrangement in T-ALL. The clinical link between HOXA11-A13 ectopic expression and poor survival identifies a potentially actionable therapeutic target in a subtype of T-ALL currently incurable by standard treatments. The study implies that 3D genome alterations, in addition to driver mutations and pathway dysregulations, play critical roles in rewiring the T-ALL transcriptome. Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors are proposed as a potential therapy for patients with ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression.

Contradictions And Limitations
The small cohort size (18 patients) limits the generalizability of findings across the full spectrum of T-ALL. The study was conducted at a single center (Peking University), introducing potential selection bias. No information on patient demographics, race, or geographical origin is provided beyond Supplementary Table 7. The paper does not report a random seed, train/test split, or other reproducibility details typically found in computational analyses. Data and code availability are not explicitly detailed beyond the GEO database mention for Loucy and Jurkat. The use of 4 healthy controls for comparison with 18 patients may introduce statistical imbalances. The translocation detection method (hic_breakfinder) was adapted, and the manual assessment of translocations introduces subjective criteria. The 45% association of upregulated genes with 3D alterations was estimated after eliminating overlapping DEGs identified by RcisTarget, and the direct vs indirect attribution (56% vs 44%) may have uncertainty. The Pearson's correlation (0.685) between expression and chromatin changes was calculated but the underlying distribution and multiple-testing corrections are not detailed. The clinical outcome analysis used a cohort with outcome information (companion paper) whose details are not fully described in this main paper. The multivariate analysis for HOXA13+ as an independent predictor does not report hazard ratios, confidence intervals, or the exact model specifications.

Claims
3D genome alterations provide a functional readout for transcriptome changes and contribute to nearly half of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. Approximately 29% of all DEGs were associated with 3D alterations. The transcriptome changes were highly consistent with 3D genome structural changes, as shown in Fig. 1a and 1b. Approximately 45% of upregulated genes showed association with 3D genome alterations. CDK6, MYB, MYCN, BCL11A, SOX4, and WT1 all exhibited increased D-scores and were upregulated. The association was only calculated after eliminating overlapping DEGs identified by RcisTarget, and the indirect contribution (44%) may involve confounding factors. The Pearson's correlation of 0.685 between expression and chromatin structural changes indicates that 3D alterations only explain a portion of the transcriptomic variation. 3D genome alterations are critical determinants of T-ALL gene expression and may serve as biomarkers. Targeting the structural basis of oncogene activation could be a therapeutic strategy.
ETP and non-ETP ALL represent different frozen stages of T cell development detectable by 3D genome organization. ETP ALL samples arrested at LMPP to Thy1 stages and non-ETP at Thy2 to Thy4 stages on the T cell developmental trajectory. ETP and non-ETP ALLs were better separated at the loop level than at the compartment level. 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops were identified in ETP samples. Gene ontology of ETP enhanced loops matched myeloid differentiation and B cell activation, consistent with ETP definition. Non-ETP enhanced loops were enriched in transcription and TCR V(D)J recombination. Sample 093 fell between ETP and non-ETP on the trajectory and had significant TCR rearrangement, indicating heterogeneity. The developmental trajectory was defined by RNA-seq, and the assumption that chromatin organization directly reflects developmental stage requires validation. T-ALL can be hierarchically classified by 3D genome organization along the T cell differentiation trajectory. Developmental arrest at specific checkpoints may be captured and targeted by 3D-disrupting therapies.
Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and fusion events drive ectopic activation of HOXA cluster and other transcription factors. 34 novel translocations and 44 translocation-mediated loops were identified. 47% of unique breakpoints were in noncoding regions and 66% in the stable A compartment. 78% of loops with CTCF motifs anchored at convergent CTCF sites, supporting loop extrusion. A complete match existed between loop-based hierarchical clustering and T-ALL clinical subtypes. The cis mechanism involved BCL11B-TLX3, TRB-TAL2, and 3 novel HOXA translocations. The trans mechanism involved PSIP1-NUP98, SET-NUP214, and MLL fusions. Translocation-mediated loops were manually recorded on Hi-C maps rather than called by an automated tool, introducing manual bias. Chromosomal rearrangements provide a structural mechanism for non-coding driven oncogenesis in T-ALL. Targeting translocation breakpoints or hijacked enhancers could disrupt oncogene activation.
Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is associated with poor survival and can be targeted by anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors. HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity (alone or combined) was associated with poor overall and event-free survivals. HOXA13+ status was an independent predictor for overall survival in pediatric and young adult T-ALL. The HOXA11-A13+ cases had DN and ETP phenotypes and a higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway mutations. Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors are suggested to benefit this group. HOXA9 positivity was not associated with survival, contrary to previous use as a biomarker. TLX positivity had no association with outcome. The multivariate analysis does not report hazard ratios, confidence intervals, or the exact model specifications. Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit T-ALL patients with ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression. HOXA11-A13+ is a potentially actionable clinical subtype of T-ALL.

Data And Code Availability
Raw RNA-seq data for Loucy and Jurkat were downloaded from the GEO database. No explicit statement is provided for the availability of the main study's Hi-C, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, or ATAC-seq data. The companion paper contains outcome information for the T-ALL cohort but is not fully described.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Differential loop calling was performed within each distance range separately and combined to minimize bias. The domain score was calculated by dividing intra-TAD interactions by all interactions connected to the corresponding TAD, providing a normalized metric. TAD boundaries were merged and assigned relative insulation scores across all samples from HiCDB. Translocations were manually assessed after filtering those detected in normal controls to confirm actual breakpoints. Chimeric reads were defined as single ends that could be mapped to two different chromatins without the BL-Hi-C bridge linker. The 56% vs 44% attribution of upregulated genes to structural alterations vs TF dysregulation was an estimation after eliminating overlapping genes. No explicit replication of Hi-C or RNA-seq experiments is reported for the patient cohort.

Ethical Considerations
Patient samples were collected under a protocol approved by the ethics committee of the Institute of Hematology at Peking University. Peripheral blood samples were obtained from four healthy donors under approval of the Peking University ethics committee. The authors do not mention informed consent, IRB number, or any additional ethical approvals for the use of patient data and tissues.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents PCA and hierarchical clustering of compartment, TAD, loop, and gene expression profiles, along with compartment and D-score changes. Figure 2 shows T-ALL samples projected onto the T cell developmental trajectory, PCA results, ETP vs non-ETP loop and D-score comparisons, and correlation plots. Figure 3 displays translocation detection in patient samples, translocation-mediated loops across chromosomes, and loop-based hierarchical clustering. Figure 4 shows HOXA gene expression clustering into subgroups, TAD boundary variations, and differential interaction intensity between E2-E6 and E8-E12. Figure 5 presents the three HOXA-T case breakpoints, translocation-mediated loop formation in the 5' TAD, and inter-TAD inversion in case 108. Figure 6 presents the survival analysis of HOXA-positive, TAL-positive, and TLX-positive T-ALL samples, with multivariate analysis and phenotype characterization. Supplementary Table 2 lists genes associated with compartment, domain score, and loop structural changes. Supplementary Table 3 provides RcisTarget predictions of transcription factors regulating upregulated genes. Supplementary Table 4 lists upregulated genes with chromatin structure changes in ETP and non-ETP ALL. Supplementary Table 5 reports the 46 translocations, precise breakpoints, and novel status. Supplementary Table 6 annotates translocation-mediated loops and associated genes. Supplementary Figure 1e shows intra-TAD interaction of CDK6. Supplementary Figure 1f shows increased D-scores for MYB, MYCN, BCL11A, SOX4, WT1. Supplementary Figure 1g shows SOX4, WT1, TFDP2 with alterations at all three levels. Supplementary Figure 2a shows lack of TCR rearrangement in ETP ALL. Supplementary Figure 2b shows different TCR rearrangements in non-ETP samples. Supplementary Figure 2f shows lack of RAG1 and PTCRA expression in ETP ALL. Supplementary Figure 2g and 2h show subtype-specific loops and expression in MEF2C and PAX9 loci. Supplementary Figure 3a and 3b show translocation breakpoint locations and novel translocations. Supplementary Figure 3c shows convergent CTCF motifs at translocation loops. Supplementary Figure 3d shows translocation-mediated gene activation mechanisms. Supplementary Figure 3e shows BCL11B-TLX3 hijacking. Supplementary Figure 3c-d show translocation-mediated loops. Supplementary Figure 3b shows cis mechanism translocations. Supplementary Figure 4a shows HOXA TAD boundaries and differential interactions. Supplementary Figure 4b-c show detailed interaction intensities. Supplementary Figure 5 shows translocation breakpoints and loop formation. Supplementary Figure 5a and 5b show new loops and gene expressions in cases 076 and 077. Supplementary Figure 5c shows the inter-TAD inversion in case 108. Supplementary Figure 5d shows CTCF binding sites C11/13, C7/9, and C10/11 in the three HOXA-T cases. Supplementary Figure 6a-b show survival curves and phenotype characterization. Supplementary Figure 6c shows JAK-STAT pathway mutation rates. Supplementary Table 7 describes patient characteristics. Supplementary Table 6 annotates translocation-mediated loops with their associated genes. Supplementary Table 5 lists translocations and precise breakpoints. Supplementary Table 4 lists chromatin-structure-altered upregulated genes in ETP and non-ETP ALL. Supplementary Table 3 provides RcisTarget transcription factor predictions.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first integrated 3D genome and RNA-seq analysis of T-ALL patients, revealing that 3D alterations account for nearly 45% of upregulated genes and that ETP and non-ETP ALL represent different frozen stages of T cell differentiation. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of 34 novel translocations, 44 translocation-mediated loops, and the mechanistic link between HOXA11-A13 ectopic expression and poor overall survival in young adult and pediatric T-ALL, validated by multivariate analysis. 3. The future path involves clinical validation of HOXA11-A13 as a prognostic biomarker and testing anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors in patients with ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression, as well as further characterizing the structural basis of T-ALL oncogenesis.

summary.executive_summary:
The paper introduces ProNetView-ccRCC, an interactive web-based portal designed to visualize and explore the phosphoproteomics co-expression network of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) derived from the CPTAC proteogenomics study. The network, constructed from 20,976 phosphopeptides in 103 ccRCC samples using a random-forest-based algorithm, comprises 3,614 genes and is presented as a 3D interactive view with 30 functional pathway-enriched network modules. Built on the Three.js framework, the portal enables users to rotate, zoom, and interactively explore the dense network topology. Users can hover over nodes to see gene names, click to view gene-level metadata, and access pathway enrichment tables (sorted by p-value). A specific query example highlights the oncogene ERG, connected to 11 genes within a module and mapping to 5 peptides, with a tumor grade association of p=0.003, FDR=0.118.

The portal supports user-defined filters on clinical variables including stage, grade, age, gender, and FDR cut-off. Each module is derived using the Glay clustering algorithm, and pathway enrichment is performed via Fisher Exact test. The portal links to the ProTrack tool for multi-omics heatmap exploration. It is an open-access, freely available resource requiring no additional plugins and running in all modern browsers, aiming to support cancer researchers with varying computational skill levels in hypothesis generation and data communication.
