judge_context:
Executive Summary
The paper introduces ProNetView-ccRCC, an interactive web-based portal designed to visualize and explore the phosphoproteomics co-expression network of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) derived from the CPTAC proteogenomics study. The network, constructed from 20,976 phosphopeptides in 103 ccRCC samples using a random-forest-based algorithm, comprises 3,614 genes and is presented as a 3D interactive view with 30 functional pathway-enriched network modules. Built on the Three.js framework, the portal enables users to rotate, zoom, and interactively explore the dense network topology. Users can hover over nodes to see gene names, click to view gene-level metadata, and access pathway enrichment tables (sorted by p-value). A specific query example highlights the oncogene ERG, connected to 11 genes within a module and mapping to 5 peptides, with a tumor grade association of p=0.003, FDR=0.118.

The portal supports user-defined filters on clinical variables including stage, grade, age, gender, and FDR cut-off. Each module is derived using the Glay clustering algorithm, and pathway enrichment is performed via Fisher Exact test. The portal links to the ProTrack tool for multi-omics heatmap exploration. It is an open-access, freely available resource requiring no additional plugins and running in all modern browsers, aiming to support cancer researchers with varying computational skill levels in hypothesis generation and data communication.

Research Context
CPTAC has performed comprehensive proteogenomic characterizations of tumor samples from breast, colon, ovarian, and kidney cancer patients. Co-expression networks derived from proteomics and phosphoproteomics data revealed the regulatory relationships between proteins and posttranscriptional modifications, bringing new insights on pathway interactions and dysfunctions. These networks contain rich information but are challenging to visually communicate due to their large dimensions and complicated topologies. These networks are best visually explored together with associated information between gene/protein activities and biological pathway annotations as well as clinical outcomes. Current network data visual exploration tools are mainly used for visually communicating networks as static 2D images in print publications. A centralized platform customized for CPTAC co-expression networks and associated meta-data is necessary to address these challenges.

Research Question And Hypothesis
There is a pressing need for a new open community resource tool for intuitive visual exploration, interpretation, and communication of gene/protein regulatory networks by the cancer research community. The paper hypothesizes that a web-based interactive portal enabling quick, user-intuitive visual interactions with the ccRCC tumor phosphoprotein co-expression network will address the visualization challenge. The portal enables quick and easy interactions with the ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network as well as 30 functional network modules. A 3D network exploration interface is needed to effectively handle dense and complex networks that are difficult to communicate as 2D images. The portal supports user-initiated queries for proteins of interest, neighbors, mapping peptides, or pathways, filtered by user-defined clinical variables.

Methodological Details
The network characterizes co-expression patterns among 20,976 phosphopeptides in ccRCC. The network was derived using a random-forest based network construction algorithm. The algorithm was based on phospho-peptide level data of 103 ccRCC samples. Two genes are connected if at least two phosphopeptides mapping to the two genes are associated to each other. Network modules were derived by using the Glay clustering algorithm. 30 modules containing at least 20 genes each were identified. For each module network, pathway enrichment analysis was performed via Fisher Exact test, and overrepresented pathways were incorporated as meta-data. The portal was built on the Three.js framework, providing an interface for WebGL. Network layouts were calculated using 3D layout algorithms within iCAVE, a previously developed desktop tool. Multiple client-side JavaScript libraries including D3.js, dataTables.js, and JQuery were utilized for user interaction events. Bootstrap v3.3.7 with custom styling was primarily used for web interface element styling. The portal runs on all modern web browsers without additional plug-ins.

Procedures And Architectures
The landing page provides the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network (Figure 1A) and links to functional modules (Figure 1B). Users can interactively explore the network topology in 3D by rotating and zooming the view. Six modules within this network were significantly associated with biological pathways, highlighted using different node coloring. Searching for an oncogene such as ERG highlights its corresponding node in red within the network exploration panel. The query returns genes whose phosphopeptides are directly connected to the queried gene, along with tumor grade association metrics. The tumor grade association for the ERG phosphoprotein is reported with p-value: 0.003 and FDR: 0.118. ERG is directly connected to 11 genes within its module and maps to 5 different peptides. Clicking a node displays the associated gene-level meta-data in a separate panel. Users can click a Heatmap link to navigate to the ProTrack tool for interactive multi-omics heatmap exploration. Clinical queries specify the phenotype of interest (e.g., grade) and an FDR cutoff value (e.g., FDR=20%). Pathway enrichment tables display pathways sorted by p-values; clicking a pathway returns the associated gene list. Node sizes are proportional to the number of connections, identifying central genes.

Key Results
The ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network comprises 3,614 genes. 30 functional pathway-enriched network modules were identified. The overall network characterizes co-expression patterns among 20,976 phosphopeptides. Each module contains at least 20 genes. The oncogene ERG is directly connected to 11 genes within its module. ERG maps to 5 different peptides. The tumor grade association for the ERG phosphoprotein yields p-value: 0.003 and FDR: 0.118. Six modules were significantly associated with biological pathways. The network was constructed from 103 ccRCC samples. Users can construct a simple query specifying phenotype and FDR cutoff (e.g., FDR=20%).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The portal enables quick, user-intuitive visual interactions with the ccRCC tumor phosphoprotein co-expression network. 30 functional network modules and their associated meta-data are integrated into a single platform. The tool aims to help guide hypothesis generation for future cancer studies. The portal facilitates researchers with a wide-spectrum of computational skill levels. The tool is freely available and runs in any modern web browser without additional plugins, promoting wide adoption. The interactive capabilities enable researchers to share and communicate their findings.

Contradictions And Limitations
No random seed or train/test split is reported for the random-forest based network construction algorithm. No evaluation of user experience, learnability, or performance metrics is reported. No comparison with existing network visualization tools is presented to validate relative performance. No benchmark on network layout quality, rendering performance, or 3D navigation efficiency is provided. The paper does not state how many individual samples contributed to each of the 30 identified modules. No explicit code repository (e.g., GitHub) or data files are cited beyond the portal URL: http://ccrcc.cptac-network-view.org/. No calibration checks or sensitivity analyses of the network construction algorithm are reported.

Claims
ProNetView-ccRCC enables intuitive 3D interactive visual exploration of the CPTAC ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network. The portal built on Three.js provides a 3D network exploration interface. Users can rotate and zoom the view to interact with the network topology. 30 functional pathway-enriched modules are available for detailed exploration. Node hover and click actions provide interactive access to gene names and metadata. The claim is qualitative; no formal evaluation of 'intuitiveness' or usability is presented. The tool can facilitate hypothesis generation for cancer researchers. The portal is open-access and accessible to researchers with diverse computational backgrounds.
Users can query association between phosphopeptide abundance in the network and clinical variables using user-defined filters. The tumor grade query for ERG returns p-value: 0.003 and FDR: 0.118. Users can specify phenotype of interest (grade) and an FDR cutoff value (e.g., FDR=20%). The query returns genes directly connected to the queried gene with clinical phenotype association. The example query is only demonstrated for tumor grade; no other clinical variables are shown. This enables data-driven hypothesis generation by linking network topology with clinical outcomes.

Data And Code Availability
The portal is an open-access freely available resource at http://ccrcc.cptac-network-view.org/. The tool runs in any modern web browser without the need for installing specific plugins. No explicit code repository (e.g., GitHub) or data files are cited outside the portal URL.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network. Figure 1B shows links to functional network modules. Figure 1C displays the oncogene ERG query highlighting the node in red. Figure 2A shows a snapshot of the Angiogenesis enriched module network (module 26). Figure 2B shows ERG in the module network, connected to 11 genes. Figure 2C shows the construction of a clinical query specifying grade and FDR=20%. Figure 2D shows highlighted genes from the clinical query. Figure 3A shows the interactive table listing enriched pathways sorted by p-values for module 18. Figure 3B shows pathway gene highlights in the network exploration panel.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is a free, open-access 3D web portal that integrates the CPTAC ccRCC phosphoproteomics co-expression network with pathway annotations and clinical metadata for intuitive interactive exploration. The strongest evidence is the practical implementation enabling user-defined queries that combine network topology (e.g., ERG connected to 11 genes) with clinical association metrics (p=0.003, FDR=0.118) in a single interface. The future path involves extending the portal to other CPTAC cancer networks and further integrating multi-omics data from ProTrack, facilitating data-driven hypothesis generation across the cancer research community.

summary.executive_summary: This study presents the first animal model of spontaneous regression of metastatic cancer foci following surgical excision of the primary tumor (PT). Using MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells engineered with a highly sensitive luciferase reporter, the authors monitored early-stage micro-metastases in BALB/c nu/nu mice. Upon reaching a total metastatic flux of 10^6 photons/second (~3-4 weeks post-injection), the primary tumor (average size 80 mm^3) was excised under isoflurane anesthesia. The study demonstrated a dramatic 100-fold decrease in metastatic bioluminescent signal within 24 hours of excision (p<0.0001), which persisted for at least 50 days as no new signal emerged and H&E staining confirmed the presence of latent malignant foci. Sham surgery without PT removal did not elicit regression (p<0.05), and supplementation with tumor-cell conditioned medium via Alzet osmotic minipumps reduced regression by 10-fold (p<0.005), directly implicating PT-secreted factors in sustaining micro-metastases. Human cytokine array and LC-MS proteomics of the MDA-MB-231 HM secretome (identifying 2,600 proteins) pinpointed four key factors: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. In vivo neutralization of these four factors with mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies completely arrested metastatic progression (p<0.0001) in the presence of the primary tumor. Retrospective analysis of a TCGA lung adenocarcinoma cohort showed that elevated levels of these four proteins correlated with significantly poorer survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05). The study concludes that PT-secreted factors promote early metastatic stages, and their removal through surgery or targeted neutralization can induce regression or latency of micro-metastases, suggesting perioperative windows for controlling minimal residual disease.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents the first animal model of spontaneous regression of metastatic cancer foci following surgical excision of the primary tumor (PT). Using MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells engineered with a highly sensitive luciferase reporter, the authors monitored early-stage micro-metastases in BALB/c nu/nu mice. Upon reaching a total metastatic flux of 10^6 photons/second (~3-4 weeks post-injection), the primary tumor (average size 80 mm^3) was excised under isoflurane anesthesia. The study demonstrated a dramatic 100-fold decrease in metastatic bioluminescent signal within 24 hours of excision (p<0.0001), which persisted for at least 50 days as no new signal emerged and H&E staining confirmed the presence of latent malignant foci. Sham surgery without PT removal did not elicit regression (p<0.05), and supplementation with tumor-cell conditioned medium via Alzet osmotic minipumps reduced regression by 10-fold (p<0.005), directly implicating PT-secreted factors in sustaining micro-metastases. Human cytokine array and LC-MS proteomics of the MDA-MB-231 HM secretome (identifying 2,600 proteins) pinpointed four key factors: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. In vivo neutralization of these four factors with mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies completely arrested metastatic progression (p<0.0001) in the presence of the primary tumor. Retrospective analysis of a TCGA lung adenocarcinoma cohort showed that elevated levels of these four proteins correlated with significantly poorer survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05). The study concludes that PT-secreted factors promote early metastatic stages, and their removal through surgery or targeted neutralization can induce regression or latency of micro-metastases, suggesting perioperative windows for controlling minimal residual disease.

Research Context
Surgical removal of the primary tumor is a standard cornerstone of cancer treatment, but has been suggested to accelerate postoperative progression of minimal residual disease. Conversely, various case studies have reported the opposite: spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastasis in breast, lung, and other cancer types. Several mechanisms have been postulated to explain this regression, including surgical trauma and elimination of primary tumor-derived stimulating factors, but no animal model of spontaneous regression previously existed. The need to study PT-metastasis interactions is stressed by the realization that the primary tumor represents a systemic disease with continuous crosstalk between the PT, its microenvironment, and distant organs. Previous studies had focused on how surgical procedures themselves might trigger progression, and few had empirically tested the proposed mechanisms for regression.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the removal of the primary tumor and its secreted factors induces spontaneous regression of early-stage metastatic foci. The hypothesis is that the primary tumor secretome supports the survival and growth of distant micro-metastases, and its elimination by surgery results in metastatic regression. A secondary hypothesis is that regression is specific to early metastatic stages, and larger, established metastases may be self-sufficient and resistant to regression. The study predicted that in vivo supplementation of tumor-derived secreted factors would diminish regression, and that specific identified factors could be neutralized to arrest metastatic progression. The authors anticipated that the identified PT-secreted factors would show clinical relevance as predictors of survival in lung adenocarcinoma patients.

Methodological Details
The model used MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells, a highly metastatic triple-negative breast adenocarcinoma variant, transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector. Eight-week old female BALB/c nu/nu mice (n = ) were injected with 2×10^5 cells in 20 μl PBS into the fourth mammary fat pad under 2% isoflurane anesthesia. Primary tumors were measured by caliper, and volume calculated as (length × width^2) × 0.5, with an average size of 80 mm^3 at excision. Metastases were assessed by bioluminescence imaging using an IVIS spectrum apparatus after i.p. injection of 150 mg/kg D-luciferin sodium salt. Primary tumor excision was performed under 2% isoflurane anesthesia with a small skin incision, verified by bioluminescence imaging, and followed by immediate skin suturing. For the sham surgery, an identical incision was made but the primary tumor was untouched, then immediately sutured. Tumor-cell conditioned medium (CM) was produced by incubating ~80% confluent MDA-MB-231 HM cells in serum-free medium for 24 h at 37°C, 5% CO2, and collected from ~30 million cells. For in vivo supplementation, CM was filtered through a 0.45 μm strainer and concentrated by 3 kDa Amicon filters to a final volume of 100 μl/mouse, stored at -20°C. Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) were loaded with CM or serum-free medium (SM) as control and implanted i.p. immediately following tumor excision. The authors estimated that excised primary tumors contain ~50×10^6 secretome-producing cells, and the osmotic pump delivery rate was ~1/8 of in vivo production per day. Adhesion studies involved incubating cells in SM or CM for 8 hours, imaged at 20-minute intervals using the IncuCyte system, and counting adhered cells. Apoptosis studies incubated cells in CM or SM for 24 hours, followed by Annexin V-FITC and 7AAD staining and flow cytometry. Tube formation assays used 24-well plates with 50 μl basement membrane extracellular matrix, seeding HUVECs reconstituted in CM or SM, imaged at 20-minute intervals for 24 h. Human cytokine analysis compared 102 soluble human proteins in CM samples and plasma samples from mice bearing a PT, one day post-excision, and control mice, each pooled from 3 mice. Mass spectrometry proteomics processed CM samples through 3 kDa Amicon filtration, 8M urea mixing, trypsin digestion overnight, C18 StageTips desalting, and UHPLC coupled to a Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer with a 140-minute linear gradient. MS/MS was performed using a top10 method with HCD fragmentation, and raw files were analyzed by MaxQuant and the Label-free quantification algorithm with a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.01. Neutralizing antibodies included mouse anti-human monoclonal IgG1 for IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF, with mouse IgG1 as isotype control, each injected once daily at 1 μg/mouse for two days. Patient outcome analysis used the public TCGA provisional dataset via cBioPortal, stratifying lung adenocarcinoma patients by RPPA-assayed protein levels of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF, with survival analyzed by Kaplan-Meier and hazard ratio in R. Statistical analysis used repeated-measures or factorial ANOVA (significance 0.05), Fisher's PLSD post-hoc tests, and student's t-test (paired/unpaired) with F-test for equality of variance, all two-sided.

Procedures And Architectures
The experimental design compared primary tumor excision, sham surgery, and PT-secretome supplementation across multiple metastatic stages and in vitro assays. Bioluminescence imaging was the primary readout, with metastases quantified as total photon counts; excision was defined at 10^6 photons/s. The in vitro assays established that CM, not SM, enhanced cancer cell viability, adhesion, and induced endothelial tube formation. The in vivo secretome supplementation design was a rescue experiment where CM (representing PT factors) was delivered via minipump at the time of excision to counteract regression. The cytokine array selection method excluded factors expressed in non-tumor-bearing mice or in plasma one day after PT excision, isolating factors unique to the PT-bearing state. The antibody neutralization cocktail was injected 24 hours prior to tumor excision at early metastatic stage (bioluminescence < 10^6 p/s), and survival was compared to IgG1 isotype control. Histology confirmed that metastatic foci were present on the day after excision and 50 days later, verified by H&E staining of 6 μm lung sections. The computational pipeline for proteomics integrated MaxQuant, the Label-free quantification algorithm, and Perseus software for statistical analysis. Pathway enrichment analysis used Gene Ontology annotations from UniProt with a Fisher exact test and FDR threshold of 0.02. Protein-protein interaction networks were constructed using the STRING database. The human cytokine array analyzed 102 soluble proteins, and the mass spectrometry identified 2,600 proteins, of which 359 were annotated as extracellular factors.

Key Results
A dramatic 100-fold decrease in metastatic bioluminescent signal was evident within 24 hours following primary tumor excision (p<0.0001). No increase in in vivo bioluminescent signal occurred for 50 days post-excision, and microscopic malignant foci were confirmed on day 1 and day 50 by H&E staining. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases (10^7 photons/sec) compared to small metastases (10^6 photons/sec), p<0.000. Metastases regressed significantly following excision of the primary tumor but continued to increase in mice subjected to sham surgery, p<0.05. Mice treated with tumor-cell conditioned medium showed 10-fold less regression than mice that received serum-free medium, p<0.005. The human cytokine array identified 28 cytokines highly expressed in cancer cell CM, four of which were unique to the PT-bearing state: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF. The LC-MS proteomics identified 2,600 proteins, with 359 annotated as extracellular factors, and pathway enrichment showed proteins engaged in apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth factor activity, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation. Antibody neutralization of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF completely blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001) in the presence of the primary tumor. No difference in regression of metastases was evident between antibody-treated and isotype-control groups on post-excision day-1, as excision removed all secreted factors in both. Larger metastases showed lower or no regression, consistent with the finding that established metastatic foci may be self-sufficient. The hazard ratio for poor survival in lung adenocarcinoma patients with high levels of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF was 2.05, p<0.05.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study demonstrates that the primary tumor secretome is a vital factor in promoting metastasis during early stages, challenging the view that the primary tumor is primarily metastasis-inhibitory. The four identified factors—IL-8, MIF, Serpin E1, and PDGFaa—are all known to promote angiogenesis and/or suppress tumor apoptosis through shared and distinct pathways. Regression was more prominent in small metastatic foci, suggesting that early-stage micrometastases rely on PT-derived factors for survival while larger, established metastases may achieve factor self-sufficiency. The finding that the perioperative period can be exploited to control minimal residual disease by blocking PT support for micro-metastases has therapeutic implications. Identifying critical pro-metastatic factors secreted by the primary tumor in each patient based on pre-operative malignant tissue biopsy could enable individually tailored neutralizing antibody combinations. The use of high-sensitivity codon-optimized luciferase was essential for detection of early-stage regression that would be overlooked with standard imaging.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study used only one tumor model (MDA-MB-231 HM) and one animal model (BALB/c nu/nu), limiting generalizability to other cancer types or syngeneic systems. The antibody neutralization study was conducted at an early metastatic stage (<10^6 p/s) and may not reflect effects at more advanced disease. The estimation that osmotic pump delivery rate was 1/8 of in vivo production is a rough calculation based on ~50×10^6 estimated cells per PT volume. The patient outcome analysis was retrospective, used a single public dataset (TCGA), and was limited to lung adenocarcinoma. The prevalence of post-operative regression of micro-metastases in cancer patients is currently unknown due to technical limitations. Other secreted factors beyond the four neutralized are likely to also be involved in supporting metastatic progression, but were not tested.

Claims
Primary tumor excision induces spontaneous regression of early-stage micro-metastases because the primary tumor secretes factors that sustain metastatic survival. A 100-fold decrease in metastatic signal within 24 hours post-excision was observed (p<0.0001). Sham surgery without PT removal did not cause regression, isolating the effect to PT elimination (p<0.05). 10-fold reduction in regression when PM-conditioned medium was supplemented via osmotic minipump (p<0.005). Regression was significantly less prominent in larger (10^7 photons/sec) metastases, indicating the effect is stage-specific. No difference in regression was observed between antibody-treated and isotype-control groups on post-excision day-1. The perioperative period represents a window of opportunity to block PT-derived pro-metastatic factors before and after surgery. Individualized combination therapy using neutralizing antibodies tailored to a patient's pre-operative tissue profile could counteract surgery-induced metastasis.
IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF are the key primary tumor-secreted factors promoting early metastatic survival and arrest of metastatic progression upon neutralization. The antibody cocktail completely blocked metastatic progression in the presence of the primary tumor (p<0.0001). The four factors were uniquely expressed in the PT-bearing state and identified by cytokine array and LC-MS proteomics. High levels of these four factors in TCGA lung adenocarcinoma correlated with poor survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05). The study only tested the combined effect of four factors; other secreted factors were likely also involved. These four factors serve as potential perioperative biomarkers and therapeutic targets for minimal residual disease. The findings may explain the rare clinical phenomenon of spontaneous regression after PT excision.

Data And Code Availability
The paper references the public TCGA provisional dataset via cBioPortal for patient outcome analysis. The exact source of the MDA-MB-231 HM cell line is noted as a gift from Dr. Zhou Ou, Fudan University. Specific software used for data analysis includes MaxQuant, Label-free quantification algorithm, Perseus, Image J, and R for Kaplan-Meier analysis. No mention of public code or data repositories beyond the TCGA dataset is provided in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The sham surgery comparison (PT excised vs. PT untouched) was used to dissociate surgical trauma effects from PT-secretome elimination. The 10-fold regression rescue with tumor-cell conditioned medium directly tested the secretome hypothesis. The comparison of small (10^6 p/s) vs. large (10^7 p/s) metastases served as a validation of stage-specificity. The cytokine array selection method (excluding factors present in non-tumor-bearing or post-excision plasma) served as a filtering procedure to identify PT-specific factors.

Ethical Considerations
All procedures were approved by Monash University or Tel-Aviv University Animal Ethics Committees. Mice were housed under SPF conditions on a 12 h dark/light cycle. Animals were randomly assigned to experimental conditions. Animals were euthanized 10 minutes following luciferin injection at the endpoint.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-B: Showed 100-fold decrease in metastatic bioluminescent signal within 24 hours of tumor excision (p<0.0001). Figure 1C: Demonstrated no increase in in vivo bioluminescent signal for 50 days post-excision. Figure 1D: H&E staining of lungs and lymph nodes on day 1 and day 50 confirmed the presence of microscopic malignant foci. Figure 1E: Showed that regression was significantly less prominent in larger (10^7 photons/sec) versus small metastases (p<0.000). Figure 1F: Compared metastatic signal between primary tumor excision and sham surgery (p<0.05). Figure 2A: CM enhanced cancer cell viability (p<0.001). Figure 2B: CM enhanced cancer cell adhesion (p<0.01). Figure 2C: CM induced tube formation of human endothelial cells (p<0.0001). Figure 2D: Showed 10-fold less regression with tumor-cell conditioned medium supplementation (p<0.005). Figure 3A: STRING database protein-protein interaction network identifying pathways involved in early metastasis. Figure 3B: Showed complete block of metastatic progression by antibody cocktail vs. IgG control (p<0.0001). Figure 3C: Showed no difference in regression on post-excision day-1, suggesting excision removed all secreted factors. Figure 3D: Kaplan-Meier survival curve showing high IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF levels correlated with poorer survival (HR=2.05, p<0.05). Table S1: Listed cytokines identified in CM but excluded from analysis because they were present in non-tumor-bearing or post-excision plasma.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first animal model of spontaneous metastatic regression following primary tumor excision, demonstrating that PT-secreted factors sustain early-stage micro-metastases and their removal induces regression. 2. The strongest evidence is the 100-fold regression within 24 hours post-excision (p<0.0001), the 10-fold rescue with tumor-cell conditioned medium (p<0.005), and the complete in vivo blockade of metastatic progression by neutralizing IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF (p<0.0001). 3. The future path involves testing these findings in syngeneic animal models, identifying other PT-secreted factors, and exploiting the perioperative window through individually tailored neutralizing antibody combinations to control minimal residual disease.

summary.title: Activation of Macrophages by CpG DNA and LPS: an FTIR Spectroscopic Study
summary.authors: Emrulla Spahiu, Senol Dogan, Jörg Schnauß, Mayda Gursel, Feride Severcan
summary.field_subfield: Immunology / FTIR Spectroscopy
summary.executive_summary:
This study uses Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells upon activation with CpG DNA (1 µM K3 ODN) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS; 0.5 µg/ml). The researchers demonstrate that FTIR spectroscopy, when combined with Principal Component Analysis (PCA), can capture global molecular changes in nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids that are not readily accessible by other omics techniques. 

Key quantitative findings include: Principal Component 1 accounted for 83% of variance, with PC-2 contributing 11%, identifying the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ IR region as the primary source of variation. CpG DNA stimulated cells showed significant increases in nucleic acid content (1238 cm⁻¹ phosphate vibration) from 10 min to 6 h post-treatment (p < 0.1), with the RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ rising significantly from the first minutes (p < 0.001) and persisting until 2 h (p < 0.1). DNA synthesis followed RNA synthesis, starting from 6 h post-CpG stimulation. LPS treatment induced increased total RNA up to 2 h post-stimulation but showed no significant changes in nucleic acid content after 6 h, consistent with its anti-proliferative effects. 

Protein content (amide I, 1639 cm⁻¹ and amide II, 1540 cm⁻¹) increased significantly from 10 min to 2 h (p < 0.001) with CpG DNA and showed a similar transient increase with LPS, before declining starting from the 2 h time point. Both CpG and LPS treatments triggered a very significant increase in triglycerides and cholesterol (1741 cm⁻¹) from the first minutes of stimulation (CpG) or after 10 min (LPS), and a significant increase in fatty acid concentration (1400 cm⁻¹), pointing to shared de novo lipogenesis pathways. The authors conclude that the 915 cm⁻¹ RNA-specific peak can define the activation state of macrophages at the very first minutes post-treatment, filling a gap in the overall picture of macrophage activation dynamics. This study marks the first demonstration of FTIR spectroscopy as an independent modality for monitoring these activation kinetics.

CpG and LPS trigger de novo lipogenesis in macrophages through shared metabolic pathways.

This study uses Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells upon activation with CpG DNA (1 µM K3 ODN) and lipopolysaccharide (LPS; 0.5 µg/ml). The researchers demonstrate that FTIR spectroscopy, when combined with Principal Component Analysis (PCA), can capture global molecular changes in nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids that are not readily accessible by other omics techniques. 

Key quantitative findings include: Principal Component 1 accounted for 83% of variance, with PC-2 contributing 11%, identifying the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ IR region as the primary source of variation. CpG DNA stimulated cells showed significant increases in nucleic acid content (1238 cm⁻¹ phosphate vibration) from 10 min to 6 h post-treatment (p < 0.1), with the RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ rising significantly from the first minutes (p < 0.001) and persisting until 2 h (p < 0.1). DNA synthesis followed RNA synthesis, starting from 6 h post-CpG stimulation. LPS treatment induced increased total RNA up to 2 h post-stimulation but showed no significant changes in nucleic acid content after 6 h, consistent with its anti-proliferative effects. 

Protein content (amide I, 1639 cm⁻¹ and amide II, 1540 cm⁻¹) increased significantly from 10 min to 2 h (p < 0.001) with CpG DNA and showed a similar transient increase with LPS, before declining starting from the 2 h time point. Both CpG and LPS treatments triggered a very significant increase in triglycerides and cholesterol (1741 cm⁻¹) from the first minutes of stimulation (CpG) or after 10 min (LPS), and a significant increase in fatty acid concentration (1400 cm⁻¹), pointing to shared de novo lipogenesis pathways. The authors conclude that the 915 cm⁻¹ RNA-specific peak can define the activation state of macrophages at the very first minutes post-treatment, filling a gap in the overall picture of macrophage activation dynamics. This study marks the first demonstration of FTIR spectroscopy as an independent modality for monitoring these activation kinetics.

Research Context
FTIR spectroscopy has developed into a powerful biomedical tool for non-destructive, rapid, and high-throughput analysis of biological systems. The infrared spectrum serves as a chemical fingerprint for all cell metabolites, with peak area providing quantitative concentration data and absorption frequencies revealing molecular bond nature. A major limitation of infrared spectroscopy is water absorbance, which superimposes on aqueous cell system signals, a challenge overcome by the Fourier transform procedure. The ATR spectroscopy configuration eliminates the need for sample preparation and requires minimal sample amount for high-quality spectra. ATR-FTIR spectroscopy has been applied in hematology, live cell activation analysis, disease screening, chemical stress response, disease state identification, and cellular differentiation. Macrophages constitute the frontline of the immune system, defending the organism against invaders with high structural and functional plasticity. CpG DNA triggers macrophage proliferation, pro-inflammatory cytokine production, induction of Th1 reactions, and activation of antigen-presenting cells. LPS stimulates monocytes and macrophages, inducing biological response mediators including TNF-α and interleukins, preventing microbial infection. LPS recognition occurs through the TLR4 pathway, sharing high homology with TLR-9 signaling carried out by CpG DNA. Both CpG and LPS require MyD88 as the adaptor protein and activate NF-κB as well as AP-1 transcription factors. Trending omics techniques provide precise quantitative data on specific molecules but require complex sample preparation that can alter chemical ratios and post-translational modifications. The simple, rapid, and non-invasive experimental setup using bulk FTIR provides a broad view of metabolite ratios not readily accessible by other techniques.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation leads to global molecular changes in cells detectable by FTIR spectroscopy. Prior work established that CpG DNA improves host survival following pathogen challenge, but how CpG ODN-mediated activation impacts relative amounts of nucleic acids, lipids, and proteins had not been studied. The authors hypothesize that ATR-FTIR spectroscopy can monitor global molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells upon activation with CpG DNA and LPS. PCA analysis was planned to identify sources of variation and guide selection of peaks for detailed spectral analysis. The study aims to examine global molecular changes in murine macrophage cells upon treatment with CpG DNA and LPS using ATR-FTIR spectroscopy. The authors expected that many cells could be probed simultaneously, yielding statistically significant data sets. A central hypothesis was that the RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ could define the activation state of macrophages at the very first minutes post-treatment. The study predicted that DNA synthesis would follow RNA synthesis in a time-dependent manner, and that LPS would inhibit DNA synthesis.

Methodological Details
Murine macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells were cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO₂ in DMEM supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 2 mM L-glutamine. Sub-culturing was performed in a 1/10 ratio upon reaching acceptable confluency, generally every 2-3 days. Cells were harvested, spun at 1000 rpm (208 g) for 10 min, and resuspended at a concentration of 2×10⁶ /mL. The control group was treated with phosphate-buffered saline (0.9% PBS) from Sigma. The CpG DNA stimulated group was treated with 1 µM K3 ODN (endotoxin-free from Integrated DNA Technologies). The LPS stimulated group was treated with 0.5 µg/ml LPS from Sigma. Four time points following treatment were used to evaluate kinetics: 10 min, 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h. When incubation time was reached, samples were spun at 1000 rpm, washed with 15 mL of sterile PBS, and spun again to remove media. For ATR-FTIR spectroscopic analysis, cell samples of 1 µl were dried with mild N₂ flux for 5 min to allow cells to settle on the crystal. The ATR unit featured a Diamond-ZnSe crystal. Cell samples were recorded in the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ region at 25°C using a Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One FTIR spectrometer. Air background was measured and subtracted automatically by the Spectrum One software; the PBS spectrum was recorded and subtracted manually. The best signal-to-noise ratio was achieved with 128 scan number and 2 cm⁻¹ spectral resolution. The ATR surface was cleaned using a water-ethanol-water sequence and then air-dried. Each group was scanned under the same conditions in three independent scans (the average constitutes a replicate). Replicates of n=5 were used in data analysis.

Procedures And Architectures
Spectra of cell samples were recorded in the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ region at 25°C using the Diamond-ZnSe ATR crystal. Air background was measured and subtracted automatically by the Spectrum One software; the PBS spectrum was recorded and subtracted manually. Cell samples of 1 µl were dried with mild N₂ flux for 5 min to allow cells to settle on the crystal. The best signal-to-noise ratio for interferogram collection was achieved with 128 scan number at 2 cm⁻¹ spectral resolution. The ATR surface was cleaned using a water-ethanol-water sequence before each measurement. Each group was scanned in three independent scans (the average constitutes a replicate). Post-processing included 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction at 3800-2750-1800-900 cm⁻¹ points using the Spectrum One software. Baseline correction was performed at 3800-2750-1800-900 cm⁻¹ points. PCA was performed using the spectra imported directly into the Unscrambler 11.0 software in the 3000-650 cm⁻¹ region. PCA was conducted on the data matrix obtained from spectral readings of 0.5 cm⁻¹ resolution. Peak assignment used the center of weight measurements and literature comparison. For the side-peak band assignment, the second derivative spectrum was used. Concentration studies were carried out by integrating the curves under the peaks. For conformational alteration studies, bandwidth measurements were done manually using the 75% height of the peaks. Normality of datasets was assessed using Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests. Statistical analysis was performed with GraphPad Prism 8.3.

Key Results
PCA revealed that Principal Component (PC)-1 accounted for 83% of the variance, identifying the vast source of variation. PC-2 had a variability of 11%, and the Loadings Plots showed the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ IR region having numerous peaks with high variation among samples. The peaks at 1238 cm⁻¹ (nucleic acids-phosphate vibration) and 1085 cm⁻¹ (symmetric PO₂⁻ stretching) showed prominent differences starting from 10 min post-treatment. CpG DNA stimulation induced significant changes in nucleic acid content (1238 cm⁻¹ peak integration) of macrophages starting from 10 min until 6 h after treatment (p < 0.1). The RNA-specific peak (ribose vibration) at 915 cm⁻¹ increased significantly from the first minutes post-stimulation (p < 0.001). This increase in the 915 cm⁻¹ peak was maintained until 2 h after stimulation (p < 0.1). DNA synthesis starts from 6 h after stimulation with CpG DNA, following RNA synthesis. CpG DNA treatment showed a significant increase in total protein content (amide I band, 1639 cm⁻¹) from 10 min to 2 h post-treatment (p < 0.001). A similar protein increase change was observed upon LPS stimulation, with the initial increase reduced starting from the 2 h time point. Triglyceride and cholesterol concentrations (1741 cm⁻¹) showed a very significant increase starting from the very first minutes of stimulation with CpG DNA. summary.title: The Foster method: Rapid and non-invasive detection of clinically significant American Foulbrood disease levels using eDNA sampling and a dual-target qPCR assay, with its potential for other hive pathogens
summary.authors: John F Mackay, Rebecca E Hewett, Noa T Smith, Tammy L Waters, John S Scandrett
summary.field_subfield: Apicultural Science / Molecular Diagnostics - American Foulbrood Detection
summary.executive_summary: The Foster method introduces a novel, non-invasive environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling approach for detecting American Foulbrood (AFB) in honeybee colonies, combined with a dual-target multiplex qPCR assay (AFBduo) for Paenibacillus larvae. AFB, caused by hardy spores of P. larvae that persist for over 30 years, is one of the most destructive bee diseases worldwide. Traditional diagnosis relies on subjective visual inspection by beekeepers, which is time-consuming and often misses infections, requiring thousands of brood cells to be examined per hive. Previous molecular testing methods necessitated hive dismantling or multiple visits to retrieve passive samples. The Foster method uses colony entrance swabs and a multiplex qPCR assay targeting both the single-copy ftsZ gene, used for spore quantification, and the multi-copy 16S gene, providing high sensitivity. In three cohorts of quarantine apiaries in New Zealand (sampled from late 2018 to early 2020), 45 hives were sampled up to six times in the first cohort, 23 hives in the second, and pooled trials used eight and later twelve swab eluate pools. The assay demonstrated analytical sensitivity down to 4 copies per 10 µL reaction, with ftsZ efficiency of 94% and 16S at 96%, showing linearity over seven orders of magnitude with r = 0.998. The 16S target amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than ftsZ due to multiple copy numbers. Binary logistic regression revealed that a spore count of 565,000 or more corresponds to a 95% probability of clinical signs. The entrance-swabbing approach eliminated the need to dismantle hives for sampling, and the method identified a pre-clinical infection in Hive 11. The method is named the Foster method and has potential application to Nosema ceranae, European foulbrood, tracheal mites, and small hive beetle detection. This rapid, one-time sampling and quantification method provides clinically significant information for AFB management.

claims.description: The Foster method enables non-invasive, rapid detection of clinically significant AFB through colony entrance swabbing and dual-target qPCR.
The dual-target qPCR (AFBduo) provides high confidence due to the integrated internal control and two markers.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The Foster method introduces a novel, non-invasive environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling approach for detecting American Foulbrood (AFB) in honeybee colonies, combined with a dual-target multiplex qPCR assay (AFBduo) for Paenibacillus larvae. AFB, caused by hardy spores of P. larvae that persist for over 30 years, is one of the most destructive bee diseases worldwide. Traditional diagnosis relies on subjective visual inspection by beekeepers, which is time-consuming and often misses infections, requiring thousands of brood cells to be examined per hive. Previous molecular testing methods necessitated hive dismantling or multiple visits to retrieve passive samples. The Foster method uses colony entrance swabs and a multiplex qPCR assay targeting both the single-copy ftsZ gene, used for spore quantification, and the multi-copy 16S gene, providing high sensitivity. In three cohorts of quarantine apiaries in New Zealand (sampled from late 2018 to early 2020), 45 hives were sampled up to six times in the first cohort, 23 hives in the second, and pooled trials used eight and later twelve swab eluate pools. The assay demonstrated analytical sensitivity down to 4 copies per 10 µL reaction, with ftsZ efficiency of 94% and 16S at 96%, showing linearity over seven orders of magnitude with r = 0.998. The 16S target amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than ftsZ due to multiple copy numbers. Binary logistic regression revealed that a spore count of 565,000 or more corresponds to a 95% probability of clinical signs. The entrance-swabbing approach eliminated the need to dismantle hives for sampling, and the method identified a pre-clinical infection in Hive 11. The method is named the Foster method and has potential application to Nosema ceranae, European foulbrood, tracheal mites, and small hive beetle detection. This rapid, one-time sampling and quantification method provides clinically significant information for AFB management.

Research Context
American Foulbrood is one of the most destructive bee diseases, caused by hardy spores of Paenibacillus larvae. These spores are extremely resistant to heat and chemical treatments, remaining infectious for over 30 years. A single infected larva can generate millions of spores, leading to rapid colony decline. Infection spreads through direct transmission, robbing, and unknowingly through beekeeper activity. In New Zealand, the percentage of hives reported as infected rose from 0.21% in 2015 to 0.46% in 2021. Traditional diagnosis is based on subjective visual inspection, requiring thousands of brood cells to be examined per hive. Prior molecular testing required dismantling the hive or multiple visits to insert and remove sampling sheets. qPCR had been used for rapid confirmation, but the quantification data generated was not previously utilized for clinical assessment. Low-level AFB infections are often not clinically relevant, creating a need for threshold quantification.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether colony entrance swabs combined with dual-target qPCR can detect clinically significant AFB before visual symptoms appear. The hypothesis is that a non-invasive entrance swab sampling method can detect relevant P. larvae levels for clinical management. A key objective is to evaluate and compare the levels of P. larvae among bees, the entire baseboard, and the entrance region. The study aims to establish a threshold spore quantity that correlates with the probability of clinical AFB signs. A secondary objective is to determine if the sampling method can detect pre-clinical or sub-clinical infections missed by visual inspection. The authors further explore whether the entrance-swabbing method can be adapted for other bee pathogens and incursion pests.

Methodological Details
Five quarantine apiaries in New Zealand from four regions (East Coast, Wellington, Wairarapa, South Canterbury) were sampled. Multiple hives were sampled two-monthly from late 2018 to early 2020. In the first cohort, 45 hives were sampled up to 6 times. Eight hives had clinical signs of AFB, and another six were presumed to have AFB. In the second cohort, 23 hives were tested, with four showing clinical signs. A third cohort involved pooling swab eluates into groups of eight and later twelve. Nurse bees were collected from brood frames using 50 mL sterile containers and frozen. Each sample contained 10 bees for practical ease of handling and throughput. Foam-tipped swabs were moistened in sterile water and applied for 3-5 seconds. Swab heads were snapped off into 2 mL microcentrifuge tubes and sent by overnight courier. Genomic DNA was extracted using the Bee Pathogen DNA/RNA Extraction Kit from dnature diagnostics. Bees were homogenized in a Mini Beadbeater 16 for 3 minutes with zirconia silica beads. The beads were 0.5 mm (~2.4 g) and 2.3 mm zirconia silica (~1 g). Tubes were incubated at 65°C for 10 minutes with manual inversion every 3 minutes. 1 mL of homogenate was centrifuged at 15,000 x g for 5 minutes. 500 µL of supernatant was transferred to a new tube with 450 µL AD buffer. Swabs were processed similarly with 0.5 mm and 2.3 mm beads and 800 µL DXL buffer. For pooled applications, individual swabs were vortexed for 10 seconds in 500 µL DXL buffer. 60 µL of each swab eluate (up to twelve swabs) was added for pooled extraction. A synthetic 153 bp ftsZ standard was quantified on a DS-11 FX microvolume spectrophotometer. Standards ranged from 10^6 copies per µL down to 2 copies per µL. The diluent was a pooled DNA sample extracted from bees free of P. larvae. Copies were calculated using the equation including Avogadro's constant and 660 g/mole. Statistical analysis included binary logistic regression and ANOVA, with p < 0.05 considered significant.

Procedures And Architectures
The AFBduo assay is a commercially available multiplex qPCR for P. larvae from Hall et al., 2021. The assay targets both the single-copy ftsZ gene and the multi-copy 16S gene. Hydrolysis probe TaqMan qPCR assays permit quantification of each target by selected fluorescent wavelengths. An internal control is included in an additional detection channel to confirm suitable quality DNA. DNA was extracted via a column-based kit in conjunction with beadbeating. Beadbeating homogenization was performed for 3 minutes in a Mini Beadbeater 16. Incubation occurred at 65°C for 10 minutes with manual inversion every 3 minutes. After centrifugation at 15,000 x g for 5 minutes, 500 µL of supernatant was used. The solution was applied to a nucleic acid binding column in two passes and centrifuged. Elution was performed in 100 µL elution buffer. For quantification, the single-copy ftsZ gene was used with a standard curve. The standard curve was prepared with a quantified synthetic template diluted in AFB-negative bee DNA. The qPCR assay utilized hydrolysis probes and internal controls for robustness.

Key Results
The AFBduo assay reliably detected P. larvae down to 4 copies per 10 µL reaction. Amplification efficiencies were 94% for ftsZ and 96% for the 16S target. The assay showed excellent linearity over seven orders of magnitude with r = 0.998. The 16S target typically amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than the ftsZ target. DNA extraction from bees yielded OD260/280 measurements between 1.8 and 1.9. Extracted DNA samples serially diluted showed the expected increase in Cq's, indicating no inhibitors. DNA yields from swabs were too low to be measured by spectrophotometer, but internal control Cq's confirmed quality. In the first cohort, 8 hives had clinical AFB signs while 6 were presumed AFB positive. Cohort one included 45 hives sampled up to 6 times during the 2018-2019/20 seasons. In the second cohort, 4 of 23 hives showed clinical AFB signs. Pooling swab eluates into groups of eight and later twelve allowed detection of single hives with higher AFB levels. Binary logistic regression and ANOVA indicated a strong relationship between spore levels and clinical signs, p = 0.00. A spore quantity of 565,000 or more revealed a 95% probability of clinical signs being present. The FtsZ gene was used for spore level conversion: Spores = 10(Cq_ftsZ-39/-3.48) x 50.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 16S marker's higher analytical sensitivity (3-5 cycles earlier) is due to its multi-copy nature. Variability in Cq difference between the two markers indicates 16S copy number varies among AFB isolates. The 16S gene cannot be relied on for quantification, making ftsZ the suitable quantification target. Entrance-swabbing removed the need to dismantle and disrupt the hive for sampling, a major practical advantage. Hive 11 showed high bee spore levels and clinical signs two weeks after the sampling, demonstrating detection of pre-clinical infection. Hive 11 and 12 showed high bee spore levels but low or undetectable hiveware levels. The low hiveware levels were explained by new hiveware (<2 weeks old) and insufficient time for spore accumulation. The method has potential for Nosema ceranae detection, with good correlation between bee and debris levels. The sampling technique combined with appropriate qPCR could detect tracheal mites, tropilaelap mites, and small hive beetle. The Foster method is named as a fast, one-time sampling and quantification method amenable to composite testing.

Contradictions And Limitations
Hives 11 and 12 showed discordance between bee and hiveware spore levels. This discrepancy was due to new hiveware and insufficient time for spore accumulation at the entrance. Further research is required to assess spore accumulation rates on the hive surface. Spore levels never increased during the monitoring time for many hives, or became undetectable in some low-spore cases. The study is limited to New Zealand quarantine apiaries, restricting external generalizability. The 16S gene copy number variability makes it unsuitable for absolute quantification. The clinical spore threshold of 565,000 is based on the limited data points available in this study. The study does not report the random seed, train/test split, or demographic details of the beekeepers.

Claims
The Foster method enables non-invasive, rapid detection of clinically significant AFB through colony entrance swabbing and dual-target qPCR. Entrance-swabbing removed the need to dismantle hives for sampling. A spore count of 565,000 or more corresponds to a 95% probability of clinical signs. The method identified Hive 11 with clinical signs two weeks after pre-clinical sampling. The assay detected down to 4 copies per 10 µL with 94% ftsZ efficiency. Hives 11 and 12 showed discordant bee and hiveware levels, with low entrance spores despite high bee levels. Spore levels never increased for many hives during the monitoring period. The study was conducted in a limited number of quarantine apiaries. Rapid, one-time sampling reduces beekeeper labor and hive disruption. The method provides early detection of infections missed by visual inspection. The quantification threshold enables targeted intervention for hives at clinical risk.
The dual-target qPCR (AFBduo) provides high confidence due to the integrated internal control and two markers. The assay targets both single-copy ftsZ and multi-copy 16S. High analytical sensitivity was demonstrated down to 4 copies. Linearity was excellent over seven orders of magnitude with r = 0.998. The internal control confirmed DNA was of suitable quality. The 16S copy number varies among isolates, precluding its use for quantification. The 16S marker showed variability in Cq difference among samples. The ftsZ gene remains the reliable target for absolute spore quantification. The internal control enhances sensitivity by mitigating inhibition effects.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The assay demonstrated robustness with an internal control for DNA quality. Sensitivity and linearity were validated with synthetic standards from 10^6 down to 2 copies per µL. A second cohort of 23 hives confirmed the method's generalizability in a different operation. Pooling of 8 and 12 swab eluates demonstrated detection of single-hive AFB within a pool. The 16S marker amplified 3-5 cycles earlier than ftsZ, confirming expected behavior. DNA purity was confirmed with OD260/280 between 1.8 and 1.9. The use of two independent targets enhances both sensitivity and specificity. The synthetic 153 bp ftsZ standard is available on request.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 shows the progression of P. larvae levels in three colonies converted to spores per 10 bee or swab sample. Table 2 compares nurse bee spore levels with entrance swab levels in the second cohort of 23 hives. Table 3 presents the results of the pooling trials with groups of eight and later twelve swab eluates. Table 4 compares spore levels among bees, whole baseboard, and entrance swabs in the first cohort. Supplementary Figure 4 displays the analysis of variance confirming the correlation between entrance spores and clinical signs. Supplementary S1 contains the standards and their resulting Cq's for conversion.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the Foster method: a non-invasive entrance-swabbing procedure combined with a dual-target qPCR assay (AFBduo) for quantification of clinically significant AFB in honeybee colonies. 2. The strongest evidence is the binary logistic regression showing that a spore quantity of 565,000 or more yields a 95% probability of clinical AFB signs, validated across multiple cohorts and pooling trials. 3. The future path includes refining the clinical spore threshold, assessing spore accumulation rates on hive surfaces, and adapting the method to other bee pathogens and biosecurity monitoring.

3. A hydrolysis probe TaqMan assay permits quantification of each target.
4. An internal control is included in an additional detection channel.
5. DNA extraction used the Bee Pathogen DNA/RNA Extraction Kit from dnature.
6. Homogenization employed a Mini Beadbeater 16 instrument.
7. Beadbeating beads were 0.5 mm and 2.3 mm zirconia silica.
8. Incubation was at 65°C with manual inversion every 3 minutes.
9. Supernatant was applied to a nucleic acid binding column in two passes.
10. Elution was performed in 100 µL elution buffer.
11. The ftsZ gene was used for quantification due to its single-copy nature.
12. The 16S gene provided higher analytical sensitivity but not quantification.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The authors develop SPOT-Contact-Single, a protein contact-map prediction method that eliminates the need for multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) or evolutionary profiles, addressing a major limitation in existing contact-map predictors that rely on homologous sequence information. The method leverages the attention maps from a pre-trained Transformer language model (ESM-1b) concatenated with one-hot amino acid encodings and one-dimensional structural feature outputs from a single-sequence predictor (SPOT-1D-Single) as input to an ensemble of residual neural networks (ResNet12 architectures). Trained on a large, non-redundant dataset of 34,691 proteins with high-resolution crystal structures (< 2.5 Å), the model uses an ensemble of six variants (three with direct contact prediction and three with distogram-based bin prediction across three feature combinations). Key results demonstrate that SPOT-Contact-Single outperforms the state-of-the-art single-sequence-based predictor SSCpred by 15% in F1-score on the independent CASP14-FM test set. On proteins without homologous sequences (Neff=1) in the independent SPOT-2018 dataset, it surpasses TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact by 48.7% and 48.5% in F1-score, respectively. The attention maps from the last layer of ESM-1b alone provide F1-scores of 0.51 and MCC of 0.50 on the validation set, representing a 242% improvement in F1 over the one-hot encoding baseline and a 178% improvement over the combination of one-hot and SPOT-1D-Single features. Feature importance analysis reveals that concatenating all features (one-hot + SPOT-1D-Single + all-layer ESM-1b attention maps) further improves F1-score by 2.92%. The method is also substantially faster than profile-based methods, requiring only 116 seconds on CPU for 15 proteins versus 1926 seconds for TrRosetta on GPU, making it suitable for genomic-scale prediction. The paper concludes that unsupervised language model features provide a viable alternative to MSA-based methods for proteins with limited homology, although performance decreases as Neff increases, highlighting that co-mutation information from MSAs still provides additional predictive signal.

Research Context
The past two decades have seen many developments in protein structure prediction, particularly for secondary structure, contact-and distance-map prediction, and tertiary structure prediction. Protein contact maps can be predicted by statistical inference based on the Potts model or deep learning-based predictors. A common trait among existing predictors is the use of multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and other homology-based profile information. However, many proteins have very few or no homologs to generate MSA and homology profiles, causing their performance to drop significantly in these cases. SSCpred is a single-sequence-based method using one-hot encoding and SPIDER3-Single one-dimensional structural properties, but it performs relatively poorer for proteins with effective homologs compared to MSA-based techniques. Unsupervised deep learning methods inspired by NLP language models have been introduced to extract protein features from reference libraries such as Uniref50, Uniclust, Pfam, and BFD. ESM-1b is a Transformer-34 model trained on Uniref50 that outputs an embedding and attention maps, and its use as an input feature was examined in this work.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the attention maps from a pre-trained Transformer language model (ESM-1b) can serve as effective input features to improve single-sequence-based protein contact-map prediction without requiring homologous sequences. The authors hypothesize that unsupervised learning features from ESM-1b, when concatenated with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs, will outperform SSCpred and MSA-based predictors for proteins with a low effective number of homologous proteins (Neff). A second hypothesis is that an ensemble of models trained through different training approaches (direct contact vs. distogram) and different feature combinations will add to the performance improvement. The authors predict that the proposed method will provide a faster and reasonably accurate alternative to evolution-based methods suitable for large-scale prediction. A sub-question is which feature combinations and training strategies yield the best performance for contact-map prediction. The method is also expected to perform better on de-novo and protein-without-homolog test sets (Neff=1) compared to profile-based methods.

Methodological Details
The authors used the ProteinNet benchmark dataset consisting of 50,914 proteins submitted to PDB before 2016 with high resolution (< 2.5 Å) crystal structures, clustered at sequence identity cut-off of 95% according to MMseqs2. To ensure independence, 100 proteins were separated as a validation set and any proteins with hits at e-value < 0.1 were removed, leaving 39,120 proteins for training. After removing proteins with length more than 500, the final training and validation sets contained 34,691 and 88 proteins, respectively. For independent testing, proteins released between May 2018 and April 2020 were downloaded, and any potential homologs in the training set were removed using HHblits at e-value < 0.1. The resulting 669 proteins form the stringent SPOT-2018 test set. A subset of 46 proteins with Neff=1 from SPOT-2018 forms the Neff1-2018 test set, where Neff is calculated with respect to the Uniclust30 reference dataset. The CASP14-FM dataset includes 15 free-modeling targets released at CASP14, which are proteins without known structural templates in PDB at the time of release. Input features include one-hot encoding of amino acids, SPOT-1D-Single outputs (three-state and eight-state secondary structure probabilities, ASA, HSE, and backbone torsion angles ψ, φ, θ, τ), and ESM-1b attention maps. One-dimensional features were converted to two-dimensional features using outer concatenation. Attention maps from all twenty heads of the last layer and all twenty heads from every layer of ESM-1b were gathered, symmetrized, and had average product corrections applied as per Rao et al. (2020). The baseline for comparison is SSCpred, which was accessed via its web-server due to a lack of stand-alone version. Profile-based methods (TrRosetta, SPOT-Contact, ESM-1b) were evaluated using inputs obtained from the SPOT-Contact MSA generation pipeline for benchmarking.

Procedures And Architectures
The model architecture is a 12-block ResNet, the maximum depth trainable on the available GPU, using a recently published version of ResNet (Duta et al., 2020) instead of vanilla ResNet. Convolutional layers have a channel size of 64 and kernel size of 3. Six models were trained with the same architectural specifications but different input feature combinations: Model 1 uses ESM-1b last-layer attention; Model 2 uses all-layer attention; Model 3 uses all-layer attention + one-hot + SPOT-1D-Single; Models 4, 5, 6 mirror these with distogram-based bin prediction. Direct contact-map models use Binary Cross-Entropy loss, while distogram-based models use Cross-Entropy loss on distance bins. All models used the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001, batch size of 1, and early stopping after 3 epochs. The ensemble (SPOT-Contact-Single) combines the mean results of all six models. The model is limited by the ESM-1b input length of 1024 amino acids, but proteins are typically composed of domains smaller than 1000 residues. Inference time for 15 proteins on CASP14-FM is 116 seconds on CPU, and TrRosetta took 1926 seconds on GPU for the same set.

Key Results
On the independent CASP14-FM test set, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved an F1-score of 0.2061 and MCC of 0.1925, representing a 15% improvement over SSCpred. On proteins without homologs (Neff=1) in the SPOT-2018 set, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved F1-scores of 0.32, 48.7% higher than TrRosetta (0.22) and 48.5% higher than SPOT-Contact (0.22). Feature importance analysis shows the one-hot encoding baseline has F1=0.15 and MCC=0.14 on the validation set. Adding SPOT-1D-Single outputs to one-hot encoding improves F1 by 22.90%. The last-layer attention map from ESM-1b alone achieves F1=0.51, MCC=0.50, precision=0.56, and AUC=0.95, a 242% improvement in F1 over the one-hot baseline and 178% over one-hot + SPOT-1D-Single. Concatenating all features (one-hot + SPOT-1D-Single + all-layer ESM-1b attention maps) provides a further 2.92% increase in F1-score over all-layer attention only. The ensemble SPOT-Contact-Single achieves 4% improvement in F1-score over the second-best individual model on the validation set. On a specific example protein (5YKZ_A) from Neff1-2018, F1-scores were 0.215 for SPOT-Contact, 0.235 for TrRosetta, 0.252 for ESM-1b, and 0.388 for SPOT-Contact-Single. The most improvement over SSCpred is in long-range contacts precision, achieving approximately 100% improvement. Direct contact-map prediction performs slightly better than distogram-based prediction, but the difference is small. The performance gap between profile-based and single-sequence methods widens as Neff increases, with profile-based predictors outperforming SPOT-1D-Single. SPOT-Contact-Single is 22 times faster than TrRosetta on CPU for 15 proteins (116 seconds vs 1926 seconds on GPU) and 42 times faster on GPU.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results demonstrate that unsupervised language model features from a transformer can capture sufficient evolutionary-free structural information to significantly improve single-sequence contact-map prediction. The 242% F1 improvement from last-layer attention alone suggests that the pre-trained attention maps encode strong spatial structural signals useful for contact prediction. The diminished performance relative to profile-based methods as Neff increases indicates that co-mutation information from homologous sequences still provides additive predictive signal not captured by unsupervised learning. The method is positioned as a viable screening tool for proteins with limited homology, where MSA-based predictors are ineffective. The speed advantage makes the method more suitable for genomic-scale prediction compared to profile-based methods that require computationally expensive MSA generation. Further improvements may come from using more advanced architectural models such as Transformer or Performer for the contact-map prediction task.

Contradictions And Limitations
The input length of ESM-1b is limited to 1024 amino acids, preventing direct prediction for proteins exceeding this length. SPOT-1D-Single is not yet as competitive as evolution-based methods for proteins with multiple homologs, as co-mutation information from MSAs is more effective. The validation set size of 88 proteins may be small for comprehensive evaluation of a 12-block ResNet across six model variants. The comparison with SSCpred was conducted via its web-server due to a lack of stand-alone version, which might introduce artifacts in benchmarking. The method was tested on the available GPU hardware, limiting the ResNet depth to 12 blocks; greater depth may be achievable. The paper does not explicitly state which random seeds or hyperparameter search spaces were used, limiting exact reproducibility.

Claims
SPOT-Contact-Single achieves superior F1-score over SSCpred on the CASP14-FM test set. SPOT-Contact-Single achieved an F1-score of 0.2061 and MCC of 0.1925, a 15% improvement over SSCpred. The most improvement over SSCpred is in long-range contacts precision, reaching approximately 100% improvement. For proteins with more effective homologs, SPOT-Contact-Single does not outperform MSA-based methods, as profile-based predictors remain more competitive. The method can replace SSCpred for single-sequence contact-map prediction in scenarios with limited homology.
SPOT-Contact-Single outperforms TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact on proteins without homologs. On Neff=1 proteins, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved 48.7% higher F1 than TrRosetta and 48.5% higher than SPOT-Contact. On example protein 5YKZ_A, F1-scores were 0.215 (SPOT-Contact), 0.235 (TrRosetta), 0.252 (ESM-1b), and 0.388 (SPOT-Contact-Single). As Neff increases, the performance gap between profile-based and single-sequence methods widens, favoring MSA-based methods. The method addresses a critical gap for proteins without naturally occurring homologous sequences, expanding the applicable range of contact-map prediction.
ESM-1b attention maps provide a powerful single-sequence feature for contact-map prediction. Last-layer attention alone achieved 242% F1 improvement over the one-hot baseline and 178% over one-hot + SPOT-1D-Single. F1 of 0.51 and MCC of 0.50 were obtained using last-layer attention maps on the validation set. All-layer attention does not improve F1-score significantly over last-layer attention, although precision is improved. Concatenating all features only yields a further 2.92% increase, diminishing returns after attention maps are included. Pre-trained Transformer attention maps capture spatial structural information relevant to inter-residue contacts without explicit structural or evolutionary labels.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Feature importance was assessed by training a ResNet12 on different input combinations: one-hot, one-hot + SPOT-1D-Single, one-hot + all-layer attention, and the full concatenation. Direct contact-map prediction was compared against distogram-based bin prediction, with direct prediction performing slightly better but with a small difference. Ensemble performance was evaluated by comparing the six individual models against their mean-combined result, showing 4% F1 improvement over the second-best individual model. Sensitivity analysis showed that all-layer attention improved precision across all three contact ranges (short, medium, long) compared to last-layer attention, as detailed in Supplementary Table S2. The model is limited by the 1024 residue input constraint of ESM-1b.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the ResNet12 architecture with convolutional layers and channel/kernel specifications. Figure 2 displays precision for top-ranked predictions across short-, medium-, and long-range contacts for various methods. Figure 3 plots F1-score as a function of Neff values, demonstrating performance scaling with homology depth. Figure 4 presents native and predicted contact-maps for example protein 5YKZ_A across four predictors. Table 1 details the six trained model variants, their feature combinations, and training strategies. Table 2 presents feature importance results on the validation set. Table 3 compares direct vs. distogram contact-map prediction strategies. Table 4 presents validation set results for all six individual models and the ensemble. Table 5 compares SPOT-Contact-Single, SPOT-Contact, TrRosetta, and ESM-1b on Neff=1 proteins. Table 6 presents comparison results on the CASP14-FM dataset.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is SPOT-Contact-Single, which demonstrates that pre-trained Transformer language model attention maps, concatenated with one-hot encodings and 1D structural features, can predict protein contact maps without MSA or evolutionary profiles, outperforming existing single-sequence predictors by 15% on CASP14-FM. 2. The strongest evidence is the 242% F1-score improvement from ESM-1b last-layer attention alone over the one-hot baseline, and the 48.7% improvement over TrRosetta on Neff=1 proteins, confirming that unsupervised transformer features capture sufficient contact-relevant structure. 3. The future path involves extending the method to more advanced architectural models such as Transformer or Performer for the contact-map prediction task, profiling against profile-based methods in terms of computational time, and addressing the 1024-residue input constraint.

summary.title: CCN2 activates ERK-signaling via integrin av and enhances the interaction of ERK and DUSP6 in lymphatic endothelial cells
summary.authors: Shiho Hashiguchi, Tomoko Tanaka, Ryosuke Mano, Seiji Kondo, Shohta Kodama
summary.field_subfield: Vascular Biology / Lymphangiogenesis / Cell Signaling
summary.type_of_paper: Primary research article (in vitro and in vivo functional study)
summary.executive_summary:
This study investigates the molecular mechanism by which Cellular Communication Network Factor 2 (CCN2), also known as Connective Tissue Growth Factor (CTGF), regulates lymphangiogenesis and intracellular signaling in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). While CCN2 is established as a potent angiogenic factor in vascular endothelial cells, its specific role in LECs was previously undefined. Using primary cultured LECs and an in vivo Matrigel plug assay, the authors first demonstrated that CCN2 upregulates key LEC markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4) in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL, with a dramatic decrease observed at 200 ng/mL. CCN2 also increased Flt4 (Vegfr3) expression but did not affect Kdr (Vegfr2), and notably, neither VEGFR2 nor VEGFR3 phosphorylation was changed by CCN2 treatment, suggesting that CCN2 signals independently of traditional VEGF-receptor activation in LECs.

Mechanistically, CCN2 selectively induces ERK phosphorylation (p<0.001) without affecting p38, JNK, AKT, NFκB, or Smad pathways. The authors identified that CCN2-mediated ERK activation is partially mediated via integrin av (Itgav), as siRNA-mediated knockdown of integrin av partially reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040). In contrast, integrin a9 and b1 knockdown did not demonstrate the same relationship, with b1 suppression causing constitutive phospho-ERK induction. Furthermore, CCN2 was found to weakly suppress LEC growth at 24 hours (p=0.003 at 50 ng/mL; p=0.02 at 100 ng/mL) and to enhance the physical interaction between ERK and the dual-specificity phosphatase DUSP6. DUSP6 knockdown abrogated the ERK-suppression mechanism, resulting in sustained CCN2-induced phospho-ERK levels at all time points. In vivo Matrigel plug assays confirmed that exogenous CCN2 increases the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels, CD31-positive cavities, and b3-Tubulin-positive peripheral nerves, with detectable phospho-ERK and DUSP6 within CCN2-treated plugs. These findings establish that CCN2 regulates lymphangiogenesis in LECs by activating ERK via integrin av while simultaneously enhancing ERK-DUSP6 interaction to limit excessive ERK signaling, positioning these components as potential therapeutic targets in conditions like tongue squamous cell carcinoma.
