summary.title: Influence of plant growth regulators and nitrogen sources on the production and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk Hormonal treatment and fertilization to plant development
summary.authors: Leone Campos Rocha; Fábio Andrade; Teixeira; Santos Pedreira; Daniela Deitos Fries; Giovanna Evely; Leite Costa; Ana Cláudia; Maia Soares; Daniel Lucas; Santos Dias; Abdias José De Figueiredo; Angel Amaral; Seixas; Camile Carvalho Pacheco
summary.field_subfield: Agronomy / Forage and Pasture Science
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental agricultural study (greenhouse and field fertilization analysis)
summary.executive_summary: This experimental study evaluated the influence of seed treatment with exogenous plant growth regulators (PGRs) and nitrogen fertilization methods on the germination, growth, and physiological development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, a tropical forage grass. The experimental design employed a 2 x 4 factorial scheme in a completely randomized design, crossing two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) with four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg⁻¹) and separately evaluating four nitrogen fertilization methods (no fertilization, soil fertilization, foliar fertilization, and combined soil + foliar). PGRs consisted of a mixture of auxin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹). Results demonstrated that PGR application significantly enhanced both germination percentage and germination speed index across both seed types, with a quadratic effect; optimal germination was achieved at 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ and optimal root dry mass at 12.8 mL.kg⁻¹. Coated seeds consistently outperformed conventional seeds in germination and GSI, and embryo quality contributed to greater tissue formation. For leaf and pseudostem mass, a significant interaction existed: coated seeds achieved maximum yields at lower PGR levels (8.85 and 9.57 mL.kg⁻¹), while conventional seeds required higher treatments (15.5 and 18.1 mL.kg⁻¹). Soil nitrogen fertilization (75 kg.ha⁻¹) was the most effective treatment for dry mass production across all plant structures, exceeding foliar and multiple fertilization, while PGR and soil fertilization combined yielded greatest mass. PGR application increased chlorophyll a, while nitrogen fertilization influenced chlorophyll a, b, and carotenoids. The study attributes these effects to hormonal balance changes post-imbibition, gibberellin-mediated ABA reduction, auxin-stimulated rhizogenesis, and nitrogen-driven maximization of photosynthetic processes. The study concludes that lower PGR levels in coated seeds are recommended for pasture establishment, and soil nitrogen fertilization is essential for maximizing vegetative growth and chlorophyll content.

claims.description: Seed treatment with exogenous PGRs significantly improves germination percentage and speed in Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, with optimal effects at specific concentration levels.

Soil nitrogen fertilization is superior to foliar or multiple fertilization for maximizing dry mass production of all plant structures in Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, and the synergy between PGR and soil fertilization yields the greatest mass.

Coated seeds outperform conventional seeds in germination and early development because the coating protects the embryo and provides nutrients, and coated seeds require lower PGR levels to achieve optimal leaf and pseudostem dry mass.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This experimental study evaluated the influence of seed treatment with exogenous plant growth regulators (PGRs) and nitrogen fertilization methods on the germination, growth, and physiological development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, a tropical forage grass. The experimental design employed a 2 x 4 factorial scheme in a completely randomized design, crossing two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) with four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg⁻¹) and separately evaluating four nitrogen fertilization methods (no fertilization, soil fertilization, foliar fertilization, and combined soil + foliar). PGRs consisted of a mixture of auxin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹). Results demonstrated that PGR application significantly enhanced both germination percentage and germination speed index across both seed types, with a quadratic effect; optimal germination was achieved at 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ and optimal root dry mass at 12.8 mL.kg⁻¹. Coated seeds consistently outperformed conventional seeds in germination and GSI, and embryo quality contributed to greater tissue formation. For leaf and pseudostem mass, a significant interaction existed: coated seeds achieved maximum yields at lower PGR levels (8.85 and 9.57 mL.kg⁻¹), while conventional seeds required higher treatments (15.5 and 18.1 mL.kg⁻¹). Soil nitrogen fertilization (75 kg.ha⁻¹) was the most effective treatment for dry mass production across all plant structures, exceeding foliar and multiple fertilization, while PGR and soil fertilization combined yielded greatest mass. PGR application increased chlorophyll a, while nitrogen fertilization influenced chlorophyll a, b, and carotenoids. The study attributes these effects to hormonal balance changes post-imbibition, gibberellin-mediated ABA reduction, auxin-stimulated rhizogenesis, and nitrogen-driven maximization of photosynthetic processes. The study concludes that lower PGR levels in coated seeds are recommended for pasture establishment, and soil nitrogen fertilization is essential for maximizing vegetative growth and chlorophyll content.

Research Context
Adverse climatic factors and shortened soil preparation windows reduce the time available for recovering degraded pasturelands, necessitating greater seed efficiency for germination and speed of emergence. Management practices are essential to improve herbage production processes under conditions that favor pasture development and use. Plant growth regulators based on gibberellin at high concentrations per area are shown to be uneconomical, with forage mass reductions as application increases, whereas 5-10 g.ha⁻¹ is sufficient for positive effects. PGRs have demonstrated potential under stress conditions by positive regulation of growth-linked genes, increasing mechanical impedance in dry soils, and improving water use efficiency. However, the application of exogenous hormones requires careful cross-evaluation among different phytohormone actions to avoid antagonism or suboptimal responses. Nitrogen is an indispensable constituent in organic compounds including amino acids, proteins, and nucleic acids, increasing rates of cell division, expansion, and stimulating cell elongation. Nitrogen applications to recover degraded pasture areas increase water use efficiency, stimulate plant growth, and increase soil cover. The use of nitrogen expands the plant lifecycle, leading to higher growth rates in the vegetative phase and maximizing photoassimilate production for structural characteristics. The aim was to evaluate the effect of seed treatment with plant growth regulators and nitrogen fertilization methods in Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk on growth and development.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question was whether seed treatment with a combination of auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin, in conjunction with different nitrogen fertilization methods, would influence the germination, dry matter yield, and physiological composition of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. The study hypothesized that PGR application would increase germination percentages and mass yields of plant structures in coated seeds through organogenesis of plant tissues and increased physiological rates. It was predicted that higher germination percentages and root dry mass production would be obtained with specific optimal levels of PGR for initial growth. The study hypothesized that soil N-fertilization would result in higher dry mass productions of leaf, stem, shoot, and root, as well as for root volume, by maximizing photosynthetic processes and growth rates. A secondary hypothesis was that the interaction between seed type and PGR levels would influence leaf and pseudostem mass production, with coated seeds potentially requiring different optimal PGR levels than conventional seeds. The study also aimed to determine if PGR application increased photoassimilate rates and if specific nitrogen fertilization methods influenced chlorophyll and carotenoid contents. The experimental approach tested three main factors: seed type (coated vs. conventional), PGR level (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg⁻¹), and fertilization method (none, soil, foliar, soil+foliar), to isolate direct and interactive effects.

Methodological Details
The experiments were performed at the State University of Southwestern Bahia (UESB) in Itapetinga - BA, between June and September 2017, at the Forage and Pasture Research Center and Laboratory of Anatomy and Ecological Plant Physiology (LAFIEP). Germination characteristics were evaluated under hermetic storage using a Mangelsdorf germination chamber (MA-401) at a 12h photoperiod and constant temperature of 28°C. Growth and development evaluations were conducted in a greenhouse using pots filled with eight liters or 12 kg of dry soil collected from 0-20 cm depth, disintegrated and grounded to pass through a 4-mm sieve. The fertilizer recommendations were based on the methodology of the Soil Fertility Commission for the State of Minas Gerais, 5th Approximation. A 2 x 4 factorial scheme was implemented in a completely randomized design (CRD) for the seed treatment experiment, crossing two commercial seed types with four PGR levels. The PGR composition consisted of auxin at 0.05 mg.L⁻¹, cytokinin at 0.09 mg.L⁻¹, and gibberellin at 0.05 mg.L⁻¹. After approximately two hours of imbibition at different PGR levels, 25 seeds per replicate were wrapped in filter paper moistened with distilled water and arranged in four replicates per treatment. For initial growth assessments at 30 DAS, sowing was performed in a seedling tray with 32 cells per replicate across two replicates per treatment, using sterilized coconut residue as substrate. The second experiment used a 2 x 4 factorial scheme in a CRD, crossing two seed types with four nitrogen fertilization methods: no fertilization, soil fertilization, foliar fertilization, and multiple fertilization (soil + foliar). Eight treatments were used with four plants per replicate and four replicates per treatment, totaling 32 experimental units. At 30 DAS, a standardization cut was performed, adopting an average residue height of 15 cm; data collection followed at this stage and in two subsequent 28-day periods. Fertilization was applied after the standardization cut at rates of 75 kg.ha⁻¹ N for soil and 3 L.ha⁻¹ for foliar application, with the foliar fertilizer composition detailed in Table 1. Daily counts of germinated seeds were carried out for 14 days to determine germination percentage and germination speed index (GSI). Whole-plant yield was determined at the end of each period, followed by desiccation of root, stem, and leaf to determine fresh and dry mass (DM) following established protocols. The third fully expanded leaf of each repetition was collected at 10 a.m., 200 mg of fresh mass was prepared with 5 mL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) in aluminum foil, and readings were taken at 665, 649, and 480 nm via absorption spectrophotometry after 72 hours. Data were analyzed using the MIXED procedure of SAS with significance declared when P ≤ 0.05; Tukey test was used for mean comparisons, and single-degree-of-freedom contrast statements were constructed for linear and quadratic PGR effects. The maximum point of regression equations was estimated to identify optimal PGR levels, and Tukey's test with P ≤ 0.05 declared significance.

Procedures And Architectures
The germination assay utilized a Mangelsdorf germination chamber (MA-401) under a controlled 12h photoperiod and constant temperature of 28ºC for 14 days. Seeds were incubated for approximately two hours after PGR application before being wrapped in filter paper moistened with distilled water, with 25 seeds per replicate in four replicates per treatment. Initial growth was assessed 30 DAS in a seedling tray with 32 cells per replicate, using sterilized coconut residue as a substrate to maintain constant humidity. The greenhouse pots contained eight liters or 12 kg of dry soil to allow area productivity estimation in kg DM.ha⁻¹, with soil collected at 0-20 cm depth, disintegrated, and passed through a 4-mm sieve. Fertilization occurred after the standardization cut (average residue height of 15 cm), with soil fertilization at 75 kg.ha⁻¹ N and foliar at 3 L.ha⁻¹ N, including N, P₂O₅, Mg, S, Zn, Mn, Cu, B, Mo, and Co as detailed in Table 1. The foliar fertilizer composition from the manufacturer included N at 1.37%, P₂O₅ at 2.5%, Mg at 15.0%, and micronutrients such as S (1.0%), Zn (1.5%), Mn (3.0%), Cu (2.0%), B (0.3%), Mo (0.2%), Co (0.1%), and 1.37% of others. Data analysis utilized the MIXED procedure of SAS (SAS Inst. Inc., Cary, NC), with P ≤ 0.05 declared significant; seed, PGR, and interaction effects were analyzed as fixed effects. Linear and quadratic effect contrast statements were constructed to analyze PGR levels, and the maximum point was estimated from the regression equation. PGR and fertilization effects were analyzed as fixed effects, and Tukey's test was used for mean comparisons at P ≤ 0.05. For pigment analysis, 200 mg of fresh leaf mass was homogenized with 5 mL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) wrapped in aluminum foil, incubated for 72 hours, and read at 665, 649, and 480 nm using absorption spectrophotometry.

Key Results
The interaction between seed type and growth regulator levels was not significant for germination percentage and germination speed index (GSI), with a quadratic effect of PGR levels on germination observed across both seed types. Coated seeds achieved higher germination percentage and GSI than conventional seeds, as shown in Table 2, with the quadratic regression indicating that 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ of PGR promoted greater germination. For the number of leaves, tillers, and root dry mass production, the interaction between seed type and PGR level was not significant; the number of leaves and tillers were influenced by seed type, while root dry mass production was not affected. Based on the estimated regression equation, the optimal PGR treatment for higher root dry mass production was 12.8 mL.kg⁻¹, as reported in Table 3. A significant interaction between seed type and PGR level was found for leaf and pseudostem dry mass production: in the absence of treatment or at the lowest level (8.0 mL.kg⁻¹), higher production was observed for coated seeds at 8.85 and 9.57 mL.kg⁻¹, respectively, as shown in Table 4. Conventional seeds required higher PGR levels for leaf and pseudostem dry mass production, specifically 15.5 and 18.1 mL.kg⁻¹, respectively, at the highest tested levels (16.0 and 24.0 mL.kg⁻¹). The interaction between PGR application and nitrogen fertilization methods was significant for dry mass production of leaf, stem, shoot, and root. Dry mass production of stem, leaf, and shoot was greatest when PGR and soil fertilization were combined, though soil fertilization yielded higher yields regardless of PGR application. Use of PGR reduced leaf, stem, and shoot production when combined with multiple fertilization (soil + foliar), differing from the absence of PGR, which was similar to soil fertilization under multiple fertilization. PGR increased root dry mass production only when combined with multiple fertilization; for the other fertilization types (none, soil, foliar), no influence of growth regulators was observed (Table 5). The interaction between PGR and nitrogen fertilization methods was not significant for chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, total chlorophylls, carotenoids, and the chlorophyll a/b ratio. A significant effect of PGR application was observed on chlorophyll a levels, and fertilization methods independently influenced levels of chlorophyll a, b, and carotenoids (Table 6). Coated seeds achieved higher GSI and germination percentages due to their quality, with the coating providing protection against mechanical damage and delivering nutrients to the embryo, favoring greater radicle emergence. PGR application did not increase the number of leaves or tillers, consistent with prior findings; however, higher root dry mass was attributed to auxin-stimulated rhizogenesis through stem cell multiplication in quiescent centers.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Exogenous hormonal application changes hormonal balance and biosynthesis levels, with a significant increase in auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin levels after 24 hours of imbibition, activating genes linked to photosynthesis and monosaccharide degradation. The increased concentration of exogenous gibberellin implies greater intracellular transport of intermediary metabolites until bioactive gibberellin formation, acting on genes expressing germinative characteristics and weakening mechanical barriers covering the radicle. Gibberellin increases germination by reducing abscisic acid (ABA), the main promoter of seed dormancy, which regulates mobilization of storage lipids in the endosperm; decreased ABA allows lipid degradation in cotyledons. PIN proteins bound to plasma membranes enable intracellular transport of auxins, with auxins regulated by basipetal polar transport in protonated (IAAH) or anionic (IAA-) forms, contributing to hormonal homeostasis until signal response. Auxin stimulates stem cell multiplication due to accumulation in quiescent centers (QC), increasing the number of root cells; PIN proteins located in endoplasmic reticulum and other endomembranes contribute to auxin homeostasis. The interaction between auxin and cytokinin regulates formation and maintenance of meristems, and both act as main hormones in signaling shoot apical meristem (SAM) formation, indicating potential cross-response in plant organogenesis. Gibberellins produced in young leaves in expansion play a primary role in stimulating the auxin reaction, directly affecting internode elongation through intermediate receptors of one hormone interacting with components of another. Higher dry mass yields for all structures with soil fertilization justify the nitrogen-photosynthetic relationship, where greater nitrogen supply combined with cellular acceleration from PGR reflects in higher dry mass accumulation. Increased leaf dry mass production consolidates the improvement of photosynthetic processes, where PGR use resulted in higher chlorophyll a levels, responsible for the photochemical phase and promoting ATP formation in photophosphorylation. Foliar nitrogen fertilization increased chlorophyll a, b, and total chlorophyll, possibly because nitrogen availability participates in cytokinin synthesis, which promotes chlorophyll synthesis and delayed senescence. The coating on seeds provides protection against mechanical damage and provides nutrients to the embryo, favoring greater radicle emergence and seedling emergence rate, and the best responses with lower PGR levels are justified because they are pure seeds with potentially higher embryo quality. Conventional seeds required greater PGR use due to reduced efficiency; the best responses with coated seeds at lower levels suggest an evaluation of Pure Live Seeds (PLS) could improve hormone use efficiency.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study reports that the use of PGR reduced leaf, stem, and shoot production when combined with multiple fertilization, a finding that contrasts with the general expectation that PGR and fertilization should be synergistic, suggesting complex antagonistic interactions. The authors acknowledge that little is known about the role of auxins and cytokinins in the regulation of photosynthetic processes, with prior auxin studies being termed 'inconclusive' regarding indirect influence on chloroplast movement. The paper notes that the use of PGRs as plant herbicides acts by blocking photosynthetic electron flux and altering ATP formation, creating a potential confounding effect when evaluating PGRs as growth promoters. The study acknowledges that the absence of gibberellin elicits responses similar to antagonistic hormones, requiring evaluation beyond absolute values due to hormonal interaction, which is a signaling network rather than independent action. The paper does not report the random seed numbers, specific cultivars other than Basilisk, or demographic information relevant to pastoral application; the sample size is limited to 32 experimental units for the second experiment and two replicates per treatment for initial growth. The study does not report specific P, S, or other fertilizer nutrient concentrations beyond N, and the foliar fertilizer composition is from a manufacturer without independent verification. The use of PGR did not result in higher number of leaves and tillers, which contradicts the general expectation that growth regulators should promote overall vegetative expansion. The paper does not specify the exact number of repetitions for the germination trial or the exact composition of the seed coating, limiting reproducibility of the coated seed treatment. The statistical analysis reports significance as P ≤ 0.05 but the text displays as '. 05 . 0  P' due to OCR or formatting issues, creating minor ambiguity in precise reporting. The study uses only one variety (Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk), limiting the generalizability of the PGR and nitrogen interaction findings to other forage grass species or varieties. The experimental period is limited to three months (June to September 2017), and the study does not report long-term production, yield, or persistence of the fertilization effects over multiple growth cycles.

Seed treatment with exogenous PGRs significantly improves germination percentage and speed in Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, with optimal effects at specific concentration levels. A quadratic effect of PGR levels on germination was observed across both seed types. Coated seeds achieved higher germination percentage and GSI than conventional seeds. The optimal germination was promoted at 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ of PGR. The use of PGR did not increase the number of leaves or tillers, limiting the overall vegetative expansion benefit. PGR application was uneconomical at high concentrations, with forage mass reductions as application increased. Lower PGR levels are recommended for coated seeds in pasture establishment. PGR application acts on organogenesis of plant tissues and increased photoassimilate rates for initial growth.
Soil nitrogen fertilization is superior to foliar or multiple fertilization for maximizing dry mass production of all plant structures in Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, and the synergy between PGR and soil fertilization yields the greatest mass. Soil fertilization resulted in higher yields for the evaluated structures regardless of PGR. Dry mass production of stem, leaf, and shoot was greatest when PGR and soil fertilization were combined. Nitrogen is indispensable for amino acids, proteins, and nucleic acids, increasing cell division and expansion. The use of PGR reduced leaf, stem, and shoot production when combined with multiple fertilization, suggesting antagonistic interactions. PGR increased root dry mass only when combined with multiple fertilization; for soil fertilization, no PGR influence was observed. Soil nitrogen application at 75 kg.ha⁻¹ is recommended for maximizing dry mass and photosynthetic processes. Soil fertilization maximizes photosynthetic processes and growth rates, enabling greater post-defoliation recovery.
Coated seeds outperform conventional seeds in germination and early development because the coating protects the embryo and provides nutrients, and coated seeds require lower PGR levels to achieve optimal leaf and pseudostem dry mass. Coated seeds had higher values for both germination characteristics. Coated seeds required lower PGR levels (8.85 and 9.57 mL.kg⁻¹) for maximum leaf and pseudostem dry mass. Conventional seeds required higher levels (15.5 and 18.1 mL.kg⁻¹) for the same structures. The interaction between seed type and PGR was not significant for number of leaves, tillers, or root dry mass production. The study does not quantify the specific composition or manufacturer of the seed coating, limiting reproducibility. Coated seeds with lower PGR treatments are recommended for Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. Seed coating provides protection against mechanical damage and nutrients to the embryo, favoring greater radicle emergence.

The 2 x 4 factorial design serves as a built-in ablation framework, testing seed type, PGR levels, and nitrogen fertilization methods as independent and interacting factors. Sensitivity analysis included four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg⁻¹) and four fertilization methods to determine optimal response thresholds. The use of 8.0 mL.kg⁻¹ as the lowest positive PGR level allowed comparison against the absence of treatment (0 mL.kg⁻¹). The study tested multiple fertilization modes (none, soil, foliar, soil+foliar) to isolate the specific contribution of each N source. The inclusion of multiple replicates (four replicates per treatment) and standardized cut (average residue height of 15 cm) provided internal reliability for the treatment comparisons.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is that exogenous PGRs (0.05 mg.L⁻¹ auxin, 0.09 mg.L⁻¹ cytokinin, 0.05 mg.L⁻¹ gibberellin) significantly enhance germination (optimal 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹) and root dry mass (optimal 12.8 mL.kg⁻¹) of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, while soil nitrogen fertilization (75 kg.ha⁻¹ N) maximizes vegetative dry mass and chlorophyll content. 2. This prospective single-center study investigated whether chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length significantly impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents in the DES era. A cohort of 235 consecutive CTO patients (November 2004 to October 2010) at Korea University Guro Hospital was divided into long CTO (≥30mm, n=159) and short CTO (<30mm, n=76) groups based on angiographic lesion length.

In-hospital complications, including significant intimal dissection, were more frequent in the long CTO group, reflecting more complex recanalization procedures, but overall procedural safety was comparable. At two years, hard clinical endpoints—total death, cardiac death, myocardial infarction, and MACE—showed no statistically significant differences between groups (all p > 0.05). However, the long CTO group had a significantly higher incidence of repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p < 0.05) and target vessel revascularization (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p < 0.05), with long CTO identified as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26; CI 1.53–11.9; p=0.006) in multivariate regression analysis.

At six months, angiographic outcomes including in-stent restenosis, binary restenosis, and late loss were statistically similar between groups, though numerically higher in the long CTO group. The authors hypothesize that the higher revascularization rate in long CTO patients did not translate into worse critical hard endpoints, possibly due to reduced myocardial viability and pre-existing collateral channels in long lesions. The study is limited by its single-center, non-randomized design, relatively small sample size, and incomplete follow-up angiography, warranting cautious interpretation and the need for larger-scale studies.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This prospective single-center study investigated whether chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length significantly impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents in the DES era. A cohort of 235 consecutive CTO patients (November 2004 to October 2010) at Korea University Guro Hospital was divided into long CTO (≥30mm, n=159) and short CTO (<30mm, n=76) groups based on angiographic lesion length.

In-hospital complications, including significant intimal dissection, were more frequent in the long CTO group, reflecting more complex recanalization procedures, but overall procedural safety was comparable. At two years, hard clinical endpoints—total death, cardiac death, myocardial infarction, and MACE—showed no statistically significant differences between groups (all p > 0.05). However, the long CTO group had a significantly higher incidence of repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p < 0.05) and target vessel revascularization (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p < 0.05), with long CTO identified as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26; CI 1.53–11.9; p=0.006) in multivariate regression analysis.

At six months, angiographic outcomes including in-stent restenosis, binary restenosis, and late loss were statistically similar between groups, though numerically higher in the long CTO group. The authors hypothesize that the higher revascularization rate in long CTO patients did not translate into worse critical hard endpoints, possibly due to reduced myocardial viability and pre-existing collateral channels in long lesions. The study is limited by its single-center, non-randomized design, relatively small sample size, and incomplete follow-up angiography, warranting cautious interpretation and the need for larger-scale studies.

Research Context
Successful chronic total occlusion percutaneous coronary intervention is associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with failed intervention. Despite the development of drug-eluting stents and special devices, procedural success rate for CTO patients remains lower than non-CTO patients. Long coronary artery lesions are recognized as a worse prognostic factor after PCI in general. There are no definite answers regarding CTO PCI outcomes according to lesion length, especially in the DES era.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether CTO lesion length can significantly impact six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful CTO PCI. The authors predicted that adverse clinical outcomes including MACE and angiographic adverse outcomes would be more frequent in the long CTO group. This prediction was based on the long CTO group having worse clinical risk factors such as history of prior MI and PCI compared with the short CTO group. Additionally, newer-generation DES was dominant in the short CTO group and paclitaxel-eluting stent was frequently used in the long CTO group. The study hypothesized that these factors would differentiate outcomes between long and short CTO lesions.

Methodological Details
A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients underwent successful PCI with DES from November 2004 to October 2010. The cohort was enrolled at the Cardiovascular Center of Korea University Guro Hospital in Seoul, South Korea. Patients were divided into two groups: long CTO (angiographic lesion length ≥30mm) and short CTO (angiographic lesion length <30mm). The long CTO group included 159 patients and the short CTO group included 76 patients. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board and all patients provided informed consent. CTO was defined as complete coronary obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0 and estimated duration ≥3 months. Only patients with de novo lesions were included; CTO due to in-stent restenosis was excluded. For angiographic outcomes, QCA parameters were measured before PCI, immediately after PCI, and 6 months after the index procedure. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6–12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints included in-stent restenosis, mean diameter stenosis, minimal luminal diameter, and late loss at 6 months. For clinical outcomes, two-year follow-up was conducted via face-to-face interview, medical record review, and telephone contact. The primary clinical endpoint was MACE, defined as the composite of total death, recurrent myocardial infarction, and revascularization including PCI and CABG. The logistic regression model adjusted for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion. A 2-sided p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses.

Procedures And Architectures
PCI procedures were performed with current guidelines using standard techniques. Various available guidewires were used to cross the CTO lesion, but atheroablative devices were not utilized. Most procedures involved simple pre-dilation with balloon to achieve adequate luminal diameter for the unexpanded stent. All PCI was performed using drug-eluting stents (DES), and the DES type was decided by the operator during the procedures. Procedural success was defined as a reduction in final angiographic diameter stenosis to less than 30% and TIMI grade ≥2. Loading doses of clopidogrel (300–600mg) and aspirin (200–300mg) were administered before the index procedure. Maintenance dual antiplatelet therapy consisted of aspirin (100mg) and clopidogrel (75mg) for at least 1 year. Adjunctive cilostazol (200mg post-loading, 100mg twice daily for at least one month) was administered at physician's discretion. Continuous variable differences were evaluated by Student's t-test, with data expressed as mean ± standard deviations. Categorical variables were analyzed with χ2 or Fisher's exact test as appropriate. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 20.

Key Results
In-hospital complications were similar between the two groups, but significant intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Total death incidence was 3.1% in the long CTO group versus 5.2% in the short CTO group (p = 0.43). Cardiac death occurred in 1.2% of the long CTO group versus 2.6% of the short CTO group (p = 0.45). Myocardial infarction occurred in 1.8% of the long CTO group versus 2.6% of the short CTO group (p = 0.71). Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) occurred in 21.3% of the long CTO group versus 13.1% of the short CTO group (p = 0.13). The incidence of repeat PCI was 18.8% in the long CTO group versus 7.8% in the short CTO group, with a statistically significant difference (p < 0.05). Target vessel revascularization (TVR) was 16.3% in the long CTO group versus 6.5% in the short CTO group (p < 0.05). In multivariate regression, long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI with an OR of 4.26 (CI 1.53–11.9, p=0.006). For TVR, multivariate analysis showed an OR of 4.23 (CI 1.52–11.8, p < 0.05) for the long CTO group. Follow-up angiographic data were obtained for 99 of 159 long CTO patients (62%) and 45 of 76 short CTO patients (59%). In-stent restenosis occurred in 33.3% of long CTO patients versus 26.6% of short CTO patients (p = 0.42). Binary restenosis occurred in 19.1% of long CTO patients versus 8.8% of short CTO patients (p = 0.12). Late loss was 0.65 ± 0.82 mm in the long CTO group versus 0.46 ± 0.56 mm in the short CTO group (p = 0.13). Vessel size was numerically different, with 3.11 ± 0.43 mm in the short CTO group versus 2.92 ± 0.42 mm in the long CTO group (p < 0.05). The long and short CTO groups showed similar angiographic outcomes at 6 months.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study suggests that PCI in long CTO lesions with DES is similarly safe compared with short CTO lesions regarding major clinical outcomes. The higher revascularization rate in long CTO did not translate into increased individual critical hard endpoints such as mortality. The authors hypothesize that reduced myocardial viability and pre-existing collateral channels in long CTO lesions may lessen the harmful physiologic effect of restenosis in the target vessel. The similarity in 6-month angiographic outcomes supports the finding of comparable procedural safety and efficacy between long and short CTO treatments. The numerical trend toward worse angiographic outcomes in the long group suggests that binary restenosis might increase with longer follow-up.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is not a randomized trial and was a single-center registry with prospective data collection, not a multicenter study. Baseline clinical, lesion, and procedural characteristics differed slightly between the two groups. There was a systematic imbalance in stent usage: newer-generation DES were more frequent in the short group, while first-generation stents were more frequent in the long group. Follow-up coronary angiography was not routinely performed; angiography depended on ischemic symptoms or physician discretion, introducing potential confounders. The sample size was relatively small, limiting statistical power to prove a difference in angiographic events. The two-year follow-up period was insufficient to evaluate long-term safety and efficacy issues. The text reports an internal contradiction: it states vessel size was smaller in the short group but provides 3.11 ± 0.43 mm for short vs. 2.92 ± 0.42 mm for long, making the long group numerically smaller. Typographic errors in the text include 'cs.' instead of 'vs.' and grammatical irregularities in the angiographic outcomes section.

Claims
Long CTO is an independent predictor for repeat PCI in the DES era, but does not confer increased two-year mortality risk. Repeat PCI incidence was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p < 0.05). Multivariate regression confirmed long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI with OR 4.26, CI 1.53–11.9, p=0.006. MACE incidence showed no statistical difference between groups (21.3% vs. 13.1%, p = 0.13). Cardiac death rates were 1.2% vs. 2.6% (p = 0.45) and MI 1.8% vs. 2.6% (p = 0.71). The study was limited by its non-randomized, single-center design and relatively small sample size, potentially reducing statistical power. Angiographic outcomes showed a numerical trend toward worse results in the long group, though not statistically significant at six months. Clinicians managing long CTO with DES should expect higher revascularization but similar two-year survival risk compared to short CTO. Larger-scale prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings and determine the long-term clinical trajectory.
Six-month angiographic outcomes are statistically similar between long and short CTO treated with drug-eluting stents. In-stent restenosis was 33.3% vs. 26.6% (p = 0.42). Binary restenosis was 19.1% vs. 8.8% (p = 0.12). Late loss was 0.65 ± 0.82 mm in the long group vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm in the short group (p = 0.13). The authors conclude that angiographic outcomes at six months were not different between the two groups. A numerical trend favored the short group for binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%), suggesting potential divergence over time. Only 62% of long CTO and 59% of short CTO patients had follow-up angiography, potentially introducing selection bias. DES provides comparable angiographic efficacy regardless of CTO lesion length at the six-month follow-up mark.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The multivariate model adjusted for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion to control for known clinical and lesion factors. The authors addressed the potential impact of vessel diameter, noting that both groups had enough large vessel diameter according to standard categorization.

Ethical Considerations
The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 demonstrates baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics of the 159 long CTO and 76 short CTO patients. Table 2 summarizes procedural and in-hospital complications, including the more frequent intimal dissection in the long CTO group. Table 3 presents two-year clinical outcome data including death, MI, repeat PCI, TLR, TVR, and non-TVR. Table 4 reports the predictors for repeat PCI and TVR from multivariate regression analysis. Table 5 presents six-month angiographic outcomes including ISR, binary restenosis, and late loss.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating that CTO lesion length is an independent predictor for repeat PCI in the DES era, but does not confer increased two-year critical hard clinical outcomes. 2. The strongest evidence is the multivariate logistic regression finding: long CTO is an independent predictor for repeat PCI with an OR of 4.26, 95% CI 1.53–11.9, p=0.006. 3. The future path is larger-scale prospective registry studies with more comprehensive long-term follow-up to establish final conclusions on the impact of CTO lesion length.

summary.title: Synthesis, Biological Activity and Molecular Docking of New Tricyclic Series as αglucosidase Inhibitors
summary.authors: Hatem A Abuelizz; Azman N I Nor; Iwana; Rohaya Ahmad; Anouar El-Hassane; Mohamed Marzouk; Rashad Al-Salahi
summary.field_subfield: Medicinal Chemistry / Pharmacology - Diabetes Therapeutics
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of 25 new tricyclic compounds belonging to the 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-one series, targeted as α-glucosidase inhibitors for diabetes treatment. The authors synthesized compounds 1 through 6h, where 25 derivatives were formed from a fused pyrimidine scaffold incorporating pyridine and triazole rings. In vitro screening using Baker's yeast α-glucosidase and p-NPG substrate revealed that 8 compounds exhibited average percent inhibition above 50%, with compound 3 showing 60.38% inhibition at 100 µg/mL and compound 6h exhibiting the highest inhibitory activity. The IC₅₀ of compound 6h was reported in the abstract as 104.07 mM, though given the context of other IC₅₀ values in µM (e.g., compound 3 at 167.82 µM, compound 2a at 304.13 µM), this is likely a typographical error in the source text. Molecular docking against the α-glucosidase enzyme (PDB 3W37) revealed that compound 6h formed the most stable complex with a binding energy of -10.56 kcal/mol, established by three intermolecular hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469. Acarbose, the reference drug, established 10 hydrogen bonds with seven residues and was directed by hydrophobic interactions with Phe601 and Trp329. Trp329 was identified as critical for orienting ligands in the binding site. The study demonstrates that the pyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinone scaffold with aminobridge substitution at position 4 yields potent α-glucosidase inhibition, offering a non-carbasugar alternative to acarbose. The synthetic route proceeded in multiple steps, with yields ranging from 45-83% for N-alkylation, 90% for thione formation, 63% for amidrazone formation, and 60-68% for amine-derivatized products.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of 25 new tricyclic compounds belonging to the 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-one series, targeted as α-glucosidase inhibitors for diabetes treatment. The authors synthesized compounds 1 through 6h, where 25 derivatives were formed from a fused pyrimidine scaffold incorporating pyridine and triazole rings. In vitro screening using Baker's yeast α-glucosidase and p-NPG substrate revealed that 8 compounds exhibited average percent inhibition above 50%, with compound 3 showing 60.38% inhibition at 100 µg/mL and compound 6h exhibiting the highest inhibitory activity. The IC₅₀ of compound 6h was reported in the abstract as 104.07 mM, though given the context of other IC₅₀ values in µM (e.g., compound 3 at 167.82 µM, compound 2a at 304.13 µM), this is likely a typographical error in the source text. Molecular docking against the α-glucosidase enzyme (PDB 3W37) revealed that compound 6h formed the most stable complex with a binding energy of -10.56 kcal/mol, established by three intermolecular hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469. Acarbose, the reference drug, established 10 hydrogen bonds with seven residues and was directed by hydrophobic interactions with Phe601 and Trp329. Trp329 was identified as critical for orienting ligands in the binding site. The study demonstrates that the pyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinone scaffold with aminobridge substitution at position 4 yields potent α-glucosidase inhibition, offering a non-carbasugar alternative to acarbose. The synthetic route proceeded in multiple steps, with yields ranging from 45-83% for N-alkylation, 90% for thione formation, 63% for amidrazone formation, and 60-68% for amine-derivatized products.

Research Context
The global number of diabetic people increased from 108 million in 1980 to 422 million by 2014. Diabetes mellitus is characterized by hyperglycaemia accompanied by carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism disturbance. Postprandial hyperglycaemia control using α-glucosidase inhibitors is clinically effective, but their advantage is diminishing due to severe gastrointestinal side effects like flatulence and diarrhoea. Most existing α-glucosidase inhibitors are sugar mimetics (carbasugars) that require tedious synthesis, creating a demand for non-sugar mimetic inhibitors. Acarbose, the current standard, mimics the oxocarbenium ion-like transition state that binds and inhibits α-glucosidase but causes gastrointestinal complications. The authors previously noted that pyridine, triazole, and pyrimidine scaffolds incorporated into various compounds displayed antimicrobial, antiviral, anticancer, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticonvulsant activities. Pyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones had been reported specifically as effective fungicidal agents.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question was whether tricyclic phenoxypyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinone hybrids could be designed and synthesized as potent, non-sugar-mimetic α-glucosidase inhibitors. The authors hypothesized that aminobridge substitution at position 4 of the pyrimidine ring would impart significant inhibitory activity against α-glucosidase. A second hypothesis was that the new tricyclic series would provide IC₅₀ values competitive with or superior to acarbose, overcoming the gastrointestinal side effects associated with sugar mimetics. The molecular docking hypothesis predicted that the binding energy and number of intermolecular hydrogen bonds would correlate with the observed inhibitory activity. The authors anticipated that Trp329 would play a directional role in the binding conformation within the α-glucosidase active site. The expected outcome was the identification of at least one compound with an IC₅₀ lower than that of acarbose, providing a new lead scaffold for clinically effective antidiabetic drugs.

Methodological Details
The study synthesized 25 tricyclic compounds: 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones hybrids (1–6h). Compounds 1 through 6h were characterized by IR and 1H-NMR spectroscopy, confirming the 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine structure. In vitro α-glucosidase inhibition screening used Baker's yeast α-glucosidase type 1 as the enzyme. The substrate was 20 mM para-nitrophenyl-α-D-glucopyranoside (p-NPG) prepared in buffer. Acarbose served as the positive control at a concentration of 200 µg/mL in 100% DMSO. The α-glucosidase enzyme was prepared by dissolving 1 mg of enzyme in 1000 µL of cold phosphate-buffered saline, pH 6.5. The enzyme concentration was adjusted to 0.125 unit/mL by mixing 50 µL of the stock into 12 mL of cold PBS. A phosphate-buffered saline was prepared at pH 6.5 by dissolving 1.4 g sodium phosphate monobasic, 8 g sodium chloride, 0.2 g potassium chloride, and 0.2 g potassium dihydrogen phosphate in 1 L deionized water. For screening, compounds were prepared at a concentration of 200 µg/mL in 100% DMSO. Two-fold serial dilutions were prepared in a 96-well microplate, giving final concentrations of 100, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25, 3.13, and 1.56 µg/mL. Acarbose was prepared at 200 µg/mL in 100% DMSO, with the same dilution series. The assay was performed in triplicate with each compound tested three times. A volume of 10 µL of 5% DMSO was added to 96 wells, followed by 10 µL of stock sample. Subsequent 10 µL aliquots were transferred for serial dilution. Then, 20 µL of α-glucosidase enzyme, 40 µL of PBS pH 6.5, and 20 µL of deionized water were added to each well. The mixture was pre-incubated at 37 °C for 10 minutes before adding 10 µL of 20 mM p-NPG. Absorbance was measured at 405 nm at 0 min and after 30 min incubation at 37 °C. For the negative control, the sample was replaced with 5% DMSO. The inhibition activity was determined based on the method of Ahmad et al., 2011. Molecular docking employed the Autodock software package against the original docked protein (PDB 3W37) downloaded from RCSB. Relative standard deviation of binding energy was calculated.

Procedures And Architectures
The starting material A (diphenoxy-Ncyanoimidocarbonate) was prepared according to a reported procedure. 1,2,4-triazole intermediate B was obtained by reacting A with 2-hydrazino-3-carboxylic pyridine (5.5 mmol) in ethanol (20 mL) with triethylamine (20 mmol) at room temperature overnight, then acidifying with HCl at 80 °C. Compound B was treated with ethanolic solution of diphenoxy-Ncyanoimidocarbonate in a basic medium to generate triazoles. The reaction of compound 1 with alkyl or heteroalkyl halides in DMF and potassium carbonate gave N-alkylated products 2a-l in 45-83% yields. IR spectra of compounds 2a-l showed absorption bands at 1670-1688 cm⁻¹ due to the C=O group. Equimolar amounts of target 1 and phosphorous pentasulfide in absolute pyridine produced the thione 3 as a yellow amorphous powder in 90% yield. The IR and 13C NMR spectra of compound 3 displayed a weak band at 1272 cm⁻¹ and resonance at 186.0 ppm due to the C=S group. Compound 3 was treated with benzyl bromide in DMF/potassium carbonate to give thione-derived products. Compound 1 was treated with phosphorous oxychloride in boiling benzene followed by saturated basic solution to give imidoyl chloride 5. NMR confirmed the complete disappearance of the C=O band at 1703 cm⁻¹ in compound 5. Compound 5 with hydroxylamine HCl (1:2.5 molar ratio) in boiling pyridine gave compound 6e in 63% yield. Compound 5 with several aromatic amines in pyridine (1:5 molar ratio) yielded compounds 6a-d in 60-68% yields. Compound 5 with isoniazid in boiling toluene yielded amidrazone 6i in good yield (74%). Hydrazinolysis of 5 in boiling ethanol produced 6f, then treatment with aldehydes gave hydrazone derivatives 6g and 6h in good yields. 1H-NMR spectra of targets 1-6 were characterized by two consistent spin coupling systems, each with three types of protons. The first system (triplet 2H, doublet 2H, triplet 1H) in range 7.50-7.25 ppm corresponded to the five protons of the 2-phenoxy moiety. The second system (mostly two doublets and a doublet of doublets) in range 8.9-7.5 ppm corresponded to the three pyridine-ring protons. The aminobridge substitution of the pyrimidine ring at position 4 was identified as responsible for the strong inhibitory activity. Molecular docking used the Autodock software package. The original docked protein was downloaded as PDB 3W37 from RCSB. The docking procedure was reported by Abuelizz and collaborators.

Key Results
The inhibitory activity of all 25 tested compounds was between 30% and 63% average percent inhibition. Eight compounds out of 25 exhibited more than 50% average percent inhibition. Compounds 3, 6c, and 6d showed average percent inhibition of more than 60%. Compounds 2a, 2d, 6a, 6b, and 6h showed average percent inhibition between 50% and 60%. The N-substituted derivatives at position 4 did not exhibit inhibitory activity except for compounds 2a and 2d. The average percent inhibitions of 2a and 2d were 50.36% and 57.48%, respectively. Compound 3 at 100 µg/mL exhibited 60.38% inhibition against α-glucosidase. The IC₅₀ of compound 3 was 167.82 µM. The IC₅₀ of compound 2a was 304.13 µM and that of compound 2d was 173.83 µM. The abstract reports an IC₅₀ of 104.07 mM for compound 6h, which is a likely typographical error for 104.07 µM. All synthesized derivatives formed a complex with the target enzyme in molecular docking. The relative standard deviation of the binding energy of the formed complex was less than 2.34 kcal/mol. The binding energy of docked 6h was the lowest at -10.56 kcal/mol among all docked derivatives. Compound 6a had a binding energy of -9.76 kcal/mol and compound 6b had -9.17 kcal/mol. Compound 2a had a binding energy of -8.12 kcal/mol. Compound 6h had a free binding energy of -10.55 kcal/mol after accounting for three hydrogen bonds. Acarbose established 10 hydrogen bonds with Asp232, Ala234, Asn237, Asp357, Arg552, Asp568, and His626. Acarbose also formed two hydrophobic interactions with Phe601 and Trp329. Compound 2a interacted with 10 residues but formed only one hydrogen bond with Arg552. Compound 6h established three hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469. Trp329 formed hydrophobic bonds with compounds 2a and 6h, directing their binding conformation. The IC₅₀ of compounds 6a, 6b, 6c, and 6d was similar to or lower than that of acarbose. The N-alkylated derivatives 2a and 2d (ethyl and 2-methylbenzyl) showed IC₅₀ values of 304.13 µM and 173.83 µM, respectively. The aminobridge substitution at position 4 was identified as responsible for the strong inhibitory activity.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The aminobridge substitution of the pyrimidine ring at position 4 is responsible for the strong inhibitory activity of compounds 6a-6i compared to 2a-2l. The higher stability of the 6a-αglucosidase complex (binding energy -9.76 kcal/mol) compared to 6b (-9.17 kcal/mol) explains why 6a exhibited higher inhibitory activity than 6b. Acarbose inhibition activity correlates with the number of hydroxyl groups and the number of hydrogen bonds between the ligand and the active site. The three hydrogen bonds formed by 6h with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469 enhance the ligand-α-glucosidase complex stability and reduce the free binding energy to -10.55 kcal/mol. Trp329 plays a critical role in directing the ligand in the binding site of the α-glucosidase enzyme, forming hydrophobic bonds with compounds 2a and 6h. The tricyclic phenoxypyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinone scaffold provides a new structural insight for developing non-carbasugar α-glucosidase inhibitors that could be transformed into clinical drugs for type II diabetes. The binding conformation is determined by the hydrophobic interaction with Trp329, similar to the binding mode of acarbose.

Contradictions And Limitations
The abstract reports an IC₅₀ of 104.07 mM for compound 6h, which is incongruent with the µM-range IC₅₀ values reported elsewhere in the paper and the biologically plausible range for an inhibitor. The enzymatic assay uses 5% DMSO, but compounds were initially prepared in 100% DMSO, potentially affecting solubility and activity. The N-substitution at position 4 was tested but only N-alkyl and N-aryl derivatives were evaluated, limiting the scope of the substitution analysis. The binding energy was reported as a single value for each compound, without explicit confidence intervals or error analysis beyond the relative standard deviation. The paper does not mention the concentration of α-glucosidase used in the assay, only the initial stock preparation details. The synthetic route for compound 6f is described but 6g and 6h are formed through hydrazone formation with aldehydes, and the specific yields for 6g and 6h are not reported.

Compound 6h is the most potent α-glucosidase inhibitor among the 25 synthesized tricyclic compounds, with an IC₅₀ lower than acarbose (though reported as 104.07 mM in the abstract). The study does not compare aminobridge vs. other bridge types at position 4. Position 4 substitution strategy should be prioritized in further structure-activity relationship (SAR) studies. The scaffold can be further elaborated at the aminobridge position.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 displays the structural relationship between acarbose, sugar mimetics, and other α-glucosidase inhibitors with their biological activities. Figure 2 illustrates the synthetic route towards fused pyrimidine derivatives, including all key reaction steps and intermediates. Figure 3 shows the average percent inhibition of 25 compounds against α-glucosidase enzyme. Figure 4 presents the IC₅₀ values of the active compounds compared to acarbose. Figure 5 displays the docking results, including binding energies, hydrogen bonds, and closest residues for acarbose and key synthesized compounds. Table 1 reports the number of established hydrogen bonds, binding energies, and closest amino acid residues for all docked complexes.

Three Takeaways
1. The tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-one scaffold with aminobridge substitution at position 4 provides a non-carbasugar approach to α-glucosidase inhibition, with compound 6h identified as the lead candidate. 2. Compound 6h achieved the lowest docking binding energy (-10.56 kcal/mol), established by three hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, and Trp329 was confirmed as critical for binding conformation. 3. Future work should resolve the IC₅₀ discrepancy for compound 6h, validate the docking results with experimental kinetic assays, and synthesize analogs for SAR at the aminobridge position.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The authors challenge the findings of Brüschweiler et al. who reported that the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3) could be refolded to homogeneity from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies in the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC) and maintained in a folded, active state for isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and NMR experiments. King et al. demonstrate that in their hands, DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3 when isolated from the inner membrane of mitochondria, contrasting with the claim of a refolded, active state. Crucially, the authors show that the CATR binding Kd reported by Brüschweiler et al. (~15 µM by ITC, ~150 µM by NMR) is three to four orders of magnitude higher than the consensus values of the low nanomolar range in the membrane. They highlight that the 192 µM Kd used as a reference by Brüschweiler et al. was a typographical error in Babot et al. (2012) and had been corrected to 192 nM in an erratum. The authors' own ITC measurements in dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin yielded an average Kd of 72 nM, 200 to 2000-fold lower than the reported value in DPC. Thermostability assays using the CPM fluorophore reveal that AAC3 in DPC is in a non-native state, showing no CATR-induced stability shift and no functional binding site. ADP binding by NMR was 500 µM, ~85-fold higher than consensus values. Furthermore, dilution into DPC before reconstitution completely abolishes CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in proteoliposomes. The authors conclude that the data from Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance, and that the observed binding in DPC is non-specific, promoted by high concentrations and temperatures in the NMR experiments.

Research Context
The subject is the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier AAC3, which the authors have studied in great detail. The authors have solved the structure of AAC3 by electron and x-ray crystallography. Interactions with the specific inhibitors atractyloside (ATR) and carboxyatractyloside (CATR) have been studied by single-molecule force spectroscopy. Brüschweiler et al. claimed that AAC3 can be refolded to homogeneity from inclusion bodies produced in Escherichia coli. The detergent used was dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC), better known as Foscholine-12. The authors claim AAC3 is maintained in a folded and active state for the duration of ITC and NMR experiments. However, the authors report that in their hands the presence of DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3. AAC3 was folded and active in the inner membrane of mitochondria, as shown by functional complementation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether AAC3 retains its native tertiary structure and functional integrity when solubilized in the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine. The authors hypothesize that DPC is harsh enough to denature functional, well-folded carrier protein prepared in mild non-ionic detergents. They predict that DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3 when isolated from the inner membrane. The authors expect to show that the Kd of CATR binding to AAC3 in DPC is several orders of magnitude higher than consensus values in the membrane. They further anticipate that NMR-measured Kd of ADP binding will be substantially higher than consensus values for the solubilized carrier. They hypothesize that CATR binding in DPC is non-specific, promoted by high concentrations and temperatures used in NMR experiments. A key predicted outcome is that dilution into DPC before reconstitution will cause complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in proteoliposomes. The authors conclude that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance.

Methodological Details
AAC3 was purified from yeast mitochondrial membranes using a nickel-sepharose high performance column on an ÄKTAprime system. The soluble fraction was loaded onto the column at 1 mL min⁻¹ after particulate material was removed by ultracentrifugation at 140,000 g for 45 min at 4 °C. The column was washed with 40 column volumes of buffer containing 20 mM PIPES pH 7.0, 150 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, 0.1% dodecyl-maltoside, and 0.1 mg mL⁻¹ tetraoleoyl cardiolipin. The column was washed with 20 column volumes of buffer B containing 100 mM NaCl in addition to the other components. The column material was resuspended with 500 μL buffer B and transferred to a vial containing 5 mM CaCl₂ and 75 μL Factor Xa for overnight incubation at 10 °C. The cleaved protein was separated by filtration and centrifugation, and the protein concentration was determined. Thermostability data were obtained using the thiol-reactive fluorophore CPM at a protein concentration of approximately 1 μM AAC3. CPM stock of 5 mg mL⁻¹ in DMSO was diluted 50-fold into buffer containing 20 mM PIPES pH 7.0, 100 mM NaCl, 0.1% dodecyl-maltoside, and 0.1 mg mL⁻¹ tetraoleoyl cardiolipin. Approximately 1.5 μg of purified protein was added into a final volume of 45 μL buffer containing either dodecyl-maltoside or 3 mM dodecyl-phosphocholine. The ITC experiments were performed at 10 °C using a NanoITC-LV isothermal titration calorimeter with 500 μM CATR titrant and 25 μM AAC3 (0.83 mg mL⁻¹). Reconstitution involved mixing L-α-phosphatidylcholine and tetraoleoyl cardiolipin in a 20:1 (w/w) ratio, totaling 10 mg lipid. 30 μg of purified AAC3 protein was added to the lipid/detergent mix, with 55 μL 25% (v/v) pentaethylene glycol monodecyl detergent used for solubilization. Detergent was stepwise removed using 4 × 30 mg and 4 × 60 mg of Bio-Beads SM-2 in 20-min intervals over 4 cycles. ADP uptake assays were performed using a Hamilton MicroLab Star robot with 100 µL of the proteoliposome suspension in a 96-well filter plate with 0.45 µm pores. Uptake of [¹⁴C]-ADP was initiated by adding 100 μL of external buffer containing 2.2 GBq mmol⁻¹ [¹⁴C]-ADP, yielding a final concentration of 1.5 µM. Transport was monitored at time points 0, 10, 20, 30, 45 s, 1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, and 15 min. The CATR:AAC3 molar ratios varied from 0 (black) to 100 (dark red), with intermediate ratios of 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, and 10. The protein was tested with CATR at molar ratios of 1 and above in thermostability assays.

Procedures And Architectures
For thermostability, a 5 mg mL⁻¹ CPM stock in DMSO was diluted 50-fold into buffer containing 20 mM PIPES, 100 mM NaCl, 0.1% dodecyl-maltoside, and 0.1 mg mL⁻¹ tetraoleoyl cardiolipin. The solution equilibrated in the dark at room temperature for 10 min before addition of 1.5 μg protein and 5 μL CPM working solution. Fluorescence was measured on a Qiagen Rotorgene Q in the HRM channel, with excitation at 440–480 nm and emission detected at 505–515 nm. Measurements were taken in 1 °C intervals from 25 to 90 °C with a 'wait between reading' of 4 s, equating to a ramp rate of 5.6 °C/min after a 90 s pre-incubation. Melting temperatures were determined with the software supplied with the instrument, defined as the peak in the derivative of the melting curve. ITC experiments involved 2 µL injections in an initial volume of 170 µL at 3-min intervals with a stirrer speed of 350 rpm. Both CATR titrant and protein samples were degassed under vacuum at 10 °C for at least 20 min before titration. Isotherms were fitted to a one-site binding model with ΔH, Kd, and stoichiometry as fitting parameters using NanoAnalyze software. Lipid was emulsified in buffer and solubilized with 55 μL 25% pentaethylene glycol monodecyl detergent on ice before adding 30 μg AAC3. Proteoliposomes were prepared by stepwise detergent removal with Bio-Beads SM-2, followed by separation using an empty spin column and exchange into external buffer. The external buffer contained 20 mM tris-HCl pH 7.4 and 50 mM NaCl, without ADP. Proteoliposomes were eluted in 1.5 mL and diluted a further 9-fold in external buffer before ADP uptake assays. Detergent was removed from the reconstitution mix through addition of 4 × 30 mg and 4 × 60 mg of Bio-Beads SM-2 in 20-min intervals.

Key Results
Native AAC3 purified in dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin yielded an average CATR binding Kd of 72 nM by ITC. Only 2 out of 10 ITC trials succeeded, due to the low enthalpic change and the very unstable apo-state in detergent. ADP transport by AAC3 is half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR, consistent with the low nanomolar consensus values. Brüschweiler et al. reported an ITC Kd of ~15 µM and an NMR-derived Kd of ~150 µM for CATR binding to DPC-refolded AAC3. The 192 µM reference Kd from Babot et al. (2012) was a typographical error and was corrected to 192 nM in an erratum. The authors' native ITC Kd (72 nM) is 200 to 2000-fold lower than the values reported in Brüschweiler et al. The NMR-measured ADP binding Kd was 500 µM, which is ~85-fold higher than published consensus values for the carrier in the mitochondrial membrane. The NMR ADP binding Kd is ~25-fold higher than for the solubilized carrier. In the DPC thermostability assay, AAC3 displayed a high signal with no transition, indicating a non-native state. Addition of CATR at molar ratios of 1 and above had no effect on the DPC thermostability curve, demonstrating no functional binding site. Dilution of AAC3 into DPC before reconstitution resulted in a complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in liposomes. In contrast, control tests with dilution into dodecyl-maltoside prior to reconstitution preserved CATR-sensitive ADP uptake. Only a limited number of chemical shift perturbations were observed for CATR binding to DPC-refolded AAC3, and all were dynamic, inconsistent with tight binding. The residues with CATR-induced chemical shift perturbations were not near the known CATR binding site nor on structural elements involved in CATR binding. In the crystal structure (AAC3 in maltoside, 5–7 days in the absence of CATR), interpretable density for CATR was observed. Binding of CATR introduces a large number of polar and van der Waals interactions that cross-link most of the transmembrane α-helices.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The authors conclude that AAC3 in DPC is soluble but in a non-native state, rather than the folded and active state claimed by Brüschweiler et al. The observed CATR and ADP binding in DPC is interpreted as non-specific interactions promoted by the high concentrations and temperatures used in NMR experiments. The discrepancy of three to four orders of magnitude between reported and consensus Kd values indicates the reported measurements lack biological relevance. The authors argue that the dynamic studies by NMR relaxation dispersion are invalid because CATR binding should lock the protein in a non-dynamic aborted state. The observed dynamics in the presence of substrate do not provide a plausible structural mechanism for transport. The isoelectric point of AAC3 (9.82) makes it highly positively charged, while CATR, ADP, and ATP are all negatively charged at neutral pH, facilitating non-specific electrostatic interactions. The ring of transmembrane α-helices is held together largely by lateral pressure of the membrane and counter pressure from the water-filled cavity, explaining why unliganded AAC3 in detergent micelles is prone to unfolding. The extremely low affinity of CATR to refolded AAC3 in DPC raises the question of whether the binding is specific at all. The data from Brüschweiler et al. are deemed to have no biological relevance for understanding AAC3 function.

Contradictions And Limitations
The ITC measurements in dodecyl-maltoside were very difficult, with only 2 out of 10 trials succeeding, indicating a technically challenging assay. The enthalpic change associated with CATR binding is low and the apo-state is very unstable in detergent, further complicating ITC measurement. The paper is a rebuttal and commentary, not a primary research study reporting a new independent structural determination. Brüschweiler et al. performed no functional transport assays to verify the activity of the refolded protein. The authors do not report a complete set of transport assays validating the activity of AAC3 in DPC. The AAC3 crystal structure was obtained in maltoside detergents in the absence of CATR for 5–7 days, adding a layer of methodological complexity. The NMR chemical shift perturbations could represent non-specific interactions promoted by high concentrations and temperatures, introducing a technical artifact. The thermodynamic data rely on a single instrument (NanoITC-LV) and a single software package (NanoAnalyze), which may not be fully generalizable.

Claims
AAC3 is in a non-native, denatured state when solubilized in dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC), rendering the reported NMR and ITC data biologically irrelevant. Thermostability assays in DPC showed a high signal with no transition and no CATR-induced stability shift, unlike the typical protein melt curve in dodecyl-maltoside. Dilution of AAC3 into DPC before reconstitution resulted in a complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in proteoliposomes. NMR chemical shift perturbations for CATR binding were limited in number, all were dynamic, and none were near the known CATR binding site. The ADP binding Kd by NMR (500 µM) was ~85-fold higher than published consensus values for the carrier in the membrane. The 192 µM Kd reference used by Brüschweiler et al. was a typographical error corrected to 192 nM in an erratum. Only a limited number of CATR-induced chemical shift perturbations were observed, and their dynamic nature is noted as inconsistent with tight binding. The ITC measurements in dodecyl-maltoside were technically difficult, with only 2 of 10 trials succeeding. The reported structure and dynamics of AAC3 in DPC cannot be interpreted as physiologically relevant. The CATR and ADP binding data reflect non-specific interactions at high concentrations rather than specific ligand binding. Future studies of AAC3 in detergent micelles must account for detergent-specific denaturation and potential non-specific binding artifacts.
The CATR binding affinity of AAC3 in the native mitochondrial membrane is in the low nanomolar range, consistent with its role as a powerful toxin. Native ITC measurements in dodecyl-maltoside yielded an average CATR binding Kd of 72 nM. ADP transport by AAC3 is half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR in the membrane. Published consensus values for CATR binding to AAC in the membrane are all in the low nanomolar range. The crystal structure shows CATR bound to AAC3 in the membrane for 5–7 days without dissociation. The authors acknowledge that the enthalpic change is low and the apo-state is very unstable, which could affect Kd measurement accuracy. CATR's nanomolar affinity is consistent with its known potency as a mitochondrial toxin. The discrepancy with the DPC-reported Kd values (three to four orders of magnitude) highlights the severe impact of detergent choice on reported affinity.
DPC is a harsh detergent capable of denaturing functional, well-folded carrier proteins, and AAC3 in DPC represents a non-native state. DPC has previously been demonstrated to solubilize unfolded mitochondrial carrier protein from E. coli inclusion bodies and denature functional well-folded carrier protein in mild detergents. Thermostability assays in 3 mM DPC showed no CATR-induced stability shift and no functional binding. The apo-state is very unstable in detergent, and few polar side chain interactions stabilize the structure. Brüschweiler et al. claimed the protein remained in a folded and active state for the duration of experiments, though this is not independently verified by this paper. Detergent choice is critical for preserving protein integrity in solution NMR and ITC studies of membrane proteins. Studies of AAC3 in DPC should be interpreted with extreme caution and verified by functional assays.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Thermostability assays were performed at CATR:AAC3 molar ratios of 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100, with the highest ratios showing no effect in DPC. Reconstitution tests included both direct addition and 20-fold dilution into dodecyl-maltoside or dodecyl-phosphocholine before reconstitution to isolate detergent effects. ITC experiments were performed at 10 °C with vacuum degassing of both titrant and protein for at least 20 min, and analyzed with NanoAnalyze software. The ADP uptake assay included transport stopping at 11 time points from 0 to 15 min, and CATR was added where required. The thermodynamic fitting used a one-site binding model with three parameters, which may not capture more complex binding scenarios.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows ADP transport by AAC3 half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. Figure 1b shows ITC measurements in dodecyl-maltoside yielding an average Kd of 72 nM for CATR binding. Figure 1c shows the protein melt curve in dodecyl-maltoside with CATR-induced stability shift. Figure 1d shows the thermostability curve in 3 mM DPC with no CATR-induced shift. Supplementary Table 1 reports 24 different binding studies for CATR and ATR, including published Kd values in the membrane. Supplementary Table 2 reports consensus Kd values of the carrier in the membrane and for the solubilized carrier. Supplementary Fig. 1a illustrates the transmembrane helical arrangement and lateral pressure of the membrane. Supplementary Fig. 1b shows CATR-induced polar and van der Waals cross-linking of transmembrane helices. Supplementary Fig. 2 shows the complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake upon DPC dilution prior to reconstitution. Figure 1 also mentions that AAC3 crystal structure was obtained in maltoside detergents for 5–7 days in the absence of CATR with interpretable density for the inhibitor.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that AAC3 in dodecyl-phosphocholine is in a non-native, denatured state, rendering the reported NMR and ITC binding measurements biologically irrelevant. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of thermostability assays in DPC showing no CATR-induced stability shift, the ~85-fold higher NMR-measured ADP binding Kd (500 µM vs consensus), and the complete loss of functional transport upon DPC dilution prior to reconstitution. 3. The future path lies in the necessity of verifying protein folding and activity through functional transport assays before attempting solution structure determination, and in using detergent conditions that preserve native conformation rather than facilitating non-specific interactions.
